results.name: Pickands' theorem on the supremum of a stationary Gaussian process
results.statement: Let p > 0 and let X(t), t ∈ [0, p], be a continuous stationary Gaussian process with E X(t) = 0 and covariance r(t) = E X(t + s)X(s) = 1 − |t|^α + o(|t|^α) as t → 0, for some α ∈ (0, 2]. Assume r(t) < 1 for 0 < t ≤ p. Let χ(t) = √2 B(t) − t^α, where B is fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index α/2 and E B(1)² = 1, and let H(T) = E exp(sup_{t∈[0,T]} χ(t)). Then the Pickands constant H_α = lim_{T→∞} H(T)/T exists and 0 < H_α < ∞, and P(sup_{t∈[0,p]} X(t) > u) = H_α p u^(2/α) Ψ(u)(1 + o(1)) as u → ∞, where Ψ(u) = 1 − Φ(u) is the standard normal tail. If instead r(t) = 1 − C|t|^α + o(|t|^α) with a constant C > 0, the same holds with H_α C^(1/α) p in place of H_α p.
hypotheses: X(t), t ∈ [0, p], is a continuous stationary Gaussian process with mean 0 and variance 1.
Local condition: r(t) = 1 − |t|^α + o(|t|^α) as t → 0, for some α ∈ (0, 2] (or 1 − C|t|^α + o(|t|^α) with C > 0).
No other perfect correlation: r(t) < 1 for 0 < t ≤ p.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 bounds the probability of the union of the interval events by the sum of their probabilities.

definitions.name: Pickands constant
definitions.text: H_α = lim_{T→∞} T⁻¹ E exp(sup_{t∈[0,T]} (√2 B_{α/2}(t) − t^α)), where B_{α/2} is fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index α/2. Known values are H_1 = 1 and H_2 = 1/√π.

definitions.name: fractional Brownian motion
definitions.text: The centred Gaussian process B_H with continuous paths and covariance E B_H(t)B_H(s) = (|t|^(2H) + |s|^(2H) − |t − s|^(2H))/2, for a Hurst index H ∈ (0, 1].

definitions.name: double sum method
definitions.text: A method that splits the time set into short intervals, bounds the probability of a high supremum above by the sum over intervals, and bounds it below by the same sum minus the double sum over pairs of intervals.

source.citation: Zbigniew Michna, Remarks on Pickands' theorem, Probability and Mathematical Statistics 37, no. 2 (2017).
source.revision: arXiv:0904.3832v3 [math.PR], 15 March 2017.
source.module: Section 3 Pickands theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 4 (Pickands) Let X(t) where t ∈ [0, p] be a continuous stationary Gaussian process with expected value EX(t) = 0 and covariance r(t) = E(X(t + s)X(s)) = 1 − |t|^α + o(|t|^α). Furthermore we assume that r(t) < 1 for all t > 0. Then P(sup_{t∈[0,p]} X(t) > u) = H_α p u^{2/α} Ψ(u)(1 + o(1)) as u → ∞ where H_α = lim_{T→∞} H(T)/T is positive and finite (Pickands constant) where H(T) is defined in (9).
source.attribution: © Zbigniew Michna. Quoted from the author's arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement writes out H(T) from relation (9) and Remark 2 of the source and states the range 0 < α ≤ 2 that the source assumes throughout. It adds the time change for a general constant C > 0. The outline follows Michna's proof of Theorem 4, which follows Piterbarg's double sum proof.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 4 in Michna (2017), pp. 11-16, which follows Piterbarg's double sum method. Steps s1, s5 and s6 take the local asymptotics (Lemma 4 and Corollary 2) and the bound for pairs of intervals (Lemma 5) from the source. Step s4 cites the Borell inequality (Theorem 3 of the source).

steps.text: Local asymptotics (Lemma 4 of the source, p. 7). For each fixed T > 0, P(sup_{t∈[0, u^(−2/α)T]} X(t) > u) = Ψ(u) H(T)(1 + o(1)) as u → ∞. The source proves this as for Lemma 3: it conditions on the value of X at the left end, and the rescaled process u(X(u^(−2/α)t) − u) converges to the drifted fractional Brownian motion χ. Corollary 2 of the source gives H(T) ≤ ⌈T⌉ H(1).

Upper bound (relation (27) of the source). Fix T and cut [0, p] into the intervals Δ_k = [k u^(−2/α)T, (k + 1) u^(−2/α)T], k = 0, …, N_p, with N_p = ⌊p u^(2/α)/T⌋. The union bound and stationarity give P(sup_{[0,p]} X > u) ≤ (N_p + 1) P(sup_{Δ_0} X > u). With step s1 this gives lim sup_u P(sup_{[0,p]} X > u)/(p u^(2/α) Ψ(u)) ≤ H(T)/T for every T > 0.

Lower bound by the double sum (relation (28) of the source). The Bonferroni inequality P(∪A_k) ≥ Σ P(A_k) − Σ_{i<j} P(A_i ∩ A_j) holds because a point in m ≥ 1 of the sets satisfies 1 ≥ m − m(m − 1)/2. Take A_k = {sup_{Δ_k} X > u} for k < N_p. Stationarity gives P(sup_{[0,p]} X > u) ≥ N_p P(sup_{Δ_0} X > u) − Σ_2, and the double sum Σ_2 is at most A_1 + A_2 + A_3. Here A_1 = N_p P(sup_{Δ_0} X > u, sup_{Δ_1} X > u), A_2 is N_p times the sum of the same probabilities for Δ_0 and Δ_k over 2 ≤ k < N_(ε/4), and A_3 is N_p times that sum over k ≥ N_(ε/4), where N_(ε/4) = ⌊(ε/4) u^(2/α)/T⌋.

Far pairs (relations (29)-(31) of the source). For t ∈ Δ_0 and s ∈ Δ_k with k ≥ N_(ε/4), Var(X(t) + X(s)) = 2 + 2r(t − s) ≤ 4 − δ with δ = 2 inf_{ε/4 ≤ s ≤ p}(1 − r(s)) > 0, because r is continuous and r < 1 on (0, p]. Let m be an upper bound for E sup (X(t) + X(s)) over these pairs. The Borell inequality (Theorem 3 of the source) gives P(sup (X(t) + X(s)) > 2u) ≤ exp(−(2u − m)²/(2(4 − δ))) ≤ exp(−(u − m/2)²/(2(1 − δ/8)²)). Divided by Ψ(u), this tends to 0 faster than any power of u, because 1 − δ/8 < 1. Since there are fewer than N_p² such pairs and N_p grows like u^(2/α), A_3/(N_p Ψ(u)) → 0.

Moderately close pairs (relation (32) of the source). For small ε the local condition gives 1 − 2|t|^α ≤ r(t) ≤ 1 − |t|^α/2 on [0, ε]. Lemma 5 of the source then proves P(sup_{Δ_0} X > u, sup_{Δ_k} X > u) ≤ C_1 ⌈C_2 T⌉ ⌈C_2(k + 1)T⌉ exp(−(k − 1)^α T^α/8) Ψ(u) for k ≥ 2 and large u. Summation over k and an incomplete gamma estimate give lim sup_u A_2/(N_p Ψ(u)) ≤ C⌈T⌉² exp(−T^α/8)(1 + O(T^(−α))).

Adjacent pairs (relations (33)-(35) of the source). Split Δ_1 into a first piece of length u^(−2/α)√T and the rest. The first piece has probability Ψ(u)H(√T)(1 + o(1)) ≤ Ψ(u)⌈√T⌉H(1)(1 + o(1)) by step s1. The rest lies at distance u^(−2/α)√T from Δ_0, so Lemma 5 bounds its joint probability with Δ_0 by C⌈T⌉⌈2T + √T⌉ exp(−T^(α/2)/8) Ψ(u). So lim sup_u A_1/(N_p Ψ(u)) ≤ ⌈√T⌉H(1) + C⌈T⌉⌈2T + √T⌉ exp(−T^(α/2)/8).

Existence of the constant and the asymptotics (relation (36) of the source). Steps s1 and s3 to s6 give lim inf_u P(sup_{[0,p]} X > u)/(p u^(2/α) Ψ(u)) ≥ f(T) = H(T)/T − e(T), where e(T) collects the three error bounds divided by T and tends to 0 as T → ∞. With step s2, lim sup_T H(T)/T ≤ lim inf_u ≤ lim sup_u ≤ lim inf_T H(T)/T. So H_α = lim H(T)/T exists, it is finite because H(T)/T ≤ ⌈T⌉H(1)/T, and the ratio tends to H_α. For r(t) = 1 − C|t|^α + o(|t|^α), the process Y(s) = X(C^(−1/α)s) on [0, C^(1/α)p] satisfies the normalized condition and has the same supremum, which gives the factor C^(1/α).

Positivity of H_α (end of the proof in the source). Restrict to the set D, the union of the even intervals Δ_(2j) inside [0, 1]. No two of them are adjacent, so the term A_1 does not occur, and the Bonferroni bound with steps s4 and s5 gives H(T)/T ≥ lim sup_u P(sup_{[0,1]} X > u)/(u^(2/α)Ψ(u)) ≥ S⁻¹(H(S)/2 − C⌈S⌉² exp(−S^α/8)(1 + O(S^(−α)))) for every large S. Since H(S) ≥ E exp(χ(0)) = 1 and the subtracted term tends to 0, the right side is positive for large S. So H_α > 0.

applications.title: High excursions of an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck signal
applications.inputs: A standardized stationary Ornstein–Uhlenbeck signal X has covariance r(t) = e^(−λ|t|) with λ = 2 per hour. We want the probability that X exceeds u = 4 standard deviations within p = 10 hours.
applications.hypotheses: X is a continuous stationary Gaussian process with mean 0 and variance 1. Its covariance is r(t) = e^(−2|t|) = 1 − 2|t| + o(|t|), so α = 1 and C = 2. Also r(t) < 1 for t > 0.

steps.text: Constants. For α = 1 the Pickands constant is H_1 = 1, and C^(1/α) = 2. So P(sup_{[0,p]} X > u) ∼ H_1 · 2 · p · u² Ψ(u) = 2p u² Ψ(u).
Prefactor. With p = 10 and u = 4 the prefactor is 2 · 10 · 4² = 320.
Normal tail. Ψ(4) ≈ 3.17 · 10^(−5), so the approximation gives P(sup_{[0,10]} X > 4) ≈ 320 · 3.17 · 10^(−5) ≈ 0.0101.

Comparison. A single time point gives only Ψ(4) ≈ 3.2 · 10^(−5). The factor 2 p u² = 320 counts the effective number of independent looks at the level, and this number grows with u because the path is rough (α = 1).

applications.conclusion: For the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck signal with λ = 2 per hour, the probability of a 4σ excursion within 10 hours is about 320 Ψ(4) ≈ 0.010.

limitations: The theorem gives only first-order asymptotics. The relative error tends to 0 slowly, and the approximation at moderate levels can be poor.
The Pickands constant is known in closed form only for α = 1 (H_1 = 1) and α = 2 (H_2 = 1/√π). For other α it is known only by bounds and simulation.
The theorem needs the local condition with an exact power α. Other local behaviours, nonstationary processes and random fields need extensions of the double sum method.

results.name: Lundberg inequality
aliases: Lundberg bound for the ruin probability
results.statement: Let the claim sizes X₁, X₂, … be i.i.d. real random variables, and let the interarrival times W₁, W₂, … be i.i.d. and strictly positive, with the two sequences independent (Sparre Andersen model). Let c > 0 be the premium rate and u ≥ 0 the initial capital. Set T_n = W₁ + ⋯ + W_n, N_t = #{n ≥ 1 : T_n ≤ t} and R_t = u + ct − Σ_{k=1}^{N_t} X_k. Let ψ(u) = P(inf_{t≥0} R_t < 0) be the ruin probability. If a constant R > 0 satisfies E[e^(R(X₁ − cW₁))] ≤ 1, then ψ(u) ≤ e^(−Ru) for every u ≥ 0. In the classical Cramér–Lundberg model the W_n are exponential with rate λ, and the condition on R reads λ(E[e^(RX₁)] − 1) ≤ cR.
hypotheses: The claim sizes X₁, X₂, … are i.i.d. The interarrival times W₁, W₂, … are i.i.d. and strictly positive. The two sequences are independent.
The premium rate c is positive and the initial capital u is nonnegative.
The constant R > 0 satisfies E[e^(R(X₁ − cW₁))] ≤ 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 applies the strong law of large numbers to min(W_k, 1) to show that the claim times T_n tend to infinity almost surely.
Step s3 applies the optional stopping theorem for supermartingales at the bounded stopping time τ ∧ n.

definitions.name: ruin probability
definitions.text: ψ(u) = P(R_t < 0 for some t ≥ 0), the probability that the reserve process that starts at u ever becomes negative.

definitions.name: Sparre Andersen model
definitions.text: A risk model in which claims arrive at the points of a renewal process with i.i.d. interarrival times W_n, independent of the i.i.d. claim sizes X_n. The Cramér–Lundberg model is the case of exponential W_n.

definitions.name: adjustment coefficient
definitions.text: A constant R > 0 with E[e^(R(X₁ − cW₁))] = 1. In the Cramér–Lundberg model it solves λ(E[e^(RX₁)] − 1) = cR. A constant with ≤ in place of = is a superadjustment coefficient.

definitions.name: supermartingale
definitions.text: An adapted integrable sequence (Z_n) with E[Z_{n+1} | F_n] ≤ Z_n for every n.

source.citation: Klaus D. Schmidt, Lectures on Risk Theory, Teubner, Stuttgart, 1996.
source.revision: Author's manuscript dated December 28, 1995 (TeX output 1995-12-28), 207 pages, from the author's TU Dresden publication page.
source.module: Chapter 7 The Reserve Process and the Ruin Problem, Section 7.3 Lundberg’s Inequality, result 7.3.4
source.excerpt: Theorem (Lundberg’s Inequality). If ρ ∈ (0, ∞) is a superadjustment coefficient for the excess premium process, then the identity P[{inf_{n∈N₀} U_n^u < 0}] ≤ e^{−ρu} holds for all u ∈ (0, ∞).
source.attribution: © Klaus D. Schmidt. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Lectures on Risk Theory for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source numbers the result 7.3.4 and states it for the modified reserve process U_n^u = u + Σ (κW_k − X_k), with independent excess premiums and a superadjustment coefficient ρ. Its Lemma 7.1.2 shows that ruin of the continuous-time reserve happens only at claim times. The authored statement restricts to i.i.d. excess premiums and states the ruin event in continuous time. The authored proof follows the source: a nonnegative supermartingale e^(−ρU_n) and a maximal bound, here obtained by optional stopping.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the supermartingale proof of Theorem 7.3.4 in Schmidt's Lectures on Risk Theory. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for the Sparre Andersen model and every u ≥ 0, with the form of the condition in the Cramér–Lundberg model.

steps.text: Reduce to claim times. Let G_k = cW_k − X_k and U_n = u + G₁ + ⋯ + G_n, with U_0 = u. The variables min(W_k, 1) are i.i.d. with a positive mean, so the strong law of large numbers gives T_n ≥ Σ_{k≤n} min(W_k, 1) → ∞ almost surely. Hence, almost surely, every t ≥ 0 lies in exactly one interval [T_n, T_{n+1}) with n ≥ 0 and T_0 = 0. On that interval N_t = n and R_t = u + ct − Σ_{k≤n} X_k increases in t. Its infimum over the interval is its value at T_n, which is u + Σ_{k≤n}(cW_k − X_k) = U_n. So inf_{t≥0} R_t = inf_{n≥0} U_n almost surely, and ψ(u) = P(τ < ∞) for τ = inf{n ≥ 0 : U_n < 0}.

Build a supermartingale. Let F_n = σ(G₁, …, G_n) and Z_n = e^(−RU_n). The G_k are i.i.d. because the pairs (W_k, X_k) are i.i.d. The variable G_{n+1} is independent of F_n, so E[Z_{n+1} | F_n] = Z_n E[e^(−RG_{n+1})] = Z_n E[e^(R(X₁ − cW₁))] ≤ Z_n. Each Z_n is nonnegative and E Z_n = e^(−Ru) (E e^(−RG₁))^n ≤ e^(−Ru), so Z_n is integrable. Hence (Z_n) is a nonnegative supermartingale with Z_0 = e^(−Ru).

Stop at ruin. The time τ is a stopping time for (F_n), because the event {τ ≤ n} depends only on U_0, …, U_n. Fix n. The time τ ∧ n is bounded, so the optional stopping theorem for supermartingales gives E Z_{τ∧n} ≤ E Z_0 = e^(−Ru). On the event {τ ≤ n} the value U_τ is negative, so Z_{τ∧n} = e^(−RU_τ) > 1. Because Z_{τ∧n} ≥ 0 everywhere, P(τ ≤ n) ≤ E[Z_{τ∧n} 1{τ ≤ n}] ≤ E Z_{τ∧n} ≤ e^(−Ru).

Let n → ∞. The events {τ ≤ n} increase to {τ < ∞}, so continuity of the probability measure from below gives P(τ < ∞) = lim_n P(τ ≤ n) ≤ e^(−Ru). Step s1 identifies P(τ < ∞) with ψ(u), so ψ(u) ≤ e^(−Ru). In the Cramér–Lundberg model, X₁ and W₁ are independent and E e^(−cRW₁) = λ/(λ + cR). So E e^(R(X₁ − cW₁)) = E[e^(RX₁)] λ/(λ + cR), and this is at most 1 exactly when λ(E[e^(RX₁)] − 1) ≤ cR.

applications.title: Capital requirement for an insurer with exponential claims
applications.inputs: Claims arrive as a Poisson process with rate λ = 1 per year. The claim sizes are exponential with rate β = 1, so the mean claim is 1. The premium rate is c = 5/4, which is a safety loading of 25 %. The initial capital is u = 10.
applications.hypotheses: The interarrival times are i.i.d. exponential, so they are strictly positive. The claim sizes are i.i.d. and independent of the arrivals. The premium rate c = 5/4 is positive and u = 10 is nonnegative. Steps a2 and a3 show that R = 1/5 satisfies the condition on R.

steps.text: For r < β the moment generating function of a claim is E e^(rX₁) = β/(β − r). The condition λ(E e^(RX₁) − 1) ≤ cR becomes λR/(β − R) ≤ cR, that is β − R ≥ λ/c. The largest admissible value is R = β − λ/c.
With λ = 1, β = 1 and c = 5/4 the largest admissible value is R = 1 − 1/(5/4) = 1/5.
Check the condition at R = 1/5: λ(E e^(RX₁) − 1) = 1/(1 − 1/5) − 1 = 1/4, and cR = (5/4)(1/5) = 1/4. The two sides are equal, so R = 1/5 is the adjustment coefficient.
The Lundberg inequality gives ψ(10) ≤ e^(−10/5) = e^(−2) ≈ 0.135. To get ψ(u) ≤ 0.01 it is sufficient that e^(−u/5) ≤ 0.01, that is u ≥ 5 log 100 ≈ 23.03.
For exponential claims the exact value is ψ(u) = (λ/(cβ)) e^(−Ru) = (4/5) e^(−u/5), which follows from the Pollaczek–Khinchine formula. So the Lundberg bound is too large only by the factor 5/4 here.

applications.conclusion: The adjustment coefficient is R = 1/5, and ψ(u) ≤ e^(−u/5) for every u ≥ 0. A capital of u = 10 gives a ruin probability of at most e^(−2) ≈ 0.135, and a capital of about 23 gives at most 1 %.

limitations: The bound needs a finite exponential moment of the claims. For heavy-tailed claims no R > 0 satisfies the condition, and ψ(u) decays more slowly than every exponential.
The bound is not sharp in the constant. In the Cramér–Lundberg model ψ(u) is asymptotic to C e^(−Ru) with a constant C ≤ 1 (Cramér–Lundberg approximation).

results.name: Pollaczek–Khinchine formula for the ruin probability
results.statement: Consider the Cramér–Lundberg model with premium rate c > 0, claim arrivals at the times of a Poisson process with rate λ > 0, and i.i.d. claim sizes ξ₁, ξ₂, … that are independent of the arrivals, with distribution function F, F(0) = 0 and finite mean μ. Let ρ = λμ/c and assume ρ < 1. For x ≥ 0 let ψ(x) = P(x + ct − Σ_{i=1}^{N_t} ξ_i < 0 for some t > 0). Let F_I(x) = μ⁻¹ ∫_0^x (1 − F(y)) dy for x ≥ 0 be the integrated tail distribution, let F_I^{*k} be its k-fold convolution power, and set F_I^{*0}(x) = 1 for x ≥ 0. Then 1 − ψ(x) = (1 − ρ) Σ_{k≥0} ρ^k F_I^{*k}(x) for every x ≥ 0. Equivalently, ψ(x) = (1 − ρ) Σ_{k≥1} ρ^k (1 − F_I^{*k}(x)). In particular ψ(0) = ρ.
hypotheses: Claims arrive at the times of a Poisson process with rate λ > 0. The claim sizes are i.i.d., positive, independent of the arrivals, with distribution function F and finite mean μ.
The premium rate c > 0 satisfies the net profit condition ρ = λμ/c < 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 integrates over the independent first claim time and size, and steps s3 and s5 exchange the order of integration in convolution integrals.
Step s2 differentiates the integral ∫_x^∞ e^(−λs/c) h(s) ds at almost every x with the Lebesgue differentiation theorem.
Step s3 integrates the almost everywhere derivative of the absolutely continuous survival function over [0, t].
Step s4 applies the strong law of large numbers to the increments cW_k − ξ_k to show that the survival probability tends to 1.
Step s4 lets t → ∞ in the integrated equation with the monotone convergence theorem to find the value at zero.

definitions.name: Cramér–Lundberg model
definitions.text: The reserve x + ct − Σ_{i=1}^{N_t} ξ_i, where N is a Poisson process with rate λ and the claim sizes ξ_i are i.i.d. positive and independent of N.

definitions.name: ruin probability
definitions.text: ψ(x) is the probability that the reserve that starts at x ≥ 0 becomes negative at some time t > 0.

definitions.name: integrated tail distribution
definitions.text: F_I(x) = μ⁻¹ ∫_0^x (1 − F(y)) dy. It is a continuous distribution function on [0, ∞) with density (1 − F(y))/μ.

definitions.name: convolution power
definitions.text: F_I^{*1} = F_I and F_I^{*(k+1)}(x) = ∫_{[0,x]} F_I^{*k}(x − y) dF_I(y). It is the distribution function of a sum of k independent variables with law F_I.

source.citation: Andreas E. Kyprianou, Gerber–Shiu Risk Theory, EAA Series, Springer International Publishing, Cham, 2013. DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-02303-8.
source.revision: Published Springer version of 2013 (95 pages) as posted on the author's Warwick book page.
source.module: Chapter 1 Introduction, Section 1.2 The Classical Problem of Ruin
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.3 (Pollaczek–Khintchine formula) Suppose that λμ/c < 1. For all x ≥ 0, 1 − P_x(τ_0^− < ∞) = (1 − ρ) Σ_{k≥0} ρ^k η^{*k}(x), where ρ = λμ/c, η(x) = (1/μ) ∫_0^x (1 − F(y)) dy, x ≥ 0, and, for k ≥ 0, we understand η^{*k} to be the k-fold convolution of η with the special understanding that η^{*0}(dx) = δ_0(dx).
source.attribution: © Andreas E. Kyprianou. Quoted from the book Gerber–Shiu Risk Theory for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source writes the integrated tail distribution as η and the ruin probability as P_x(τ_0^− < ∞), with τ_0^− = inf{t > 0 : X_t < 0}. The authored statement adds the equivalent form for ψ and the value ψ(0) = ρ. The source proves the formula later with scale functions. The authored proof follows instead the classical renewal argument of first-claim conditioning, as in Bingham's lecture notes, and solves the renewal equation by iteration.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the first-claim renewal argument in Bingham's lecture notes on the ruin problem. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every x ≥ 0 under the net profit condition ρ < 1, with both forms of the formula and the value ψ(0) = ρ.

steps.text: First claim. Let φ = 1 − ψ, let W_k be the interarrival times and let V = inf_{n≥1} Σ_{k=2}^{n} (cW_k − ξ_k), where the empty sum for n = 1 is 0, so V ≤ 0. The Poisson arrival times tend to infinity almost surely, and the reserve increases between claims, so ruin can happen only at a claim time. Hence the company survives exactly when Z + V ≥ 0, where Z = x + cW₁ − ξ₁. The variable V is independent of (W₁, ξ₁) and has the law of inf_{n≥0} Σ_{k=1}^{n} (cW_k − ξ_k). So φ(z) = P(z + V ≥ 0) for every real z, and φ(z) = 0 for z < 0. Fubini's theorem gives φ(x) = E φ(Z) = ∫_0^∞ λe^(−λt) h(x + ct) dt with h(s) = ∫_{(0,s]} φ(s − y) dF(y). The substitution s = x + ct gives φ(x) = (λ/c) e^(λx/c) ∫_x^∞ e^(−λs/c) h(s) ds.

Differentiate. A larger initial capital survives on every path where a smaller one survives, so φ is nondecreasing with values in [0, 1]. Hence h is Borel with 0 ≤ h ≤ 1. The function A(x) = ∫_x^∞ e^(−λs/c) h(s) ds is absolutely continuous on [0, ∞), and the Lebesgue differentiation theorem gives A'(x) = −e^(−λx/c) h(x) for almost every x. So φ(x) = (λ/c) e^(λx/c) A(x) is continuous and absolutely continuous on every interval [0, t], and φ'(x) = (λ/c)(φ(x) − h(x)) for almost every x.

Integrate. The fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions gives φ(t) − φ(0) = (λ/c) ∫_0^t φ(x) dx − (λ/c) ∫_0^t h(x) dx. Fubini's theorem gives ∫_0^t h(x) dx = ∫_{(0,t]} ∫_0^{t−y} φ(z) dz dF(y) = ∫_0^t φ(z) F(t − z) dz. Hence φ(t) = φ(0) + (λ/c) ∫_0^t φ(t − y)(1 − F(y)) dy for every t ≥ 0.

Value at zero. The increments cW_k − ξ_k are i.i.d. with mean c/λ − μ > 0, because ρ < 1. The strong law of large numbers gives Σ_{k≤n}(cW_k − ξ_k) → ∞ almost surely, so V is finite almost surely and φ(t) = P(V ≥ −t) → 1 as t → ∞. In step s3 the integrand φ(t − y) 1{y ≤ t} (1 − F(y)) increases in t to 1 − F(y), because φ is nondecreasing. The monotone convergence theorem and μ = ∫_0^∞ (1 − F(y)) dy give 1 = φ(0) + λμ/c. So φ(0) = 1 − ρ.

Solve the renewal equation. The measure (λ/c)(1 − F(y)) dy equals ρ dF_I(y). So steps s3 and s4 give φ = (1 − ρ) + ρ F_I * φ on [0, ∞), where (G * g)(t) = ∫_{[0,t]} g(t − y) dG(y). Insert this identity into itself n times. Associativity of convolution, which follows from Fubini's theorem, gives φ(t) = (1 − ρ) Σ_{k=0}^{n} ρ^k F_I^{*k}(t) + ρ^{n+1} (F_I^{*(n+1)} * φ)(t). The remainder lies in [0, ρ^{n+1}], because 0 ≤ φ ≤ 1 and F_I^{*(n+1)} is a probability distribution. It tends to 0 because ρ < 1, and the series formula follows. Subtract it from 1 = (1 − ρ) Σ_{k≥0} ρ^k to get the formula for ψ. The law F_I has no atom at 0, so F_I^{*k}(0) = 0 for k ≥ 1 and ψ(0) = (1 − ρ) Σ_{k≥1} ρ^k = ρ.

applications.title: Exact ruin probability for exponential claims
applications.inputs: Claims arrive as a Poisson process with rate λ = 10 per month. The claim sizes are exponential with mean μ = 1 (in thousands), so F(y) = 1 − e^(−y). The premium rate is c = 12 per month. The initial capital is x = 12.
applications.hypotheses: The arrivals are Poisson and the claims are i.i.d., positive and independent of the arrivals, with finite mean 1. The load factor is ρ = λμ/c = 5/6 < 1, so the net profit condition holds.

steps.text: The load factor is ρ = λμ/c = 10 · 1/12 = 5/6.

The integrated tail is F_I(x) = ∫_0^x e^(−y) dy = 1 − e^(−x), so F_I = F is again exponential with rate 1. Its convolution power F_I^{*k} is the gamma law with shape k, and 1 − F_I^{*k}(x) = e^(−x) Σ_{j=0}^{k−1} x^j/j!.
Insert this into the formula and exchange the two sums: ψ(x) = e^(−x) Σ_{j≥0} (x^j/j!) (1 − ρ) Σ_{k≥j+1} ρ^k = e^(−x) Σ_{j≥0} (x^j/j!) ρ^(j+1) = ρ e^(−(1−ρ)x).
With ρ = 5/6 the decay rate is 1 − ρ = 1/6, so ψ(x) = (5/6) e^(−x/6). In particular ψ(0) = 5/6.
For the initial capital x = 12 the ruin probability is ψ(12) = (5/6) e^(−2) ≈ 0.1128. Without capital, ruin happens with probability 5/6.

applications.conclusion: For exponential claims the formula gives the closed form ψ(x) = ρ e^(−(1−ρ)x/μ). With λ = 10, μ = 1 and c = 12 this is ψ(x) = (5/6) e^(−x/6), and ψ(12) ≈ 0.113.

limitations: The formula is an infinite series of convolution powers. Closed forms exist only for special claim laws, such as exponential, mixtures of exponentials or phase-type laws.
The proof needs Poisson arrivals. With renewal arrivals the ruin probability is still a geometric compound, but the ladder height law is no longer F_I.

results.name: Embrechts–Veraverbeke theorem
results.statement: Consider the Cramér–Lundberg model with premium rate c > 0, Poisson claim arrivals with rate λ > 0, and i.i.d. positive claim sizes independent of the arrivals, with distribution function F and finite mean μ. Assume ρ = λμ/c < 1. Let ψ(u) be the ruin probability for the initial capital u ≥ 0, and let F_I(x) = μ⁻¹ ∫_0^x (1 − F(y)) dy be the integrated tail distribution. If F_I is subexponential, then ψ(u)/(1 − F_I(u)) → ρ/(1 − ρ) as u → ∞. Equivalently, ψ(u) ∼ (λ/(c − λμ)) ∫_u^∞ (1 − F(y)) dy.
hypotheses: Claims arrive at the times of a Poisson process with rate λ > 0. The claim sizes are i.i.d., positive, independent of the arrivals, with distribution function F and finite mean μ.
The net profit condition ρ = λμ/c < 1 holds.
The integrated tail distribution F_I is subexponential: 1 − F_I(x) > 0 for all x and (1 − F_I^{*2}(x))/(1 − F_I(x)) → 2 as x → ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 writes ψ(u) as the geometric series (1 − ρ) Σ ρ^n (1 − F_I^{*n}(u)) of the Pollaczek–Khinchine formula.
Step s2 uses the limit (1 − F_I^{*n}(u))/(1 − F_I(u)) → n, and step s3 uses Kesten's bound K(1 + ε)^n for the same ratio.
Step s4 exchanges the limit u → ∞ with the infinite series by the dominated convergence theorem for the counting measure.

definitions.name: subexponential distribution
definitions.text: A distribution function H on [0, ∞) with 1 − H(x) > 0 for all x and (1 − H^{*2}(x))/(1 − H(x)) → 2 as x → ∞. Then (1 − H^{*n}(x))/(1 − H(x)) → n for every n ≥ 1.

definitions.name: integrated tail distribution
definitions.text: F_I(x) = μ⁻¹ ∫_0^x (1 − F(y)) dy for x ≥ 0. Its tail 1 − F_I(u) = μ⁻¹ ∫_u^∞ (1 − F(y)) dy is the normalized second tail of F.

definitions.name: Kesten's bound
definitions.text: For a subexponential H and every ε > 0 there is K < ∞ with 1 − H^{*n}(x) ≤ K(1 + ε)^n (1 − H(x)) for all x ≥ 0 and n ≥ 1.

source.citation: Stan Zachary, A note on Veraverbeke's theorem, Queueing Systems 46 (2004), 9-14.
source.revision: arXiv:1410.8551v1 [math.PR], 30 October 2014, 6 pages.
source.module: Section 2 Veraverbeke’s Theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 1 (Veraverbeke). (i) Suppose that, in addition to (4), F^s is long-tailed. Then lim inf_{x→∞} P(M > x)/F̄^s(x) ≥ 1/a. (ii) Suppose that, in addition to (4), F^s is subexponential. Then lim_{x→∞} P(M > x)/F̄^s(x) = 1/a.
source.attribution: © Stan Zachary. Quoted from the author's arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the result for the maximum M of a random walk with i.i.d. increments of mean −a < 0 and second tail F^s. In the Cramér–Lundberg model ψ(u) = P(M > u) for the increments ξ_k − cW_k, with a = c/λ − μ, and the second tail of these increments is asymptotic to μ(1 − F_I(u)) because F_I is long-tailed. So part (ii) gives the same limit ρ/(1 − ρ). The authored proof does not follow the one-big-jump proof of the source: it follows the Pollaczek–Khinchine and dominated convergence route of Embrechts and Veraverbeke, as presented in Mikosch's survey, relations (2.8)-(2.11).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the Pollaczek–Khinchine and dominated convergence argument of relations (2.8)-(2.11) in Mikosch's survey of subexponential distributions. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement in the Cramér–Lundberg model under the listed hypotheses. The converse implication of the original theorem is not proved.

steps.text: Series for the ratio. Write G(u) = 1 − F_I(u), which is positive for every u because F_I is subexponential. The Pollaczek–Khinchine formula gives ψ(u) = (1 − ρ) Σ_{n≥1} ρ^n (1 − F_I^{*n}(u)). Division by G(u) gives ψ(u)/G(u) = (1 − ρ) Σ_{n≥1} ρ^n a_n(u), with a_n(u) = (1 − F_I^{*n}(u))/G(u).
Limit of each term. Because F_I is subexponential, the convolution tails satisfy a_n(u) → n as u → ∞ for every fixed n ≥ 1. So the n-th term of the series tends to (1 − ρ) n ρ^n.

Uniform domination. Choose ε > 0 so small that (1 + ε)ρ < 1. This is possible because ρ < 1. Kesten's bound for the subexponential law F_I gives a constant K = K(ε) with a_n(u) ≤ K(1 + ε)^n for all u ≥ 0 and all n ≥ 1. Hence the n-th term of the series is at most K((1 + ε)ρ)^n for every u, and Σ_{n≥1} K((1 + ε)ρ)^n < ∞.

Exchange of limit and sum. Steps s2 and s3 give pointwise convergence of the terms and a summable bound that does not depend on u. The dominated convergence theorem for the counting measure on n ≥ 1 gives lim_{u→∞} ψ(u)/G(u) = (1 − ρ) Σ_{n≥1} n ρ^n = (1 − ρ) ρ/(1 − ρ)² = ρ/(1 − ρ). Finally G(u) = μ⁻¹ ∫_u^∞ (1 − F(y)) dy and ρ/((1 − ρ)μ) = λ/(c − λμ), which gives the second form.

applications.title: Ruin probability with Pareto-type claims
applications.inputs: Claims arrive as a Poisson process with rate λ = 1 per day. The claim sizes have the tail 1 − F(x) = (1 + x)^(−3) for x ≥ 0, so the mean is μ = ∫_0^∞ (1 + x)^(−3) dx = 1/2. The premium rate is c = 5/8 per day.
applications.hypotheses: The arrivals are Poisson and the claims are i.i.d., positive and independent of the arrivals, with finite mean 1/2. The load factor is ρ = 4/5 < 1. The integrated tail is 1 − F_I(u) = (1 + u)^(−2), which is regularly varying with index −2, so F_I is subexponential.

steps.text: The load factor is ρ = λμ/c = (1/2)/(5/8) = 4/5.
The integrated tail is 1 − F_I(u) = μ⁻¹ ∫_u^∞ (1 + y)^(−3) dy = 2 · (1 + u)^(−2)/2 = (1 + u)^(−2).
The constant of the theorem is ρ/(1 − ρ) = (4/5)/(1/5) = 4, so ψ(u) ∼ 4(1 + u)^(−2) as u → ∞.
For the capital u = 100 the approximation gives ψ(100) ≈ 4/101² = 4/10201 ≈ 3.9 · 10^(−4).
Compare with exponential claims of the same mean 1/2. Then ψ(u) = (4/5) e^(−2u/5), and ψ(100) = (4/5) e^(−40) ≈ 3.4 · 10^(−18). The heavy tail raises the ruin probability by a factor of about 10^14.

applications.conclusion: With Pareto-type claims of tail (1 + x)^(−3), λ = 1 and c = 5/8, the ruin probability decays only like a power: ψ(u) ∼ 4(1 + u)^(−2), and ψ(100) ≈ 3.9 · 10^(−4).

limitations: The result is asymptotic. The relative error ψ(u)(1 − F_I(u))⁻¹ − ρ/(1 − ρ) can tend to 0 arbitrarily slowly, so the approximation may be poor for moderate u.
Embrechts and Veraverbeke also prove the converse: subexponentiality of F_I is equivalent to the tail equivalence of ψ and 1 − F_I. This record proves only the direct implication.
The condition is on F_I, not on F. For example, a regularly varying claim tail with index −α, α > 1, makes F_I regularly varying with index 1 − α and hence subexponential.

results.name: Ruin probability of Brownian motion with positive drift
results.statement: Let B be a standard linear Brownian motion with B₀ = 0, and let x > 0, µ > 0 and σ > 0 be constants. Let X_t = x + µt + σB_t for t ≥ 0, and let τ = inf{t ≥ 0 : X_t = 0}, with inf ∅ = ∞. Then P(τ < ∞) = exp(−2µx/σ²).
hypotheses: B is a standard linear Brownian motion that starts at 0.
The initial capital x, the drift µ and the volatility σ are strictly positive constants.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 applies the optional stopping theorem to the martingale M at the bounded stopping time t ∧ τ.
Step s3 applies the strong law of large numbers to the independent standard normal increments B_k − B_(k−1) to get B_n/n → 0.
Step s3 bounds E Y₀² ≤ 4 for the oscillation Y₀ = sup over s ≤ 1 of |B_s| with Doob's L² maximal inequality.
Step s3 applies Markov's inequality to Y_n² to get P(Y_n > εn) ≤ 4/(ε²n²).
Step s3 uses the Borel–Cantelli lemma with the summable bound 4/(ε²n²) to get Y_n ≤ εn for all large n.
Step s4 passes to the limit t → ∞ in E M_(t∧τ) = 1 with the dominated convergence theorem and the constant bound e^(θx).

definitions.name: Brownian motion with drift
definitions.text: The process X_t = x + µt + σB_t, where B is a standard Brownian motion. Over a time h, its increment has the normal law with mean µh and variance σ²h, independently of the past.

definitions.name: ruin time
definitions.text: τ = inf{t ≥ 0 : X_t = 0}, the first time at which the surplus reaches 0. τ = ∞ when the surplus stays positive at all times.

definitions.name: adjustment coefficient
definitions.text: θ = 2µ/σ², the unique positive number θ for which exp(−θ(X_t − x)) is a martingale.

source.citation: Peter Mörters and Yuval Peres, Brownian Motion, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics 30, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
source.revision: Authors' version of the book (PDF created 2010-01-06), posted on the first author's home page.
source.module: Chapter 2, Exercises (Brownian motion as a strong Markov process), with the solution in Hints and solutions for selected exercises
source.excerpt: (c) Find E[T²] for T = min{t ⩾ 0 : B(t) ∈ {a, b}} and a < 0 < b. Exercise 2.16. Let {B(t) : t ⩾ 0} be a linear Brownian motion and a, b > 0. Show that P0{B(t) = a + bt for some t > 0} = e^{−2ab}.
source.attribution: © Peter Mörters and Yuval Peres. Quoted from the authors' version of Brownian Motion for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states that a Brownian motion B hits the line a + bt with probability e^(−2ab). The authored statement is the same result for the surplus x + µt + σB_t: it hits 0 exactly when the Brownian motion −B hits the line x/σ + (µ/σ)t, so a = x/σ and b = µ/σ give e^(−2ab) = exp(−2µx/σ²). The authored proof follows the solution on p. 368 with the exponential martingale and the bounded stopped process, and it adds the proof that the martingale tends to 0 when ruin never occurs. The excerpt starts with the last line of Exercise 2.15, which directly precedes Exercise 2.16.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the exponential martingale solution of the cited exercise. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for all positive x, µ and σ. The case µ ≤ 0 is not covered.

steps.text: Let θ = 2µ/σ² and let (F_t) be the filtration of B. For real λ, the process exp(λB_t − λ²t/2) is a martingale: B_t − B_s is independent of F_s and has the law N(0, t − s), so E[exp(λ(B_t − B_s)) | F_s] = exp(λ²(t − s)/2). Take λ = −θσ. Then λ²/2 = θ²σ²/2 = 2µ²/σ² = θµ, so M_t = exp(−θσB_t − θµt) = exp(−θ(X_t − x)) is a positive martingale with M₀ = 1.

The time τ is a stopping time, because X has continuous paths and {0} is a closed set. For s ≤ τ, X_s ≥ 0, because X₀ = x > 0, X is continuous and τ is its first zero. Hence 0 < M_(t∧τ) = e^(θx) e^(−θX_(t∧τ)) ≤ e^(θx). The optional stopping theorem at the bounded stopping time t ∧ τ gives E M_(t∧τ) = E M₀ = 1 for every t ≥ 0.

B_t/t → 0 almost surely. The increments B_k − B_(k−1), k ≥ 1, are independent with law N(0, 1), so the strong law of large numbers gives B_n/n → 0. Let Y_n = sup_(0≤s≤1) |B_(n+s) − B_n|. Each Y_n has the law of Y₀. Doob's L² maximal inequality on finite sets of dyadic times in [0, 1], extended by path continuity and monotone limits, gives E Y₀² ≤ 4 E B₁² = 4. For ε > 0, Markov's inequality gives P(Y_n > εn) ≤ 4/(ε²n²), which is summable in n. The Borel–Cantelli lemma gives Y_n ≤ εn for all large n, almost surely. For t ∈ [n, n + 1], |B_t|/t ≤ (|B_n| + Y_n)/n. So lim sup |B_t|/t ≤ ε almost surely, for every rational ε > 0.

On the event {τ = ∞}, X_t = t(µ + x/t + σB_t/t) → ∞ almost surely by step s3, because µ > 0. So M_(t∧τ) = M_t = e^(θx) e^(−θX_t) → 0 there. On the event {τ < ∞}, M_(t∧τ) = M_τ = e^(θx) for all t ≥ τ, because X_τ = 0. The bound 0 < M_(t∧τ) ≤ e^(θx) of step s2 allows the dominated convergence theorem as t → ∞: 1 = lim E M_(t∧τ) = e^(θx) P(τ < ∞). Hence P(τ < ∞) = e^(−θx) = exp(−2µx/σ²).

applications.title: Capital requirement in the diffusion approximation of an insurance surplus
applications.inputs: The surplus of an insurer, in millions of euros, is modelled as X_t = x + µt + σB_t with net premium drift µ = 1/2 per year and volatility σ = 2 per square root of a year. The initial capital x is to be chosen.
applications.hypotheses: B is a standard Brownian motion, and x > 0, µ = 1/2 > 0 and σ = 2 > 0. So the theorem applies for every positive capital x.

steps.text: The adjustment coefficient is θ = 2µ/σ² = 2 · (1/2)/2² = 1/4 per million euros.
The theorem gives the ruin probability ψ(x) = P(τ < ∞) = e^(−x/4). For a capital x = 10 million, ψ(10) = e^(−2.5) ≈ 0.082.
The formula is multiplicative in the capital: ψ(x + y) = ψ(x)ψ(y). The capital x₀ = 4 ln 10 ≈ 9.21 million gives ψ(x₀) = 1/10, so three times this capital gives ψ(3x₀) = (1/10)³ = 1/1000.
A ruin probability of at most 0.1% thus needs x ≥ 12 ln 10 ≈ 27.6 million. If the volatility doubles to σ = 4, then θ becomes 1/16, and the same target needs four times this capital.

applications.conclusion: ψ(x) = e^(−x/4) in millions of euros. A ruin probability of 0.1% needs a capital of 12 ln 10 ≈ 27.6 million, and the required capital is proportional to σ²/(2µ).

limitations: If µ ≤ 0, the surplus reaches 0 almost surely, so P(τ < ∞) = 1. The formula covers only a positive drift.

The model is the diffusion approximation of a risk process. For the compound Poisson (Cramér–Lundberg) surplus, the same martingale method gives only the Lundberg bound ψ(x) ≤ e^(−Rx), because the surplus jumps below 0 with an overshoot.

results.name: Ladder height distribution in the Cramér–Lundberg model
aliases: Integrated tail formula for the ladder height
Ladder height distribution for Poisson arrivals
results.statement: In the Cramér–Lundberg model, claims arrive at the jump times of a Poisson process of rate λ > 0. The claim sizes Y₁, Y₂, … are i.i.d., nonnegative and independent of the arrivals, with distribution function B, tail B̄ = 1 − B and finite mean µ_B. Premiums come in at rate c > 0, and ρ = λµ_B/c < 1. Let S(t) = Σ_(i≤N(t)) Y_i − ct be the claim surplus process and τ₊ = inf{t ≥ 0 : S(t) > 0}. Then for every z ≥ 0, P(τ₊ < ∞, S(τ₊) > z) = (λ/c) ∫_z^∞ B̄(y) dy. So the first ladder height S(τ₊) has the defective density (λ/c) B̄(y) on (0, ∞), and P(τ₊ < ∞) = ρ.
hypotheses: Claims arrive at the jump times of a Poisson process of rate λ > 0, independent of the claim sizes.
The claim sizes are i.i.d. and nonnegative with distribution function B and finite mean µ_B.
The net profit condition holds: ρ = λµ_B/c < 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses the strong law of large numbers to show that the reflected walk with positive mean step reaches a new maximum with probability one.
Steps s3, s4 and s5 exchange sums and integrals of nonnegative terms with Tonelli's theorem.

definitions.name: claim surplus process
definitions.text: S(t) = Σ_(i≤N(t)) Y_i − ct, where N(t) is the number of claims by time t. Ruin from initial reserve u happens when S(t) > u for some t.

definitions.name: ladder height
definitions.text: The value S(τ₊) of the claim surplus at the first time τ₊ that it is above 0. It is the deficit at ruin when the initial reserve is 0.

definitions.name: ladder point measure
definitions.text: For a random walk W with W₀ = 0, the measure ψ(A) = expected number of n ≥ 0 with W_n > W_k for all k < n and W_n ∈ A.

source.citation: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th edition, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
source.revision: Author's online version of January 11, 2019 (PTE5_011119.pdf).
source.module: Chapter 5 Markov Chains, Section 5.8.4 GI/G/1 queue
source.excerpt: Using (5.8.1) now and integrating by parts gives P(S̄τ ≤ x) = ∫_{y≤x} (1 + α(x − y)) dF(y) = F(x) + α∫_{−∞}^x F(y) dy for x ≤ 0 (5.8.2). Since P(S̄n = 0) = 0 for n ≥ 1, −S̄τ has the same distribution as ST, where T = inf{n : Sn > 0}.
source.attribution: © Rick Durrett. Quoted from the author's online version of Probability: Theory and Examples for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source works with the GI/G/1 walk S_n = Σ(η_(i−1) − ζ_i) with exponential interarrival times ζ of rate α and proves formula (5.8.2) for the first weak descending ladder height of S̄ = −S. With η = Y and α = λ/c this walk is the claim surplus at the claim times of the Cramér–Lundberg model. The authored statement is the integrated form of (5.8.2), and step s5 computes it from (5.8.2). The source proof cites 'Exercise 5.8.13', which is Lemma 5.8.13 on p. 327.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, Example 5.8.15, with an added computation of the integrated tail. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement.

steps.text: Reduction to a random walk. Let E_i be the i.i.d. Exp(λ) times between claims and S_n = Σ_(i≤n) (Y_i − cE_i), the claim surplus just after claim n. Between claims S(t) decreases, so S first exceeds 0 at a claim time, and S(τ₊) = S_T with T = inf{n ≥ 1 : S_n > 0}. Let S̄_n = −S_n, a random walk with steps ξ̄_i = cE_i − Y_i, where cE_i is exponential with rate α = λ/c. Then E ξ̄ = 1/α − µ_B > 0 because ρ < 1. For n ≥ 1, c(E₁ + ⋯ + E_n) has a density and is independent of the claims, so P(S_n = 0) = 0. With τ = inf{n ≥ 1 : S̄_n ≤ 0}, almost surely T = τ, and P(T < ∞, S_T ≥ z) = P(τ < ∞, S̄_τ ≤ −z) for z ≥ 0.

Exponential right tail of the steps. For x ≥ 0, independence gives P(ξ̄ > x) = ∫ P(cE > x + y) B(dy) = e^(−αx) ∫ e^(−αy) B(dy) = a e^(−αx), where a = P(ξ̄ > 0) from x = 0. This is Lemma 5.8.13 of the source.

Ladder heights of S̄. By the strong law of large numbers S̄_n/n → E ξ̄ > 0, so T̄ = inf{n : S̄_n > 0} is finite almost surely. For x ≥ 0, condition on ξ̄₁, …, ξ̄_(n−1): on {T̄ > n − 1} we have s = S̄_(n−1) ≤ 0 and P(ξ̄_n > x − s) = e^(−αx) P(ξ̄_n > −s) by step s2. So P(T̄ = n, S̄_n > x) = e^(−αx) P(T̄ = n), and the first ladder height is Exp(α). T̄ is a stopping time, so the walk after T̄ is a new copy, independent of the past. The ladder heights V_k = J₁ + ⋯ + J_k therefore have i.i.d. Exp(α) increments J_i. Tonelli and Σ_(k≥1) α^k s^(k−1)/(k−1)! = α e^(αs) give Σ_(k≥1) P(V_k ≤ w) = ∫₀^w α ds = αw.

Reversal and the first step below 0. Let ψ_n(A) = P(S̄₁ > 0, …, S̄_n > 0, S̄_n ∈ A), with ψ₀ = δ₀. The reversed walk S̄_n − S̄_(n−k), 0 ≤ k ≤ n, has the same law as S̄_k, 0 ≤ k ≤ n, so ψ_n(A) is the probability that n is a strict ascending ladder epoch of S̄ with S̄_n ∈ A. By step s3, ψ = Σ_n ψ_n satisfies ψ[0, w] = 1 + αw, so ψ = δ₀ + α · Lebesgue measure on (0, ∞). For x ≤ 0 and F(x) = P(ξ̄ ≤ x), independence of ξ̄_(n+1) gives P(τ = n + 1, S̄_τ ≤ x) = ∫ F(x − s) ψ_n(ds). Tonelli gives P(τ < ∞, S̄_τ ≤ x) = F(x) + α ∫₀^∞ F(x − s) ds = F(x) + α ∫_(−∞)^x F(y) dy, which is formula (5.8.2).

Integrated tail. Let g(u) = F(−u) = P(Y − cE ≥ u). For u ≥ 0, g(u) = E[1{Y > u}(1 − e^(−α(Y−u)))]. Tonelli gives α ∫_z^∞ g(u) du = E[1{Y > z}(α(Y − z) − 1 + e^(−α(Y−z)))] = α E(Y − z)⁺ − g(z), and E(Y − z)⁺ = ∫_z^∞ B̄(y) dy. With x = −z in step s4 and step s1, P(T < ∞, S_T ≥ z) = g(z) + α ∫_z^∞ g(u) du = (λ/c) ∫_z^∞ B̄(y) dy. The right side is continuous in z, so the same holds for S_T > z. At z = 0 the value is λµ_B/c = ρ.

applications.title: First deficit of an insurer with uniform claims
applications.inputs: Claims arrive at rate λ = 1 per day. Claim sizes are uniform on [0, 2], so µ_B = 1 and B̄(y) = 1 − y/2 for 0 ≤ y ≤ 2. The premium rate is c = 5/4 per day, and the initial reserve is 0.
applications.hypotheses: The arrivals are Poisson and independent of the i.i.d. claims, and ρ = λµ_B/c = 4/5 < 1.

steps.text: With zero initial reserve, ruin happens at τ₊. The theorem gives the ruin probability P(τ₊ < ∞) = ρ = 4/5.
The deficit at ruin is the ladder height S(τ₊). The theorem gives P(τ₊ < ∞, S(τ₊) > 1) = (4/5) ∫₁² (1 − y/2) dy = (4/5)(1 − 3/4) = 1/5.
Given ruin, the deficit is above 1 with probability (1/5)/(4/5) = 1/4. Its conditional density B̄(y)/µ_B = 1 − y/2 on [0, 2] is the integrated tail distribution of the claims.
The mean deficit given ruin is E Y²/(2µ_B) = (4/3)/2 = 2/3, which is less than the mean claim 1. The deficit is the ruinous claim minus the reserve that the premiums built up before it.

applications.conclusion: With zero reserve the insurer is ruined with probability 4/5, and the deficit at ruin has density 1 − y/2 on [0, 2] given ruin, with mean 2/3.

limitations: The Poisson arrivals are essential. The proof uses the exponential tail of the steps of S̄, and for other interarrival laws the ladder height law is in general not the integrated tail.
The result gives only the first ladder height. The ruin probability for a positive initial reserve follows from it as a geometric compound sum, which is the Pollaczek–Khinchine formula.
The net profit condition ρ < 1 is needed. For ρ ≥ 1 the claim surplus reaches a new maximum almost surely, and for ρ > 1 the total mass ρ of the formula is above 1.

results.name: Lindley recursion and the supremum representation of waiting times
results.statement: Let U₁, U₂, … be independent and identically distributed real random variables. Let S₀ = 0, S_k = U₁ + ⋯ + U_k, M_n = max_(0≤k≤n) S_k and M = sup_(k≥0) S_k ∈ [0, ∞]. Define W₀ = 0 and W_n = max(W_(n−1) + U_n, 0) for n ≥ 1. Then (i) W_n = max_(0≤k≤n) (U_(n−k+1) + ⋯ + U_n) = S_n − min_(0≤i≤n) S_i for every n, where the empty sum is 0. (ii) W_n has the same law as M_n. (iii) For every real x, P(W_n > x) increases with n to P(M > x), and P(W_n ≥ x) increases to P(S_k ≥ x for some k ≥ 0). (iv) If E|U₁| < ∞ and E U₁ < 0, then M < ∞ almost surely, so W_n converges in distribution to the law of M. In a G/G/1 queue with interarrival times X_n and service times Y_n, all independent, U_n = Y_(n−1) − X_n and W_n is the waiting time of customer n.
hypotheses: The increments U₁, U₂, … are independent and identically distributed real random variables.
For part (iv) only: E|U₁| < ∞ and E U₁ < 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 applies the strong law of large numbers, S_k/k → E U₁ < 0, to show that the supremum M is finite almost surely.

definitions.name: Lindley recursion
definitions.text: W₀ = 0 and W_n = max(W_(n−1) + U_n, 0). In the G/G/1 queue, W_n is the waiting time of customer n, and U_n = Y_(n−1) − X_n is the service time of customer n − 1 minus the interarrival time before customer n.

definitions.name: running maximum
definitions.text: M_n = max_(0≤k≤n) S_k and M = sup_(k≥0) S_k for the random walk S₀ = 0, S_k = U₁ + ⋯ + U_k.

definitions.name: G/G/1 queue
definitions.text: A single-server queue with first-come first-served service, independent and identically distributed interarrival times, and independent and identically distributed service times that are independent of the arrivals.

source.citation: Robert G. Gallager, Discrete Stochastic Processes, Chapter 7: Random Walks, Large Deviations, and Martingales, course notes for MIT 6.262, Spring 2011, MIT OpenCourseWare. A revised version appeared as Stochastic Processes: Theory for Applications, Cambridge University Press, 2013.

source.module: Chapter 7, Section 7.2 The queueing delay in a G/G/1 queue
source.excerpt: Theorem 7.2.1. Let {Xi; i ≥ 1} be the IID interarrival intervals of a G/G/1 queue, let {Yi; i ≥ 0} be the IID service times, and assume that the system is empty at time 0 when customer 0 arrives. Let Wn be the queueing delay for the nth customer. Let Un = Yn−1 − Xn for n ≥ 1 and let Zin = Un + Un−1 + · · · + Un−i+1 for 1 ≤ i ≤ n. Then for every α > 0, and n ≥ 1, Wn = max[0, Z1n, Z2n, . . . , Znn]. …
source.attribution: © Robert G. Gallager. Quoted from the MIT OpenCourseWare notes Discrete Stochastic Processes, Chapter 7, for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the pathwise formula for W_n, the equality of P(W_n ≥ α) with the probability that the random walk crosses α by trial n, and the limit as the probability of ever crossing α. The authored statement uses a general i.i.d. increment sequence, adds the form S_n − min S_i, and adds part (iv) on the finiteness of M under a negative mean. The authored proof follows the source: iteration of the recursion (7.5), reversal of the increments, and monotonicity in n.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the iteration and time-reversal argument of the cited source. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Parts (i) to (iii) for every i.i.d. increment law, and part (iv) for an integrable increment with negative mean.

steps.text: Part (i) by induction on n. Let V_n = max_(0≤k≤n) (U_(n−k+1) + ⋯ + U_n), with the term 0 for k = 0. Then V₀ = 0 = W₀. If W_(n−1) = V_(n−1), then W_(n−1) + U_n = max_(0≤k≤n−1) (U_(n−k) + ⋯ + U_n) = max_(1≤j≤n) (U_(n−j+1) + ⋯ + U_n) with j = k + 1. Taking the maximum with 0 adds the term j = 0, so W_n = V_n. Since U_(n−k+1) + ⋯ + U_n = S_n − S_(n−k), also W_n = S_n − min_(0≤i≤n) S_i.

Part (ii) by reversal. Let g(u₁, …, u_n) = max_(0≤k≤n) (u₁ + ⋯ + u_k). Step s1 gives W_n = g(U_n, U_(n−1), …, U₁), and M_n = g(U₁, …, U_n) by definition. The joint law of (U₁, …, U_n) is the product of n copies of one law, so it does not change under the permutation that reverses the order. Hence (U_n, …, U₁) and (U₁, …, U_n) have the same law, and W_n and M_n have the same law.

Part (iii). The running maximum M_n is nondecreasing in n and tends to M pathwise. So the events {M_n > x} increase with union {M > x}, and the events {M_n ≥ x} increase with union {S_k ≥ x for some k ≥ 0}. Continuity of the probability measure from below and step s2 give P(W_n > x) = P(M_n > x) ↑ P(M > x) and P(W_n ≥ x) ↑ P(S_k ≥ x for some k).

Part (iv). If E|U₁| < ∞ and E U₁ < 0, the strong law of large numbers gives S_k/k → E U₁ < 0 almost surely. So S_k → −∞, and on this event only finitely many S_k are larger than S₀ = 0. Hence M is a maximum of finitely many finite values, and M < ∞ almost surely. By step s3, P(W_n ≤ x) = 1 − P(M_n > x) → P(M ≤ x) for every real x, and P(M ≤ x) → 1 as x → ∞. So W_n converges in distribution to the proper law of M.

applications.title: Waiting times in a queue with constant service time
applications.inputs: Every customer needs a service time Y = 2 minutes. The interarrival times X_n are independent, equal to 1 minute with probability 1/3 and to 3 minutes with probability 2/3. Customer 0 arrives at an empty system at time 0.
applications.hypotheses: The increments U_n = Y − X_n are independent and identically distributed, with U_n = 1 with probability 1/3 and U_n = −1 with probability 2/3. Their mean is E U₁ = −1/3 < 0, so part (iv) applies.

steps.text: Part (i) on one path: the interarrival times (1, 1, 3) give U = (1, 1, −1). The recursion gives W₁ = 1, W₂ = 2, W₃ = 1, and indeed W₃ = max(0, −1, 1 − 1, 1 + 1 − 1) = 1.
Part (ii) for customer 3: P(W₃ ≥ 1) = P(M₃ ≥ 1). The walk stays at or below 0 up to time 3 exactly when U₁ = −1 and not U₂ = U₃ = 1. So P(W₃ ≥ 1) = 1 − (2/3)(1 − (1/3)²) = 11/27.

Part (iii) gives P(W_n ≥ k) ↑ P(S reaches k). The function 2^s is harmonic for this walk, because (1/3)2^(s+1) + (2/3)2^(s−1) = 2^s. Optional stopping gives P(S reaches k before −m) = (1 − 2^(−m))/(2^k − 2^(−m)), which tends to 2^(−k) as m → ∞.

So the steady-state wait W satisfies P(W ≥ k) = 2^(−k) for k ≥ 0, and E W = Σ_(k≥1) 2^(−k) = 1 minute. The probability of a wait is 1/3 for customers 1 and 2, then 11/27 for customer 3, and it increases to 1/2.

applications.conclusion: The waiting time of customer n has the law of the running maximum of a ±1 random walk with downward drift. In steady state the wait in minutes is geometric with P(W ≥ k) = 2^(−k) and mean 1 minute.

limitations: The representation gives the law of each W_n separately, but not the joint law of successive waiting times. The reversed walks for different n are different.

If E U₁ > 0, then M = ∞ almost surely and W_n → ∞ in probability. If E U₁ = 0 and U₁ is not almost surely 0, also M = ∞ almost surely, because a mean-zero random walk oscillates. These cases are not covered by part (iv).
The law of M is explicit only in special cases, for example with exponential service or interarrival times. In general it follows from Spitzer's identity or from ladder heights.

results.name: Spitzer's identity
results.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be i.i.d. real random variables with law f, S₀ = 0, S_n = X₁ + ⋯ + X_n, S_n⁺ = max(S_n, 0) and M_n = max(S₀, S₁, …, S_n). Let 𝔐 be the Banach algebra of finite complex Borel measures on ℝ, with convolution as product, total variation as norm and unit δ₀, and let exp be the exponential series in 𝔐. Then for every complex x with |x| < 1, Σ_(n≥0) xⁿ P(M_n ∈ ·) = exp(Σ_(n≥1) (xⁿ/n) P(S_n⁺ ∈ ·)) in 𝔐. In particular, for every real θ, Σ_(n≥0) xⁿ E[e^(iθM_n)] = exp(Σ_(n≥1) (xⁿ/n) E[e^(iθS_n⁺)]).
hypotheses: The increments X₁, X₂, … are independent and identically distributed real random variables. No moment condition is needed.
The generating variable x is a complex number with |x| < 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 uses the Lindley recursion and its representation by reversed partial sums to show that the reflected walk W_n has the law of the maximum M_n.

definitions.name: measure algebra
definitions.text: The space 𝔐 of finite complex Borel measures on ℝ with convolution as product and total variation as norm. It is a commutative Banach algebra with unit δ₀.

definitions.name: projection P
definitions.text: Pµ is the image of the measure µ under the map y ↦ max(y, 0). It moves all mass of (−∞, 0] to the point 0.

source.citation: J. F. C. Kingman, The use of Spitzer's identity in the investigation of the busy period and other quantities in the queue GI/G/1, Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society 2 (1962), 345-356.
source.revision: Journal version, Cambridge Core PDF (scanned, 12 pages), DOI 10.1017/S1446788700026938.
source.module: Section 2, Spitzer's identity
source.excerpt: LEMMA 1. Let 𝔐 be the Banach algebra of totally finite complex Borel measures on a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, with convolution as multiplication, total variation as norm, and identity e. Let f be a probability measure, and let P be a linear transformation of 𝔐 into itself, such that P² = P, ‖P‖ ≤ 1, Pe = e, and such that P𝔐 and (I − P)𝔐 are sub-algebras. If we define a sequence g_n in 𝔐 by the equations g₀ = e, …
source.attribution: © Australian Mathematical Society. Quoted from J. F. C. Kingman, J. Austral. Math. Soc. 2 (1962), for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states Spitzer's identity for a general projection P on the measure algebra, as a restatement of results of Wendel, and gives no proof. Section 4 (p. 347) of the source applies it to a random walk with an impenetrable barrier at 0, with g₀ = e and g_(n+1) = P(f g_n). The authored statement is the case of ℝ with P the image under y ↦ max(y, 0), where g_n is the law of the maximum M_n, together with the form for characteristic functions. The authored proof writes out the Banach algebra argument for this projection.

results.proof_status: authored proof by the Banach algebra method of Lemma 1 in Kingman (1962), which restates results of Wendel. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for every law f and every complex x with |x| < 1.

steps.text: The projection. 𝔐 is a commutative Banach algebra with unit δ₀, because ‖µ ∗ ν‖ ≤ ‖µ‖ ‖ν‖. Pµ = µ restricted to (0, ∞) plus µ((−∞, 0]) δ₀, so P is linear, ‖Pµ‖ ≤ ‖µ‖, P² = P and Pδ₀ = δ₀. Its range 𝔐₊ is the set of measures carried by [0, ∞). The range 𝔐₋ of I − P is the set of measures carried by (−∞, 0] with total mass 0, which is the kernel of P. Both sets are closed, and both are subalgebras, because supports add under convolution and total masses multiply. If µ ∈ 𝔐₊ ∩ 𝔐₋, then µ = Pµ = 0.

Lindley recursion. Let W₀ = 0 and W_(n+1) = max(W_n + X_(n+1), 0), and let g_n be the law of W_n. X_(n+1) is independent of W_n, so W_n + X_(n+1) has law g_n ∗ f and g_(n+1) = P(g_n ∗ f). By induction W_n = max_(0≤k≤n) (X_(k+1) + ⋯ + X_n), with the empty sum 0 for k = n. The reversed vector (X_n, …, X_1) has the law of (X₁, …, X_n), so W_n has the law of max_(0≤j≤n) S_j = M_n. Hence g_n = P(M_n ∈ ·).

The equation for the generating series. Since ‖g_n‖ = 1 and |x| < 1, G = Σ_(n≥0) xⁿ g_n converges in norm, and G ∈ 𝔐₊ because 𝔐₊ is closed. Multiplication of the recursion by x^(n+1), summation and continuity of P give G − δ₀ = P(x f ∗ G). Let A = δ₀ − x f. Since PG = G, P(G ∗ A) = G − P(x f ∗ G) = δ₀. Hence G ∗ A = δ₀ + m with m = (I − P)(G ∗ A) ∈ 𝔐₋.

Factorization of A. Let L = Σ_(n≥1) (xⁿ/n) f^(∗n), which converges in norm because ‖f^(∗n)‖ = 1. For |z| < 1, exp(−Σ_(n≥1) zⁿ/n) = 1 − z as power series. In 𝔐 the same identity holds for x f, because the double series that defines exp(−L) converges absolutely: its norms are bounded by Σ_k (Σ_n |x|ⁿ/n)^k/k! = 1/(1 − |x|). So A = exp(−L). PL and (I − P)L commute and add to L, so A = exp(−PL) ∗ exp(−(I − P)L), and step s3 gives G ∗ exp(−PL) = (δ₀ + m) ∗ exp((I − P)L).

Separation of the two sides. The left side of the last equation is in 𝔐₊, because G ∈ 𝔐₊ and exp(−PL) = δ₀ + Σ_(k≥1) (−PL)^k/k! with PL in the closed subalgebra 𝔐₊. On the right side, exp((I − P)L) = δ₀ + c with c ∈ 𝔐₋, so the product is δ₀ + (m + c + m ∗ c) ∈ δ₀ + 𝔐₋. Since δ₀ ∈ 𝔐₊, G ∗ exp(−PL) − δ₀ is in 𝔐₊ ∩ 𝔐₋ = {0}. Hence G = exp(PL). Here f^(∗n) is the law of S_n, so PL = Σ_(n≥1) (xⁿ/n) P(S_n⁺ ∈ ·), which is the identity in 𝔐.

Characteristic functions. For real θ, the map µ ↦ ∫ e^(iθy) µ(dy) is linear, multiplicative for convolution, bounded by ‖µ‖ and equal to 1 at δ₀. So it maps norm-convergent series term by term and maps exp(ν) to exp of the image of ν. Applied to the identity of step s5, it gives Σ_(n≥0) xⁿ E[e^(iθM_n)] = exp(Σ_(n≥1) (xⁿ/n) E[e^(iθS_n⁺)]).

applications.title: Persistence of a symmetric random walk
applications.inputs: A log-price or a particle position moves by i.i.d. steps X_i with a symmetric continuous law, for example a centred Gaussian or Laplace law. We want P(S₁ ≤ 0, …, S_n ≤ 0), the probability that the walk stays at or below its start for n steps, for n = 3.
applications.hypotheses: The steps are i.i.d., and the identity needs no other condition. Each S_n is symmetric and has a continuous law, so P(S_n ≤ 0) = 1/2.

steps.text: On measures carried by [0, ∞), the map µ ↦ µ({0}) is linear, bounded and multiplicative, because y + z = 0 with y, z ≥ 0 forces y = z = 0. Both sides of the identity are in this subalgebra, so Σ_n xⁿ P(M_n = 0) = exp(Σ_(n≥1) (xⁿ/n) P(S_n ≤ 0)).
With P(S_n ≤ 0) = 1/2 the right side is exp(−(1/2) log(1 − x)) = (1 − x)^(−1/2) = Σ_n C(2n, n) (x/4)ⁿ. So P(S₁ ≤ 0, …, S_n ≤ 0) = P(M_n = 0) = C(2n, n)/4ⁿ for every n.
For n = 3, C(6, 3)/4³ = 20/64 = 5/16. The walk stays at or below its start for three steps with probability 5/16, whatever the symmetric continuous step law is.
Stirling's formula gives C(2n, n)/4ⁿ ~ 1/√(πn). This universal decay of the persistence probability is the Sparre Andersen law of random walk theory.

applications.conclusion: For every symmetric continuous step law, the probability that the walk stays at or below its start for n steps is C(2n, n)/4ⁿ, which is 5/16 for n = 3.

limitations: The identity gives the law of M_n only through a transform. Explicit distributions need a factorization of 1 − x E e^(iθX), for example when X has a rational characteristic function.
The limit law of M_n as n → ∞ needs E X₁ < 0, or a weaker condition that makes Σ_n P(S_n > 0)/n finite.
The identity needs i.i.d. steps. It does not apply directly to walks with dependent or Markov-modulated increments.

results.name: Renewal-reward theorem
aliases: Strong law of large numbers for renewal-reward processes
results.statement: Let (r₁, t₁), (r₂, t₂), … be independent and identically distributed pairs of random variables with t_i ≥ 0, 0 < µ = E t₁ < ∞ and E|r₁| < ∞. Let T_n = t₁ + ⋯ + t_n, N(t) = max{n ≥ 0 : T_n ≤ t} and R(t) = Σ_(i=1)^(N(t)) r_i, the total reward of the cycles that end by time t. Then R(t)/t → E r₁ / E t₁ almost surely as t → ∞.
hypotheses: The cycle pairs (r_i, t_i) are independent and identically distributed. The reward r_i can depend on the length t_i of its own cycle.
The cycle lengths are nonnegative with finite positive mean 0 < E t₁ < ∞.
The reward of a cycle is integrable: E|r₁| < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s3 apply the strong law of large numbers to the cycle lengths t_i and to the rewards r_i.

definitions.name: renewal counting process
definitions.text: N(t) = max{n ≥ 0 : T_n ≤ t}, the number of cycles that end by time t, where T_n = t₁ + ⋯ + t_n.

definitions.name: renewal-reward process
definitions.text: R(t) = Σ_(i=1)^(N(t)) r_i, where the reward r_i is earned at the end of cycle i and the pairs (r_i, t_i) are i.i.d.

source.revision: Author's online version, marked 'Almost Final Version of the 2nd Edition, December, 2011' (EOSP2E.pdf).
source.module: Chapter 3 Renewal Processes, Section 3.1 Laws of Large Numbers
source.excerpt: … total amount of rewards earned by time t. The main result about renewal reward processes is the following strong law of large numbers. Theorem 3.3. With probability one, R(t)/t → Eri/Eti
source.attribution: © Rick Durrett. Quoted from the author's online version of Essentials of Stochastic Processes, 2nd edition, for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source defines R(t) = Σ_(i≤N(t)) r_i on p. 102 for i.i.d. pairs (r_i, t_i) and states the almost sure limit as Theorem 3.3 on p. 103. The authored statement adds the integrability conditions that the source leaves implicit. The authored proof follows the source proof of Theorems 3.1 and 3.3, and adds the details that make N(t) finite and let the strong law pass along the random index N(t).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorems 3.1 and 3.3 in Durrett, Essentials of Stochastic Processes. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement.

steps.text: The cycle lengths t_i are i.i.d. and nonnegative with mean µ ∈ (0, ∞), so the strong law of large numbers gives T_n/n → µ almost surely. On this event T_n → ∞, so for every t the set {n : T_n ≤ t} is finite and N(t) is finite. Each T_n is finite, so N(t) ≥ n for t ≥ T_n. Hence N(t) is nondecreasing and N(t) → ∞ as t → ∞.

For t with N(t) ≥ 1 the definition of N(t) gives T_(N(t)) ≤ t < T_(N(t)+1). Division by N(t) gives T_(N(t))/N(t) ≤ t/N(t) < (T_(N(t)+1)/(N(t)+1)) · ((N(t)+1)/N(t)). If a_n → a and N(t) → ∞ through the integers, then a_(N(t)) → a: for ε > 0 take n₀ with |a_n − a| < ε for n ≥ n₀, and then t₀ with N(t) ≥ n₀ for t ≥ t₀. So both bounds tend to µ, and N(t)/t → 1/µ almost surely.

The rewards r_i are i.i.d. with E|r₁| < ∞, so the strong law of large numbers gives (1/n) Σ_(i=1)^n r_i → E r₁ almost surely. The rule of step s2 for limits along N(t) gives R(t)/N(t) = (1/N(t)) Σ_(i=1)^(N(t)) r_i → E r₁ almost surely as t → ∞.

The events of steps s1, s2 and s3 each have probability one, so their intersection has probability one. On it, for all large t, N(t) ≥ 1 and R(t)/t = (R(t)/N(t)) · (N(t)/t). The product of the two limits gives R(t)/t → E r₁ · (1/µ) = E r₁ / E t₁.

applications.title: Long-run cost of an age replacement policy
applications.inputs: A component has a lifetime L that is uniform on [0, 10] years. It is replaced at failure or at age 5, whichever comes first. A planned replacement costs 1 unit and a replacement after failure costs 3 units. Each new component is independent of the earlier ones.
applications.hypotheses: Cycle i ends at a replacement, so t_i = min(L_i, 5) and r_i = 3 if L_i < 5, else r_i = 1. The pairs (r_i, t_i) are i.i.d., 0 < E t₁ ≤ 5 and |r_i| ≤ 3, so the theorem applies.

steps.text: The mean cycle length is E min(L, 5) = ∫₀⁵ P(L > x) dx = ∫₀⁵ (1 − x/10) dx = 5 − 25/20 = 15/4 years.
A failure comes before age 5 with probability 1/2, so the mean cost per cycle is E r₁ = 1 · 1/2 + 3 · 1/2 = 2 units.
The theorem gives the long-run cost per year R(t)/t → E r₁ / E t₁ = 2/(15/4) = 8/15 almost surely.
Without planned replacements, each cycle is a full lifetime with mean 5 years and cost 3, so the long-run cost per year is 3/5 = 9/15. The age 5 policy saves 1/15 unit per year.

applications.conclusion: Replacement at failure or at age 5 costs 8/15 unit per year in the long run, which is less than the 3/5 unit per year of replacement at failure only.

limitations: The theorem counts the reward of a cycle at its end. For rewards that accumulate during a cycle, a separate argument must show that the partial reward of the current cycle is small compared with t, for example a bound by an integrable variable Y_(N(t)+1).
The almost sure limit does not by itself give E R(t)/t → E r₁/E t₁. That version needs Wald's equation, the elementary renewal theorem and control of the last cycle.
If E t₁ = ∞, then N(t)/t → 0 and R(t)/t → 0 almost surely, which this statement does not include.

results.name: Erdős–Feller–Pollard renewal theorem
results.statement: Let f₁, f₂, … be nonnegative numbers with Σ_k f_k = 1, such that the greatest common divisor of {k ≥ 1 : f_k > 0} is 1, and let µ = Σ_k k f_k ∈ [1, ∞]. Define u₀ = 1 and u_n = Σ_(k=1)^n f_k u_(n−k) for n ≥ 1. Then u_n → 1/µ as n → ∞, with 1/∞ = 0. In terms of a random walk S_m = X₁ + ⋯ + X_m with independent steps of law P(X_i = k) = f_k, u_n is the probability that S_m = n for some m ≥ 0.
hypotheses: The numbers f_k, k ≥ 1, are nonnegative with sum 1. Their mean µ = Σ_k k f_k can be infinite.
The greatest common divisor of the support {k : f_k > 0} is 1.
The sequence u solves the renewal equation u₀ = 1 and u_n = Σ_(k=1)^n f_k u_(n−k) for n ≥ 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 exchanges the order of the nonnegative double sum Σ_k Σ_(j>k) f_j = Σ_j j f_j with Tonelli's theorem to get Σ_k r_k = µ.
Step s3 uses Bézout's identity Σ c_i a_i = 1 for finitely many support points to write every large integer as a nonnegative combination of them.

definitions.name: renewal sequence
definitions.text: The solution u of u₀ = 1 and u_n = Σ_(k=1)^n f_k u_(n−k). It equals the probability that the random walk with step law f visits the integer n.

definitions.name: aperiodic step law
definitions.text: A law f on {1, 2, …} whose support {k : f_k > 0} has greatest common divisor 1.

definitions.name: tail sum
definitions.text: r_k = Σ_(j>k) f_j = P(X₁ > k) for k ≥ 0. The tail sums add up to the mean: Σ_(k≥0) r_k = µ.

source.citation: Steven P. Lalley, Renewal Theory, lecture notes, University of Chicago.
source.revision: PDF of the notes on the author's course page (13 pages, PDF created 2018-05-10).
source.module: Section 2, The Feller-Erdös-Pollard renewal theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 1. (Feller-Erdös-Pollard) Let (Sn)n≥0 be an ordinary arithmetic renewal process whose inter-occurrence time distribution fk = P{Xi = k} has finite mean 0 < µ < ∞ and is not supported by any proper additive subgroup of the integers (i.e., there is no m ≥ 2 such that P{Xi ∈ mZ} = 1). Let u be the associated renewal measure. Then lim_{k→∞} u(k) = lim_{k→∞} P{Sn = k for some n ≥ 0} = 1/µ.
source.attribution: © Steven P. Lalley. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Renewal Theory for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the theorem for a finite mean and proves it with a Markov chain and with a coupling. The authored statement works with the renewal equation (the source's Proposition 1) and includes the infinite mean case with limit 0, as in the original paper of Erdős, Feller and Pollard (Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 55 (1949), 201-204). The authored proof follows the elementary proof of that paper on pp. 203-204, with an explicit Bézout bound for the representation of large integers.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the elementary proof of Erdős, Feller and Pollard (1949). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for finite and infinite mean. Step s5 is needed only when µ < ∞.

steps.text: Bounds and tail identity. By strong induction, 0 ≤ u_n ≤ Σ_(k=1)^n f_k ≤ 1. Let r_k = Σ_(j>k) f_j for k ≥ 0, so r₀ = 1 and r_(k−1) − r_k = f_k. Let D_n = Σ_(k=0)^n r_k u_(n−k). Then D₀ = 1, and for n ≥ 1, D_n − D_(n−1) = u_n + Σ_(k=1)^n (r_k − r_(k−1)) u_(n−k) = u_n − Σ_(k=1)^n f_k u_(n−k) = 0. Hence Σ_(k=0)^n r_k u_(n−k) = 1 for every n ≥ 0. Tonelli's theorem for the nonnegative double sum gives Σ_(k≥0) r_k = Σ_j j f_j = µ.

Shifts along a lim sup sequence. Let λ = lim sup u_n and choose n_v → ∞ with u_(n_v) → λ. Let f_j > 0 and λ′ = lim inf_v u_(n_v − j), and suppose λ′ < λ. Fix ε > 0 and N ≥ j with Σ_(k>N) f_k < ε. For all large v, u_(n_v − k) ≤ λ + ε for k ≤ N, and u ≤ 1, so u_(n_v) ≤ (1 − f_j)(λ + ε) + f_j u_(n_v − j) + ε. Along a subsequence with u_(n_v − j) → λ′, this gives λ ≤ (1 − f_j)(λ + ε) + f_j λ′ + ε. As ε → 0, f_j λ ≤ f_j λ′, so λ ≤ λ′, a contradiction. Hence u_(n_v − j) → λ. The sequence n_v − j has the same property as n_v, so by induction u_(n_v − s) → λ for every finite sum s of points of A = {k : f_k > 0}.

Large integers are sums of support points. The greatest common divisor of A ∩ [1, n] is a nonincreasing positive integer for n ≥ min A, so it is eventually constant, equal to some g. Every point of A lies in some A ∩ [1, n], so g divides every point of A and g = 1. Hence finitely many points a₁, …, a_t of A have greatest common divisor 1, and Bézout's identity gives integers c_i with Σ c_i a_i = 1. Let N₀ = (a₁ − 1) Σ_i |c_i| a_i. For n ≥ N₀ write n − N₀ = q a₁ + ρ with q ≥ 0 and 0 ≤ ρ < a₁. Then n = q a₁ + Σ_i (ρ c_i + (a₁ − 1)|c_i|) a_i, and each coefficient is at least (a₁ − 1 − ρ)|c_i| ≥ 0. By step s2, u_(n_v − s) → λ for every fixed s ≥ N₀.

Upper bound. Fix M. For large v, the tail identity at index n_v − N₀ and the positivity of all terms give 1 ≥ Σ_(k=0)^M r_k u_(n_v − N₀ − k). By step s3 each term tends to r_k λ as v → ∞, so λ Σ_(k=0)^M r_k ≤ 1. Letting M → ∞ gives λµ ≤ 1. If µ = ∞, then λ = 0, and u_n → 0 = 1/µ because u_n ≥ 0.

Lower bound when µ < ∞. Let λ_* = lim inf u_n and choose n′_v with u_(n′_v) → λ_*. If f_j > 0 and λ″ = lim sup_v u_(n′_v − j) > λ_*, fix ε > 0 and N as in step s2, and let ℓ = max(λ_* − ε, 0). For large v, u_(n′_v − k) ≥ ℓ for k ≤ N, so u_(n′_v) ≥ (1 − f_j − ε)ℓ + f_j u_(n′_v − j). Along a subsequence, λ_* ≥ (1 − f_j − ε)ℓ + f_j λ″, and ε → 0 gives λ_* ≥ λ″, a contradiction. With step s3, u_(n′_v − s) → λ_* for every s ≥ N₀. Since u ≤ 1, the tail identity at n′_v − N₀ gives 1 ≤ Σ_(k=0)^M r_k u_(n′_v − N₀ − k) + Σ_(k>M) r_k, so 1 ≤ λ_* Σ_(k≤M) r_k + Σ_(k>M) r_k. As M → ∞, with Σ_k r_k = µ < ∞, λ_* µ ≥ 1. With step s4, u_n → 1/µ.

applications.title: Density of tile boundaries in a random monomer–dimer tiling
applications.inputs: Tiles of length 1 (monomers) and length 2 (dimers) are laid on the sites of a line from site 0 to the right. Each tile is independently a monomer or a dimer with probability 1/2. u_n is the probability that a tile boundary falls at site n.
applications.hypotheses: The step law is f₁ = f₂ = 1/2, so the support {1, 2} has greatest common divisor 1 and µ = 1 · 1/2 + 2 · 1/2 = 3/2. The last tile before a boundary at n has length 1 or 2, so u solves the renewal equation.

steps.text: The theorem gives u_n → 1/µ = 2/3. Far from the origin, two sites in three carry a tile boundary.
The renewal equation is u_n = u_(n−1)/2 + u_(n−2)/2 with u₀ = 1 and u₁ = 1/2. Its characteristic roots are 1 and −1/2, and the initial values give u_n = 2/3 + (1/3)(−1/2)^n.
For example, the recursion gives u₂ = 3/4, u₃ = 5/8 and u₄ = (5/8 + 3/4)/2 = 11/16, and the closed form gives u₄ = 2/3 + (1/3)(1/16) = 11/16.
The error |u_n − 2/3| = (1/3) 2^(−n) decays geometrically. With dimers only (f₂ = 1) the greatest common divisor is 2, and u_n alternates between 1 and 0, so the gcd condition cannot be dropped.

applications.conclusion: The density of tile boundaries converges to 1/µ = 2/3, the inverse of the mean tile length, at the geometric rate 2^(−n).

limitations: The gcd condition is necessary. If the support lies in dℤ with d ≥ 2, then u_n = 0 for n ∉ dℤ, and u_(nd) → d/µ instead.
The theorem gives no rate of convergence. A geometric rate needs more, for example an exponential moment of the step law.
The analogue for nonarithmetic step laws on the real line is the Blackwell renewal theorem.
