results.name: Lévy–Itô decomposition
aliases: Itô–Lévy decomposition of a Lévy process
results.statement: Let X = (X_t)_{t≥0} be a Lévy process in ℝⁿ with respect to a filtration (F_t): X is adapted, X_0 = 0, for all s, t ≥ 0 the increment X_{t+s} − X_t is independent of F_t and has the law of X_s, and t ↦ X_t is continuous in probability. Take the càdlàg version of X and write ΔX_s = X_s − X_{s−}. For a Borel set A ⊂ ℝⁿ∖{0} let N_t(A) = #{s ∈ (0, t] : ΔX_s ∈ A} and ν(A) = E[N_1(A)]. Then (i) ν is a measure on ℝⁿ∖{0} with ∫ min(1, |x|²) ν(dx) < ∞. (ii) For every Borel set A with 0 ∉ Ā, (N_t(A))_{t≥0} is a Poisson process with rate ν(A) < ∞, and N(A) and N(A′) are independent processes when A ∩ A′ = ∅. (iii) The vector γ = E[X_1 − ∑_{s≤1} ΔX_s 1(|ΔX_s| ≥ 1)] ∈ ℝⁿ exists, and there is a centered Gaussian Lévy process (B_t)_{t≥0} with continuous paths, independent of the jump counts N, such that for every t ≥ 0, almost surely, X_t = B_t + γt + ∑_{s≤t} ΔX_s 1(|ΔX_s| ≥ 1) + X^d_t. Here the sum of the big jumps has finitely many terms almost surely, and X^d_t = lim_{ε↓0} (∑_{s≤t} ΔX_s 1(ε ≤ |ΔX_s| < 1) − t ∫_{ε≤|x|<1} x ν(dx)), where the limit exists in L²(P).
hypotheses: X is an ℝⁿ-valued Lévy process with respect to a filtration (F_t): adapted, X_0 = 0, X_{t+s} − X_t independent of F_t with the law of X_s, and continuous in probability.
The càdlàg version of X is used. Every such process has one.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses optional sampling for the exponential martingales to get the strong Markov property, which gives the moment bound for bounded jumps.
Steps s3 and s5 use Doob's L² inequality E[sup_{s≤t} M_s²] ≤ 4E[M_t²] to make the martingale space complete and to get uniform convergence of paths.
Steps s3 and s4 use dominated convergence to pass from step functions and fine partitions to the limit.
Step s6 expands exp(iuB) to second order with a Taylor remainder along a partition of [0, t].
Step s6 bounds the Taylor remainder on the event of a large oscillation with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

definitions.name: Lévy process
definitions.text: An adapted process with X_0 = 0 whose increment X_{t+s} − X_t is independent of F_t and has the law of X_s, and which is continuous in probability.

definitions.name: Lévy measure of X
definitions.text: The measure ν(A) = E[N_1(A)] on ℝⁿ∖{0}, the mean number of jumps with value in A during one unit of time.

definitions.name: compensated small-jump integral
definitions.text: X^d_t, the L² limit as ε ↓ 0 of the sum of the jumps with ε ≤ |ΔX_s| < 1 up to time t minus its mean t ∫_{ε≤|x|<1} x ν(dx).

source.excerpt: Theorem 3.12 (A) Let X be an n–dimensional Lévy process. Then … where Bt is a centered Gaussian Lévy process with a.s. continuous sample paths. Nt (dx) is a family of Poisson processes, independent of Bt , with Nt (A) idependent of Nt (B) if A ∩ B = ∅, and with ν(dx) = E[N1 (dx)].

source.alignment: Theorem 3.12 (A) of the source states the decomposition X_t = B_t + tE[X_1 − ∫_{|x|>1} x N_1(dx)] + ∫_{|x|≥1} x N_t(dx) + ∫_{|x|<1} x (N_t(dx) − tν(dx)) with the properties of B, N and ν that the authored statement lists. The source states the drift with |x| > 1 and the big jumps with |x| ≥ 1. The authored statement uses |x| ≥ 1 in both places, which the proof of the source supports. The authored statement writes the stochastic integrals as finite sums and as an L² limit of compensated sums.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 3.12 (A) in Bretagnolle's notes as translated by Ouwehand (arXiv:1506.06624), Sections 1-3. Steps s1, s3, s4 and s6 take Corollary 1.5, Theorem 2.1, Lemmas 3.5-3.7 and Lemma 3.11 from the source. Parts (B)-(D) of the source theorem, the Lévy–Khintchine formula, are not covered here.

steps.text: Regular paths and moments. Theorem 1.2 of the source gives a càdlàg version, because each M^u_t = e^{i⟨u,X_t⟩}/E[e^{i⟨u,X_t⟩}] is a martingale and so has limits along countable sets. Theorem 1.4 proves the strong Markov property with optional sampling. Corollary 1.5 uses it as follows: if no jump has size M or more, the stopping times T_k = inf{t > T_{k−1} : |X_t − X_{T_{k−1}}| ≥ M} have i.i.d. increments, so E[e^{−T_k}] = a^k with a = E[e^{−T_1}] < 1. Since |X_t| ≥ 2kM forces T_k ≤ t, P(|X_t| ≥ 2kM) ≤ e^t a^k, and X_t has exponential moments.

Jump counts and removal of the big jumps. For a Borel set A with 0 ∉ Ā, càdlàg paths have finitely many jumps in A on [0, t], so N_t(A) is finite. Lemmas 3.1-3.4 of the source show that N(A), X_t(A) = ∑_{s≤t} ΔX_s 1(ΔX_s ∈ A) and X − X(A) are Lévy processes. A Lévy process that grows only by jumps of size 1 is a Poisson process (Section 2 of the source), so ν(A) < ∞. For A = {|x| ≥ 1}, X′ = X − X(A) has jumps of size below 1. By s1 it has moments of all orders, the bound is uniform for t ≤ 1, and the mean is additive in t. Hence E[X′_t] = γt, and X″_t = X′_t − γt is a centered Lévy process and a square-integrable martingale.

Compensated isometry. Lemma 3.5 of the source proves, for 0 ∉ B̄ and f1_B ∈ L²(ν), that E[∫_B f dN_t] = t∫_B f dν and E[(∫_B f dN_t − t∫_B f dν)²] = t∫_B f² dν. For step functions this uses Var N_t(B) = tν(B) and Theorem 2.1: E[M_t N_t] = E[∑_k (M_{T_k} − M_{T_k−}) 1(T_k ≤ t)] for a centered square-integrable martingale M and a Poisson process N with jump times T_k, so compensated counts of disjoint sets are uncorrelated. Dominated convergence extends the formulas to all f. Doob's inequality makes the space 𝓜 of càdlàg centered square-integrable martingales complete for the seminorms q_t(M) = E[M_t²]^{1/2}, and Lemma 3.6 shows that the compensated integrals H_B form a closed subspace.

Orthogonality gives independence. Lemma 3.7 of the source shows with Theorem 2.1 that a martingale in 𝓜 without jumps at the jump times of N(B) is orthogonal to H_B. Corollary 3.8 applies the same partition argument to the normalized exponential martingales e^{i⟨u,Z_t⟩}/E[e^{i⟨u,Z_t⟩}] − 1 and e^{i⟨v,Z′_t⟩}/E[e^{i⟨v,Z′_t⟩}] − 1 of two processes Z, Z′ without common jump times, where one of them has paths of finite variation on [0, t]. The sum of the products of their increments over a fine partition tends to the sum of the products of their common jumps, which is zero, so their product has mean zero. This factorizes the joint characteristic function. Hence X(B_1) and X(B_2) are independent for disjoint B_1 and B_2, and so are the jump counts of disjoint sets.

Small jumps. Let B_k = {1/(k+1) ≤ |x| < 1/k}, A_m = B_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ B_m and Y_t(B) = X_t(B) − t∫_B x ν(dx). By s4, Y(A_m) and X″ − Y(A_m) are independent and centered, so E|X″_t|² = E|X″_t − Y_t(A_m)|² + t∫_{A_m} |x|² ν(dx) by s3. Hence ∫_{0<|x|<1} |x|² ν(dx) ≤ E|X″_1|² < ∞ (Remark 3.10 of the source), and Y(A_m) is a Cauchy sequence in 𝓜 with limit X^d (Lemma 3.9). Doob's inequality gives uniform convergence on [0, t] along a subsequence, almost surely. The process X″ − Y(A_m) has no jump of size 1/(m+1) or more, so the limit X^c = X″ − X^d has continuous paths. It is a centered Lévy process as a limit of Lévy processes.

The continuous part is Gaussian. Lemma 3.11 of the source treats a one-dimensional centered Lévy process B with continuous paths and E[B_1²] = 1. It has all moments by s1, and E[B_s⁴] is a polynomial in s without constant term. Along a partition of [0, t], a second-order Taylor expansion gives E[e^{iuB_t}] − 1 = −(u²/2) ∑_j E[e^{iuB_{t_j}}] Δt_j + R. On the event A_α that every oscillation on a partition cell is below α, the remainder is at most (1/2)α|u|³ ∑(ΔB_j)². Off A_α, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds it by u² P(A_α^c)^{1/2} E[(∑(ΔB_j)²)²]^{1/2}. Continuity of the paths gives P(A_α^c) → 0. Hence e^{−tψ(u)} − 1 = −(u²/2)∫_0^t e^{−sψ(u)} ds, so ψ(u) = u²/2. One-dimensional projections then give a Gaussian vector process.

Assembly. By construction X_t = X^c_t + γt + X_t({|x| ≥ 1}) + X^d_t, which is the decomposition with B = X^c. B is Gaussian by s6. The exponential martingales of B are continuous, so the argument of s4 makes B independent of all jump counts. N({|x| ≥ 1}) is a Poisson process with finite rate, so ν({|x| ≥ 1}) < ∞, and with s5 this gives ∫ min(1, |x|²) ν(dx) < ∞. Finally, the compensated sums over ε ≤ |x| < 1 differ from Y(A_m) by a term with second moment t∫_{ε≤|x|<1/(m+1)} |x|² ν(dx), which tends to 0, so the L² limit as ε ↓ 0 equals X^d.

applications.title: Thermal noise and active kicks on a tracer particle
applications.inputs: A tracer particle in a bath of active swimmers moves along one axis. Its displacement is X_t = W_t + (3/2)t + ∑_{k≤K_t} J_k. Here W is a standard Brownian motion (thermal noise with variance 1 per unit time), 3/2 is the drift from a weak external force, K is a Poisson process of rate 4 (kicks from swimmers), and the kicks J_k are i.i.d. with P(J = −1/2) = P(J = 2) = 1/2, independent of W and K.
applications.hypotheses: X is a sum of independent Lévy processes, so it is a Lévy process with càdlàg paths. Its jumps are the kicks, so the Lévy measure is ν = 2δ_{−1/2} + 2δ_2.

steps.text: The Lévy measure is finite: ∫ min(1, x²) ν(dx) = 2 · (1/2)² + 2 · 1 = 5/2 < ∞. The big jumps are the kicks of size 2, and they form a Poisson process of rate ν({2}) = 2.
The drift of the decomposition is γ = E[X_1] − E[sum of big jumps up to time 1]. E[X_1] = 3/2 + 4 · E[J] with E[J] = 3/4, and the big jumps have mean 2 · 2 = 4. So γ = 3/2 + 3 − 4 = 1/2.

The small jumps form −(1/2)(N_t({−1/2}) − 2t), a compensated Poisson process. The decomposition reads X_t = W_t + t/2 + 2N_t({2}) − (1/2)(N_t({−1/2}) − 2t). The drift terms add to t/2 + t = (3/2)t, as in the model.
The three random parts are independent, so Var X_t = t(1 + ∫ x² ν(dx)) = t(1 + 2 · 2² + 2 · (1/2)²) = 19t/2. The kicks raise the effective diffusion constant from 1/2 to 19/4.

applications.conclusion: The tracer displacement splits into thermal noise W, drift t/2, a Poisson stream of large kicks of size 2 at rate 2 and a compensated stream of small kicks of size −1/2 at rate 2. The variance per unit time is 19/2, so the effective diffusion constant is 19/4.

limitations: The decomposition describes the paths of one given Lévy process. The explicit characteristic exponent (the Lévy–Khintchine formula) and its uniqueness need the further parts (B)-(D) of the source theorem.
The small-jump sum is only an L² limit of compensated sums. Without compensation the sum ∑_{s≤t} |ΔX_s| can diverge when ∫_{|x|<1} |x| ν(dx) = ∞.
The cut-off 1 between big and small jumps is a convention. Another cut-off changes γ by an explicit integral of x against ν.

results.name: Characteristic functions of stable distributions
aliases: canonical representation of stable characteristic functions
results.statement: Call a probability distribution on ℝ stable if, for every n ≥ 1, independent random variables X₁, …, X_n with this distribution satisfy X₁ + ⋯ + X_n = a_n X₁ + b_n in distribution for some constants a_n > 0 and b_n ∈ ℝ. A function φ: ℝ → ℂ is the characteristic function of a stable distribution if and only if φ(t) = exp ψ(t) for all t ∈ ℝ, with ψ(t) = iµt − |ct|^α (1 − iβ sign(t) ω_α(t)) and ψ(0) = 0, where ω_α(t) = tan(πα/2) for α ≠ 1 and ω_1(t) = −(2/π) log|t|, for some real α, c, β, µ with 0 < α ≤ 2, c ≥ 0 and |β| ≤ 1. If the distribution is not a point mass, then c > 0 and the norming constants are a_n = n^{1/α}. For α = 2 the law is normal with mean µ and variance 2c², and β has no effect.
hypotheses: The distribution is a probability measure on ℝ. Stability means that for every n ≥ 1 there are a_n > 0 and b_n ∈ ℝ such that the sum of n independent copies X₁, …, X_n has the law of a_n X₁ + b_n.
In the formula the parameters satisfy 0 < α ≤ 2, c ≥ 0, |β| ≤ 1 and µ ∈ ℝ.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the sufficiency half of the Lévy–Khintchine formula: an exponent built from a drift and a Lévy measure is the logarithm of a characteristic function.
Step s6 uses the central limit theorem in the case α = 2: the normalized sums of a law with finite variance must converge to the standard normal law, which forces c′ = 0.
Step s7 uses dominated convergence, with the regular-variation bounds of the source, for the limit of K₂(x)/(x² V(1/x)) as x → ∞.

definitions.name: stable distribution
definitions.text: A probability distribution on ℝ such that for every n ≥ 1 the sum of n independent copies X₁, …, X_n has the law of a_n X₁ + b_n for some a_n > 0 and b_n ∈ ℝ. Point masses are stable in this sense.

definitions.name: index of stability
definitions.text: The number α ∈ (0, 2] in the formula. For a stable law that is not a point mass, the norming constants are a_n = n^{1/α}.

definitions.name: skewness parameter
definitions.text: The number β ∈ [−1, 1] in the formula. For 0 < α < 2 the Lévy measure of the law has density proportional to (1 + β)|x|^{−1−α} on x > 0 and to (1 − β)|x|^{−1−α} on x < 0, so β = 0 for a symmetric law.

source.citation: E. J. G. Pitman and Jim Pitman, A direct approach to the stable distributions, arXiv:1604.07350 [math.PR], 2016.
source.module: Section 1 Introduction, with the proof in Sections 4-8
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.1. (Lévy-Khintchine representation of stable distributions [19],[17]) A function φ is the characterisic function of a stable probability distribution on the real line if and only if φ(t) = exp[ψ(t)] with ψ(t) = ψ_{α,c,β,µ}(t) := iµt − |ct|^α (1 − iβ sign(t) ω_α(t)) where ω_α(t) = tan(πα/2) if α ≠ 1, ω_α(t) = −(2/π) log |t| if α = 1 … for some real α, c, β, µ with 0 < α ≤ 2, c ≥ 0 and |β| ≤ 1.

source.alignment: The authored statement is Theorem 1.1 of the source with the definition (1.2) of stability written out. It adds the norming constants a_n = n^{1/α} (Proposition 5.1 and Corollary 2.1 of the source) and the remark on α = 2 from Definition 1.2. The outline follows the proof of the source: Section 4 for the sufficiency, Section 5 for the functional equation, and Sections 6-8 for the bounds on the skewness constant.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 1.1 in E. J. G. Pitman and J. Pitman, A direct approach to the stable distributions (arXiv:1604.07350), Sections 4-8. Step s1 takes the Eulerian integrals of Lemma 4.2 from the source. Steps s6 and s7 take the tail estimates of Lemma 6.1, Theorem 6.3, Theorem 6.4 and Lemma 7.1 from the source. Steps s2-s5 are the elementary analysis of the functional equation in Section 5.

steps.text: Sufficiency. For α = 2, exp ψ is the normal characteristic function with mean µ and variance 2c². For 0 < α < 2, Lemma 4.2 of the source evaluates the Eulerian integrals ∫₀^∞ (e^{itx} − 1 − it sin x) x^{−1−α} dx = −K(α)[|t|^α − it tan(πα/2)(|t|^{α−1} − 1)] for α ≠ 1 and −(π/2)|t| − it log|t| for α = 1, with K(α) = −Γ(−α) cos(πα/2) > 0 and K(1) = π/2. Corollary 4.1 adds the two half-lines: the Lévy measure L(dx) = [(1 − β)1(x < 0) + (1 + β)1(x > 0)] c^α dx / (2K(α)|x|^{1+α}) gives ∫ (e^{itx} − 1 − it sin x) L(dx) = ψ(t) − ibt with b = µ + βc^α tan(πα/2) for α ≠ 1 and b = µ for α = 1. The Lévy–Khintchine formula makes exp ψ a characteristic function. Since |n^{1/α}ct|^α = n|ct|^α, nψ_{α,c,β,µ} = ψ_{α,n^{1/α}c,β,nµ}, so the sum of n copies has the law of n^{1/α}X + µ(n − n^{1/α}) for α ≠ 1 and of nX + (2/π)cβ n log n for α = 1 (Corollary 2.2). The law is stable.

Functional equation. Let φ be the characteristic function of a stable law. A point mass at µ gives φ(t) = e^{iµt}, the case c = 0. Otherwise |φ(t)| < 1 for some t, and stability reads φ(t)^n = φ(a_n t) e^{ib_n t} (2.2). Lemma 5.2: |φ(ct)| ≤ |φ(t)| for all t forces |c| ≥ 1 (iterate and let cⁿt → 0), and |φ(c₁t)| = |φ(c₂t)| for all t forces c₁ = c₂. Lemma 5.3: |φ(a_{n+1}t)| = |φ(t)| |φ(a_n t)| gives 1 = a₁ < a₂ < ⋯. From |φ(t/a₂)|² = |φ(t)|, a zero at t gives zeros at t/a₂^j → 0, which contradicts φ(0) = 1, so φ has no real zero. Writing φ(t)^{mn} in two ways gives a_{mn} = a_m a_n and b_m(n − a_n) = b_n(m − a_m). Lemma 5.4 compares n^p ≤ m^q < n^{p+1} and shows that a strictly increasing multiplicative sequence is a_n = n^k with k > 0. Put α = 1/k. Let log φ be the continuous logarithm with log φ(0) = 0. Both sides of n log φ(t) = log φ(a_n t) + ib_n t are continuous, agree at 0 and differ by a multiple of 2πi, so they are equal.

The case α ≠ 1 (Section 5.1). For n ≥ 2, n − n^k ≠ 0, so b_m(n − a_n) = b_n(m − a_m) gives b_n = γ(n − n^k) for a real constant γ. The function ψ₀(t) = log φ(t) − iγt then satisfies ψ₀(n^k t) = nψ₀(t), hence ψ₀((m/n)^k t) = (m/n)ψ₀(t), and by continuity ψ₀(rt) = r^α ψ₀(t) for all real r, t > 0. So ψ₀(t) = −(c − ic₁)t^α for t > 0. Since φ(−t) is the complex conjugate of φ(t), log φ(t) = iγt − c|t|^α (1 − ic′ sign(t)) with c′ = c₁/c (5.11). The bound |φ(t)| = e^{−c|t|^α} ≤ 1 and the exclusion of point masses give c > 0.

The case α = 1 (Section 5.2). Then a_n = n. The numbers B_n = b_n/n satisfy B_{mn} = B_m + B_n, and B_{m/n} = B_m − B_n extends them to positive rationals with r log φ(t) = log φ(rt) + iB_r rt (5.12). By continuity this defines B_r for all real r > 0 with B_{rs} = B_r + B_s. The function p ↦ B(e^p) is continuous and additive, so B(r) = λ log r. Put t = 1 and log φ(1) = −c + iy. Then log φ(r) = iyr − cr − iλ r log r for r > 0, so |φ(r)| = e^{−cr} and c > 0. With λ = cc′ this is log φ(t) = iyt − c(t + ic′ t log t) for t > 0 (5.15).

The index is at most 2 (Lemma 5.5). Let U = Re φ. For α ≠ 1, (5.11) gives 1 − U(t) ∼ c|t|^α as t → 0. For every random variable, 2(1 − U(t))/t² → E[X²] as t → 0, finite or infinite. Indeed (1 − cos tX)/t² ≤ X²/2, and Fatou's lemma gives the lower bound. If α > 2, this limit is 0, so E[X²] = 0 and X = 0 almost surely. This contradicts the assumption that the law is not a point mass. Hence 0 < α ≤ 2.

The skewness constant for α ≠ 1 (Lemma 5.6, proved in Section 8). Shift X so that γ = 0. Then 1 − U(t) ∼ ct^α and V(t) = Im φ(t) ∼ cc′t^α as t ↓ 0. For α = 2, X has variance 2c and mean 0, and φ(t/√(2cn))^n = exp(−t²(1 − ic′)/2) for t > 0 and every n. The central limit theorem forces this to equal e^{−t²/2}, so c′ = 0. For 0 < α < 2, Theorem 6.4 of the source gives c′ = β tan(πα/2) with β = lim K(x)/H(x) ∈ [−1, 1], where H(x) = 1 − F(x) + F(−x) and K(x) = 1 − F(x) − F(−x). Its proof takes Lemma 6.1 (E. J. G. Pitman, 1968) for H(x) ∼ (1 − U(1/x))/S(α), Lemma 6.2 for the imaginary part W of the characteristic function of |X|, and Theorem 6.3 (proved in Section 7) for the right tail R = (H + K)/2. The result is R(x)/H(x) → (1 + c′/tan(πα/2))/2. Since 0 ≤ R ≤ H, |c′/tan(πα/2)| ≤ 1. Theorem 6.3 needs C(α) + c′S(α) ≠ 0. The excluded case is c′/tan(πα/2) = −1, which is already in [−1, 1].

The skewness constant for α = 1 (Lemma 5.7) and assembly. From (5.15), 1 − U(t) ∼ ct and V(t) ∼ −cc′ t log t as t ↓ 0. If c′ = 0, put β = 0. Otherwise V has one sign near 0, and Lemma 7.1 of the source integrates the inversion formula K(u) = (2/π)∫₀^∞ (V(t)/t) cos ut dt twice: K₂(x) = ∫₀^x ∫₀^u K(v) dv du = (2/π)∫₀^∞ V(t)(1 − cos xt) t^{−3} dt. Regular variation of V and dominated convergence give K₂(x) ∼ x² V(1/x) (2/π)∫₀^∞ (1 − cos t) t^{−2} dt = x² V(1/x) ∼ cc′ x log x. Lemma 6.1 gives H(x) ∼ 2c/(πx), so H₂(x) = ∫₀^x ∫₀^u H(v) dv du ∼ (2c/π) x log x. Since |K| ≤ H, |K₂| ≤ H₂, so |c′| ≤ 2/π and c′ = 2β/π with |β| ≤ 1. To assemble, for α ≠ 1 write the constant c of (5.11) as c^α in the notation of the theorem and put µ = γ and c′ = β tan(πα/2). For α = 1 put µ = y and c′ = 2β/π, and extend (5.15) to t < 0 by conjugation. Both cases give the stated form of ψ.

applications.title: The Holtsmark law of the electric microfield in an ideal plasma
applications.inputs: Ions of equal charge q form a homogeneous Poisson process Π of density ρ in ℝ³, as in an ideal plasma without correlations. In units with Coulomb constant 1, the x-component of the electric field at the origin is X = lim_{R→∞} ∑_{y∈Π, |y|<R} q y₁/|y|³. Let φ be its characteristic function.
applications.hypotheses: The limit exists in L² after the ions in the unit ball are separated: for 1 ≤ R < R′ the ions with R ≤ |y| < R′ give a centered term with variance (4πρq²/3)(1/R − 1/R′). Step a1 checks stability. X is not a point mass, because the ions in the unit ball give an independent compound Poisson term that is not constant.

steps.text: Stability. n independent Poisson processes of density ρ superpose to one of density nρ, so X₁ + ⋯ + X_n has the law of the field X^{(nρ)} at density nρ. The scaled process n^{−1/3}Π has density nρ, and each term q y₁/|y|³ is multiplied by n^{2/3}. So X₁ + ⋯ + X_n has the law of n^{2/3} X, with b_n = 0.
Index. The theorem gives a_n = n^{1/α} for a law that is not a point mass. Here a_n = n^{2/3}, so 1/α = 2/3 and α = 3/2.

Symmetry. The reflection y₁ ↦ −y₁ keeps the law of Π and changes the sign of X, so φ is real. Then Im ψ is continuous with values in πℤ and Im ψ(0) = 0, so Im ψ = 0. With tan(3π/4) = −1, Im ψ(t) = µt − βc^{3/2} sign(t)|t|^{3/2}. At t = 1 and t = 4 this gives µ = βc^{3/2} and 4µ = 8βc^{3/2}. So βc^{3/2} = 0, and c > 0 gives β = 0 and µ = 0.

No finite variance. Now φ(t) = exp(−c^{3/2}|t|^{3/2}), so 2(1 − φ(t))/t² ∼ 2c^{3/2}|t|^{−1/2} → ∞ as t → 0. Hence E[X²] = ∞, and a normal approximation of the microfield with a mean-square field strength is wrong.
Density dependence. At density 8ρ the field has the law of 8^{2/3} X = 4X, because 4³ = 8². Its characteristic function is φ(t)^8 = exp(−8c^{3/2}|t|^{3/2}) = φ(4t), since 4^{3/2} = 8.

applications.conclusion: The x-component of the Holtsmark microfield has the characteristic function exp(−c^{3/2}|t|^{3/2}) for some c > 0. It is the symmetric stable law with index 3/2, its variance is infinite, and its scale grows as ρ^{2/3}.

limitations: The theorem gives the characteristic functions but no closed form of the densities. Closed forms are known for α = 2 (normal), for α = 1 with β = 0 (Cauchy) and for α = 1/2 with |β| = 1 (one-sided Lévy law).
The parametrization is discontinuous at α = 1 when β ≠ 0. The centering b = µ + βc^α tan(πα/2) of the Lévy–Khintchine form diverges as α → 1.
The theorem is about laws on ℝ. Stable laws on ℝ^d need a spectral measure on the unit sphere in place of the two numbers c and β.

results.name: Generalized central limit theorem for regularly varying tails
aliases: stable limit theorem for heavy-tailed sums
results.statement: Let X_1, X_2, … be i.i.d. real random variables. Suppose that P(|X_1| > x) = x^(−α) L(x) for some α ∈ (0, 2) and a slowly varying function L, and that P(X_1 > x)/P(|X_1| > x) → θ ∈ [0, 1] as x → ∞. Let S_n = X_1 + ⋯ + X_n, a_n = inf{x : P(|X_1| > x) ≤ 1/n} and b_n = n E[X_1 1(|X_1| ≤ a_n)]. Then (S_n − b_n)/a_n converges in distribution to a nondegenerate random variable Y with E e^(itY) = exp ∫ (e^(itx) − 1 − itx 1(|x| ≤ 1)) ν(dx), where ν(dx) = θα x^(−α−1) dx on x > 0 and ν(dx) = (1 − θ)α |x|^(−α−1) dx on x < 0.
hypotheses: The variables X_1, X_2, … are independent and identically distributed.
The tail T(x) = P(|X_1| > x) is regularly varying with index −α for some 0 < α < 2: T(x) = x^(−α) L(x) with L(λx)/L(x) → 1 for every λ > 0.
The tails are balanced: P(X_1 > x)/P(|X_1| > x) → θ ∈ [0, 1] as x → ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Step s6 uses Lévy's continuity theorem to pass from pointwise convergence of the characteristic functions to convergence in distribution.
Step s5 bounds the truncated mean E[|X_1|/a_n; |X_1| ≤ εa_n] by the square root of the truncated second moment with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
Step s6 uses dominated convergence to show that the exponent ψ(t) = ∫ h_t dν is continuous at t = 0.

definitions.name: slowly varying function
definitions.text: A measurable function L, positive for large x, with L(λx)/L(x) → 1 as x → ∞ for every λ > 0.

definitions.name: Lévy measure of the limit
definitions.text: ν(dx) = θα x^(−α−1) dx on x > 0 and (1 − θ)α |x|^(−α−1) dx on x < 0. It satisfies ∫ min(1, x²) ν(dx) < ∞ because 0 < α < 2.

source.excerpt: Y has a nondegenerate distribution. Remark. This is not much of a generalization of the example, but the conditions are necessary for the existence of constants an and bn so that (Sn − bn)/an ⇒ Y, where Y is nondegenerate. Proofs of necessity can be found in Chapter 9 of Breiman (1968) or in Gnedenko and Kolmogorov (1954).

source.alignment: The authored statement has the hypotheses, a_n and b_n of Theorem 3.8.2 (p. 186), and the excerpt quotes its conclusion and the remark after it. The source writes α < 2 and assumes 0 < α < 2 throughout the section. The limit exponent is the ε → 0 limit of the source's formula (3.8.9). The authored proof uses the scale limit (3.8.6), the tail limits (3.8.7) and the halving bound of Lemma 3.8.3 from the source, and replaces the Poisson point process step by a direct characteristic function computation.

proof.scope: Sufficiency of the regular variation and tail balance conditions for 0 < α < 2. The necessity of the conditions and the closed form of the characteristic function are not proved.

steps.text: Scale. Put T(x) = P(|X_1| > x). T is positive, nonincreasing and right-continuous, so T(a_n) ≤ 1/n < T(x) for x < a_n, and a_n → ∞. For λ > 1, T(a_n/λ) > 1/n gives nT(a_n) ≥ T(a_n)/T(a_n/λ) → λ^(−α). Let λ ↓ 1: nT(a_n) → 1. Hence nT(xa_n) → x^(−α) for x > 0, and with the balance condition nP(X_1 > xa_n) → θx^(−α) and nP(X_1 < −xa_n) → (1 − θ)x^(−α).

Halving bound. Fix δ = (2 − α)/2. Choose t_0 with T(s/2) ≤ 2^(α+δ) T(s) for s ≥ t_0. Let t ≥ t_0 and 2^(−k−1) < y ≤ 2^(−k). If t2^(−i) ≥ t_0 for i = 0, …, k, then k + 1 halvings give T(yt) ≤ 2^((α+δ)(k+1)) T(t) ≤ 2^(α+δ) y^(−α−δ) T(t). Otherwise let j ≤ k be the first index with t2^(−j) < t_0. Then T(t) ≥ 2^(−(α+δ)j) T(t_0), so T(yt) ≤ 1 ≤ y^(−α−δ) T(t)/T(t_0). So T(yt) ≤ C y^(−α−δ) T(t) for t ≥ t_0 and 0 < y ≤ 1.
Small values. For 0 < ε ≤ 1 and a_n ≥ t_0, n E[(X_1/a_n)²; |X_1| ≤ εa_n] ≤ ∫_0^ε 2y nT(ya_n) dy ≤ nT(a_n) C ∫_0^ε 2y^(1−α−δ) dy ≤ K ε^(2−α−δ) with K = 2C/(2 − α − δ), by s2 and nT(a_n) ≤ 1.

Exponent. Let ν_n(A) = nP(X_1/a_n ∈ A), χ_n(t) = E e^(itX_1/a_n), β_n = E[(X_1/a_n) 1(|X_1| ≤ a_n)] and h_t(x) = e^(itx) − 1 − itx 1(|x| ≤ 1). Then c_n(t) = n(χ_n(t) − 1) − itnβ_n = ∫ h_t dν_n. By s1 the tail functions of ν_n on (ε, ∞) and on (−∞, −ε) converge at every point to those of ν, which has no atoms. So these finite measures converge weakly. h_t is bounded there and continuous except on the ν-null set {±1}, so ∫_{|x|>ε} h_t dν_n → ∫_{|x|>ε} h_t dν. On |x| ≤ ε, |h_t(x)| ≤ t²x²/2, so s3 bounds the rest by t²Kε^(2−α−δ)/2, and ∫_{|x|≤ε} x² ν(dx) = αε^(2−α)/(2 − α). Let n → ∞ and then ε → 0: c_n(t) → ψ(t) = ∫ h_t dν.

Centering and product. Split β_n at ε. Cauchy–Schwarz on |X_1| ≤ εa_n and |X_1|/a_n ≤ 1 on the rest give |β_n| ≤ (E[(X_1/a_n)²; |X_1| ≤ εa_n])^(1/2) + T(εa_n). So nβ_n² ≤ 2Kε^(2−α−δ) + 2 nT(εa_n) T(εa_n), and limsup nβ_n² ≤ 2Kε^(2−α−δ) for every ε. Hence nβ_n² → 0 and n|χ_n(t) − 1|² ≤ 2|c_n(t)|²/n + 2t²nβ_n² → 0. For |z| ≤ 1 and |z − 1| ≤ 1, |z^n − e^(n(z−1))| ≤ n|z − e^(z−1)| ≤ n|z − 1|². With Z_n = (S_n − b_n)/a_n we have E e^(itZ_n) = e^(−itnβ_n) χ_n(t)^n = e^(c_n(t)) + o(1) → e^(ψ(t)).

Limit. For |t| ≤ 1, |h_t(x)| ≤ x²/2 on |x| ≤ 1 and ≤ 2 on |x| > 1, which is ν-integrable. So ψ is continuous at 0 by dominated convergence, and Lévy's continuity theorem gives Z_n ⇒ Y with E e^(itY) = e^(ψ(t)). Finally Re ψ(t) = ∫ (cos tx − 1) ν(dx) < 0 for t ≠ 0, because ν has a positive density on at least one half-line. So |E e^(itY)| < 1 for t ≠ 0, and Y is not degenerate.

applications.title: Superdiffusive spreading of a Lévy flight
applications.inputs: A tracer in a flow with long jumps makes i.i.d. flights X_1, X_2, … along a line. The flight lengths have the symmetric Pareto tail P(X_1 > x) = P(X_1 < −x) = x^(−3/2)/2 for x ≥ 1. The position after n flights is S_n.
applications.hypotheses: T(x) = x^(−3/2) for x ≥ 1, so α = 3/2 with L ≡ 1, and θ = 1/2. The law is symmetric, so b_n = 0.

steps.text: a_n solves T(a_n) = 1/n, so a_n = n^(2/3). For n = 10⁶ this is a_n = 10⁴, because (10⁴)³ = (10⁶)².
The Lévy measure has density (3/4)|x|^(−5/2) on each half-line. Its mass outside [−1, 1] is 2 · (3/4)/(3/2) = 1, which matches nP(|X_1| > a_n) = 1.
By symmetry the compensator terms cancel, and the theorem gives S_n/n^(2/3) ⇒ Y with E e^(itY) = exp(−c|t|^(3/2)) for a constant c > 0.
So the spread of the tracer grows like n^(2/3), faster than the diffusive n^(1/2). This is superdiffusion with a symmetric 3/2-stable profile, the index of the Holtsmark law.

applications.conclusion: A Lévy flight with symmetric Pareto flights of index 3/2 spreads on the scale n^(2/3), and the rescaled position converges to a symmetric 3/2-stable law.

limitations: Only sufficiency is proved. The source states that regular variation and tail balance are also necessary for a nondegenerate limit, and refers to Breiman and to Gnedenko and Kolmogorov for the proof.
The case α = 2 with infinite variance belongs to the normal domain of attraction and needs a different truncation.
The closed form exp(itc − b|t|^α(1 + iκ sgn(t) w_α(t))) of the limit is not derived here.

results.name: Domain of attraction of the normal law
aliases: Lévy–Feller–Khinchin criterion for the normal domain of attraction
results.statement: Let X_1, X_2, … be i.i.d. real random variables whose common law is not concentrated at one point. Put S_n = X_1 + ⋯ + X_n, T(y) = P(|X_1| > y) and U(y) = E[X_1² 1(|X_1| ≤ y)]. There are constants a_n > 0 and b_n ∈ ℝ such that (S_n − b_n)/a_n converges in distribution to the standard normal law N(0, 1) if and only if y² T(y)/U(y) → 0 as y → ∞.
hypotheses: The variables X_1, X_2, … are independent and identically distributed.
X_1 is nondegenerate, that is, X_1 is not almost surely constant.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the classical central limit theorem for the case of a finite second moment.
Step s3 applies the Lindeberg–Feller theorem to the truncated and centered triangular array Y_{n,m}.
Step s3 uses Slutsky's theorem to remove the truncation error, which vanishes with probability tending to 1.
Step s3 bounds the truncated mean E[|X_1|; s < |X_1| ≤ a_n] by (U(a_n)T(s))^(1/2) with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
Step s4 uses that a sequence which converges in distribution on ℝ is tight, the easy half of Prokhorov's theorem.
Steps s2 and s6 use dominated (bounded) convergence for U(y)/y² → 0 and for the integral of 4f_n(t) − f_n(2t) over [0, 1].
Step s6 exchanges the t-integral and the expectation (Tonelli) to write the integral as n E[G(X^s/a_n)].

definitions.name: truncated second moment
definitions.text: U(y) = E[X_1² 1(|X_1| ≤ y)]. It is nondecreasing and right-continuous, and it tends to E X_1² ∈ (0, ∞] as y → ∞.

definitions.name: domain of attraction of the normal law
definitions.text: The set of laws of X_1 for which some a_n > 0 and b_n make (S_n − b_n)/a_n converge in distribution to N(0, 1).

definitions.name: symmetrization
definitions.text: X^s = X_1 − X′_1, where X′_1 is an independent copy of X_1. Its characteristic function is |φ|², where φ is that of X_1.

source.alignment: Theorem 3.4.14 (p. 152) states the criterion, due to Lévy, for constants with (Sn − an)/bn ⇒ χ, and the source gives no proof. The authored statement writes a_n for the scale and b_n for the centering, and adds the hypothesis that X_1 is nondegenerate, without which the criterion fails for a constant X_1 ≠ 0. The authored proof is not taken from the source: sufficiency uses truncation and the Lindeberg–Feller theorem (Theorem 3.4.10 of the source), and necessity uses symmetrization and characteristic functions.

results.proof_status: authored proof of the criterion that Durrett states without proof as Theorem 3.4.14, with sufficiency by truncation and the Lindeberg–Feller theorem and necessity by symmetrization. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Both directions of the criterion for nondegenerate X_1.

steps.text: Finite variance. If E X_1² < ∞, then σ² = Var X_1 > 0 and the classical central limit theorem gives (S_n − nE X_1)/(σ√n) ⇒ N(0, 1). In this case the condition also holds, because y²T(y) ≤ E[X_1²; |X_1| > y] → 0 while U(y) → E X_1² > 0. So both directions only need proof when E X_1² = ∞.

Sufficiency, choice of a_n. Assume y²T(y)/U(y) → 0 and E X_1² = ∞. For λ > 1, 0 ≤ U(λy) − U(y) ≤ λ²y²T(y), so U(λy)/U(y) → 1: U is slowly varying, and U(y) → ∞. By dominated convergence U(y)/y² → 0. Fix y_0 with U(y_0) > 0. The function g(y) = y²/U(y) on [y_0, ∞) is right-continuous, tends to ∞ and has only downward jumps, because U is nondecreasing and right-continuous. For large n put a_n = inf{y ≥ y_0 : g(y) ≥ n}. Right continuity gives g(a_n) ≥ n, and the left limit gives a_n²/U(a_n−) ≤ n. Since U(a_n−) ≤ U(a_n), we get nU(a_n) = a_n². Also a_n → ∞.

Sufficiency, truncation. Let μ_n = E[X_1; |X_1| ≤ a_n], b_n = nμ_n and Y_{n,m} = (X_m 1(|X_m| ≤ a_n) − μ_n)/a_n for m ≤ n. (i) P(S_n ≠ Σ_m X_m 1(|X_m| ≤ a_n)) ≤ nT(a_n) = a_n²T(a_n)/U(a_n) → 0. (ii) For fixed s, Cauchy–Schwarz gives |μ_n| ≤ s + (U(a_n)T(s))^(1/2), so nμ_n²/a_n² = μ_n²/U(a_n) ≤ 2s²/U(a_n) + 2T(s), and letting n → ∞ and then s → ∞ gives nμ_n²/a_n² → 0. (iii) Each row is independent and centered, with Σ_m E Y_{n,m}² = 1 − nμ_n²/a_n² → 1. (iv) Fix 0 < ε < 1. Once |μ_n| < εa_n, the event |Y_{n,m}| > 2ε forces εa_n < |X_m| ≤ a_n, and Y_{n,m}² ≤ 2X_m²1(|X_m| ≤ a_n)/a_n² + 2μ_n²/a_n². So the Lindeberg sum is at most 2(U(a_n) − U(εa_n))/U(a_n) + 2nμ_n²/a_n², which tends to 0 by slow variation. The Lindeberg–Feller theorem gives Σ_m Y_{n,m} ⇒ N(0, 1), and with (i) and Slutsky's theorem (S_n − b_n)/a_n ⇒ N(0, 1).

Necessity, symmetrization. Assume (S_n − b_n)/a_n ⇒ N(0, 1) with a_n > 0. Let X′_1, X′_2, … be an independent copy of the sequence, X^s = X_1 − X′_1, ψ(u) = E cos(uX^s) = |E e^(iuX_1)|² ∈ [0, 1], and T^s, U^s the functions T, U of X^s. Then W_n = (S_n − S′_n)/a_n has characteristic function ψ(t/a_n)^n = |E e^(it(S_n − b_n)/a_n)|² → e^(−t²). The sequence W_n is tight, so for ε > 0 there is K with P(|W_n| > K) ≤ ε for all n, and |E e^(itW_n) − E e^(isW_n)| ≤ K|t − s| + 2ε. These characteristic functions are therefore equicontinuous, and together with the pointwise limit this gives ψ(t/a_n)^n → e^(−t²) uniformly on compact sets.

Necessity, a_n → ∞. Suppose a_{n_k} → a ∈ [0, ∞) along a subsequence. By s4, ψ(t)^{n_k} = ψ(ta_{n_k}/a_{n_k})^{n_k} → e^(−a²t²) > 0 for every t, which forces ψ(t) = 1 for every t. Then cos(tX^s) = 1 almost surely for t = 1 and t = √2, so X^s ∈ 2πℤ ∩ √2πℤ = {0} almost surely. Thus X_1 = X′_1 almost surely, and independence gives P(X_1 ≤ x) = P(X_1 ≤ x)² for every x, so X_1 is constant. This contradicts the hypothesis, so a_n → ∞.

Necessity, no large values. Let f_n(t) = n(1 − ψ(t/a_n)). Since ψ(t/a_n)^n → e^(−t²) > 0, n log ψ(t/a_n) → −t², so ψ(t/a_n) → 1 and f_n(t) → t². By s4, ψ(t/a_n)^n ≥ e^(−5) on [0, 2] for large n, and 1 − x ≤ −log x gives f_n ≤ 5 there. The identity 2(1 − cos x)² = 4(1 − cos x) − (1 − cos 2x) gives n E[2(1 − cos(tX^s/a_n))²] = 4f_n(t) − f_n(2t), which tends to 0 and is at most 20 for t ∈ [0, 1]. Integrate over t ∈ [0, 1] with bounded convergence and Tonelli: n E[G(X^s/a_n)] → 0, where G(x) = ∫_0^1 2(1 − cos tx)² dt. G is continuous, positive for x ≠ 0 and tends to 3 as |x| → ∞, so c_ε = inf_{|x|≥ε} G(x) > 0. Hence nT^s(εa_n) ≤ n E[G(X^s/a_n)]/c_ε → 0 for every ε > 0.

Necessity, second moment. Let V_n(ε) = nU^s(εa_n)/a_n². Write 1 − cos y = y²/2 − r(y) with 0 ≤ r(y) ≤ y⁴/24. Then n E[1 − cos(X^s/a_n); |X^s| ≤ εa_n] lies between (1/2 − ε²/24)V_n(ε) and V_n(ε)/2. It equals f_n(1) minus a term in [0, 2nT^s(εa_n)], so it tends to 1 by s6. Hence 2 ≤ liminf V_n(ε) and limsup V_n(ε) ≤ 24/(12 − ε²). For 0 < η < ε, V_n(η) ≤ V_n(ε) ≤ V_n(η) + ε² nT^s(ηa_n). Let η → 0: V_n(ε) → 2 for every ε > 0.

Necessity, all large y. First, a_{n+1}/a_n is bounded. If r_n = a_{n+1}/a_n → ∞ along a subsequence, then U^s(z) ≤ U^s(a_n) + z²T^s(a_n) for z ≥ a_n gives V_{n+1}(1) ≤ ((n+1)/n)(V_n(1)/r_n² + nT^s(a_n)) → 0, which contradicts s7. So a_{n+1} ≤ K a_n for n ≥ n_1. For large y let n = max{k ≥ n_1 : a_k ≤ y}. This exists by s5, and n → ∞ as y → ∞. Then a_n ≤ y < a_{n+1} ≤ Ka_n, so y²T^s(y)/U^s(y) ≤ K² a_n²T^s(a_n)/U^s(a_n) = K² nT^s(a_n)/V_n(1) → 0.

Necessity, back to X_1. Let m be a median of X_1 and Y = X_1 − m. Since P(X_1 − X′_1 > y) ≥ P(X_1 − m > y) P(X′_1 ≤ m) and similarly on the left, P(|Y| > y) ≤ 2T^s(y). Since min((u − v)², y²) ≤ 2 min(u², y²) + 2 min(v², y²), U^s(y) ≤ 4E[min(Y², y²)] = 4(U_Y(y) + y²P(|Y| > y)). So U_Y(y) ≥ U^s(y)/4 − 2y²T^s(y) ≥ U^s(y)/8 for large y, by s8, and y²P(|Y| > y)/U_Y(y) ≤ 16y²T^s(y)/U^s(y) → 0. By s1 we may assume E Y² = ∞, so U_Y(y) → ∞. For y ≥ 2|m|, T(y) ≤ P(|Y| > y/2) and U(y) ≥ U_Y(y/2)/2 − m² ≥ U_Y(y/2)/4 for large y, because (Y + m)² ≥ Y²/2 − m². Hence y²T(y)/U(y) ≤ 16 (y/2)²P(|Y| > y/2)/U_Y(y/2) → 0.

applications.title: The marginal Weierstrass random walk
applications.inputs: The Weierstrass random walk of Hughes, Shlesinger and Montroll with b = 2 and N = 4 has the jumps X = ±2^J with a fair sign and P(J = j) = (3/4) 4^(−j) for j = 0, 1, 2, …. Its index log N/log b equals 2, the marginal value between Gaussian and Lévy behaviour.
applications.hypotheses: The jumps are i.i.d. and not constant. E X² = Σ_j 4^j (3/4) 4^(−j) = ∞, so the classical central limit theorem does not apply.

steps.text: The truncated second moment at y = 2^k is U(2^k) = Σ_{j≤k} 4^j (3/4) 4^(−j) = (3/4)(k + 1). For k = 3 this is 3.
The tail is T(2^k) = P(J > k) = 4^(−k−1), so y²T(y) = 1/4 at every y = 2^k. For k = 3, 8² · 4^(−4) = 1/4.
For 2^k ≤ y < 2^(k+1), T(y) = T(2^k), U(y) = U(2^k) and y² < 4 · 4^k. So y²T(y)/U(y) < 4/(3(k + 1)), which tends to 0. The criterion holds.
The proof gives the scale a_n with a_n² = nU(a_n), so a_n² ~ (3/4) n log₂ a_n ~ (3/8) n log₂ n. By symmetry b_n = 0. Hence S_n/√((3/8) n log₂ n) ⇒ N(0, 1).

applications.conclusion: The marginal Weierstrass walk is in the domain of attraction of the normal law: it spreads diffusively up to a logarithmic factor, with S_n/√((3/8) n log₂ n) ⇒ N(0, 1), although its jumps have infinite variance.

limitations: The criterion does not give a rate of convergence. With infinite variance the convergence can be very slow because of the logarithmic scale.
The constants a_n and b_n are not explicit in general. The proof gives them as solutions of nU(a_n) = a_n² and b_n = nE[X_1; |X_1| ≤ a_n].
For stable limits with index α < 2 the corresponding criterion uses regular variation of the tail and a tail balance condition.

results.name: Stable laws are the only limits of normalized sums of i.i.d. variables
aliases: characterization of stable laws as limit laws
results.statement: Let Y be a nondegenerate real random variable. Then the following are equivalent. (a) There are i.i.d. real random variables X_1, X_2, … and constants a_n > 0 and b_n ∈ ℝ such that (X_1 + ⋯ + X_n − b_n)/a_n converges in distribution to Y. (b) Y has a stable law: for every integer k ≥ 1 there are constants α_k > 0 and β_k ∈ ℝ such that (Y_1 + ⋯ + Y_k − β_k)/α_k has the law of Y whenever Y_1, …, Y_k are i.i.d. copies of Y.
hypotheses: Y is a nondegenerate real random variable, that is, Y is not almost surely constant.
In (a) the variables X_i are i.i.d., the scale constants a_n are positive and the centering constants b_n are real.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 uses Lévy's continuity theorem to show that a sum of k independent block sums converges in distribution to Y_1 + ⋯ + Y_k.
Step s3 uses Slutsky's theorem to identify the limit of α_n W_n + β_n as αW + β once α_n → α and β_n → β.

definitions.name: stable law
definitions.text: The law of Y is stable if for every k ≥ 1 there are α_k > 0 and β_k ∈ ℝ with Y_1 + ⋯ + Y_k equal in law to α_k Y + β_k, where Y_1, …, Y_k are i.i.d. copies of Y.

definitions.name: quantile function
definitions.text: For a random variable V with distribution function F, q_V(y) = inf{x : F(x) ≥ y} for 0 < y < 1. It is nondecreasing, and q_{αV+β} = α q_V + β for α > 0.

source.alignment: Theorem 3.8.8 states that Y is the limit of (X1 + · · · + Xk − bk)/ak for some i.i.d. sequence if and only if Y has a stable law, and the excerpt quotes its block decomposition. The authored statement adds the assumptions a_n > 0 and Y nondegenerate, which the proof in the source uses through the convergence of types theorem (Theorem 3.8.9). The authored proof follows the block argument of the source and proves convergence of types with quantile functions instead of characteristic functions.

proof.scope: The full equivalence for nondegenerate Y. The explicit form of the stable characteristic functions is not derived.

steps.text: From (b) to (a). Let X_1, X_2, … be i.i.d. copies of Y and put a_n = α_n and b_n = β_n. By (b), (X_1 + ⋯ + X_n − b_n)/a_n has the law of Y for every n, so it converges in distribution to Y.

Quantiles converge. Let V_n ⇒ V with distribution functions F_n and F, and let y ∈ (0, 1) be a continuity point of q = q_V. Fix ε > 0. Pick y′ < y < y″ in (0, 1) with q(y′) > q(y) − ε and q(y″) < q(y) + ε. Pick continuity points c and d of F with q(y) − 2ε < c < q(y′) and q(y″) < d < q(y) + 2ε. Since c < q(y′), F(c) < y′ < y, so F_n(c) < y for large n, and then q_{V_n}(y) ≥ c. Since d > q(y″), right continuity gives F(d) ≥ y″ > y, so F_n(d) ≥ y for large n, and then q_{V_n}(y) ≤ d. Hence q_{V_n}(y) → q(y).

Convergence of types. Let W_n ⇒ W and α_n W_n + β_n ⇒ W′ with α_n > 0, where W and W′ are nondegenerate. A nondegenerate law has q(y_1) < q(y_2) for some y_1 < y_2, so there is η ∈ (0, 1/2) with q_W(η) < q_W(1 − η) and q_{W′}(η) < q_{W′}(1 − η). Monotone functions have at most countably many discontinuities, so we can pick y_1 ∈ (0, η] and y_2 ∈ [1 − η, 1) where q_W and q_{W′} are both continuous. By s2 and q_{αV+β} = α q_V + β, q_{W_n}(y_i) → q_W(y_i) and α_n q_{W_n}(y_i) + β_n → q_{W′}(y_i). Subtracting the values at y_1 and y_2 gives α_n → α = (q_{W′}(y_2) − q_{W′}(y_1))/(q_W(y_2) − q_W(y_1)) > 0, and then β_n → β = q_{W′}(y_1) − α q_W(y_1). Slutsky's theorem gives α_n W_n + β_n ⇒ αW + β, so W′ has the law of αW + β.

Blocks. Assume (a) and fix k. Put Z_n = (S_n − b_n)/a_n with S_n = X_1 + ⋯ + X_n, and split S_{nk} into the k block sums S_n^(j) = X_{(j−1)n+1} + ⋯ + X_{jn}. The blocks are independent and each has the law of S_n. So W′_n = Σ_j (S_n^(j) − b_n)/a_n has characteristic function E[e^(itZ_n)]^k, which tends to the characteristic function of Y_1 + ⋯ + Y_k for i.i.d. copies Y_j of Y. By Lévy's continuity theorem W′_n ⇒ Y_1 + ⋯ + Y_k. Algebra gives W′_n = (a_{nk}/a_n) Z_{nk} + (b_{nk} − k b_n)/a_n, and Z_{nk} ⇒ Y as a subsequence of Z_n.

The sum Y_1 + ⋯ + Y_k is nondegenerate. If Y_1 + V = c almost surely with V = Y_2 + ⋯ + Y_k independent of Y_1, then Y_1 = c − V is independent of itself and so is constant, which contradicts the hypothesis on Y. Now apply s3 with W_n = Z_{nk}, W = Y, α_n = a_{nk}/a_n and β_n = (b_{nk} − k b_n)/a_n. It gives constants α_k > 0 and β_k such that Y_1 + ⋯ + Y_k has the law of α_k Y + β_k. This holds for every k, so Y is stable.

applications.title: The Boltzmann law of a two-dimensional kinetic energy is not a limit of normalized sums
applications.inputs: In a classical ideal gas in two dimensions at temperature T, the kinetic energy of one particle is E = (p_x² + p_y²)/2m. Its law is exponential: Y = E/k_BT has density e^(−y) on y > 0. The question is whether Y can be the limit of (X_1 + ⋯ + X_n − b_n)/a_n for some i.i.d. microscopic contributions X_i.
applications.hypotheses: Y is nondegenerate, so the theorem applies. Y has finite moments of every order, so its cumulants κ_2(Y) = 1 and κ_3(Y) = 2 exist.

steps.text: If Y were a limit, the theorem with k = 2 would give α_2 > 0 and β_2 with Y_1 + Y_2 equal in law to α_2 Y + β_2. Cumulants add over independent sums and κ_r(αY + β) = α^r κ_r(Y) for r ≥ 2.
The variances give 2 κ_2(Y) = α_2² κ_2(Y), so α_2² = 2.
The third cumulants give κ_3(Y_1 + Y_2) = 2 + 2 = 4 and κ_3(α_2 Y + β_2) = 2 α_2³. Square both sides: the left side gives 16.
The right side gives 4 α_2⁶ = 4 · 2³ = 32, which differs from 16. This is a contradiction, so the exponential law is not stable.

applications.conclusion: The exponential Boltzmann law of a two-dimensional kinetic energy is not the limit in distribution of (X_1 + ⋯ + X_n − b_n)/a_n for any i.i.d. sequence and any constants a_n > 0 and b_n. In contrast, the total energy of n particles, suitably normalized, tends to the normal law, which is stable.

limitations: The theorem does not give the explicit form of the stable characteristic functions exp(itc − b|t|^α(1 + iκ sgn(t) w_α(t))). That form needs a separate analysis.
Degenerate limits are excluded. Every constant is a trivial limit of (S_n − b_n)/a_n, for example with a_n → ∞ fast.
The theorem concerns one i.i.d. sequence. Limits of row sums of general triangular arrays form the larger class of infinitely divisible laws.

results.name: Khinchin's theorem on limits of infinitesimal triangular arrays
aliases: infinitesimal triangular array limits are infinitely divisible
Khinchin's limit theorem for null arrays
results.statement: For each n ≥ 1 let X_{n,1}, …, X_{n,k_n} be independent real random variables, and assume that the array is infinitesimal: for every ε > 0, max_{1≤k≤k_n} P(|X_{n,k}| > ε) → 0 as n → ∞. Let S_n = X_{n,1} + ⋯ + X_{n,k_n}. If there are constants a_n ∈ ℝ such that S_n − a_n converges in distribution to a random variable Z, then Z has an infinitely divisible distribution: for every m ≥ 1 there are i.i.d. random variables V_1, …, V_m with V_1 + ⋯ + V_m equal in law to Z.
hypotheses: The variables in each row are independent. Variables in different rows may be dependent, and they need not have the same law.
The array is infinitesimal: max_{1≤k≤k_n} P(|X_{n,k}| > ε) → 0 as n → ∞ for every ε > 0.
S_n − a_n converges in distribution to Z for some real constants a_n.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Prokhorov's theorem to extract a convergent subsequence from the tight family of m-th convolution roots.
Step s2 uses Lévy's continuity theorem to turn pointwise convergence of the accompanying characteristic functions into convergence in distribution.
Step s4 uses the Taylor bound |e^{iy} − 1 − iy| ≤ y²/2 for the truncated part of each summand.
Step s5 uses Tonelli's theorem to exchange the expectation and the integral over t of 1 − cos(tV).

definitions.name: infinitesimal array
definitions.text: A triangular array with max_{1≤k≤k_n} P(|X_{n,k}| > ε) → 0 for every ε > 0. Each single summand becomes negligible, uniformly in its row. Other names are null array and uniformly asymptotically negligible array.

definitions.name: infinitely divisible distribution
definitions.text: The law of Z is infinitely divisible if for every m ≥ 1 it is the law of a sum of m i.i.d. random variables.

definitions.name: symmetrization
definitions.text: For a random variable X, X^s = X − X′ with X′ an independent copy of X. Its characteristic function is |φ_X(t)|², which is real and in [0, 1].

source.excerpt: Let us emphasize that the limit in Theorem 1 is always an infinitely divisible distribution, although we did not assume that the terms in the sums we have considered are identically distributed.

source.alignment: Theorem 1 of the source assumes a triangular array with independent rows that satisfies the uniform smallness condition, lim_k max_j P(|ξ_{k,j}| > ε) = 0, and normalized sums S_k − b̄_k that converge in distribution. It describes the limit by the formula (1.7) with a canonical measure, and the quoted remark states that this limit is always infinitely divisible. The authored statement keeps only this conclusion. The authored proof does not compute the canonical measure. It compares the sums with accompanying compound Poisson laws, as the associated distributions of the source do, and closes the class of infinitely divisible laws under limits.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the method of accompanying infinitely divisible laws behind Theorem 1 of Major's lecture notes, with symmetrization estimates instead of the canonical measure. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for real random variables. The proof shows that the limit is infinitely divisible but does not identify its Lévy–Khintchine triple.

steps.text: Limits of infinitely divisible laws are infinitely divisible. Let μ_j be infinitely divisible with μ_j ⇒ μ, and fix m. Write μ_j = ν_j^{*m} and take Y_1, …, Y_m i.i.d. with law ν_j. If every Y_i exceeds y, then the sum exceeds my, so ν_j((y, ∞))^m ≤ μ_j((my, ∞)), and similarly ν_j((−∞, −y))^m ≤ μ_j((−∞, −my)). The convergent sequence (μ_j) is tight, so (ν_j) is tight. By Prokhorov's theorem a subsequence ν_{j_i} converges to some ν. Then the characteristic functions satisfy ν̂_{j_i}(t)^m = μ̂_{j_i}(t), and the limit gives ν̂(t)^m = μ̂(t), so μ = ν^{*m}.

Accompanying laws. Let φ_{n,k} be the characteristic function of X_{n,k}, put b_{n,k} = E[X_{n,k} 1(|X_{n,k}| < 1)], Y_{n,k} = X_{n,k} − b_{n,k}, with characteristic function χ_{n,k}, and B_n = ∑_k b_{n,k}. Then E[e^{it(S_n − a_n)}] = e^{it(B_n − a_n)} ∏_k χ_{n,k}(t). Put G_n(t) = e^{it(B_n − a_n)} ∏_k exp(χ_{n,k}(t) − 1). Each factor exp(χ_{n,k}(t) − 1) is the characteristic function of a compound Poisson sum with Poisson(1) many i.i.d. copies of Y_{n,k}. Its m-th root exp((χ_{n,k}(t) − 1)/m) is again compound Poisson, so G_n is the characteristic function of an infinitely divisible law. If G_n(t) − E[e^{it(S_n − a_n)}] → 0 for every t, then G_n(t) → E[e^{itZ}], a continuous function. Lévy's continuity theorem then gives convergence in distribution of these infinitely divisible laws to the law of Z, and s1 shows that Z is infinitely divisible. Steps s3-s6 prove this convergence.

The centered summands are uniformly small. For 0 < ε < 1, |b_{n,k}| ≤ E[|X_{n,k}| 1(|X_{n,k}| < 1)] ≤ ε + P(|X_{n,k}| > ε), so max_k |b_{n,k}| → 0 by infinitesimality. Once max_k |b_{n,k}| ≤ ε, the event |Y_{n,k}| > 2ε implies |X_{n,k}| > ε. Hence |χ_{n,k}(t) − 1| ≤ E[min(2, |tY_{n,k}|)] ≤ 2|t|ε + 2P(|X_{n,k}| > ε), and max_k |χ_{n,k}(t) − 1| → 0 for every t.

One summand is controlled by its symmetrization. Fix X = X_{n,k}, write U = X 1(|X| < 1), so b = E[U] and |b| < 1, and let X′, U′ be independent copies and X^s = X − X′. Since E[Y 1(|X| < 1)] = b P(|X| ≥ 1), the Taylor bound |e^{iy} − 1 − iy| ≤ y²/2 gives |χ(t) − 1| ≤ (t²/2) E[Y² 1(|X| < 1)] + (|t| + 2) P(|X| ≥ 1). Next, E[Y² 1(|X| < 1)] ≤ Var U = E[(U − U′)²]/2. On {|X| < 1, |X′| < 1} we have U − U′ = X^s and |X^s| < 2, and elsewhere (U − U′)² < 4, so Var U ≤ E[min((X^s)², 4)]/2 + 4P(|X| ≥ 1). If P(|X| ≥ 1/2) ≤ 1/2, which holds for large n by infinitesimality, then P(|X^s| > 1/2) ≥ P(|X| ≥ 1) P(|X′| < 1/2) ≥ P(|X| ≥ 1)/2, and P(|X^s| > 1/2) ≤ 4E[min((X^s)², 4)]. With min(x², 4) ≤ 4 min(x², 1) these bounds give |χ(t) − 1| ≤ C(t) E[min(1, (X^s)²)] with C(t) = 65t² + 32|t| + 64.

The symmetrized row sums are bounded. Let ψ_{n,k}(t) = |φ_{n,k}(t)|² = E[cos(tX^s_{n,k})] and S^s_n = ∑_k X^s_{n,k}, whose characteristic function is ψ_n = ∏_k ψ_{n,k}. Convergence in distribution makes (S_n − a_n) tight, so there is M ≥ 1 with P(|S_n − a_n| > M) ≤ 1/16 for all n, hence P(|S^s_n| > 2M) ≤ 1/8. Then 1 − ψ_n(t) ≤ t²(2M)²/2 + 2/8, so ψ_n(t) ≥ 5/8 for |t| ≤ δ = 1/(4M). Since 1 − x ≤ −log x on (0, 1], ∑_k (1 − ψ_{n,k}(t)) ≤ −log ψ_n(t) ≤ log(8/5) there. For real v, ∫_0^δ (1 − cos(tv)) dt = δ(1 − sin(δv)/(δv)), and 1 − sin(w)/w ≥ min(1, w²)/7 (by the Taylor series for |w| ≤ 1 and by |sin(w)/w| ≤ sin 1 for |w| ≥ 1). With δ ≤ 1 and Tonelli this gives ∑_k E[min(1, (X^s_{n,k})²)] ≤ (7/δ³) ∫_0^δ ∑_k (1 − ψ_{n,k}(t)) dt ≤ (7/δ²) log(8/5) for every n.

Comparison of the products. By s4 and s5, ∑_k |χ_{n,k}(t) − 1| ≤ K(t) = C(t)(7/δ²) log(8/5) for all large n. For complex numbers with |z_k|, |w_k| ≤ 1, |∏ z_k − ∏ w_k| ≤ ∑ |z_k − w_k|. Here z_k = χ_{n,k}(t) and w_k = exp(χ_{n,k}(t) − 1), and |w_k| = e^{Re χ_{n,k}(t) − 1} ≤ 1. By s3, |χ_{n,k}(t) − 1| ≤ 1 for large n, and |e^u − 1 − u| ≤ (e − 2)|u|² ≤ |u|² for |u| ≤ 1. Hence |E[e^{it(S_n − a_n)}] − G_n(t)| ≤ ∑_k |χ_{n,k}(t) − 1|² ≤ max_k |χ_{n,k}(t) − 1| · K(t) → 0 by s3. This is the convergence that s2 needs, so Z is infinitely divisible.

applications.title: The random field of many weak impurities cannot be uniformly distributed
applications.inputs: In the n-th sample of a disordered crystal, a probe site feels the local field S_n = X_{n,1} + ⋯ + X_{n,k_n}, the sum of independent contributions of k_n impurities. Each impurity is weak: max_k P(|X_{n,k}| > ε) → 0 for every ε > 0. The question is whether S_n − a_n can converge in distribution to the uniform law on [−1, 1] in units of a field h_0.
applications.hypotheses: The contributions in one sample are independent, the array is infinitesimal by assumption, and the question asks about a limit in distribution of S_n − a_n. So the theorem applies, and any such limit must be infinitely divisible.

steps.text: The uniform law U on [−1, 1] has variance (1 − (−1))²/12 = 1/3.

Suppose that U is infinitely divisible and take m = 4: U has the law of V_1 + V_2 + V_3 + V_4 with V_i i.i.d. If V_1 > 1/4 with positive probability, then all four exceed 1/4 with probability P(V_1 > 1/4)⁴ > 0, and then the sum exceeds 1, which is impossible. The same holds for V_1 < −1/4, so |V_1| ≤ 1/4 almost surely.
Variances add over independent terms, so Var U = 4 Var V_1 ≤ 4 E[V_1²] ≤ 4 · (1/4)² = 1/4.
The bound 1/4 contradicts Var U = 1/3, because 1/3 − 1/4 = 1/12 > 0. So U is not infinitely divisible, and by the theorem it is not a possible limit.

applications.conclusion: No choice of weak independent impurity fields and centering constants gives a uniformly distributed limiting local field. The same argument with general m shows that no nondegenerate bounded law is a possible limit. The possible limits are the infinitely divisible laws, for example normal, Cauchy and other stable laws.

limitations: The theorem does not say when the sums converge or which infinitely divisible law appears. The Gnedenko–Kolmogorov conditions in Theorem 1 of the source answer both questions.
The infinitesimality condition is necessary in general. Without it, a single summand can carry any law, for example a uniform law, which is not infinitely divisible.
Every infinitely divisible law appears as such a limit, for example as the row sums of an array with i.i.d. rows of n-th convolution roots, so the theorem is sharp.

results.name: Lindeberg–Feller central limit theorem
results.statement: For each n ≥ 1 let X_{n,1}, …, X_{n,k_n} be independent real random variables with E X_{n,m} = 0 and E X_{n,m}² < ∞, and let S_n = X_{n,1} + ⋯ + X_{n,k_n}. Suppose that (i) Σ_m E X_{n,m}² → σ² as n → ∞, where 0 < σ² < ∞, and (ii) for every ε > 0, Σ_m E[X_{n,m}² 1(|X_{n,m}| > ε)] → 0 (the Lindeberg condition). Then S_n converges in distribution to the normal law N(0, σ²).
hypotheses: In each row n, the variables X_{n,1}, …, X_{n,k_n} are independent, have mean 0 and have finite variance.
The row variances satisfy Σ_m E X_{n,m}² → σ² with 0 < σ² < ∞.
The Lindeberg condition holds: Σ_m E[X_{n,m}²; |X_{n,m}| > ε] → 0 for every ε > 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 reduces convergence in distribution of S_n to pointwise convergence of its characteristic function, and step s4 concludes with the same theorem.
Step s2 bounds e^(ix) − 1 − ix + x²/2 by the third-order remainder of Taylor's theorem.

definitions.name: triangular array
definitions.text: A family of random variables X_{n,m}, 1 ≤ m ≤ k_n, n ≥ 1, where the variables in each row n are independent. Different rows need not be independent of each other.

definitions.name: Lindeberg condition
definitions.text: For every ε > 0, Σ_m E[X_{n,m}²; |X_{n,m}| > ε] → 0 as n → ∞. Here E[Y; A] = E[Y 1_A]. The condition says that no single summand carries a fixed part of the variance.

definitions.name: convergence in distribution
definitions.text: S_n converges in distribution to a law μ if E g(S_n) → ∫ g dμ for every bounded continuous g: ℝ → ℝ.

To see that Theorem 3.4.10 contains our first central limit theorem, let Y1, Y2 . . . be i.i.d. with EYi = 0 and EYi² = σ² ∈ (0, ∞), and let X_{n,m} = Y_m/n^{1/2}.

The source uses rows of length n and writes σχ for N(0, σ²). The authored statement allows rows of any length k_n and states the finite-variance assumption explicitly. The authored proof follows the proof in the source (p. 149) with a Taylor bound on each characteristic function, the product comparison of Lemma 3.4.3 and the limit of a product of factors 1 − c_{n,m}.

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses. The converse of Feller is not proved.

steps.text: Fix t ∈ ℝ. Let φ_{n,m}(t) = E e^(itX_{n,m}) and σ_{n,m}² = E X_{n,m}². By independence within the row, E e^(itS_n) = Π_m φ_{n,m}(t). The function exp(−σ²t²/2) is the characteristic function of N(0, σ²). So by Lévy's continuity theorem it suffices to prove Π_m φ_{n,m}(t) → exp(−σ²t²/2) for every t.

For real x, Taylor's theorem gives |e^(ix) − 1 − ix + x²/2| ≤ |x|³/6. Also |e^(ix) − 1 − ix| ≤ x²/2, so the same quantity is at most x². Put x = tX_{n,m} and take expectations. The linear term vanishes because E X_{n,m} = 0, so with w_{n,m} = 1 − t²σ_{n,m}²/2 we get |φ_{n,m}(t) − w_{n,m}| ≤ E min(|tX_{n,m}|³/6, t²X_{n,m}²). Split the expectation at |X_{n,m}| = ε: the bound is at most (|t|³ε/6) E[X_{n,m}²; |X_{n,m}| ≤ ε] + t² E[X_{n,m}²; |X_{n,m}| > ε]. Sum over m and use (i) and (ii): limsup_n Σ_m |φ_{n,m}(t) − w_{n,m}| ≤ |t|³εσ²/6. Since ε > 0 is arbitrary, Σ_m |φ_{n,m}(t) − w_{n,m}| → 0.

For every ε > 0, σ_{n,m}² ≤ ε² + E[X_{n,m}²; |X_{n,m}| > ε]. Hence max_m σ_{n,m}² ≤ ε² + Σ_m E[X_{n,m}²; |X_{n,m}| > ε], and (ii) gives max_m σ_{n,m}² → 0. So for large n every w_{n,m} lies in [0, 1]. For complex numbers z_m, w_m of modulus at most 1, |Π_m z_m − Π_m w_m| ≤ Σ_m |z_m − w_m|. This follows by induction from z₁Z − w₁W = z₁(Z − W) + (z₁ − w₁)W. Apply it with z_m = φ_{n,m}(t), which has modulus at most 1. Step s2 then gives |Π_m φ_{n,m}(t) − Π_m w_{n,m}| → 0.

Set c_{n,m} = t²σ_{n,m}²/2, so w_{n,m} = 1 − c_{n,m}. By s3, max_m c_{n,m} → 0, and by (i), Σ_m c_{n,m} → t²σ²/2. For 0 ≤ c ≤ 1/2, |log(1 − c) + c| = Σ_{k≥2} c^k/k ≤ c²/(2(1 − c)) ≤ c². Hence |log Π_m w_{n,m} + Σ_m c_{n,m}| ≤ Σ_m c_{n,m}² ≤ (max_m c_{n,m}) Σ_m c_{n,m} → 0. So Π_m w_{n,m} → exp(−σ²t²/2). With s3, Π_m φ_{n,m}(t) → exp(−σ²t²/2), and step s1 gives S_n ⇒ N(0, σ²).

applications.title: Magnetization fluctuations of a paramagnet with two sublattices
applications.inputs: N = 2K independent Ising spins σ_i ∈ {−1, +1} in a paramagnet. The spins on odd sites feel a field with βh = artanh(1/2), so E σ_i = 1/2. The spins on even sites feel no field, so E σ_i = 0. The magnetization is M_N = Σ_i σ_i. Take N = 400 for the numbers.
applications.hypotheses: Put V_N = Var M_N and X_{N,i} = (σ_i − E σ_i)/√V_N. The variables in row N are independent with mean 0 and finite variance. Step a2 shows (i) with σ² = 1, and step a3 shows the Lindeberg condition.

steps.text: A spin with mean m has variance 1 − m². So the odd sites contribute K(1 − 1/4) = 3K/4 and the even sites contribute K. Hence E M_N = K/2 = N/4 and V_N = 7K/4 = 7N/8.
By construction Σ_i E X_{N,i}² = V_N/V_N = 1 for every N, so condition (i) holds with σ² = 1.
Each |σ_i − E σ_i| ≤ 2, so |X_{N,i}| ≤ 2/√V_N. If V_N > 4/ε², that is N > 32/(7ε²), no term has |X_{N,i}| > ε and the Lindeberg sum is exactly 0. So (ii) holds.
The theorem gives (M_N − N/4)/√(7N/8) ⇒ N(0, 1). For N = 400, P(M_400 ≥ 100 + 1.96 · √350) is close to 0.025, and 1.96 · √350 is about 36.7.

applications.conclusion: The magnetization of the two-sublattice paramagnet has Gaussian fluctuations: (M_N − N/4)/√(7N/8) converges in distribution to N(0, 1), although the spins are not identically distributed.

limitations: Feller's converse is not proved here: if max_m E X_{n,m}² → 0 and S_n ⇒ N(0, σ²), then the Lindeberg condition holds.
The theorem gives no rate of convergence. The Berry–Esseen theorem gives a rate under a third-moment condition.
Lyapunov's condition Σ_m E|X_{n,m}|^(2+δ) → 0 implies the Lindeberg condition, so Lyapunov's central limit theorem is a special case.

results.name: Local limit theorem for lattice random walks
results.statement: Let X_1, X_2, … be i.i.d. real random variables with E X_1 = 0 and E X_1² = σ² ∈ (0, ∞). Suppose that X_1 has a lattice distribution with span h > 0: P(X_1 ∈ b + hℤ) = 1 for some real b, and no larger h has this property. Put S_n = X_1 + ⋯ + X_n, L_n = {(nb + hz)/√n : z ∈ ℤ}, p_n(x) = P(S_n/√n = x) and g(x) = (2πσ²)^(−1/2) exp(−x²/(2σ²)). Then sup_{x ∈ L_n} |(√n/h) p_n(x) − g(x)| → 0 as n → ∞.
hypotheses: The variables X_1, X_2, … are independent and identically distributed.
E X_1 = 0 and E X_1² = σ² with 0 < σ² < ∞.
X_1 has a lattice distribution with span h: P(X_1 ∈ b + hℤ) = 1 for some b, and h is the largest number with this property.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses the classical central limit theorem to get the pointwise limit φ(t/√n)^n → exp(−σ²t²/2) of the characteristic functions.
Step s2 writes the Gaussian density g as the Fourier inversion integral of its characteristic function exp(−σ²t²/2).
Step s4 uses the Taylor bound |e^(iy) − 1 − iy + y²/2| ≤ min(|y|³/6, y²) to control φ near 0.
Steps s4 and s6 use dominated (bounded) convergence for the remainder E min(|u||X|³/6, X²) and for the integral over a fixed interval [−A, A].

definitions.name: lattice distribution
definitions.text: A random variable X has a lattice distribution if P(X ∈ b + hℤ) = 1 for some real b and some h > 0, where b + hℤ = {b + hz : z ∈ ℤ}.

definitions.name: span
definitions.text: The span of a lattice distribution is the largest h > 0 such that P(X ∈ b + hℤ) = 1 for some b.

Let Y be a random variable with P(Y ∈ a + θZ) = 1 and ψ(t) = E exp(itY). It follows from part (iii) of Exercise 3.3.2 that

proof.scope: The full statement for lattice distributions with finite variance. The nonlattice case (Durrett's Theorem 3.5.4) is not treated.

steps.text: Lattice inversion. Let Y take values in a + θℤ with ψ(t) = E e^(itY). For x = a + θj, e^(−itx) ψ(t) = Σ_k P(Y = a + θk) e^(itθ(k − j)). The series converges absolutely and uniformly in t, and ∫_{−π/θ}^{π/θ} e^(itθ(k−j)) dt equals 2π/θ if k = j and 0 otherwise. So P(Y = x) = (θ/2π) ∫_{−π/θ}^{π/θ} e^(−itx) ψ(t) dt. Apply this to Y = S_n/√n, which takes values in L_n with θ = h/√n, and let φ(t) = E e^(itX_1). Then (√n/h) p_n(x) = (1/2π) ∫_{|t| ≤ π√n/h} e^(−itx) φ(t/√n)^n dt for x ∈ L_n.

Subtract the Gaussian. Fourier inversion gives g(x) = (1/2π) ∫ e^(−itx) exp(−σ²t²/2) dt. Since |e^(−itx)| = 1, for every x ∈ L_n we get |(√n/h) p_n(x) − g(x)| ≤ (1/2π) [∫_{|t| ≤ π√n/h} |φ(t/√n)^n − exp(−σ²t²/2)| dt + ∫_{|t| > π√n/h} exp(−σ²t²/2) dt]. The bound does not depend on x. The second integral tends to 0. It remains to show that the first integral I_n tends to 0.

Pointwise limit. By the central limit theorem, S_n/√n converges in distribution to N(0, σ²). Since x ↦ e^(itx) is bounded and continuous, φ(t/√n)^n = E e^(itS_n/√n) → exp(−σ²t²/2) for every t. The integrand of I_n is at most 2, so for each fixed A the part of I_n over |t| ≤ A tends to 0 by bounded convergence.

Gaussian bound near 0. From |e^(iy) − 1 − iy + y²/2| ≤ min(|y|³/6, y²) and E X_1 = 0 we get |φ(u) − 1 + σ²u²/2| ≤ u² r(u) with r(u) = E min(|u||X_1|³/6, X_1²). Dominated convergence gives r(u) → 0 as u → 0. Choose δ > 0 with r(u) ≤ σ²/4 and σ²u² ≤ 2 for |u| ≤ δ. Then |φ(u)| ≤ 1 − σ²u²/2 + σ²u²/4 ≤ exp(−σ²u²/4). Hence |φ(t/√n)^n| ≤ exp(−σ²t²/4) for |t| ≤ δ√n, and the part of I_n over A < |t| ≤ δ√n is at most 2 ∫_{|t| > A} exp(−σ²t²/4) dt.

Away from 0 the span gives decay. Suppose |φ(u)| = 1 for some u with 0 < u < 2π/h. Write φ(u) = e^(iuc). Then E[1 − cos(u(X_1 − c))] = 0, so u(X_1 − c) ∈ 2πℤ almost surely, that is X_1 ∈ c + (2π/u)ℤ. Since 2π/u > h, this contradicts the maximality of the span. So |φ(u)| < 1 on the compact set δ ≤ |u| ≤ π/h, and by continuity |φ(u)| ≤ η there for some η < 1. The part of I_n over δ√n < |t| ≤ π√n/h is then at most (2π√n/h) η^n + ∫_{|t| > δ√n} exp(−σ²t²/2) dt, which tends to 0.
Combine. By s3, s4 and s5, limsup_n I_n ≤ 2 ∫_{|t| > A} exp(−σ²t²/4) dt for every A > 0. Let A → ∞ to get I_n → 0. With s2, sup_{x ∈ L_n} |(√n/h) p_n(x) − g(x)| → 0.

applications.title: Magnetization histogram of a spin-1 paramagnet
applications.inputs: N independent spin-1 variables σ_i ∈ {−1, 0, 1}, as in a Blume–Capel model with no coupling. The crystal field gives the weight e^(−βΔ) = 1/2 to the states ±1 and the weight 1 to the state 0. So P(σ_i = 0) = 1/2 and P(σ_i = ±1) = 1/4. The magnetization is M_N = σ_1 + ⋯ + σ_N.
applications.hypotheses: The spins are i.i.d. with mean 0. They take values in ℤ, and the values 0 and 1 have positive probability, so no lattice b + hℤ with h > 1 contains them. The span is h = 1 with b = 0.

steps.text: The variance of one spin is σ² = (1/4) · 1 + (1/2) · 0 + (1/4) · 1 = 1/2.
Here L_N = ℤ/√N and g(x) = (2π · 1/2)^(−1/2) e^(−x²) = π^(−1/2) e^(−x²). The theorem gives P(M_N = m) = N^(−1/2) π^(−1/2) e^(−m²/N) + o(N^(−1/2)) uniformly in the integers m.
A direct count for N = 2 gives P(M_2 = 0) = P(0, 0) + 2 P(1, −1) = 1/4 + 1/8 = 3/8. The local formula gives (2π)^(−1/2) ≈ 0.399, which is already close to 0.375.

The ratio of the probabilities of the magnetizations m and 0 is then e^(−m²/N)(1 + o(1)) for |m| ≤ C√N. So the free energy of the constrained ensemble is quadratic in m/√N, with no correction from the lattice.

applications.conclusion: The histogram of the magnetization of the spin-1 paramagnet has the Gaussian shape P(M_N = m) ≈ e^(−m²/N)/√(πN) at each single value m, not only for intervals.

limitations: The theorem gives no rate. Under a third moment condition the error is O(1/√n) uniformly.
Only the lattice case is treated. For nonlattice laws the analogue concerns P(S_n ∈ (x_n + a, x_n + b)), which is Durrett's Theorem 3.5.4.
The uniform error o(1) is small relative to g(x) only where g(x) is not small. Far in the tails the relative error can be large, and large deviation estimates are needed there.

results.name: Lamperti's theorem on self-similar limit processes
aliases: Lamperti's limit theorem for scaling limits
results.statement: Let (Y(t))_{t≥0} be a real-valued stochastic process and f : (0, ∞) → (0, ∞) a function with f(a) → ∞ as a → ∞. Assume that, as a → ∞, the finite-dimensional distributions of (Y(at)/f(a))_{t≥0} converge to those of a process (X(t))_{t≥0} that is continuous in probability and proper: X(t) is not almost surely constant for any t > 0. Then there is H > 0 such that f(ab)/f(a) → b^H for every b > 0, so f(a) = a^H L(a) with L slowly varying. Moreover X(0) = 0 almost surely, and X is H-self-similar: for every b > 0 the processes (X(bt))_{t≥0} and (b^H X(t))_{t≥0} have the same finite-dimensional distributions. Conversely, every H-self-similar process X with H > 0 is such a limit, for example with Y = X and f(a) = a^H.
hypotheses: f(a) > 0 for all a > 0 and f(a) → ∞ as a → ∞.
The finite-dimensional distributions of (Y(at)/f(a))_{t≥0} converge to those of X as a → ∞.
X is continuous in probability on [0, ∞), and X(t) is not almost surely constant for any t > 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses Slutsky's theorem to multiply a convergent random vector by the deterministic factors f(ab)/f(b) → a^H.

definitions.name: H-self-similar process
definitions.text: A process X with (X(bt))_{t≥0} equal to (b^H X(t))_{t≥0} in finite-dimensional distributions for every b > 0. Lamperti called such processes semi-stable.

definitions.name: slowly varying function
definitions.text: A positive function L with L(ab)/L(a) → 1 as a → ∞ for every b > 0.

source.citation: Youri Davydov and Vygantas Paulauskas, Lamperti type theorems for random fields, arXiv:1705.00182, 2017. Theorem 3 there restates J. Lamperti, Semi-stable stochastic processes, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 104 (1962), 62-78.

source.alignment: Theorem 3 of the source restates Lamperti's 1962 theorem for ℝ^m-valued processes with a centering function k(a): if (Y(at) + k(a))/f(a) converges to a proper stochastically continuous X in finite-dimensional distributions, then X is self-similar of order H > 0, f(a) = a^H L(a) and k(a) = ω(a) a^H L(a) with ω(a) → w = X(0). The authored statement is the real-valued case with k ≡ 0, where w = 0. It writes self-similarity in the modern form X(bt) = b^H X(t) in finite-dimensional distributions.

source_references.alignment: Theorem 18 extends the case k ≡ 0 of Lamperti's theorem to random fields indexed by ℝ^d_+ with diagonal normalizations. Its proof, which the source says follows Lamperti's proof, applies Lamperti's lemma on types to get lim f(at)/f(a), identifies the limit as a power, and proves self-similarity by a double limit. For d = m = 1 these are steps s1-s3 of the outline. The source states H > 0 without the hypothesis f → ∞. Step s4 of the outline uses f → ∞ and continuity at t = 0 for this.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 18 in Davydov and Paulauskas (arXiv:1705.00182) for d = m = 1, which the authors say follows Lamperti's 1962 proof of Theorem 3. Step s1 takes the lemma on types from Lamperti (p. 71 of his paper) as cited by the source. Steps s2 and s4 replace the citation of the theory of regularly varying functions by short direct arguments. The centering k(a) of Lamperti's general theorem is not treated.

steps.text: Convergence of types. Fix b > 0 and a sequence a_n → ∞. The one-dimensional laws give W_n = Y(a_n b)/f(a_n b) ⇒ X(1), because a_n b → ∞, and α_n W_n = Y(a_n b)/f(a_n) ⇒ X(b) with α_n = f(a_n b)/f(a_n) > 0. Both limits are nondegenerate because X is proper. The lemma on types that the source takes from Lamperti (p. 71) gives α_n → l(b) ∈ (0, ∞) and X(b) = l(b) X(1) in law. Two quantiles of X(1) and X(b) fix l(b), so the limit does not depend on the sequence, and f(ab)/f(a) → l(b) as a → ∞.

The limit is a power. Since ab → ∞ when a → ∞, l(bc) = lim [f(abc)/f(ab)] [f(ab)/f(a)] = l(c) l(b). As b → b_0 > 0, continuity in probability gives l(b) X(1) = X(b) ⇒ X(b_0) = l(b_0) X(1) in law, and the lemma on types gives l(b) → l(b_0). So g(x) = log l(e^x) is continuous and additive, hence linear, and l(b) = b^H with H = log l(e). Then L(a) = f(a) a^{−H} satisfies L(ab)/L(a) → 1, so L is slowly varying. The source reaches the same conclusion with its Proposition 9 on regularly varying functions.

Self-similarity by a double limit. Fix a > 0 and times t_1, …, t_k. As b → ∞, the finite-dimensional convergence at the times a t_i gives (Y(a b t_i)/f(b))_i ⇒ (X(a t_i))_i. At the times t_i with the scale ab it gives (Y(a b t_i)/f(ab))_i ⇒ (X(t_i))_i, and multiplication by f(ab)/f(b) → a^H with Slutsky's theorem gives (Y(a b t_i)/f(b))_i ⇒ (a^H X(t_i))_i. Limits in distribution are unique, so (X(a t_i))_i and (a^H X(t_i))_i have the same law. This is the last part of the proof of Theorem 18 in the source.

The index is positive and X(0) = 0. The variable Y(0) does not depend on a and f(a) → ∞, so Y(0)/f(a) → 0 in probability and X(0) = 0. If H < 0, then f(2^n)/f(2^{n−1}) → 2^H < 1 forces f(2^n) → 0, which contradicts f → ∞. If H = 0, then s1 gives X(t) = X(1) in law for all t > 0. Continuity in probability at 0 gives X(t) → X(0) = 0 as t ↓ 0, so X(1) = 0 almost surely, which contradicts properness. Hence H > 0.

Converse. If X is H-self-similar with H > 0, put Y = X and f(a) = a^H, which tends to ∞. Then (Y(at)/f(a))_t = (a^{−H} X(at))_t has the finite-dimensional laws of (X(t))_t for every a, so the convergence holds trivially. Lamperti's theorem therefore identifies the class of proper, stochastically continuous scaling limits with the class of self-similar processes of positive index.

applications.title: Subdiffusive scaling of a tagged particle in single-file diffusion
applications.inputs: In single-file diffusion, particles on a line cannot pass each other, and the displacement Y(t) of a tagged particle grows like t^{1/4}. Assume that Y(at)/f(a) converges in finite-dimensional distributions to a proper process X that is continuous in probability, with f(a) = a^{1/4} in units where the mean square of X(1) is σ² = 1.
applications.hypotheses: f(a) = a^{1/4} is positive and tends to ∞. X is proper and continuous in probability by assumption. So the theorem applies.

steps.text: The index is fixed by f: f(16a)/f(a) = 16^{1/4} = 2, so l(16) = 2 and 16^H = 2. Since 2⁴ = 16, H = 1/4.
Self-similarity gives X(81t) = 81^{1/4} X(t) = 3X(t) in law, because 3⁴ = 81.
Mean squares scale with the square of the factor: E[X(81)²] = 3² E[X(1)²] = 9. In general E[X(t)²] = t^{2H} = t^{1/2}, a subdiffusive mean-square displacement.
X(0) = 0 almost surely, and the theorem rules out any proper limit X with a scaling exponent different from 1/4. For example, a factor 16 in time must multiply the mean square by 16^{1/2} = 4 = 2².

applications.conclusion: Any proper, stochastically continuous scaling limit of the tagged-particle displacement with normalization t^{1/4} is self-similar with index H = 1/4. Its mean-square displacement grows like t^{1/2}, which is the subdiffusive law of single-file diffusion.

limitations: The theorem gives the scaling of the limit but not its law. Brownian motion, fractional Brownian motion and stable Lévy processes are all possible limits with different indices.
Without continuity in probability or properness the conclusion H > 0 can fail. For example Y(t) = log(t) Z for t ≥ 1 with f(a) = log a gives the limit X(t) = Z for t > 0, which is constant in t.
The record omits the centering function k(a) of Lamperti's general theorem, which changes only the location of X(0).

aliases: Marcinkiewicz strong law of large numbers
results.statement: Let 1 < p < 2 and let X_1, X_2, … be i.i.d. real random variables with E X_1 = 0 and E|X_1|^p < ∞. Put S_n = X_1 + ⋯ + X_n. Then S_n / n^(1/p) → 0 almost surely.

E|X_1|^p < ∞ for some p with 1 < p < 2.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Borel–Cantelli lemma to show that X_k equals its truncation Y_k for all large k, almost surely.
Step s2 exchanges the sum over m and the expectation of a nonnegative series (Tonelli) to bound the variance series.
Step s3 uses the sufficiency part of Kolmogorov's series criterion: centered independent terms with summable variances give an almost surely convergent series.

definitions.name: truncation
definitions.text: Y_k = X_k 1(|X_k| ≤ k^(1/p)) keeps X_k when |X_k| ≤ k^(1/p) and replaces it by 0 otherwise. The truncated variables have finite variance.

definitions.name: Kronecker's lemma
definitions.text: If 0 < a_n ↑ ∞ and the series Σ x_m/a_m converges, then a_n^(−1) Σ_{m≤n} x_m → 0.

The authored proof follows the proof in the source with truncation at k^(1/p), the Borel–Cantelli lemma, a variance series, Theorem 2.5.6 with Kronecker's lemma (Theorem 2.5.9) and a bound on the truncated means. proof.scope: The full statement for 1 < p < 2. The cases 0 < p < 1 and p = 1 are not treated.

steps.text: Truncate. Put Y_k = X_k 1(|X_k| ≤ k^(1/p)) and T_n = Y_1 + ⋯ + Y_n. Since the X_k have the law of X_1, Σ_k P(Y_k ≠ X_k) = Σ_{k≥1} P(|X_1|^p > k) ≤ ∫_0^∞ P(|X_1|^p > u) du = E|X_1|^p < ∞. By the Borel–Cantelli lemma, almost surely X_k = Y_k for all k larger than some random K. Then S_n − T_n is eventually constant, so (S_n − T_n)/n^(1/p) → 0 almost surely. It remains to show T_n/n^(1/p) → 0 almost surely.

Bound the variances. Let q = 2/p > 1. For an integer M ≥ 1, Σ_{m≥M} m^(−q) ≤ M^(−q) + ∫_M^∞ x^(−q) dx ≤ C_p M^(1−q) with C_p = 1 + p/(2 − p). By Tonelli, Σ_m Var(Y_m)/m^q ≤ Σ_m E[Y_m²]/m^q = E[X_1² Σ_{m ≥ 1, m ≥ |X_1|^p} m^(−q)]. The smallest admissible m is at least max(1, |X_1|^p), and 1 − q < 0, so the inner sum is at most C_p max(1, |X_1|^p)^(1−q). If |X_1| ≤ 1 the integrand is at most C_p. If |X_1| > 1 it is at most C_p X_1² |X_1|^(p−2) = C_p |X_1|^p. Hence Σ_m Var(Y_m/m^(1/p)) ≤ C_p (1 + E|X_1|^p) < ∞.

Center and sum. Let μ_m = E Y_m. The variables (Y_m − μ_m)/m^(1/p) are independent, centered and have summable variances by s2. So Kolmogorov's criterion gives that Σ_m (Y_m − μ_m)/m^(1/p) converges almost surely. Kronecker's lemma with a_m = m^(1/p) then gives n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤n} (Y_m − μ_m) → 0 almost surely. Kronecker's lemma follows by summation by parts: with b_n = Σ_{m≤n} x_m/a_m → b and a_0 = 0, a_n^(−1) Σ_{m≤n} x_m = b_n − a_n^(−1) Σ_{m<n} (a_{m+1} − a_m) b_m, and the last average of the b_m with weights a_{m+1} − a_m ≥ 0 also tends to b.

Control the means. Since E X_1 = 0, μ_m = −E[X_1; |X_1| > m^(1/p)]. On the event |X_1| > m^(1/p) we have |X_1| = |X_1|^p |X_1|^(1−p) ≤ |X_1|^p m^((1−p)/p), because 1 − p < 0. So |μ_m| ≤ m^(1/p − 1) ε_m with ε_m = E[|X_1|^p; |X_1| > m^(1/p)]. Dominated convergence gives ε_m → 0. The function x ↦ x^(1/p − 1) decreases, so Σ_{m≤n} m^(1/p − 1) ≤ ∫_0^n x^(1/p − 1) dx = p n^(1/p). Fix M. Then n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤n} |μ_m| ≤ n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤M} |μ_m| + p sup_{m>M} ε_m. Let n → ∞ and then M → ∞: n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤n} μ_m → 0.
Combine. S_n/n^(1/p) = (S_n − T_n)/n^(1/p) + n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤n} (Y_m − μ_m) + n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤n} μ_m. The three terms tend to 0 almost surely by s1, s3 and s4. Hence S_n/n^(1/p) → 0 almost surely.

applications.title: The clock of a trap model with heavy-tailed trapping times
applications.inputs: In the mean-field version of Bouchaud's trap model, a walker visits a new trap at each step. A trap of depth E holds the walker for the time τ = e^(E/T), and the depths are exponential with P(E > x) = e^(−x/T_g). Then P(τ > t) = t^(−T/T_g) for t ≥ 1. Take T = 3T_g/2, so P(τ > t) = t^(−3/2). The trapping times τ_1, τ_2, … are i.i.d., and T_n = τ_1 + ⋯ + τ_n is the time of the n-th exit.
applications.hypotheses: Put X_k = τ_k − E τ_k and p = 5/4. The X_k are i.i.d. with mean 0. Step a2 shows E|X_1|^p < ∞, and 1 < 5/4 < 2.

steps.text: The mean is E τ = 1 + ∫_1^∞ t^(−3/2) dt = 1 + 1/(3/2 − 1) = 3. The second moment is infinite because ∫_1^∞ 2t · t^(−3/2) dt diverges. So the classical central limit theorem does not apply.
The theorem with p = 5/4 gives (T_n − 3n)/n^(4/5) → 0 almost surely. So the exit times satisfy T_n = 3n + o(n^(4/5)) on almost every path.
The same argument works for every p < 3/2. Since 1/p decreases to 2/3 as p increases to 3/2, T_n − 3n = o(n^(2/3 + δ)) almost surely for every δ > 0.

applications.conclusion: On almost every path the trap-model clock grows like 3n with an error o(n^(2/3+δ)) for every δ > 0, although the trapping times have infinite variance.

limitations: The theorem does not give a limit law for (T_n − nE τ)/n^(1/p). The generalized central limit theorem gives a stable limit on the scale n^(1/α) under a regular variation assumption.
For 0 < p < 1 the same conclusion holds without centering, and p = 1 is Kolmogorov's strong law. These cases are not proved here.
The converse also holds: if S_n/n^(1/p) → 0 almost surely, then E|X_1|^p < ∞. The converse is not proved here.
