results.name: Gibbs variational principle for finite systems
results.statement: Let Ω be a nonempty finite set, let H: Ω → ℝ be a function (the Hamiltonian) and let β ∈ ℝ. Put Z = ∑_{ω∈Ω} e^(−βH(ω)) and μ_β(ω) = e^(−βH(ω))/Z. For a probability distribution μ on Ω, let S(μ) = −∑_ω μ(ω) log μ(ω), with 0 log 0 = 0, and ⟨H⟩_μ = ∑_ω μ(ω) H(ω). Then S(μ) − β⟨H⟩_μ ≤ log Z for every probability distribution μ on Ω, and equality holds if and only if μ = μ_β. So the Gibbs distribution μ_β is the unique maximizer of μ ↦ S(μ) − β⟨H⟩_μ, and the maximum value is log Z.
hypotheses: The configuration set Ω is finite and nonempty, and H is a real function on Ω.
The parameter β is a real number.
The distribution μ is a probability distribution on Ω. Its entropy uses the convention 0 log 0 = 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 applies Jensen's inequality to the concave logarithm, with the weights μ(ω) on the support of μ.
Step s4 uses the strict form of Jensen's inequality: equality forces the values on the support of μ to be equal.

definitions.name: Gibbs distribution
definitions.text: The probability distribution μ_β(ω) = e^(−βH(ω))/Z on Ω, where Z = ∑_ω e^(−βH(ω)) is the partition function.

definitions.name: Shannon entropy
definitions.text: S(μ) = −∑_ω μ(ω) log μ(ω), with the convention 0 log 0 = 0. It is the entropy in natural units (nats).

definitions.name: mean energy
definitions.text: ⟨H⟩_μ = ∑_ω μ(ω) H(ω), the average of the Hamiltonian under μ.

source.citation: Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems: A Concrete Mathematical Introduction, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Authors' online version, revised version of August 22, 2017.
source.module: Chapter 6, Section 6.9.1 Formulation in the finite case
source.excerpt: Lemma 6.74 (Variational principle, finite version). For all µΛ ∈ M1(ΩΛ), WΛ(µΛ) ≤ WΛ(µΛ^Gibbs). Moreover, µΛ^Gibbs is the unique maximizer of WΛ(·).
source.attribution: © Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik. Quoted from the authors' online version of Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source defines W_Λ(µ_Λ) = S_Λ(µ_Λ) − β⟨H_Λ⟩_{µ_Λ} in (6.86) on p. 297 and notes that W_Λ(µ_Λ^Gibbs) = log Z_Λ. The authored statement makes the value log Z explicit, allows every real β and states the convention 0 log 0 = 0. The authored proof follows the source's Jensen argument and adds the support argument that the equality case needs.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Lemma 6.74 in Friedli and Velenik, which applies Jensen's inequality to the logarithm. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every real β and every probability distribution μ on Ω, with the equality case.

steps.text: Let A = {ω ∈ Ω : μ(ω) > 0} be the support of μ. A is nonempty because the weights of μ sum to 1. The terms with μ(ω) = 0 contribute 0 to S(μ) and to ⟨H⟩_μ. So W(μ) := S(μ) − β⟨H⟩_μ = ∑_{ω∈A} μ(ω)(−log μ(ω) − βH(ω)) = ∑_{ω∈A} μ(ω) log x_ω, where x_ω = e^(−βH(ω))/μ(ω) > 0 for ω ∈ A.

The logarithm is concave on (0, ∞), and the weights μ(ω), ω ∈ A, are positive with sum 1. Jensen's inequality gives ∑_{ω∈A} μ(ω) log x_ω ≤ log ∑_{ω∈A} μ(ω) x_ω = log ∑_{ω∈A} e^(−βH(ω)). Every term e^(−βH(ω)) is positive, and the logarithm is increasing, so log ∑_{ω∈A} e^(−βH(ω)) ≤ log ∑_{ω∈Ω} e^(−βH(ω)) = log Z. Hence W(μ) ≤ log Z.

The Gibbs distribution attains the bound. Every weight μ_β(ω) = e^(−βH(ω))/Z is positive, so its support is Ω. For each ω, −log μ_β(ω) − βH(ω) = βH(ω) + log Z − βH(ω) = log Z. Averaging over ω with the weights μ_β(ω) gives W(μ_β) = log Z.

Assume that W(μ) = log Z. Then both inequalities of step s2 are equalities. Equality in the second inequality means ∑_{ω∉A} e^(−βH(ω)) = 0. Each term is positive, so A = Ω. The logarithm is strictly concave, so equality in Jensen's inequality forces x_ω to take one value c on A = Ω. Then μ(ω) = e^(−βH(ω))/c for every ω, and the normalization ∑_ω μ(ω) = 1 gives c = Z. So μ = μ_β. With step s3, μ_β is the unique maximizer and the maximum value is log Z.

applications.title: Maximum entropy at fixed mean energy for a three-level system
applications.inputs: Three states with energies H = 0, 1, 2 and an inverse temperature β with e^(−β) = 1/2, so β = log 2. A competing distribution μ = (5/7, 0, 2/7) on the three states.
applications.hypotheses: The state space has three elements, H is real and β = log 2 is real. Both μ_β and μ are probability distributions, so the principle applies to each of them.

steps.text: The Boltzmann weights are 1, 1/2 and 1/4. Their sum is Z = 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 = 7/4, so the Gibbs distribution is μ_β = (4/7, 2/7, 1/7).
The mean energy of the Gibbs distribution is U = 0·(4/7) + 1·(2/7) + 2·(1/7) = 4/7.
The competing distribution has the same mean energy: 0·(5/7) + 1·0 + 2·(2/7) = 4/7.

For every μ with ⟨H⟩_μ = U the principle gives S(μ) ≤ log Z + βU, and the right side equals S(μ_β) by step s3 of the proof. Here S(μ_β) = log(7/4) + (4/7) log 2 ≈ 0.956 nats. The competing distribution has S(μ) = −(5/7) log(5/7) − (2/7) log(2/7) ≈ 0.598 nats, which is strictly smaller, as the uniqueness part requires.

applications.conclusion: Among all distributions on the three levels with mean energy 4/7, the Gibbs distribution (4/7, 2/7, 1/7) has the largest entropy, log(7/4) + (4/7) log 2 ≈ 0.956 nats, and it is the only maximizer.

limitations: The principle concerns a finite configuration set. For infinite lattice systems one needs specific entropy and energy density, and the variational principle then characterizes translation-invariant Gibbs measures (Theorem 6.82 of the source).
The gap log Z − W(μ) equals the relative entropy of μ with respect to μ_β. So the principle is equivalent to the nonnegativity of relative entropy on a finite set.

results.name: Gibbs–Bogoliubov–Feynman inequality
results.statement: Let H and H₀ be Hermitian operators on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space and let β > 0. Put Z = Tr e^(−βH), Z₀ = Tr e^(−βH₀), F = −β⁻¹ log Z and F₀ = −β⁻¹ log Z₀. Write ⟨X⟩ = Tr(X e^(−βH))/Z and ⟨X⟩₀ = Tr(X e^(−βH₀))/Z₀ for the Gibbs expectations of H and H₀. Then F₀ + ⟨H − H₀⟩ ≤ F ≤ F₀ + ⟨H − H₀⟩₀. Equality holds in either inequality if and only if H − H₀ is a multiple of the identity. In particular, F is at most the infimum of F₀ + ⟨H − H₀⟩₀ over all trial Hamiltonians H₀.
hypotheses: The Hilbert space is finite-dimensional, and H and H₀ are Hermitian operators on it.
The inverse temperature β is a positive real number.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s2, s3 and s4 use the relative-entropy case of Klein's inequality, with its equality condition, for the two Gibbs states.
Step s1 uses the spectral theorem to compute the logarithm of a Gibbs state.

definitions.name: Gibbs state
definitions.text: For a Hermitian operator H and β > 0, the density matrix ρ = e^(−βH)/Tr e^(−βH).

definitions.name: free energy
definitions.text: F = −β⁻¹ log Tr e^(−βH), the Helmholtz free energy of H at inverse temperature β.

definitions.name: relative entropy
definitions.text: For density matrices σ and ρ with ρ positive definite, D(σ‖ρ) = Tr σ(log σ − log ρ).

source.citation: Benedikt M. Reible, Carsten Hartmann and Luigi Delle Site, Two-sided Bogoliubov inequality to estimate finite size effects in quantum molecular simulations, Letters in Mathematical Physics 112 (2022), article 97.
source.revision: arXiv:2111.10282v3 [math-ph], 5 September 2022.
source.module: Section IV Two-sided quantum Bogoliubov inequality
source.excerpt: Theorem IV.1. Let the partition functions Z0, Z > 0 in (9) be finite and U = H − H0, with Eρ0[U] < ∞ and Eρ[U] < ∞. Then Eρ[U] ≤ ∆F ≤ Eρ0[U].
source.attribution: © The authors. Quoted from the arXiv version for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source works with Gibbs states ρ0 and ρ of H0 and H = H0 + U on a possibly infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, with ∆F = −β⁻¹ log(Z/Z0) = F − F0. The authored statement restricts to finite dimension, writes Eρ0[U] as ⟨H − H₀⟩₀, and adds the equality condition. The upper bound is the Gibbs-Bogoliubov-Feynman inequality. The authored proof follows the source's proof from the non-negativity of the relative entropy (inequality (8) and the computation before Theorem IV.1).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the relative-entropy proof of Theorem IV.1 in Reible, Hartmann and Delle Site (2022). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement in finite dimension: both bounds and the equality condition.

steps.text: Logarithms of the Gibbs states. Put ρ₀ = e^(−βH₀)/Z₀ and ρ = e^(−βH)/Z. By the spectral theorem, H₀ = ∑_λ λ P_λ with orthogonal projections P_λ that sum to I. Then ρ₀ = ∑_λ (e^(−βλ)/Z₀) P_λ, so ρ₀ is positive definite with trace 1, and log ρ₀ = ∑_λ (−βλ − log Z₀) P_λ = −βH₀ − (log Z₀) I. In the same way, ρ is positive definite with trace 1, and log ρ = −βH − (log Z) I.

Upper bound. Apply the relative-entropy case of Klein's inequality with A = ρ and B = ρ₀: Tr ρ₀(log ρ₀ − log ρ) ≥ Tr(ρ₀ − ρ) = 0. By step s1, log ρ₀ − log ρ = β(H − H₀) + (log Z − log Z₀) I, and Tr ρ₀ = 1. So β⟨H − H₀⟩₀ + log Z − log Z₀ ≥ 0. Substitute log Z = −βF and log Z₀ = −βF₀ and divide by β > 0. This gives F ≤ F₀ + ⟨H − H₀⟩₀.

Lower bound. Apply the same case of Klein's inequality with A = ρ₀ and B = ρ: Tr ρ(log ρ − log ρ₀) ≥ 0. By step s1, log ρ − log ρ₀ = −β(H − H₀) + (log Z₀ − log Z) I. So −β⟨H − H₀⟩ + log Z₀ − log Z ≥ 0, which is −β⟨H − H₀⟩ − βF₀ + βF ≥ 0. Divide by β to get F ≥ F₀ + ⟨H − H₀⟩.

Equality. The computations in steps s2 and s3 are identities except for Klein's inequality, so equality holds in either bound if and only if equality holds in Klein's inequality, that is, if and only if ρ₀ = ρ. If ρ₀ = ρ, then step s1 gives β(H − H₀) = (log Z₀ − log Z) I, a multiple of the identity. Conversely, if H − H₀ = cI, then H and H₀ commute and e^(−βH) = e^(−βc) e^(−βH₀). So Z = e^(−βc) Z₀ and ρ = ρ₀.

Variational form. Step s2 holds for every Hermitian H₀ on the same space. So F ≤ F₀ + ⟨H − H₀⟩₀ for every trial Hamiltonian H₀, and F is at most the infimum of the right side over all trial Hamiltonians.

applications.title: Weiss mean-field theory of the Ising model as a variational bound
applications.inputs: Ising spins σ_i = ±1 on the N vertices of a finite q-regular graph with Nq/2 edges, coupling J > 0, field h and inverse temperature β > 0. The Hamiltonian is H = −J ∑_edges σ_i σ_j − h ∑_i σ_i, and the trial Hamiltonian is H₀ = −h_eff ∑_i σ_i with a free parameter h_eff. Numerical instance: h = 0, βqJ = (5/3) log 2 and e^(βh_eff) = 2.
applications.hypotheses: Both H and H₀ are diagonal in the product basis of (ℂ²)^⊗N, so they are Hermitian operators on a space of dimension 2^N, and β > 0.

steps.text: Under the Gibbs state of H₀ the spins are independent, with ⟨σ_i⟩₀ = m = tanh(βh_eff) and ⟨σ_i σ_j⟩₀ = m² for i ≠ j. Also Z₀ = (2 cosh βh_eff)^N. The upper bound gives F/N ≤ Φ(h_eff)/N with Φ(h_eff)/N = −β⁻¹ log(2 cosh βh_eff) − (qJ/2)m² − hm + h_eff m.

Differentiate: d(Φ/N)/dh_eff = −m − qJm m′ − hm′ + m + h_eff m′ = (h_eff − h − qJm) m′, with m′ = β(1 − m²) > 0. So the stationary points satisfy h_eff = h + qJm, which is the Weiss equation m = tanh(β(h + qJm)).
With e^(βh_eff) = 2, m = (2² − 1)/(2² + 1) = 3/5. For h = 0 the Weiss equation then holds when βqJ = βh_eff/m = (5/3) log 2.
At this point 2 cosh(log 2) = 5/2 and β(qJ/2)m² = (5/6)(9/25) log 2 = (3/10) log 2. So βΦ/N = −log(5/2) − (3/10) log 2 + (3/5) log 2 = −log(5/2) + (3/10) log 2.

Compare with the trial h_eff = 0, which gives βΦ/N = −log 2. The tenth powers of e^(−βΦ/N) are (5/2)^10 · 2^(−3) = 9765625/8192 ≈ 1192.1 and 2^10 = 1024. The magnetized trial gives the larger value, so it gives the lower and better upper bound on F.

applications.conclusion: For every finite q-regular graph, F/N ≤ min over h_eff of Φ(h_eff)/N, and the minimizer satisfies the Weiss equation m = tanh(β(h + qJm)). For h = 0 and βqJ = (5/3) log 2, the trial with m = 3/5 gives F/N ≤ −β⁻¹(log(5/2) − (3/10) log 2), below the bound −β⁻¹ log 2 from h_eff = 0.

limitations: The statement is for finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. For unbounded Hamiltonians the source needs finite partition functions and finite expectations of H − H₀.
The inequality gives an upper bound on F only. It does not show that the mean-field bound is close to F, and for finite N the mean-field magnetization m ≠ 0 does not imply a phase transition.

results.name: Peierls–Bogoliubov inequality
results.statement: Let H and K be Hermitian n × n matrices. Then log(Tr e^(H+K) / Tr e^H) ≥ Tr(K e^H) / Tr e^H. Equality holds if and only if K is a real multiple of the identity matrix. Equivalently, if ρ = e^H / Tr e^H is the Gibbs state of H, then Tr e^(H+K) ≥ Tr e^H · exp(Tr(ρK)).
hypotheses: The matrices H and K are Hermitian of the same size n × n.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 applies Klein's trace inequality to the strictly convex function exp at the matrices H + cI and H + K, and step s4 uses its equality case.

definitions.name: matrix exponential of a Hermitian matrix
definitions.text: If H = ∑_λ λ P_λ is the spectral decomposition of H, then e^H = ∑_λ e^λ P_λ. It is positive definite, so Tr e^H > 0.

definitions.name: Gibbs state
definitions.text: The density matrix ρ = e^H / Tr e^H. For H = −βh with a Hamiltonian h, it is the thermal state at inverse temperature β.

source.citation: David Sutter, Approximate Quantum Markov Chains, SpringerBriefs in Mathematical Physics, vol. 28, Springer, 2018.
source.revision: arXiv:1802.05477v1, 15 February 2018.
source.module: Chapter 2 Preliminaries, Section 2.3 Functions on Hermitian operators
source.excerpt: … called Peierls-Bogoliubov inequality in the literature. Corollary 2.12. Let H1, H2 ∈ H(A). Then log (tr e^(H1+H2) / tr e^(H1)) ≥ tr H2 e^(H1) / tr e^(H1).
source.attribution: © David Sutter. Quoted from the arXiv version of Approximate Quantum Markov Chains for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the source's Corollary 2.12 with H1 = H and H2 = K, and it adds the equality case. The source derives the corollary from the convexity of H ↦ log tr e^H (Theorem 2.11), which rests on a variational formula for relative entropy. The authored proof follows the shorter route of Carlen and Lieb, arXiv:1709.05450, Appendix A, (A.3): Klein's inequality for f = exp with a well-chosen constant shift.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the derivation of (A.3) from Klein's inequality in Carlen and Lieb, arXiv:1709.05450, Appendix A. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for Hermitian matrices, with the equality case.

steps.text: Put Z = Tr e^H. The matrix e^H = ∑_λ e^λ P_λ is positive definite, so Z > 0. Put c = Tr(K e^H)/Z. The number Tr(K e^H) = Tr(e^(H/2) K e^(H/2)) is real, because e^(H/2) K e^(H/2) is Hermitian and its trace is the sum of its real diagonal entries. So c is a real number.

The function f = exp is differentiable and strictly convex on I = ℝ, and f′ = exp. Apply Klein's inequality with A = H + cI and B = H + K, which are Hermitian. Since H and cI commute, the spectral decomposition of H gives f(A) = f′(A) = e^c e^H. Klein's inequality then reads Tr e^(H+K) ≥ e^c Tr e^H + e^c Tr[e^H (K − cI)].

By the choice of c, Tr[e^H (K − cI)] = Tr(K e^H) − cZ = cZ − cZ = 0. So step s2 gives Tr e^(H+K) ≥ e^c Z. Both sides are positive. The logarithm is increasing, so log(Tr e^(H+K)/Z) ≥ c = Tr(K e^H)/Tr e^H. This is the inequality. With ρ = e^H/Z it reads Tr e^(H+K) ≥ Z exp(Tr(ρK)).

Equality case. Equality in the final inequality holds exactly when equality holds in step s2. Since exp is strictly convex, the equality case of Klein's inequality gives A = B, that is, K = cI. Conversely, if K = aI with a real, then e^(H+K) = e^a e^H, the left side equals a, and the right side equals a Tr e^H / Tr e^H = a.

applications.title: Free-energy bound for a spin in a rotated field
applications.inputs: A spin 1/2 with Pauli matrices σ_x and σ_z, an inverse temperature β > 0, a field h along z and an extra field g along the unit vector n = (sin θ, 0, cos θ). The partition function is Z = Tr exp(β(h σ_z + g (cos θ σ_z + sin θ σ_x))). Numbers: βh = βg = log 2 and θ = π/3.
applications.hypotheses: Take H = βh σ_z and K = βg (cos θ σ_z + sin θ σ_x). Both are Hermitian 2 × 2 matrices, so the inequality applies.

steps.text: The unperturbed partition function is Z₀ = Tr e^(βhσ_z) = 2 cosh(βh). With e^(βh) = 2 this is 2 + 1/2 = 5/2.
The matrix e^(βhσ_z) is diagonal and σ_x has a zero diagonal, so Tr(σ_x e^(βhσ_z)) = 0. Also Tr(σ_z e^(βhσ_z))/Z₀ = tanh(βh) = (2 − 1/2)/(2 + 1/2) = 3/5.
So Tr(K e^H)/Tr e^H = βg cos θ tanh(βh) = (log 2)(1/2)(3/5) = (3/10) log 2. The inequality gives log Z ≥ log(5/2) + (3/10) log 2 ≈ 1.124.

Exact value for comparison. The total field h e_z + g n has squared length h²(1 + 1 + 2 cos θ) = 3h², so the eigenvalues of H + K are ±√3 log 2 and log Z = log(2^√3 + 2^(−√3)) ≈ 1.287. The bound holds and is strict, because K is not a multiple of the identity.

applications.conclusion: For βh = βg = log 2 and θ = π/3, the Peierls–Bogoliubov inequality gives log Z ≥ log(5/2) + (3/10) log 2 ≈ 1.124, below the exact value ≈ 1.287. In free-energy form, F ≤ F₀ − g cos θ tanh(βh): the first-order perturbation estimate is an upper bound on the free energy.

limitations: The inequality gives only a lower bound on log Tr e^(H+K). The gap is the relative entropy of the Gibbs state of H with respect to the Gibbs state of H + K.
The statement is for matrices. Araki extended it to general von Neumann algebras.

results.name: Klein's inequality
results.statement: Let I ⊆ ℝ be an interval and let f: I → ℝ be convex and differentiable at every interior point of I. Let A and B be Hermitian n × n matrices such that every eigenvalue of A lies in the interior of I and every eigenvalue of B lies in I. Then Tr f(B) − Tr f(A) ≥ Tr[f′(A)(B − A)]. If f is strictly convex, equality holds if and only if A = B. In particular, for A positive definite and B positive semidefinite, Tr[B(log B − log A)] ≥ Tr(B − A), with 0 log 0 = 0, and equality holds if and only if A = B.
hypotheses: The function f is convex on an interval I and differentiable at every interior point of I.
The matrices A and B are Hermitian. The spectrum of A lies in the interior of I, and the spectrum of B lies in I.
For the equality statement, f is strictly convex on I.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 writes A and B with the spectral theorem as real combinations of orthogonal spectral projections that sum to the identity.

definitions.name: function of a Hermitian matrix
definitions.text: If A = ∑_λ λ P_λ is the spectral decomposition of a Hermitian matrix, with distinct eigenvalues λ and orthogonal projections P_λ that sum to I, then f(A) = ∑_λ f(λ) P_λ for every f defined on the spectrum of A.

definitions.name: strictly convex function
definitions.text: A function f on an interval with f((1 − t)x + ty) < (1 − t)f(x) + t f(y) for all x ≠ y in the interval and all t in (0, 1).

source.citation: David Sutter, Approximate Quantum Markov Chains, SpringerBriefs in Mathematical Physics, vol. 28, Springer, 2018.
source.revision: arXiv:1802.05477v1, 15 February 2018.
source.module: Chapter 2 Preliminaries, Section 2.3 Functions on Hermitian operators
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.14 (Klein's inequality). Let B1, B2 ∈ P(A) and f : (0, ∞) → ℝ be differentiable and convex. Then tr f(B1) − tr f(B2) ≥ tr (B1 − B2) f′(B2). If f is strictly convex, there is equality if and only if B1 = B2.
source.attribution: © David Sutter. Quoted from the arXiv version of Approximate Quantum Markov Chains for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the inequality for nonnegative operators and a function on (0, ∞). The authored statement allows any interval, asks for differentiability only on its interior, and adds the relative-entropy case f(x) = x log x. The source proves the inequality by differentiating t ↦ tr f(tB1 + (1 − t)B2) at t = 0. The authored proof follows the spectral double-sum proof in Appendix A, (A.1) and (A.2), of Carlen and Lieb, arXiv:1709.05450.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the spectral double-sum proof of Klein's inequality in Carlen and Lieb, arXiv:1709.05450, Appendix A. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, with the equality case for strictly convex f and the relative-entropy case.

steps.text: Tangent line bound. Let λ be an interior point of I. For x ≠ λ in I, the slope q(x) = (f(x) − f(λ))/(x − λ) is nondecreasing in x by convexity, and q(x) → f′(λ) as x → λ. So q(x) ≥ f′(λ) for x > λ and q(x) ≤ f′(λ) for x < λ. In both cases, multiplication by x − λ gives d(x, λ) := f(x) − f(λ) − f′(λ)(x − λ) ≥ 0 for every x ∈ I. If f is strictly convex and d(x, λ) = 0 for some x ≠ λ, then the midpoint m = (x + λ)/2 satisfies f(m) < (f(x) + f(λ))/2 = f(λ) + f′(λ)(m − λ). This contradicts d(m, λ) ≥ 0. So strict convexity gives d(x, λ) > 0 for every x ≠ λ.

Spectral expansion. By the spectral theorem, A = ∑_i λ_i P_i and B = ∑_j μ_j Q_j, with distinct eigenvalues λ_i and μ_j and orthogonal projections that satisfy ∑_i P_i = ∑_j Q_j = I. Then f(A) = ∑_i f(λ_i) P_i, f′(A) = ∑_i f′(λ_i) P_i and f(B) = ∑_j f(μ_j) Q_j. Insert ∑_i P_i = I or ∑_j Q_j = I into each trace. This gives Tr f(B) = ∑_{i,j} f(μ_j) Tr(P_i Q_j), Tr f(A) = ∑_{i,j} f(λ_i) Tr(P_i Q_j) and Tr[f′(A)(B − A)] = ∑_{i,j} f′(λ_i)(μ_j − λ_i) Tr(P_i Q_j). Hence Tr f(B) − Tr f(A) − Tr[f′(A)(B − A)] = ∑_{i,j} d(μ_j, λ_i) Tr(P_i Q_j).

Positivity of the weights. Since P_i and Q_j are orthogonal projections, Tr(P_i Q_j) = Tr(P_i P_i Q_j Q_j) = Tr(Q_j P_i P_i Q_j) = Tr((P_i Q_j)*(P_i Q_j)) ≥ 0, by cyclicity of the trace. It is the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of P_i Q_j. Every d(μ_j, λ_i) is nonnegative by step s1, because λ_i is interior and μ_j ∈ I. So the double sum of step s2 is nonnegative, which is the inequality.

Equality case. If A = B, both sides are equal. Conversely, let f be strictly convex and assume equality. Then every term of the double sum vanishes. For μ_j ≠ λ_i, d(μ_j, λ_i) > 0 by step s1, so ‖P_i Q_j‖₂ = 0 and Q_j P_i = (P_i Q_j)* = 0. Therefore B P_i = ∑_j μ_j Q_j P_i = λ_i ∑_{j: μ_j = λ_i} Q_j P_i = λ_i ∑_j Q_j P_i = λ_i P_i. Summing over i gives B = ∑_i B P_i = ∑_i λ_i P_i = A.

Relative-entropy case. Take I = [0, ∞) and f(x) = x log x with f(0) = 0. This f is continuous and strictly convex on I, since f″(x) = 1/x > 0 on (0, ∞), and f′(x) = log x + 1 on the interior. A positive definite has its spectrum in (0, ∞), and B positive semidefinite has its spectrum in I. The inequality gives Tr B log B − Tr A log A ≥ Tr[(log A + I)(B − A)] = Tr B log A − Tr A log A + Tr(B − A). Cancel Tr A log A to get Tr[B(log B − log A)] ≥ Tr(B − A), with equality if and only if A = B by step s4.

applications.title: Free energy of a nonequilibrium qubit state
applications.inputs: A qubit with Hamiltonian H = diag(0, ε) and an inverse temperature β with βε = log 3. The Gibbs state σ = e^(−βH)/Z and the pure state ρ = |+⟩⟨+|, where |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2.
applications.hypotheses: The Gibbs state σ is positive definite and the pure state ρ is positive semidefinite. So the relative-entropy case of Klein's inequality applies with A = σ and B = ρ.

steps.text: The Boltzmann weights are 1 and e^(−βε) = 1/3, so Z = 4/3 and σ = diag(3/4, 1/4). The ground-state weight is 1/(1 + 1/3) = 3/4.

Since log σ = −βH − (log Z) I, Klein's inequality with A = σ and B = ρ gives −S(ρ) + β Tr(ρH) + log Z ≥ Tr(ρ − σ) = 0, where S(ρ) = −Tr ρ log ρ. So the free energy F(ρ) = Tr(ρH) − S(ρ)/β is at least F(σ) = −(log Z)/β, with equality only for ρ = σ.
For the pure state, S(ρ) = 0 and Tr(ρH) = ε/2. In units of ε, the mean energy is 1/2 · 0 + 1/2 · 1 = 1/2. So βF(ρ) = (log 3)/2 ≈ 0.549.

For the Gibbs state, βF(σ) = −log(4/3) ≈ −0.288. The gap βF(ρ) − βF(σ) = (1/2) log 3 + log(4/3) = (1/2) log(16/3) ≈ 0.837 equals the relative entropy Tr ρ(log ρ − log σ), which is positive because ρ ≠ σ.

applications.conclusion: The pure state |+⟩⟨+| has free energy (log 3)/(2β), strictly above the Gibbs free energy −log(4/3)/β. Klein's inequality shows that the Gibbs state uniquely minimizes the free energy of the qubit.

limitations: The inequality is for traces. The operator inequality f(B) ≥ f(A) + f′(A)(B − A) can fail for a convex f that is not operator convex.
The statement is for matrices. For trace-class operators on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, the same proof needs extra conditions so that every trace is finite.

results.name: Lieb's concavity theorem
results.statement: Let n ≥ 1, let X be a complex n × n matrix and let p, q > 0 with p + q ≤ 1. Then F(A, B) = Tr(A^q X* B^p X) is jointly concave on pairs of positive definite n × n matrices: for positive definite A₁, A₂, B₁, B₂ and c ∈ [0, 1], F(cA₁ + (1 − c)A₂, cB₁ + (1 − c)B₂) ≥ c F(A₁, B₁) + (1 − c) F(A₂, B₂). The same holds on positive semidefinite matrices.
hypotheses: The exponents satisfy p > 0, q > 0 and p + q ≤ 1.
The matrix X is a fixed complex n × n matrix.
The matrices A and B range over the positive definite (or positive semidefinite) n × n matrices.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s3, s4 and s5 use the spectral theorem: commuting positive operators are diagonal in one basis, and functions of left and right multiplication operators are computed eigenvalue by eigenvalue.

definitions.name: jointly concave function
definitions.text: A function F on a convex set of pairs (A, B) with F(c(A₁, B₁) + (1 − c)(A₂, B₂)) ≥ c F(A₁, B₁) + (1 − c) F(A₂, B₂) for all c ∈ [0, 1].

definitions.name: operator convex function
definitions.text: A real function f on an interval with f(cS + (1 − c)T) ≤ c f(S) + (1 − c) f(T) in the matrix order, for all Hermitian S, T of every size with spectra in the interval.

definitions.name: matrix power
definitions.text: For a positive semidefinite A = ∑_λ λ P_λ and r > 0, A^r = ∑_λ λ^r P_λ.

source.citation: Eric A. Carlen, On some convexity and monotonicity inequalities of Elliott Lieb, in: The Physics and Mathematics of Elliott Lieb, The 90th Anniversary, Volume I, EMS Press, 2022.
source.module: Section 1.2 The first three theorems in Lieb's 1973 matrix inequality paper
source.excerpt: (Lieb, Theorem 1). For 0 ≤ s, t and s + t ≤ 1, and any fixed K ∈ Mn(C), the function (X, Y) ↦ Tr[K*Y^s K X^t] is jointly concave on Mn+(C) × Mn+(C).
source.attribution: © Eric A. Carlen. Quoted from the arXiv version of the survey for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source's Theorem 1.1 uses (X, Y, K, s, t) where the record uses (A, B, X, p, q), with Tr[K*Y^s K X^t] = Tr(A^q X* B^p X). The authored statement takes p, q > 0. The outline follows the proof of Corollary 3.3 in Effros, A matrix convexity approach to some celebrated quantum inequalities, PNAS 106 (2009) 1006-1008, arXiv:0802.1234, which uses the Hansen-Pedersen-Jensen inequality and matrix perspectives.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Corollary 3.3 in Effros (2009), Sections 2-3. Step s2 cites the source's Theorem 3.1, the Hansen-Pedersen-Jensen inequality, and step s4 cites the Löwner-Heinz operator convexity of −x^s and operator concavity of y^t. Step s6 adds the extension to positive semidefinite matrices.

steps.text: Reduction. Since q < 1, put s = q and t = p/(1 − q). Then 0 < s < 1, 0 < t ≤ 1 because p ≤ 1 − q, and (1 − s)t = p. So it suffices to show that (A, B) ↦ −Tr(A^s X* B^((1−s)t) X) is jointly convex. This is the source's rewriting of p + q as the convex combination (1 − t)q + t · 1.

Theorem 3.1 of the source, the subhomogeneous Hansen-Pedersen-Jensen inequality, proves: if f is operator convex on an interval that contains 0, f(0) ≤ 0, and the matrices C and D satisfy C*C + D*D ≤ I, then f(C*T₁C + D*T₂D) ≤ C* f(T₁) C + D* f(T₂) D for all Hermitian T₁, T₂ with spectra in the interval. The source refers to Hansen and Pedersen for its proof.

Theorem 3.2 of the source: let f be as in step s2 and let h > 0 be operator concave. For commuting positive operators L and R put (f∆h)(L, R) = h(R)^(1/2) f(h(R)^(−1/2) L h(R)^(−1/2)) h(R)^(1/2). Then f∆h is jointly convex on commuting positive pairs. Proof: let L = cL₁ + (1 − c)L₂ and R = cR₁ + (1 − c)R₂ with [L_j, R_j] = 0. Operator concavity gives c h(R₁) + (1 − c) h(R₂) ≤ h(R). So C = c^(1/2) h(R₁)^(1/2) h(R)^(−1/2) and D = (1 − c)^(1/2) h(R₂)^(1/2) h(R)^(−1/2) satisfy C*C + D*D ≤ I. Since L_j commutes with h(R_j), h(R)^(−1/2) L h(R)^(−1/2) = C*(L₁ h(R₁)^(−1))C + D*(L₂ h(R₂)^(−1))D. Step s2 and a multiplication by h(R)^(1/2) on both sides give (f∆h)(L, R) ≤ c(f∆h)(L₁, R₁) + (1 − c)(f∆h)(L₂, R₂).

Choice of functions. For 0 < s < 1 the function f(x) = −x^s is operator convex on [0, ∞) with f(0) = 0, and for 0 < t ≤ 1 the function h(y) = y^t is operator concave and positive on (0, ∞). The source cites these Löwner-Heinz facts. For commuting positive L and R, simultaneous diagonalization gives (f∆h)(L, R) = −R^t (L R^(−t))^s = −L^s R^((1−s)t).

Left and right multiplication. Give M_n the inner product ⟨Y, Z⟩ = Tr(Y Z*). For positive definite A and B, the maps L_A(Y) = AY and R_B(Y) = YB are positive definite operators on M_n, they commute, and they depend linearly on A and B. Their powers are L_A^s = L_(A^s) and R_B^r = R_(B^r). Step s3 with L = L_A and R = R_B makes (A, B) ↦ −L_(A^s) R_(B^p) jointly convex in the operator order on M_n. Evaluate the quadratic form at Y = X*: ⟨−L_(A^s) R_(B^p)(X*), X*⟩ = −Tr(A^s X* B^p X). A quadratic form preserves the operator order, so −F is jointly convex and F is jointly concave on positive definite pairs.

Positive semidefinite matrices. For positive semidefinite A₁, A₂, B₁, B₂ and ε > 0, apply step s5 to A_j + εI and B_j + εI. The maps A ↦ A^q and B ↦ B^p are continuous on positive semidefinite matrices because p, q > 0. Letting ε → 0 in the concavity inequality gives joint concavity on positive semidefinite pairs.

applications.title: Convexity of the Wigner–Yanase skew information of a qubit
applications.inputs: The Wigner–Yanase–Dyson skew information I_p(ρ, K) = Tr(ρK²) − Tr(ρ^p K ρ^(1−p) K) of a density matrix ρ and a Hermitian observable K, with 0 < p < 1. Numerical instance: p = 1/2, K = σ_x, ρ₁ = diag(4/5, 1/5), ρ₂ = diag(1/5, 4/5) and the mixture ρ = (ρ₁ + ρ₂)/2 = I/2.
applications.hypotheses: Take q = 1 − p, X = K and A = B = ρ. Then p, q > 0 and p + q = 1, so the theorem applies. The density matrices are positive semidefinite.

steps.text: Restrict the jointly concave map to the diagonal A = B = ρ. Then ρ ↦ Tr(ρ^(1−p) K ρ^p K) is concave. The term Tr(ρK²) is linear in ρ. So ρ ↦ I_p(ρ, K) is convex: mixing states cannot increase the skew information.
For ρ = diag(a, b) and K = σ_x, one has σ_x ρ^(1/2) σ_x = diag(√b, √a), so Tr(ρ^(1/2) σ_x ρ^(1/2) σ_x) = 2√(ab). Since σ_x² = I, I_(1/2)(ρ, σ_x) = 1 − 2√(ab).
For ρ₁ and ρ₂, √(ab) = √(4/25) = 2/5, so both skew informations equal 1 − 2 · (2/5) = 1/5.
For the mixture ρ = I/2, √(ab) = 1/2 and I_(1/2)(I/2, σ_x) = 1 − 2 · (1/2) = 0. Convexity requires 0 ≤ (1/5 + 1/5)/2 = 1/5, which holds.

applications.conclusion: The skew information I_(1/2)(ρ, σ_x) equals 1/5 for each of the states diag(4/5, 1/5) and diag(1/5, 4/5) and 0 for their equal mixture I/2. Lieb's concavity theorem gives this convexity for every state and every observable, which settles the Wigner–Yanase–Dyson conjecture.

limitations: The outline needs p, q > 0. If p = 0 or q = 0, the map reduces to the operator concavity of x^r for 0 ≤ r ≤ 1.
Joint concavity fails in general when p + q > 1. Ando's convexity theorem (Theorem 1.5 of the source) gives joint convexity of Tr(X* A^q X B^(−r)) for 1 ≤ q ≤ 2, 0 ≤ r ≤ 1 and q − r ≥ 1.

results.name: Strong subadditivity of von Neumann entropy
results.statement: Let H_A, H_B and H_C be finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and let ρ_ABC be a density matrix on H_A ⊗ H_B ⊗ H_C, with marginals ρ_AB, ρ_BC and ρ_B obtained by partial traces. Write S(ρ) = −Tr ρ log ρ. Then S(ρ_ABC) + S(ρ_B) ≤ S(ρ_AB) + S(ρ_BC). Equivalently, the quantum conditional mutual information I(A:C|B) = S(ρ_AB) + S(ρ_BC) − S(ρ_ABC) − S(ρ_B) is nonnegative.
hypotheses: The Hilbert spaces H_A, H_B and H_C are finite-dimensional.
The operator ρ_ABC is a density matrix: positive semidefinite with trace 1.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s2 and s4 use the spectral theorem for positive operators on the Hilbert–Schmidt space of matrices to define the logarithm of the relative modular operator.
Step s6 extends the inequality from invertible to all density matrices with the continuity of the entropy, which follows from a uniform polynomial approximation of −x log x.

definitions.name: quantum relative entropy
definitions.text: S(ρ‖σ) = Tr ρ(log ρ − log σ) for density matrices ρ and σ with σ invertible.

definitions.name: relative modular operator
definitions.text: For invertible density matrices ρ and σ on H, the linear map Δ(X) = σXρ^(−1) on the matrices on H, with the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product ⟨X, Y⟩ = Tr(X*Y).

definitions.name: operator convex function
definitions.text: A function f on an interval with f(pX + (1 − p)Y) ≤ p f(X) + (1 − p) f(Y) for all Hermitian X, Y of every size with spectra in the interval and all p ∈ [0, 1].

source.citation: Eric A. Carlen, On some convexity and monotonicity inequalities of Elliott Lieb, in: The Physics and Mathematics of Elliott Lieb, The 90th Anniversary, Volume I, EMS Press, 2022.
source.module: Section 1.4 Strong subadditivity of the quantum entropy
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.15 (Lieb Ruskai 1973, SSA and two equivalent formulations). The following statements are all true, and equivalent in that once any one of them is proven, simple arguments yield the other two: (1) For all density matrices ρ123 on H1 ⊗ H2 ⊗ H3, (1.4.1) is satisfied. …
source.attribution: © Eric A. Carlen. Quoted from the arXiv version of the survey for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Part (1) of the source's Theorem 1.15 is the inequality (1.4.1), S12 + S23 ≥ S123 + S2, displayed on p. 16. The authored statement is (1.4.1) with 1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C. The source derives (1) from the monotonicity of relative entropy under partial traces, part (3). The outline proves that monotonicity by the relative modular operator method of Petz, as presented by Nielsen and Petz, Quantum Inf. Comput. 5 (2005) 507–513, arXiv:quant-ph/0408130.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow Petz's proof as presented by Nielsen and Petz (2005), Sections 1-4: strong subadditivity follows from the monotonicity of relative entropy, which follows from the relative modular operator. Steps s3 and s4 cite the source for its Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 on operator convex functions. Step s6 adds the continuity argument that the source omits.

steps.text: Reduction to monotonicity. Assume first that ρ_ABC is invertible, so that every marginal is invertible. Let τ = I_A/d_A. Since log(τ ⊗ ρ_B) = −(log d_A) I + I_A ⊗ log ρ_B, one finds S(ρ_AB ‖ τ ⊗ ρ_B) = log d_A − S(ρ_AB) + S(ρ_B) and S(ρ_ABC ‖ τ ⊗ ρ_BC) = log d_A − S(ρ_ABC) + S(ρ_BC). The partial trace over C maps ρ_ABC to ρ_AB and τ ⊗ ρ_BC to τ ⊗ ρ_B. So the monotonicity S(ρ_X ‖ σ_X) ≤ S(ρ_XY ‖ σ_XY) for invertible states on H_X ⊗ H_Y, with X = AB and Y = C, gives S(ρ_ABC) + S(ρ_B) ≤ S(ρ_AB) + S(ρ_BC). This is the identity (5)-(6) of the source and the step (3) ⇒ (1) of Carlen's Theorem 1.15.

Relative modular operator. For invertible ρ and σ on H, define L(Z) = σZ and R(Z) = Zρ^(−1) on the matrices on H with ⟨Z, W⟩ = Tr(Z*W). Both maps are strictly positive and they commute, so Δ = LR is strictly positive and log Δ = log L + log R, where (log L)(Z) = (log σ)Z and (log R)(Z) = −Z log ρ. Hence ⟨ρ^(1/2), −(log Δ)(ρ^(1/2))⟩ = Tr ρ log ρ − Tr ρ log σ = S(ρ‖σ). This is equation (7) of the source.

Lemma 1 of the source proves that −log is operator convex on (0, ∞). The source first shows that 1/x is operator convex: the case X = I reduces to scalar convexity because I commutes with Y, and the congruence Y ↦ X^(−1/2) Y X^(−1/2) gives the general case. Then −log X = ∫₀^∞ ((X + tI)^(−1) − (1 + t)^(−1) I) dt, and each integrand is operator convex in X.

Lemma 2 of the source proves an operator Jensen inequality: if f is operator convex and U: V → W is an isometry, then f(U†XU) ≤ U† f(X) U for every Hermitian X on W with spectrum in the domain of f. The source proves it with the projector P onto the range of U and a unitary dilation that mixes P X P with Q X Q, where Q = I − P. Here it is applied on the Hilbert–Schmidt spaces of matrices, with f = −log.

The isometry. For invertible states ρ_XY and σ_XY with marginals ρ_X and σ_X, define U(Z) = (Z ρ_X^(−1/2) ⊗ I_Y) ρ_XY^(1/2) from matrices on H_X to matrices on H_X ⊗ H_Y. Then U(ρ_X^(1/2)) = ρ_XY^(1/2). A direct computation with the partial trace gives ⟨UZ, UZ′⟩ = Tr(ρ_XY (ρ_X^(−1/2) Z* Z′ ρ_X^(−1/2) ⊗ I)) = Tr(Z* Z′), so U is an isometry. The same computation gives U† Δ_XY U = Δ_X, where Δ_X and Δ_XY are the relative modular operators of the pairs (ρ_X, σ_X) and (ρ_XY, σ_XY).

Conclusion. By steps s2, s5, s3 and s4, S(ρ_X‖σ_X) = ⟨ρ_X^(1/2), −log(U†Δ_XY U) ρ_X^(1/2)⟩ ≤ ⟨ρ_X^(1/2), −U† log(Δ_XY) U ρ_X^(1/2)⟩ = ⟨ρ_XY^(1/2), −log(Δ_XY) ρ_XY^(1/2)⟩ = S(ρ_XY‖σ_XY). This is the monotonicity used in step s1, so strong subadditivity holds for invertible ρ_ABC. For a general ρ_ABC, apply it to ρ_ε = (1 − ε)ρ_ABC + ε I/(d_A d_B d_C) and let ε → 0. The entropy is continuous on density matrices, because −x log x is a uniform limit of polynomials on [0, 1], and the marginals of ρ_ε converge to those of ρ_ABC.

applications.title: Concavity of block entropies on a translation-invariant spin ring
applications.inputs: A ring of N qubits in a translation-invariant state, and S_n the entropy of n consecutive sites, with S_0 = 0. Numerical instance: the GHZ state (|0000⟩ + |1111⟩)/√2 on N = 4 sites, with entropies in bits.
applications.hypotheses: Every block of sites is a finite-dimensional system and the global state is a density matrix. A change of logarithm base multiplies all entropies by one positive constant, so the inequality holds in bits.

steps.text: For 1 ≤ n ≤ N − 1, take A = site 1, B = sites 2, …, n and C = site n + 1. By translation invariance S(ABC) = S_(n+1), S(B) = S_(n−1) and S(AB) = S(BC) = S_n. Strong subadditivity gives S_(n+1) + S_(n−1) ≤ 2S_n. So the increments S_(n+1) − S_n do not increase: the block entropy is concave in n. For n = 1 the block B is empty and the inequality is subadditivity.

For the GHZ ring, the marginal on any block of 1, 2 or 3 sites is (|0…0⟩⟨0…0| + |1…1⟩⟨1…1|)/2, with entropy 1 bit, and the full state is pure. So (S_0, …, S_4) = (0, 1, 1, 1, 0) and the increments are 1, 0, 0, −1, which do not increase.
The second difference at n = 3 is S_4 + S_2 − 2S_3 = 0 + 1 − 2 = −1 ≤ 0, as concavity requires.
For the tripartition A = site 1, B = site 2, C = site 3, the conditional mutual information is I(A:C|B) = S_2 + S_2 − S_3 − S_1 = 1 + 1 − 1 − 1 = 0 bits.

On an infinite chain, the increments S_(n+1) − S_n decrease. Since S_n ≥ 0 for all n, their limit s is finite and nonnegative, and S_n/n → s by averaging. This limit is the mean entropy of the state, the problem that motivated the conjecture of Lanford and Robinson.

applications.conclusion: Strong subadditivity makes the block entropy S_n of a translation-invariant state concave in n. For the GHZ ring of 4 qubits the block entropies (0, 1, 1, 1, 0) have nonincreasing increments, and on infinite chains concavity gives the existence of the mean entropy lim S_n/n.

limitations: The outline proves the inequality for finite-dimensional systems. The extension to infinite dimensions needs finite entropies and a separate argument.
The statement does not describe the equality case. Petz showed that equality holds exactly when a recovery map that acts on B rebuilds ρ_ABC from ρ_AB.

results.name: Araki–Lieb triangle inequality
results.statement: Let H_A and H_B be finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, let ρ_AB be a density matrix on H_A ⊗ H_B, and let ρ_A = Tr_B ρ_AB and ρ_B = Tr_A ρ_AB be its marginals. Write S(ρ) = −Tr ρ log ρ for the von Neumann entropy, with 0 log 0 = 0. Then |S(ρ_A) − S(ρ_B)| ≤ S(ρ_AB) ≤ S(ρ_A) + S(ρ_B).
hypotheses: The Hilbert spaces H_A and H_B are finite-dimensional.
The operator ρ_AB is a density matrix on H_A ⊗ H_B: positive semidefinite with trace 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 proves subadditivity with the relative-entropy case of Klein's inequality, applied to ρ_AB and ρ_A ⊗ ρ_B.
Step s2 approximates −x log x uniformly on [0, 1] by polynomials to show that the von Neumann entropy is continuous.
Steps s1 and s3 use the spectral theorem to diagonalize ρ_A ⊗ ρ_B and ρ_AB, and step s4 uses it for the eigenspaces of C*C.

definitions.name: von Neumann entropy
definitions.text: S(ρ) = −Tr ρ log ρ = −∑_k p_k log p_k, where p_k are the eigenvalues of the density matrix ρ, with 0 log 0 = 0.

definitions.name: partial trace
definitions.text: The linear map Tr_B from operators on H_A ⊗ H_B to operators on H_A with Tr[(Tr_B X) Y] = Tr[X (Y ⊗ I_B)] for every operator Y on H_A.

definitions.name: purification
definitions.text: A unit vector ψ in H_A ⊗ H_B ⊗ H_R such that Tr_R |ψ⟩⟨ψ| = ρ_AB.

source.citation: Eric A. Carlen, On some convexity and monotonicity inequalities of Elliott Lieb, in: The Physics and Mathematics of Elliott Lieb, The 90th Anniversary, Volume I, EMS Press, 2022.
source.module: Section 1.5 The Araki-Lieb inequality
source.excerpt: … Triangle Inequality). Let ρ12 be any density matrix on the tensor product of finite dimensional Hilbert spaces, H1 ⊗ H2. Then |S1 − S2| ≤ S12.
source.attribution: © Eric A. Carlen. Quoted from the arXiv version of the survey for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states Theorem 1.19 (Araki-Lieb Triangle Inequality) with S_j the entropy of the marginal ρ_j. The authored statement adds the upper bound by subadditivity, which the source quotes in Section 1.4. The authored proof follows the source's proof by purification (Lemma 1.20 and (1.5.4)) and adds a proof of subadditivity by Klein's inequality and a continuity argument.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the purification proof of Theorem 1.19 in Carlen (2022), with a proof of subadditivity by Klein's inequality. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for finite-dimensional systems, both the lower and the upper bound.

steps.text: Subadditivity when ρ_A and ρ_B are positive definite. Then σ = ρ_A ⊗ ρ_B is positive definite. If ρ_A = ∑ a_i |e_i⟩⟨e_i| and ρ_B = ∑ b_j |f_j⟩⟨f_j|, then σ has eigenvectors e_i ⊗ f_j with eigenvalues a_i b_j, so log σ = log ρ_A ⊗ I + I ⊗ log ρ_B. The relative-entropy case of Klein's inequality gives Tr ρ_AB(log ρ_AB − log σ) ≥ Tr(ρ_AB − σ) = 1 − 1 = 0. By the defining property of the partial trace, Tr[ρ_AB(log ρ_A ⊗ I)] = Tr ρ_A log ρ_A, and likewise for B. So −S(ρ_AB) + S(ρ_A) + S(ρ_B) ≥ 0.

Subadditivity in general. Let η(x) = −x log x on [0, 1], with η(0) = 0. It is continuous, so by the Weierstrass theorem there are polynomials p_k with sup_[0,1] |η − p_k| → 0. For a density matrix ρ on a space of dimension d, |Tr η(ρ) − Tr p_k(ρ)| ≤ d sup |η − p_k|, because the eigenvalues of ρ lie in [0, 1]. Each Tr p_k(ρ) is a polynomial in the entries of ρ. So S = Tr η is a uniform limit of continuous functions and is continuous. For 0 < ε < 1, put ρ_ε = (1 − ε)ρ_AB + ε I/(d_A d_B). Its marginals (1 − ε)ρ_A + ε I/d_A and (1 − ε)ρ_B + ε I/d_B are positive definite. Step s1 applies to ρ_ε, and ε → 0 gives S(ρ_AB) ≤ S(ρ_A) + S(ρ_B).

Purification. By the spectral theorem, ρ_AB = ∑_k p_k |u_k⟩⟨u_k| with an orthonormal basis (u_k) of H_A ⊗ H_B and p_k ≥ 0. Let H_R have an orthonormal basis (r_k) of the same size, and put ψ = ∑_k √p_k u_k ⊗ r_k. Then ‖ψ‖² = ∑ p_k = 1, Tr_R |ψ⟩⟨ψ| = ∑_{k,l} √(p_k p_l) ⟨r_l, r_k⟩ |u_k⟩⟨u_l| = ρ_AB, and ρ_R = Tr_AB |ψ⟩⟨ψ| = ∑_k p_k |r_k⟩⟨r_k|. So ρ_R and ρ_AB have the same eigenvalues and S(ρ_R) = S(ρ_AB).

Pure states have equal marginal entropies. Let φ be a unit vector in H_X ⊗ H_Y, written φ = ∑_{i,j} C_ij x_i ⊗ y_j in orthonormal bases. Then ρ_X has the matrix CC* and ρ_Y has the matrix (C*C)^T, which has the same eigenvalues as C*C. If C*Cv = λv with λ > 0, then CC*(Cv) = λCv and ‖Cv‖² = λ‖v‖². So v ↦ Cv/√λ maps the λ-eigenspace of C*C isometrically into the λ-eigenspace of CC*, and the same argument with C* gives the reverse map. Hence CC* and C*C have the same nonzero eigenvalues with the same multiplicities, and S(ρ_X) = S(ρ_Y), because zero eigenvalues contribute 0. With X = A and Y = BR, this gives S(ρ_A) = S(ρ_BR) for the state ψ of step s3.

Conclusion. Subadditivity (step s2) on H_B ⊗ H_R and steps s3 and s4 give S(ρ_A) = S(ρ_BR) ≤ S(ρ_B) + S(ρ_R) = S(ρ_B) + S(ρ_AB). So S(ρ_A) − S(ρ_B) ≤ S(ρ_AB). The same argument with the roles of A and B exchanged gives S(ρ_B) = S(ρ_AR) ≤ S(ρ_A) + S(ρ_AB). Together these give |S(ρ_A) − S(ρ_B)| ≤ S(ρ_AB). Step s2 gives the upper bound S(ρ_AB) ≤ S(ρ_A) + S(ρ_B).

applications.title: Negative conditional entropy of a Bell pair with an extra noisy qubit
applications.inputs: Three qubits A, B1 and B2, with B = B1B2. The state is ρ_AB = |Φ⁺⟩⟨Φ⁺|_(AB1) ⊗ (I/2)_(B2), where Φ⁺ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 is a Bell state. Entropies are in bits (logarithm to base 2).
applications.hypotheses: H_A has dimension 2 and H_B has dimension 4. The state ρ_AB is a density matrix. A change of the logarithm base multiplies every entropy by the same positive constant, so the inequality holds in bits.

steps.text: The entropy of a tensor product is the sum of the entropies, because its eigenvalues are the products of the eigenvalues of the factors. So S(AB) = S(Φ⁺) + S(I/2) = 0 + 1 = 1 bit, since Φ⁺ is pure.
The marginal of Φ⁺ on A is I/2, so S(A) = 1 bit. The marginal on B is (I/2) ⊗ (I/2), so S(B) = 1 + 1 = 2 bits.
The lower bound reads |S(A) − S(B)| = |1 − 2| = 1 ≤ S(AB) = 1. It holds with equality. The upper bound reads 1 ≤ 1 + 2 = 3 and is strict.

The conditional entropy is S(A|B) = S(AB) − S(B) = 1 − 2 = −1 bit. The triangle inequality says S(A|B) ≥ −S(A) = −1, so this state reaches the lowest possible conditional entropy. A negative conditional entropy is impossible for a classical joint distribution.

applications.conclusion: For the Bell pair with an extra maximally mixed qubit, S(A) = 1, S(B) = 2 and S(AB) = 1 bit. The Araki–Lieb bound |S(A) − S(B)| ≤ S(AB) holds with equality, and the conditional entropy S(A|B) = −1 reaches its lowest value −S(A).

limitations: The proof uses finite dimensions for the purification and the continuity argument. In infinite dimensions the entropies can be infinite, and the statement needs extra conditions.
The statement does not describe the states that give equality. Reference [23] of the source determines these cases.

results.name: Classification calibration of convex surrogate losses
results.statement: Let φ: ℝ → [0, ∞) be convex. For η ∈ [0, 1] and α ∈ ℝ put C_η(α) = ηφ(α) + (1 − η)φ(−α), H(η) = inf_{α ∈ ℝ} C_η(α) and H⁻(η) = inf {C_η(α) : α(2η − 1) ≤ 0}. Call φ classification-calibrated if H⁻(η) > H(η) for every η ∈ [0, 1] with η ≠ 1/2. Then φ is classification-calibrated if and only if φ is differentiable at 0 and φ′(0) < 0.
hypotheses: The loss φ is a convex function from ℝ to [0, ∞).
Classification calibration is the strict inequality H⁻(η) > H(η) for every η ≠ 1/2 in [0, 1].
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only the monotonicity of the difference quotients of a convex function on ℝ, which step s1 proves from the definition of convexity.

definitions.name: classification-calibrated
definitions.text: H⁻(η) > H(η) for every η ≠ 1/2: a score with the wrong sign, or the score 0, always has a strictly larger optimal conditional φ-risk.

proof.scope: The full statement: both directions of the equivalence for every convex φ: ℝ → [0, ∞).

steps.text: One-sided derivatives. Let g: ℝ → ℝ be convex and q(t) = (g(t) − g(0))/t for t ≠ 0. For 0 < s < t, convexity gives g(s) ≤ (s/t)g(t) + (1 − s/t)g(0), so q(s) ≤ q(t). The same argument gives q(s) ≤ q(t) for s < t < 0. For s < 0 < t, 0 = (t/(t − s))s + (−s/(t − s))t, and convexity gives (t − s)g(0) ≤ t g(s) − s g(t), which rearranges to q(s) ≤ q(t). So q is nondecreasing on ℝ ∖ {0}, and the one-sided derivatives a = lim_{t↑0} q(t) and b = lim_{t↓0} q(t) exist with q(s) ≤ a ≤ b ≤ q(t) for s < 0 < t. Hence g(α) ≥ g(0) + bα for α > 0 and g(α) ≥ g(0) + aα for α < 0. If g is differentiable at 0, then a = b = g′(0) and g(α) ≥ g(0) + g′(0)α for all α.

Reduction to η > 1/2. For all η and α, C_η(α) = C_{1−η}(−α), and the constraint α(2η − 1) ≤ 0 becomes (−α)(2(1 − η) − 1) ≤ 0. So H(η) = H(1 − η) and H⁻(η) = H⁻(1 − η), and it is enough to treat η ∈ (1/2, 1]. For such η, H⁻(η) = inf_{α ≤ 0} C_η(α) ≤ C_η(0) = φ(0).

Forward direction, first part. Let φ be classification-calibrated and let a ≤ b be the one-sided derivatives of φ at 0 from step s1. Fix η ∈ (1/2, 1]. For α > 0, step s1 gives φ(α) ≥ φ(0) + bα and φ(−α) ≥ φ(0) − aα, so C_η(α) ≥ φ(0) + (ηb − (1 − η)a)α. Suppose ηb − (1 − η)a ≥ 0. Then C_η(α) ≥ φ(0) ≥ H⁻(η) for every α > 0 by step s2, and C_η(α) ≥ H⁻(η) for every α ≤ 0 by definition. So H(η) ≥ H⁻(η), which contradicts calibration. Hence ηb < (1 − η)a for every η ∈ (1/2, 1].

Forward direction, conclusion. Since a ≤ b and 1 − η > 0, step s3 gives ηb < (1 − η)a ≤ (1 − η)b, so (2η − 1)b < 0 and b < 0. Letting η decrease to 1/2 in ηb < (1 − η)a gives b/2 ≤ a/2, so b ≤ a. With a ≤ b this gives a = b. So φ is differentiable at 0 and φ′(0) = b < 0.

Converse. Let φ be differentiable at 0 with φ′(0) < 0, and fix η ∈ (1/2, 1]. C_η is convex as a sum of convex functions with nonnegative weights, and it is differentiable at 0 with C_η′(0) = ηφ′(0) − (1 − η)φ′(0) = (2η − 1)φ′(0) < 0. Step s1 for g = C_η gives C_η(α) ≥ C_η(0) + αC_η′(0) ≥ C_η(0) for every α ≤ 0, so H⁻(η) = C_η(0) = φ(0). Because C_η′(0) < 0, some α₀ > 0 has C_η(α₀) < C_η(0). So H(η) ≤ C_η(α₀) < φ(0) = H⁻(η). By step s2 the same strict inequality holds for η ∈ [0, 1/2), so φ is classification-calibrated.

applications.title: The hinge loss is calibrated and the perceptron loss is not
applications.inputs: The hinge loss φ(α) = max(0, 1 − α) of support vector machines, the perceptron loss φ_p(α) = max(0, −α), and the conditional probability η = 3/4 that the label is +1.
applications.hypotheses: Both losses are maxima of affine functions, so they are convex, and both take values in [0, ∞).

steps.text: The hinge loss has its only kink at α = 1, so it is differentiable at 0 with φ′(0) = −1 < 0. By the criterion it is classification-calibrated.
Scores α ≤ 0 give C_η(α) ≥ C_η(0) = (3/4)·1 + (1/4)·1 = 1, so H⁻(3/4) = 1 = φ(0) > 1/2 = H(3/4), as the criterion predicts.

The perceptron loss has one-sided derivatives −1 and 0 at 0, so it is not differentiable at 0 and the criterion says it is not calibrated. Directly, at η = 3/4 its conditional risk (3/4)max(0, −α) + (1/4)max(0, α) is at least 0 = C_η(0), and positive scores are no better: C_η(1) = (3/4)·0 + (1/4)·1 = 1/4 > 0. So H(3/4) = H⁻(3/4) = 0.

applications.conclusion: For η = 3/4 the hinge loss separates the right sign from the wrong sign by H⁻(3/4) − H(3/4) = 1/2. The perceptron loss gives the gap 0, because the score 0 is already optimal, so minimizing it does not force the sign of the Bayes classifier.

limitations: The criterion is for convex losses only. For a nonconvex loss, classification calibration must be checked from the definition.
Calibration is a pointwise, qualitative condition. The quantitative relation between the excess φ-risk and the excess 0-1 risk is the ψ-transform of the source, which this statement does not include.

results.name: Chernoff–Stein lemma
results.statement: Let P and Q be probability measures on a measurable space (X, 𝓕), and let D(P‖Q) ∈ [0, ∞] be the relative entropy, with D(P‖Q) = ∞ unless P ≪ Q. For n ≥ 1 let Pⁿ and Qⁿ be the n-fold product measures on (Xⁿ, 𝓕^⊗n). For 0 < ε < 1 let β_n(ε) = inf {Qⁿ(A) : A ∈ 𝓕^⊗n, Pⁿ(A) ≥ 1 − ε}, the smallest type-II error of a test that accepts P on A with type-I error at most ε. Then lim_{n→∞} −(1/n) log β_n(ε) = D(P‖Q) for every ε ∈ (0, 1), with −log 0 = ∞.
hypotheses: P and Q are probability measures on the same measurable space (X, 𝓕).
The observations X₁, …, X_n are independent with common law P under the null hypothesis and common law Q under the alternative.
The bound ε on the type-I error is fixed in the open interval (0, 1).

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Radon–Nikodym theorem for the density h = dP/dQ.
Step s1 uses Tonelli's theorem to integrate the product density over a measurable rectangle.
Step s1 extends the product-density formula from measurable rectangles to all of 𝓕^⊗n with the π-λ theorem.
Step s2 applies the weak law of large numbers to the log-likelihood ratio and to its truncations.
Step s2 uses monotone convergence for the truncated log-likelihood ratio when D(P‖Q) = ∞.
Step s5 bounds the Qⁿ-probability that some observation falls in a Q-null set.

definitions.name: type-I and type-II error
definitions.text: For a test that accepts P on the set A ⊆ Xⁿ, the type-I error is Pⁿ(Xⁿ ∖ A) and the type-II error is Qⁿ(A).

definitions.name: log-likelihood ratio
definitions.text: For P ≪ Q with h = dP/dQ, L_n(x) = ∑_{i=1}^n log h(x_i) on Xⁿ, with log 0 = −∞.

source.citation: Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu, Information Theory: From Coding to Learning, Cambridge University Press, 2025.
source.revision: Prepublication version on the authors' homepage, export of August 16, 2024.
source.module: Section 14.5 Asymptotics: Stein's regime
source.excerpt: Theorem 14.14 (Stein's lemma) Consider the iid setting (14.14) where PXn = P^n and QXn = Q^n. Then Vϵ = D(P‖Q), ∀ϵ ∈ (0, 1). Consequently, V = D(P‖Q).
source.attribution: © Yury Polyanskiy and Yihong Wu. Prepublication version that the authors provide free for personal use. Quoted for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source defines the exponent V_ϵ in Definition 14.13 with randomized tests and a lower limit. The authored statement uses deterministic tests, writes the optimal type-II error as β_n(ε), and shows that the limit exists and equals D(P‖Q). The authored proof follows the source's proof: a threshold test on the log-likelihood ratio with the weak law of large numbers, a change-of-measure converse, and the test 'some observation lies in a Q-null set' when P is not absolutely continuous with respect to Q. It adds a truncation argument for the law of large numbers when D(P‖Q) = ∞.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 14.14 in Polyanskiy and Wu. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every ε ∈ (0, 1), including the cases D(P‖Q) = ∞.

steps.text: Product density. Assume P ≪ Q and let h = dP/dQ (Radon–Nikodym). Put h_n(x) = ∏_{i=1}^n h(x_i) and L_n = ∑_{i=1}^n log h(x_i) ∈ [−∞, ∞), so h_n = e^(L_n). For a measurable rectangle R = A₁ × … × A_n, Tonelli's theorem gives ∫_R h_n dQⁿ = ∏_i ∫_{A_i} h dQ = ∏_i P(A_i) = Pⁿ(R). Measurable rectangles form a π-system that generates 𝓕^⊗n, and A ↦ ∫_A h_n dQⁿ and Pⁿ are probability measures that agree on it. By the π-λ theorem, Pⁿ(A) = ∫_A h_n dQⁿ for every A ∈ 𝓕^⊗n.

Law of large numbers for L_n. Under Pⁿ the coordinates are independent with law P, so Y_i = log h(x_i) are independent and identically distributed. They are real-valued almost surely because P(h = 0) = 0. Also E[Y_i⁻] = ∫ h (log h)⁻ dQ ≤ 1/e and E[Y_i] = D(P‖Q). If D(P‖Q) < ∞, the Y_i are integrable, and the weak law gives Pⁿ(|L_n/n − D(P‖Q)| > η) → 0 for every η > 0. If D(P‖Q) = ∞, fix t ∈ ℝ. By monotone convergence, E[min(Y_i, M)] = E[min(Y_i⁺, M)] − E[Y_i⁻] → ∞ as M → ∞, so some M ≥ 0 has E[min(Y_i, M)] > t. The weak law for the integrable variables min(Y_i, M) and L_n ≥ ∑_i min(Y_i, M) give Pⁿ(L_n ≤ nt) → 0.

Achievability when P ≪ Q. Fix a real t < D(P‖Q) and let A_n = {L_n > nt}. By step s2, Pⁿ(A_n) → 1, so Pⁿ(A_n) ≥ 1 − ε for all large n. On A_n, h_n > e^(nt), so by step s1, 1 ≥ Pⁿ(A_n) = ∫_{A_n} h_n dQⁿ ≥ e^(nt) Qⁿ(A_n). Hence β_n(ε) ≤ Qⁿ(A_n) ≤ e^(−nt) for all large n, and lim inf −(1/n) log β_n(ε) ≥ t. Letting t increase to D(P‖Q) gives lim inf −(1/n) log β_n(ε) ≥ D(P‖Q). This finishes the proof when D(P‖Q) = ∞.

Converse when P ≪ Q and D = D(P‖Q) < ∞. Fix δ > 0 and put B_n = {L_n ≤ n(D + δ)} and p_n = Pⁿ(Xⁿ ∖ B_n). Let A ∈ 𝓕^⊗n with Pⁿ(A) ≥ 1 − ε. On B_n, h_n ≤ e^(n(D+δ)), so by step s1, Pⁿ(A ∩ B_n) ≤ e^(n(D+δ)) Qⁿ(A). Hence 1 − ε ≤ Pⁿ(A) ≤ e^(n(D+δ)) Qⁿ(A) + p_n. By step s2, p_n → 0, so p_n ≤ (1 − ε)/2 for all large n. For such n, every admissible A has Qⁿ(A) ≥ e^(−n(D+δ)) (1 − ε)/2, and so β_n(ε) ≥ e^(−n(D+δ)) (1 − ε)/2 > 0. Then −(1/n) log β_n(ε) ≤ D + δ + (1/n) log(2/(1 − ε)), so lim sup −(1/n) log β_n(ε) ≤ D + δ. Let δ → 0 and combine with step s3.

The case where P is not absolutely continuous with respect to Q. Then D(P‖Q) = ∞ and there is B ∈ 𝓕 with Q(B) = 0 < P(B). Let A_n = {x : x_i ∈ B for some i}. By the union bound, Qⁿ(A_n) ≤ n Q(B) = 0. Also Pⁿ(A_n) = 1 − (1 − P(B))ⁿ → 1, so Pⁿ(A_n) ≥ 1 − ε for all large n. For such n, β_n(ε) = 0 and −(1/n) log β_n(ε) = ∞ = D(P‖Q).

applications.title: Testing a fair coin against a biased coin
applications.inputs: Independent coin flips with P = Bernoulli(1/2) under the null hypothesis and Q = Bernoulli(1/4) under the alternative. A fixed bound ε ∈ (0, 1) on the type-I error. Sample size n = 20 for the numerical value.
applications.hypotheses: P and Q are probability measures on X = {0, 1} with all subsets measurable, and P ≪ Q because Q gives positive mass to both points.

steps.text: The lemma gives β_n(ε) = e^(−n(D(P‖Q) + o(1))) for every fixed ε. For n = 20 the leading factor is e^(−20 D(P‖Q)) = (3/4)^10 = 59049/1048576 ≈ 0.056.
If the roles are exchanged, so that the test must keep the error under Q small, the exponent is D(Q‖P) = (1/4) log(1/2) + (3/4) log(3/2) = (1/4) log((1/2)(3/2)³) = (1/4) log(27/16).

Since (1/2) log(4/3) = (1/4) log(16/9), the comparison of the two exponents is the comparison of 16/9 and 27/16, that is, of 16 · 16 = 256 and 9 · 27 = 243. The difference 13 is positive, so D(P‖Q) > D(Q‖P).

applications.conclusion: When the type-I error is held below a fixed ε, the best type-II error for testing Bernoulli(1/2) against Bernoulli(1/4) decays at the rate (1/2) log(4/3) per flip. With the roles exchanged the rate is (1/4) log(27/16), which is smaller, so the choice of the protected hypothesis changes the error exponent.

limitations: The lemma fixes ε and gives only the exponential rate. It does not give the factor e^(o(n)) in β_n(ε) or how it depends on ε.
When both error probabilities must decay exponentially, the trade-off between the two exponents is the Chernoff regime, which this statement does not cover.

results.name: Prékopa–Leindler inequality
results.statement: Let n ≥ 1 and 0 < λ < 1. Let f, g, h: ℝⁿ → [0, ∞] be Lebesgue measurable functions such that h((1 − λ)x + λy) ≥ f(x)^(1−λ) g(y)^λ for all x, y ∈ ℝⁿ, with the conventions 0 · ∞ = 0 and ∞^α = ∞ for α > 0. Then ∫_ℝⁿ h dx ≥ (∫_ℝⁿ f dx)^(1−λ) (∫_ℝⁿ g dx)^λ, where the integrals take values in [0, ∞]. In particular, the inequality holds for nonnegative integrable functions f, g and h.
hypotheses: The parameter λ lies in the open interval (0, 1).
The functions f, g and h are Lebesgue measurable on ℝⁿ with values in [0, ∞].
For all x, y ∈ ℝⁿ, h((1 − λ)x + λy) ≥ f(x)^(1−λ) g(y)^λ.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses Tonelli's theorem for the layer-cake formula, and step s5 uses it to integrate over slices and to show that the slice integrals are Borel functions.
Step s4 removes the truncation of F and G with the monotone convergence theorem.

definitions.name: Minkowski combination
definitions.text: For sets A, B ⊆ ℝⁿ and 0 < λ < 1, (1 − λ)A + λB = {(1 − λ)a + λb : a ∈ A, b ∈ B}.

definitions.name: level set
definitions.text: For a function F ≥ 0 and t > 0, the set {F ≥ t} = {x : F(x) ≥ t}.

source.citation: Richard J. Gardner, The Brunn-Minkowski inequality, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society (New Series) 39 (2002), no. 3, 355–405.
source.revision: Journal version, electronically published on April 8, 2002 (open back issue on ams.org).
source.module: Section 7 The move to analysis II: The Prékopa-Leindler inequality
source.excerpt: Theorem 7.1. Let 0 < λ < 1 and let f, g, and h be nonnegative integrable functions on ℝⁿ satisfying h((1 − λ)x + λy) ≥ f(x)^(1−λ) g(y)^λ, for all x, y ∈ ℝⁿ. Then ∫ h(x) dx ≥ (∫ f(x) dx)^(1−λ) (∫ g(x) dx)^λ.
source.attribution: © American Mathematical Society and Richard J. Gardner. Quoted from the Bulletin of the AMS for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the inequality for nonnegative integrable functions. The authored statement allows measurable functions with values in [0, ∞] and infinite integrals, which the induction needs. The source proves the case n = 1 by a transport argument (p. 369). The authored proof follows the route of Brascamp and Lieb that the source describes on p. 370: the one-dimensional Brunn-Minkowski inequality for level sets, then induction on n with Fubini's theorem.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the level-set proof of Brascamp and Lieb described by Gardner (2002) on p. 370. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, first for Borel functions with values in [0, ∞] by induction on n, then for Lebesgue measurable functions.

steps.text: One-dimensional Brunn-Minkowski for compact sets. Let K, L ⊂ ℝ be nonempty and compact, a = max K and b = min L. Put K′ = K − a ⊆ (−∞, 0] and L′ = L − b ⊆ [0, ∞), so 0 ∈ K′ ∩ L′. Then (1 − λ)K′ + λL′ contains (1 − λ)K′ ∪ λL′, and these two sets meet at most in {0}. So |(1 − λ)K′ + λL′| ≥ (1 − λ)|K| + λ|L|. The set (1 − λ)K + λL is compact and is a translate of (1 − λ)K′ + λL′, so |(1 − λ)K + λL| ≥ (1 − λ)|K| + λ|L|.

Extension to Borel sets. Let A, B ⊆ ℝ be nonempty Borel sets and let C be a Borel set that contains (1 − λ)A + λB. For nonempty compact K ⊆ A and L ⊆ B, step s1 gives |C| ≥ |(1 − λ)K + λL| ≥ (1 − λ)|K| + λ|L|. Lebesgue measure is inner regular on Borel sets, also when the measure is infinite, and a single point is a compact subset of measure 0. Taking suprema over K and L gives |C| ≥ (1 − λ)|A| + λ|B|.

Dimension one, bounded case. Let F, G, H: ℝ → [0, ∞] be Borel with H((1 − λ)x + λy) ≥ F(x)^(1−λ) G(y)^λ, and assume 0 < sup F < ∞ and 0 < sup G < ∞. Dividing F by a = sup F, G by b = sup G and H by a^(1−λ) b^λ keeps the hypothesis and scales both sides of the conclusion equally, so let sup F = sup G = 1. For 0 < t < 1, the level sets {F ≥ t} and {G ≥ t} are nonempty, and F(x) ≥ t, G(y) ≥ t imply H((1 − λ)x + λy) ≥ t. So (1 − λ){F ≥ t} + λ{G ≥ t} ⊆ {H ≥ t}, and step s2 gives |{H ≥ t}| ≥ (1 − λ)|{F ≥ t}| + λ|{G ≥ t}|. The layer-cake formula ∫F = ∫₀^∞ |{F ≥ t}| dt follows from Tonelli's theorem, and the integrand vanishes for t > 1. So ∫H ≥ ∫₀¹ |{H ≥ t}| dt ≥ (1 − λ)∫F + λ∫G. The concavity of the logarithm gives (1 − λ)u + λv ≥ u^(1−λ) v^λ for u, v ∈ [0, ∞]. So ∫H ≥ (∫F)^(1−λ) (∫G)^λ.

Dimension one, general case. If ∫F = 0 or ∫G = 0, the right side is 0 and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise put F_M = min(F, M) 1_[−M, M] and G_M = min(G, M) 1_[−M, M] for M > 0. Then F_M ≤ F and G_M ≤ G, so H((1 − λ)x + λy) ≥ F_M(x)^(1−λ) G_M(y)^λ. For large M, ∫F_M > 0 and ∫G_M > 0, so 0 < sup F_M ≤ M and 0 < sup G_M ≤ M. Step s3 gives ∫H ≥ (∫F_M)^(1−λ) (∫G_M)^λ. As M → ∞, F_M increases to F and G_M increases to G, so the monotone convergence theorem gives ∫F_M → ∫F and ∫G_M → ∫G in [0, ∞]. Hence ∫H ≥ (∫F)^(1−λ) (∫G)^λ.

Induction on n for Borel functions with values in [0, ∞]. Step s4 is the case n = 1. Let n ≥ 2 and assume the case n − 1. Write points of ℝⁿ as (s, z) with s ∈ ℝ and z ∈ ℝ^(n−1), and put F(s) = ∫ f(s, z) dz, G(s) = ∫ g(s, z) dz and H(s) = ∫ h(s, z) dz. By Tonelli's theorem these are Borel functions with values in [0, ∞]. For s₀, s₁ ∈ ℝ and s = (1 − λ)s₀ + λs₁, the functions z ↦ f(s₀, z), z ↦ g(s₁, z) and z ↦ h(s, z) satisfy the hypothesis in ℝ^(n−1), so the case n − 1 gives H(s) ≥ F(s₀)^(1−λ) G(s₁)^λ. Step s4 then gives ∫H ≥ (∫F)^(1−λ) (∫G)^λ, and Tonelli's theorem turns this into ∫h ≥ (∫f)^(1−λ) (∫g)^λ.

Lebesgue measurable functions. Every Lebesgue measurable function equals a Borel function outside a Lebesgue null set, and every Lebesgue null set lies in a Borel null set. So there are Borel functions f′ ≤ f and g′ ≤ g, equal to f and g almost everywhere: set them to 0 on the Borel null set. There is a Borel function h″ ≥ h, equal to h almost everywhere: set it to ∞ on the null set. Then h″((1 − λ)x + λy) ≥ f′(x)^(1−λ) g′(y)^λ for all x and y. Step s5 applies to (f′, g′, h″), and the integrals of f′, g′ and h″ equal those of f, g and h.

applications.title: Convexity of the effective potential after integrating out variables
applications.inputs: A convex potential V: ℝ^m × ℝ^k → ℝ of two groups of variables x and y, with Z(x) = ∫ e^(−V(x, y)) dy < ∞ for all x. The effective potential is W(x) = −log Z(x). Numerical instance: m = k = 1 and V(x, y) = (y − x)²/2 + y²/2.
applications.hypotheses: Fix x₀, x₁ and λ ∈ (0, 1), and put x = (1 − λ)x₀ + λx₁. The functions f(y) = e^(−V(x₀, y)), g(y) = e^(−V(x₁, y)) and h(y) = e^(−V(x, y)) are continuous, hence measurable, and nonnegative. Convexity of V gives V(x, (1 − λ)y₀ + λy₁) ≤ (1 − λ)V(x₀, y₀) + λV(x₁, y₁), which is the hypothesis h((1 − λ)y₀ + λy₁) ≥ f(y₀)^(1−λ) g(y₁)^λ.

steps.text: The inequality gives Z(x) ≥ Z(x₀)^(1−λ) Z(x₁)^λ. Taking −log gives W((1 − λ)x₀ + λx₁) ≤ (1 − λ)W(x₀) + λW(x₁). So W is convex: integrating out the variables y keeps the effective potential convex (Prékopa's theorem).

For V(x, y) = (y − x)²/2 + y²/2, the Hessian [[1, −1], [−1, 2]] has determinant 1 > 0 and trace 3 > 0, so V is convex. Completing the square gives V = (y − x/2)² + x²/4, so Z(x) = √π e^(−x²/4) and W(x) = x²/4 − log √π.
Check at x₀ = 0, x₁ = 2 and λ = 1/2. The average of the quadratic parts at the end points is (1/2)(0²/4) + (1/2)(2²/4) = 1/2.
At the midpoint x = 1 the quadratic part is 1²/4 = 1/4 ≤ 1/2, as convexity requires. The constant −log √π cancels on both sides.

applications.conclusion: For every convex potential V with finite partial partition functions, the effective potential W(x) = −log ∫ e^(−V(x, y)) dy is convex. For V = (y − x)²/2 + y²/2 it is x²/4 − log √π.

limitations: The inequality gives no equality conditions in ℝⁿ. The source notes that equality conditions are known only in dimension one.

Applied to indicator functions it gives the Brunn-Minkowski inequality in the multiplicative form |(1 − λ)A + λB| ≥ |A|^(1−λ) |B|^λ. The additive form with the exponent 1/n needs a further homogeneity argument.

results.name: Sanov's theorem for a finite alphabet
results.statement: Let E be a finite set, let µ be a probability measure on E, and let X₁, X₂, … be independent random variables with law µ. Let L_N = N⁻¹ Σ_{i≤N} δ_{X_i} be the empirical measure, a random element of the simplex M₁(E) of probability measures on E with the total variation metric. Let H(ν|µ) = Σ_{x∈E} ν(x) log(ν(x)/µ(x)) when ν(x) = 0 for every x with µ(x) = 0, with 0 log 0 = 0, and let H(ν|µ) = +∞ otherwise. Then for every set A ⊂ M₁(E), −inf_{ν∈A°} H(ν|µ) ≤ liminf_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log P(L_N ∈ A) ≤ limsup_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log P(L_N ∈ A) ≤ −inf_{ν∈A} H(ν|µ). Moreover, H(·|µ) is a convex good rate function. So (L_N) satisfies the large deviation principle with speed N and rate function H(·|µ).
hypotheses: The set E is finite and µ is a probability measure on E.
The random variables X₁, X₂, … are independent and each has the law µ.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses the multinomial theorem to show that the probabilities of all types under ν^⊗N add up to (Σ_y ν(y))^N = 1.
Step s7 uses Gibbs' inequality to show that the relative entropy H(ν|µ) is nonnegative and vanishes only at ν = µ.
Step s7 uses the Heine–Borel theorem to show that the simplex M₁(E) is compact, so that the closed level sets of H(·|µ) are compact.

definitions.name: empirical measure
definitions.text: L_N = N⁻¹ Σ_{i≤N} δ_{X_i}. It gives each point x ∈ E the fraction of the indices i ≤ N with X_i = x.

definitions.name: type and type class
definitions.text: A type of length N is a ν ∈ M₁(E) with Nν(x) ∈ ℤ for every x. Its type class T_N(ν) is the set of sequences in E^N whose empirical measure is ν.

definitions.name: good rate function
definitions.text: A function I: M₁(E) → [0, +∞] whose level sets {I ≤ α} are compact for every α ≥ 0. Then I is lower semicontinuous.

definitions.name: relative entropy
definitions.text: H(ν|µ) = Σ_x ν(x) log(ν(x)/µ(x)) if ν is zero wherever µ is zero, and +∞ otherwise. It is also called the Kullback–Leibler divergence.

source.citation: Stefan Adams, MA4L3 – Large Deviation Theory, Lecture Notes, University of Warwick, 2023.

source.module: Chapter 2 Methods of types and Sanov's theorem, Section 2.1 The empirical measure LDP - Sanov's theorem
source.excerpt: Let (Xi)i∈N be an independent, identically distributed sequence of E-valued random variables with law µ ∈ M1(E). Denote µN the distribution of LN under µ⊗N, i.e., µN = µ⊗N ◦ LN⁻¹. Then the sequence (µN)N∈N satisfies the LDP on M1(E) with rate N and rate function Iµ(ν) = H(ν|µ).
source.attribution: © Stefan Adams. Quoted from the author's MA4L3 lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the large deviation principle on M₁(E) with rate function H(·|µ) and leaves the properties of H(·|µ) to Exercise 2.5. The authored statement writes out both bounds, gives the upper bound for every set A and not only for closed sets, and includes convexity and goodness of the rate function. The authored proof follows the method of types of Lemmas 2.8 and 2.9. It replaces the Stirling estimate of Lemma 2.9 by an exact comparison of type probabilities.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the method of types in the cited proof of Theorem 2.7 and Lemmas 2.8 and 2.9. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: the upper bound for every set A, the lower bound with the interior of A, and the convexity and goodness of the rate function.

steps.text: Types. Let 𝓛_N be the set of ν ∈ M₁(E) with Nν(x) ∈ ℤ for every x ∈ E. The empirical measure L_N takes its values in 𝓛_N. Each value ν(x) lies in {0, 1/N, …, 1}, so |𝓛_N| ≤ (N + 1)^|E|. For ν ∈ 𝓛_N, the type class T_N(ν) is the set of x ∈ E^N with empirical measure ν. Its size is the multinomial coefficient N!/Π_y (Nν(y))!.

Probability of one sequence. Write H(ν) = −Σ_y ν(y) log ν(y). For x ∈ T_N(ν), independence gives P((X₁, …, X_N) = x) = Π_i µ(x_i) = Π_y µ(y)^(Nν(y)). If ν(y) > 0 = µ(y) for some y, this is 0, which agrees with H(ν|µ) = +∞. Otherwise it equals exp(N Σ_y ν(y) log µ(y)) = exp(−N(H(ν) + H(ν|µ))). Hence P(L_N = ν) = |T_N(ν)| exp(−N(H(ν) + H(ν|µ))).

Size of a type class. Apply step s2 with µ replaced by ν. Then 1 ≥ P_ν(L_N = ν) = |T_N(ν)| e^(−N H(ν)), so |T_N(ν)| ≤ e^(N H(ν)). For the lower bound, compare with another type ν′ ∈ 𝓛_N. If ν′(y) > 0 = ν(y) for some y, then P_ν(L_N = ν′) = 0. Otherwise P_ν(L_N = ν)/P_ν(L_N = ν′) = Π_y [(Nν′(y))!/(Nν(y))!] ν(y)^(N(ν(y) − ν′(y))), with the product over the y with ν(y) > 0. The bound m!/n! ≥ n^(m−n), valid for integers m ≥ 0 and n ≥ 1, shows that this ratio is at least Π_y N^(N(ν′(y) − ν(y))) = N^0 = 1. So P_ν(L_N = ν) is the largest of at most (N + 1)^|E| numbers. By the multinomial theorem these numbers add up to (Σ_y ν(y))^N = 1. Hence P_ν(L_N = ν) ≥ (N + 1)^(−|E|) and |T_N(ν)| ≥ (N + 1)^(−|E|) e^(N H(ν)).
Probability of a type. Put the two bounds of step s3 into the formula of step s2. For every ν ∈ 𝓛_N, (N + 1)^(−|E|) e^(−N H(ν|µ)) ≤ P(L_N = ν) ≤ e^(−N H(ν|µ)). Both bounds are 0 when H(ν|µ) = +∞.

Upper bound. Let A ⊂ M₁(E) be any set. The event {L_N ∈ A} is the disjoint union of the events {L_N = ν} with ν ∈ A ∩ 𝓛_N. Steps s1 and s4 give P(L_N ∈ A) ≤ (N + 1)^|E| exp(−N inf_{ν∈A} H(ν|µ)). Since N⁻¹ |E| log(N + 1) → 0, limsup N⁻¹ log P(L_N ∈ A) ≤ −inf_A H(·|µ).

Lower bound. Let ν ∈ A° with H(ν|µ) < ∞, so the support S of ν lies in the support of µ. List S = {y₁, …, y_k}. Set ν_N(y_j) = ⌊Nν(y_j)⌋/N for j < k, ν_N(y_k) = 1 − Σ_{j<k} ν_N(y_j), and ν_N = 0 off S. Then ν_N(y_k) ≥ ν(y_k) > 0, ν_N ∈ 𝓛_N, the support of ν_N lies in S, and |ν_N(y) − ν(y)| ≤ |E|/N for every y. So ν_N → ν, and ν_N ∈ A for all large N because A° is open. On the measures supported in the support of µ, H(·|µ) is a finite sum of the continuous functions t ↦ t log(t/µ(y)) on [0, 1]. Hence H(ν_N|µ) → H(ν|µ). Step s4 gives N⁻¹ log P(L_N ∈ A) ≥ N⁻¹ log P(L_N = ν_N) ≥ −N⁻¹ |E| log(N + 1) − H(ν_N|µ). So liminf N⁻¹ log P(L_N ∈ A) ≥ −H(ν|µ). The supremum over ν ∈ A° gives the lower bound.

The rate function. Gibbs' inequality gives H(ν|µ) ≥ 0, with equality only at ν = µ. The set D of measures supported in the support of µ is convex and closed, and H(·|µ) = +∞ off D. On D, H(·|µ) is a sum of convex continuous functions of the coordinates ν(y), because t ↦ t log t is convex and continuous on [0, 1]. So H(·|µ) is convex, and each level set {H(·|µ) ≤ α} is a closed subset of D. The simplex M₁(E) is closed and bounded in ℝ^E, so it is compact by the Heine–Borel theorem. Hence the level sets are compact and H(·|µ) is a good rate function. With A° ⊂ A ⊂ Ā, steps s5 and s6 give the large deviation principle.

applications.title: Rare high mean energy of a three-level gas
applications.inputs: N independent particles, each with an energy ε ∈ E = {0, 1, 2}. The prior law of each energy is uniform, µ = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). The event is that the mean energy is at least 10/7, while the typical mean energy is 1.
applications.hypotheses: E is finite and the energies are independent with law µ. The mean energy is m(L_N) = L_N(1) + 2L_N(2), so the event is {L_N ∈ A} with the closed convex set A = {ν : ν(1) + 2ν(2) ≥ 10/7}. The set A is the closure of its interior {ν : ν(1) + 2ν(2) > 10/7}.

steps.text: Since µ has full support, H(·|µ) is finite and continuous on all of M₁(E). A is the closure of A°, so inf over A° equals inf over A. Sanov's theorem then gives lim N⁻¹ log P(L_N ∈ A) = −inf_A H(·|µ).
Tilt µ by the weight 2^ε. The normalizer is Z = Σ_ε µ(ε) 2^ε = (1 + 2 + 4)/3 = 7/3, and the tilted law is ν*(ε) = µ(ε) 2^ε / Z, that is ν* = (1/7, 2/7, 4/7).
The mean energy of ν* is (0·1 + 1·2 + 2·4)/7 = 10/7. So ν* lies in A, on its boundary.

For every ν, log(ν(ε)/µ(ε)) = log(ν(ε)/ν*(ε)) + ε log 2 − log(7/3). Summation against ν gives H(ν|µ) = H(ν|ν*) + m(ν) log 2 − log(7/3). For ν ∈ A, H(ν|ν*) ≥ 0 and m(ν) ≥ 10/7. So H(ν|µ) ≥ (10/7) log 2 − log(7/3), with equality only at ν = ν*.

The rate is I = (10/7) log 2 + log 3 − log 7 ≈ 0.1429. For δ > 0 the set A minus the open ball of radius δ around ν* is closed and does not contain ν*. Its infimum of H(·|µ) is larger than I, because the level sets are compact and ν* is the only minimizer on A. So the upper bound shows that P(d(L_N, ν*) ≥ δ | L_N ∈ A) → 0.

applications.conclusion: P(mean energy ≥ 10/7) = e^(−N(I + o(1))) with I = (10/7) log 2 − log(7/3) ≈ 0.1429. Given the rare event, the empirical law of the energies concentrates at the tilted law ν* = (1/7, 2/7, 4/7).

limitations: The theorem gives only the exponential rate. The polynomial prefactor of P(L_N ∈ A) is not determined.
The finite alphabet is essential for this counting proof. For a Polish space E, Sanov's theorem holds in the weak topology, with a proof by projective limits or by the Gärtner–Ellis method.
