results.name: Gärtner–Ellis theorem
results.statement: Let X_N be random vectors in ℝ^d with laws µ_N. Assume that for every λ ∈ ℝ^d the limit Λ(λ) = lim_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log E e^(N⟨λ, X_N⟩) exists in [−∞, +∞], and that 0 is an interior point of D_Λ = {λ : Λ(λ) < ∞}. Let Λ*(x) = sup_{λ∈ℝ^d} (⟨λ, x⟩ − Λ(λ)). Then (a) Λ* is a convex good rate function, and limsup_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log µ_N(F) ≤ −inf_F Λ* for every closed F ⊂ ℝ^d. (b) liminf_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log µ_N(G) ≥ −inf_{G∩𝓔} Λ* for every open G ⊂ ℝ^d. Here 𝓔 is the set of points y with an exposing hyperplane η in the interior of D_Λ, that is, ⟨η, y⟩ − Λ*(y) > ⟨η, z⟩ − Λ*(z) for all z ≠ y. (c) If Λ is lower semicontinuous and essentially smooth, then (µ_N) satisfies the large deviation principle with speed N and the good rate function Λ*. Essentially smooth means that the interior of D_Λ is nonempty, Λ is differentiable there, and |∇Λ(λ_n)| → ∞ whenever λ_n in the interior of D_Λ converge to a boundary point of D_Λ.
hypotheses: X_N are random vectors in ℝ^d with laws µ_N.
For every λ ∈ ℝ^d the limit Λ(λ) = lim N⁻¹ log E e^(N⟨λ, X_N⟩) exists in [−∞, +∞].
The origin is an interior point of D_Λ = {λ : Λ(λ) < ∞}.
For part (c): Λ is lower semicontinuous and essentially smooth.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Hölder's inequality to show that each λ ↦ log E e^(⟨λ, X_N⟩) is convex, so that the limit Λ is convex.
Steps s2 and s3 use Markov's inequality for exponentials (the exponential Chebyshev bound) on half-spaces and on coordinate tails.

definitions.name: scaled cumulant generating function
definitions.text: Λ(λ) = lim N⁻¹ log E e^(N⟨λ, X_N⟩), the limit of the rescaled logarithmic moment generating functions of X_N.

definitions.name: Legendre–Fenchel transform
definitions.text: Λ*(x) = sup_λ (⟨λ, x⟩ − Λ(λ)). It is convex and lower semicontinuous as a supremum of affine functions.

definitions.name: exposed point
definitions.text: A point y is an exposed point of Λ* with exposing hyperplane η if ⟨η, y⟩ − Λ*(y) > ⟨η, z⟩ − Λ*(z) for every z ≠ y.

definitions.name: essentially smooth
definitions.text: A convex Λ is essentially smooth if the interior of its domain is nonempty, Λ is differentiable there, and |∇Λ| tends to infinity at the boundary of the domain.

source.module: Chapter 4 The Gärtner-Ellis theorem, Section 4.1 Gärtner-Ellis for Rd
source.excerpt: Theorem 4.2 (Gärtner-Ellis for Rd) … Assume that … Λ(λ) := lim_{N→∞} (1/N) ΛµN(Nλ) exists as an extended real number for all λ ∈ Rd, (4.5) and 0 ∈ D̊Λ. … (c) If Λ is an essentially smooth, lower semi continuous function, then (µN)N∈N satisfies the LDP with good rate function Λ*.
source.attribution: © Stefan Adams. Quoted from the author's MA4L3 lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source prints the limit in (4.5) as lim N⁻¹ log Λ_µN(Nλ), where Λ_µN is already the logarithm. The authored statement writes the intended limit N⁻¹ log E e^(N⟨λ, X_N⟩) and states parts (a), (b) and (c) with the definitions of exposed points and essential smoothness from Definition 4.1 and Remark 4.3. The outline follows the proof of Theorem 4.2 and Lemma 4.4 on pp. 35-39. In part (c) it uses a point y of the domain of Λ* and a point z of its relative interior, which is the intended form of the source's argument.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 4.2 and Lemma 4.4 in Adams's MA4L3 notes, pp. 35-39. Step s6 uses a theorem of Rockafellar on essentially smooth convex functions, which the source cites without proof.

steps.text: Lemma 4.4 of the source. By Hölder's inequality each λ ↦ N⁻¹ log E e^(N⟨λ, X_N⟩) is convex, so Λ is convex, and Λ(0) = 0. If Λ(λ) = −∞ for some λ, convexity and Λ(0) = 0 force Λ = +∞ on points −tλ with small t > 0, which contradicts 0 ∈ int D_Λ. So Λ > −∞. Λ* is convex and lower semicontinuous as a supremum of affine functions, and Λ* ≥ −Λ(0) = 0. A convex function is continuous on the interior of its domain, so Λ ≤ C on a ball B_δ(0) ⊂ int D_Λ. Then Λ*(x) ≥ δ|x| − C, the level sets of Λ* are closed and bounded, and Λ* is a good rate function.

Upper bound for compact sets. For x ∈ ℝ^d and δ > 0 choose λ_x with ⟨λ_x, x⟩ − Λ(λ_x) ≥ min(Λ*(x) − δ, 1/δ), and a ball A_x around x on which ⟨λ_x, y − x⟩ ≥ −δ. The exponential Chebyshev inequality gives µ_N(A_x) ≤ e^(Nδ − N⟨λ_x, x⟩) E e^(N⟨λ_x, X_N⟩). A compact K is covered by finitely many A_{x_i}, so limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(K) ≤ δ − min_i min(Λ*(x_i) − δ, 1/δ) ≤ δ − inf_K min(Λ* − δ, 1/δ). Letting δ → 0 gives −inf_K Λ*.

Exponential tightness and closed sets. Since 0 ∈ int D_Λ, there is δ > 0 with Λ(δe_i) < ∞ and Λ(−δe_i) < ∞ for every coordinate vector e_i. The source bounds P(X_N^(i) ≥ M) ≤ e^(−NδM) E e^(NδX_N^(i)) and the lower tail in the same way. This gives limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(ℝ^d ∖ [−M, M]^d) ≤ −δM + max_i max(Λ(δe_i), Λ(−δe_i)), which tends to −∞ as M → ∞. For a closed F, apply step s2 to the compact set F ∩ [−M, M]^d and add the tail. This proves part (a).

Exponential tilting at an exposed point. Let y ∈ 𝓔 with exposing hyperplane η ∈ int D_Λ, and let δ > 0. For large N, E e^(N⟨η, X_N⟩) < ∞, and µ̃_N(dz) = exp(N⟨η, z⟩ − log E e^(N⟨η, X_N⟩)) µ_N(dz) is a probability measure. On B_δ(y), ⟨η, z⟩ ≤ ⟨η, y⟩ + |η|δ. So N⁻¹ log µ_N(B_δ(y)) ≥ N⁻¹ log E e^(N⟨η, X_N⟩) − ⟨η, y⟩ − |η|δ + N⁻¹ log µ̃_N(B_δ(y)). The first two terms tend to Λ(η) − ⟨η, y⟩ ≥ −Λ*(y). It remains to show µ̃_N(B_δ(y)) → 1.

The tilted laws concentrate at y. The source computes the limit for µ̃_N: Λ̃(λ) = Λ(λ + η) − Λ(η), which satisfies the hypotheses because η ∈ int D_Λ. Its transform is Λ̃*(x) = Λ*(x) − ⟨η, x⟩ + Λ(η). Part (a) for µ̃_N and the closed set B_δ(y)^c gives the exponent −inf over B_δ(y)^c of Λ̃*. Since Λ̃* is good, a finite infimum is attained at some x₀ ≠ y. With Λ(η) ≥ ⟨η, y⟩ − Λ*(y), exposedness gives Λ̃*(x₀) ≥ Λ*(x₀) − ⟨η, x₀⟩ + ⟨η, y⟩ − Λ*(y) > 0. So µ̃_N(B_δ(y)^c) → 0. For open G and y ∈ G ∩ 𝓔, take B_δ(y) ⊂ G and let δ → 0. This proves part (b).

Full principle under essential smoothness. A theorem of Rockafellar, cited by the source, states that for a lower semicontinuous, essentially smooth convex Λ every point of the relative interior ri(D_Λ*) belongs to 𝓔. Let G be open and y ∈ G with Λ*(y) < ∞, and pick z ∈ ri(D_Λ*). For small t > 0 the point tz + (1 − t)y lies in G ∩ ri(D_Λ*), and convexity gives Λ*(tz + (1 − t)y) ≤ tΛ*(z) + (1 − t)Λ*(y) → Λ*(y). Hence inf_{G∩𝓔} Λ* = inf_G Λ*, and parts (a) and (b) give the large deviation principle of part (c).

applications.title: Magnetization of the one-dimensional Ising ring
applications.inputs: N spins σ_i ∈ {−1, 1} on a ring, with coupling β given by e^β = 4/3 and zero external field. The Gibbs law is proportional to exp(β Σ_i σ_i σ_{i+1}). The variable is the magnetization X_N = M_N = N⁻¹ Σ_i σ_i, and the target value is m = 4/5.
applications.hypotheses: E e^(NλM_N) = Z_N(λ)/Z_N(0), where Z_N(h) = tr T_h^N with the positive 2 × 2 transfer matrix T_h(σ, σ′) = exp(βσσ′ + h(σ + σ′)/2). Its eigenvalues are ρ_±(h) = e^β cosh h ± (e^(2β) sinh² h + e^(−2β))^(1/2). Since ρ_+ + ρ_− = 2e^β cosh h > 0 and ρ_+ > ρ_−, |ρ_−| < ρ_+. So Λ(λ) = log ρ_+(λ) − log ρ_+(0) exists, is finite and is differentiable on ℝ. With D_Λ = ℝ, Λ is essentially smooth and continuous.

steps.text: Part (c) gives the large deviation principle for M_N with rate Λ*(m) = sup_λ (λm − Λ(λ)). For a differentiable convex Λ the supremum is attained where Λ′(λ) = m. Here Λ′(λ) is the magnetization sinh λ / (sinh² λ + e^(−4β))^(1/2) of the ring in the field λ.
At the field λ = log 2, cosh λ = 5/4 and sinh λ = 3/4. Then e^β cosh λ = 5/3, and (e^(2β) sinh² λ + e^(−2β))^(1/2) = (1 + 9/16)^(1/2) = 5/4. So ρ_+(log 2) = 5/3 + 5/4 = 35/12.
The magnetization in the field log 2 is (3/4)/((3/4)² + (3/4)⁴)^(1/2), because e^(−4β) = (3/4)⁴. The radicand is 225/256, its square root is 15/16, and the magnetization is (3/4)/(15/16) = 4/5.

applications.conclusion: lim_{δ→0} lim_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log P(|M_N − 4/5| < δ) = −Λ*(4/5) = −((4/5) log 2 − log(7/5)) ≈ −0.2180. The spins are dependent, so Cramér's theorem does not apply, but the Gärtner–Ellis theorem does.

limitations: At a first-order phase transition Λ has a corner. Then Λ is not essentially smooth, part (c) fails, and Λ* is only the convex hull of the true rate function, which may be nonconvex.
The theorem gives only convex rate functions. Nonconvex rate functions need other methods, such as contraction or direct counting.

results.name: Varadhan's integral lemma
results.statement: Let E be a metric space, and let the probability measures µ_N on the Borel sets of E satisfy the large deviation principle with speed N and a good rate function I. Let H: E → ℝ be continuous. Assume either the tail condition lim_{M→∞} limsup_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log ∫_{H≥M} e^(NH) dµ_N = −∞, or the moment condition limsup_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log ∫ e^(γNH) dµ_N < ∞ for some γ > 1. Then lim_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log ∫_E e^(NH) dµ_N = sup_{x∈E} (H(x) − I(x)), and this supremum is a finite real number. Every H that is continuous and bounded above satisfies the tail condition.
hypotheses: The probability measures µ_N on the metric space E satisfy the large deviation principle with speed N and a good rate function I.
The function H: E → ℝ is continuous.
H satisfies the tail condition, or the moment condition with some γ > 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 uses Hölder's inequality with exponents γ and γ/(γ − 1) to show that the moment condition implies the tail condition.
Step s4 bounds µ_N(H ≥ M) by e^(−γNM) ∫ e^(γNH) dµ_N with Markov's inequality applied to e^(γNH).

definitions.name: large deviation principle
definitions.text: Probability measures µ_N satisfy the large deviation principle with speed N and rate function I if −inf_{A°} I ≤ liminf N⁻¹ log µ_N(A) ≤ limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(A) ≤ −inf_{Ā} I for every Borel set A.

definitions.name: good rate function
definitions.text: A function I: E → [0, +∞] whose level sets {I ≤ α}, α ≥ 0, are compact. Such a function is lower semicontinuous.

definitions.name: principle of the largest term
definitions.text: For finitely many sequences a_N^(1), …, a_N^(k) ≥ 0, limsup N⁻¹ log Σ_i a_N^(i) = max_i limsup N⁻¹ log a_N^(i), because the sum lies between the largest term and k times it.

source.module: Chapter 3 General Theory, Section 3.3 Varadhan's Integral Lemma
source.excerpt: (Varadhan Lemma) Suppose that (µN)N∈N satisfies the LDP with a good rate function I : E → [0, ∞], and let H : E → ℝ be a continuous function. Assume that either the tail-condition lim_{M→∞} lim sup_{N→∞} (1/N) log E_µN[e^{NH} 1{H ≥ M}] = −∞ (3.10), or the moment condition for γ > 1, lim sup_{N→∞} (1/N) log E[e^{γNH}] < ∞ (3.11), hold. Then lim_{N→∞} (1/N) log E_µN[e^{NH}] = sup_{x∈E} {H(x) − I(x)}.
source.attribution: © Stefan Adams. Quoted from the author's MA4L3 lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement matches Theorem 3.10 on a metric space and adds that the supremum is finite. The authored proof follows the source: the lower bound of Lemma 3.12, the upper bound of Lemma 3.13 by a finite cover of a level set and truncation, and the Hölder argument of Remark 3.11 (b). The authored upper bound applies the large deviation upper bound to closed balls, so that it uses only closed sets.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the cited proof of Theorem 3.10 through Lemmas 3.12 and 3.13 and Remark 3.11. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under both alternative conditions, with the finiteness of the supremum.

steps.text: Lower bound. Let x ∈ E with I(x) < ∞ and let δ > 0. The set G = {y : H(y) > H(x) − δ} is open because H is continuous, and x ∈ G. Then ∫ e^(NH) dµ_N ≥ e^(N(H(x) − δ)) µ_N(G). The lower bound of the large deviation principle gives liminf N⁻¹ log µ_N(G) ≥ −inf_G I ≥ −I(x). Hence liminf N⁻¹ log ∫ e^(NH) dµ_N ≥ H(x) − I(x) − δ. Let δ → 0 and take the supremum over x. Points with I(x) = ∞ do not change the supremum.

Upper bound when H ≤ M on E. Fix α ≥ 0 and δ > 0. The level set K = {I ≤ α} is compact. For x ∈ K, lower semicontinuity of I and continuity of H give r_x > 0 such that I ≥ I(x) − δ and H ≤ H(x) + δ on the closed ball B̄(x, r_x). The open balls B(x, r_x) cover K, so finitely many of them, centered at x₁, …, x_k, cover K. The complement C of their union is closed and I > α on C. Then ∫ e^(NH) dµ_N ≤ Σ_i e^(N(H(x_i) + δ)) µ_N(B̄(x_i, r_i)) + e^(NM) µ_N(C). Apply the upper bound of the large deviation principle to each closed set and the principle of the largest term to the k + 1 summands. This gives limsup N⁻¹ log ∫ e^(NH) dµ_N ≤ max(max_i (H(x_i) − I(x_i) + 2δ), M − α) ≤ max(sup_E (H − I) + 2δ, M − α). Let δ → 0 and α → ∞.

Upper bound under the tail condition. For M > 0 let H_M = min(H, M). It is continuous and bounded above by M. Since H_M = H on {H < M}, ∫ e^(NH) dµ_N ≤ ∫ e^(NH_M) dµ_N + ∫_{H≥M} e^(NH) dµ_N. Let T_M = limsup N⁻¹ log ∫_{H≥M} e^(NH) dµ_N. Step s2 for H_M and the principle of the largest term give limsup N⁻¹ log ∫ e^(NH) dµ_N ≤ max(sup_E (H_M − I), T_M) ≤ max(sup_E (H − I), T_M). The tail condition gives T_M → −∞ as M → ∞, so the limsup is at most sup_E (H − I). With step s1 the limit exists and equals sup_E (H − I).

The moment condition implies the tail condition. Let C = limsup N⁻¹ log ∫ e^(γNH) dµ_N < ∞. Hölder's inequality with exponents γ and γ/(γ − 1) gives ∫_{H≥M} e^(NH) dµ_N ≤ (∫ e^(γNH) dµ_N)^(1/γ) µ_N(H ≥ M)^(1 − 1/γ). Markov's inequality applied to e^(γNH) gives µ_N(H ≥ M) ≤ e^(−γNM) ∫ e^(γNH) dµ_N. Together, ∫_{H≥M} e^(NH) dµ_N ≤ e^(−(γ − 1)NM) ∫ e^(γNH) dµ_N. So T_M ≤ C − (γ − 1)M → −∞. If H ≤ M₀ on E, then T_M = −∞ for every M > M₀, so the tail condition holds.

Finiteness. The upper bound of the large deviation principle with A = E gives 0 ≤ −inf_E I, so inf_E I = 0. The level set {I ≤ 1} is compact and nonempty, and the lower semicontinuous I attains its minimum there at some x₀ with I(x₀) = 0. So sup_E (H − I) ≥ H(x₀) > −∞. By steps s1 and s3, sup_E (H − I) ≤ max(sup_E (H_M − I), T_M) ≤ max(M, T_M) for every M. For large M, T_M < ∞, so the supremum is finite.

applications.title: Free energy of the Curie–Weiss model in the ordered phase
applications.inputs: N Ising spins σ_i ∈ {−1, 1}, the magnetization M_N = N⁻¹ Σ_i σ_i, and the partition function Z_N(β) = Σ_σ exp(βN M_N²/2) at zero field. The inverse temperature is β = (5/3) log 2 ≈ 1.155, which is above the critical value 1.
applications.hypotheses: Under the uniform law on {−1, 1}^N the spins are independent fair signs. Cramér's theorem gives the large deviation principle of M_N with the good rate function I(m) = ((1 + m)/2) log(1 + m) + ((1 − m)/2) log(1 − m) on [−1, 1] and I = +∞ elsewhere. H(m) = βm²/2 is continuous. Since |M_N| ≤ 1, the integrand on {H ≥ M} vanishes for M > β/2, so the tail condition holds.

steps.text: Write Z_N(β) = 2^N E[exp(N H(M_N))]. Varadhan's lemma gives lim N⁻¹ log Z_N(β) = log 2 + sup_{m∈[−1,1]} g(m), with g(m) = βm²/2 − I(m).

g is even and g′(m) = βm − artanh(m). On (0, 1) the zeros of g′ solve m = tanh(βm). The function tanh(βm) − m is concave on [0, 1], vanishes at 0, has slope β − 1 > 0 there and is negative at 1. So it has exactly one zero m* in (0, 1), and g attains its maximum at ±m*.
Try m = 3/5. Then βm = log 2 and tanh(log 2) = (2² − 1)/(2² + 1) = 3/5. So m* = 3/5.
The energy term is βm*²/2 = (5/3)(3/5)²/2 · log 2 = (3/10) log 2. The entropy term is I(3/5) = (4/5) log(8/5) + (1/5) log(2/5) = (13/5) log 2 − log 5.
Hence sup g = (3/10) log 2 − (13/5) log 2 + log 5 = log 5 − (23/10) log 2 ≈ 0.0152 > 0 = g(0). The limit of N⁻¹ log Z_N(β) is log 2 + sup g = log 5 − (13/10) log 2 ≈ 0.7083.

applications.conclusion: At β = (5/3) log 2 the Curie–Weiss free energy is lim N⁻¹ log Z_N(β) = log 5 − (13/10) log 2 ≈ 0.7083. The maximizers m = ±3/5 are the two values of the spontaneous magnetization.

limitations: The lemma gives only the exponential order of the integral. Prefactors need a finer analysis, such as a Laplace expansion near a nondegenerate maximizer.
Without the tail or moment condition the conclusion can fail: unbounded H can make the integral grow faster than any rate that the large deviation principle sees.

results.name: contraction principle (large deviations)
aliases: contraction principle for large deviation principles
results.statement: Let E and Y be metric spaces, let T: E → Y be continuous, and let I: E → [0, +∞] be a good rate function, that is, every level set {I ≤ α} with α ≥ 0 is compact. Define J(y) = inf{I(x) : x ∈ E, T(x) = y} for y ∈ Y, with inf ∅ = +∞. Then (a) J is a good rate function on Y, and the infimum that defines J(y) is attained whenever J(y) < ∞. (b) If the probability measures µ_N on the Borel sets of E satisfy the large deviation principle with speed N and rate function I, then the image measures µ_N ∘ T⁻¹ on Y satisfy the large deviation principle with speed N and rate function J.
hypotheses: E and Y are metric spaces and T: E → Y is continuous.
I: E → [0, +∞] is a good rate function: each level set {I ≤ α} is compact.
For part (b): the probability measures µ_N on E satisfy the large deviation principle with speed N and rate function I.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Cantor's intersection theorem for the decreasing nonempty compact sets T⁻¹({y}) ∩ {I ≤ J(y) + 1/n}, which gives a minimizer.

definitions.name: large deviation principle
definitions.text: Probability measures µ_N satisfy the large deviation principle with speed N and rate function I if −inf_{A°} I ≤ liminf N⁻¹ log µ_N(A) ≤ limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(A) ≤ −inf_{Ā} I for every Borel set A.

definitions.name: good rate function
definitions.text: A function I: E → [0, +∞] whose level sets {I ≤ α}, α ≥ 0, are compact. Compact sets in a metric space are closed, so I is lower semicontinuous.

definitions.name: image measure
definitions.text: For a measurable map T, the image measure µ ∘ T⁻¹ gives each Borel set B ⊂ Y the mass µ(T⁻¹(B)).

source.citation: Stefan Adams, MA4L3 – Large Deviation Theory, Lecture Notes, University of Warwick, 2023.
source.revision: Version "2023, update 01.11.2023" (PDF created 2023-11-01), 85 pages.
source.module: Chapter 3 General Theory, Section 3.2 Contraction principle
source.excerpt: Theorem 3.6 (Contraction Principle) Let (E, d) and (Y, dY) be metric spaces and T : E → Y a continuous function. Suppose that I : E → [0, ∞] is a good rate function and define J(y) := inf{I(x)} … (a) Then J is a good rate function on Y, where the infimum in (3.3) over the empty set is taken as ∞. (b) If I is the rate function for a large deviation principle (LDP) associated with a sequence (µN)N∈N of probability measures µN ∈ M1(E) on E, then J controls the LDP on Y for the sequence (µN ◦ T⁻¹)N∈N …
source.attribution: © Stefan Adams. Quoted from the author's MA4L3 lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The excerpt omits the index set of the infimum in (3.3), which the source prints as y = I(x) by a misprint for y = T(x). The authored statement writes the infimum over T(x) = y and adds that the infimum is attained when it is finite. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 3.6: attainment by compactness, the level sets as images of level sets, and the identity inf_B J = inf_{T⁻¹(B)} I.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the cited proof of Theorem 3.6. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, parts (a) and (b).

steps.text: Attainment. Fix y ∈ Y with α = J(y) < ∞. The fiber T⁻¹({y}) is closed in E, because {y} is closed in the metric space Y and T is continuous. For n ≥ 1 let K_n = T⁻¹({y}) ∩ {I ≤ α + 1/n}. Each K_n is nonempty by the definition of the infimum. Each K_n is a closed subset of the compact level set {I ≤ α + 1/n}, so K_n is compact. The sets K_n decrease in n. Cantor's intersection theorem gives a point x in every K_n. Then T(x) = y and I(x) ≤ α, so I(x) = J(y) and the infimum is attained.

Level sets of J. Let α ≥ 0. If I(x) ≤ α, then J(T(x)) ≤ I(x) ≤ α. Conversely, if J(y) ≤ α, step s1 gives x with T(x) = y and I(x) = J(y) ≤ α. Hence {J ≤ α} = T({I ≤ α}). The set {I ≤ α} is compact, and a continuous image of a compact set is compact: an open cover (U_i) of T({I ≤ α}) pulls back to the open cover (T⁻¹(U_i)) of {I ≤ α}, a finite subcover exists, and the images of its members cover T({I ≤ α}). So each level set of J is compact. Compact subsets of the metric space Y are closed, so J is also lower semicontinuous. Since J ≥ 0, J is a good rate function. This proves part (a).

Infimum identity. For every set B ⊂ Y, inf_{y∈B} J(y) = inf_{y∈B} inf{I(x) : T(x) = y} = inf{I(x) : T(x) ∈ B} = inf_{x∈T⁻¹(B)} I(x). Both sides are +∞ when B misses T(E). The identity uses only the definition of J.

Transfer of the bounds. Let F ⊂ Y be closed. Then T⁻¹(F) is closed, and the upper bound of the large deviation principle for µ_N with A = T⁻¹(F) gives limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(T⁻¹(F)) ≤ −inf_{T⁻¹(F)} I = −inf_F J by step s3. Let G ⊂ Y be open. Then T⁻¹(G) is open, and the lower bound gives liminf N⁻¹ log µ_N(T⁻¹(G)) ≥ −inf_{T⁻¹(G)} I = −inf_G J. Now let B ⊂ Y be a Borel set. Monotonicity gives µ_N(T⁻¹(B°)) ≤ µ_N(T⁻¹(B)) ≤ µ_N(T⁻¹(B̄)). Apply the closed-set bound to B̄ and the open-set bound to B°. This gives −inf_{B°} J ≤ liminf N⁻¹ log µ_N∘T⁻¹(B) ≤ limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N∘T⁻¹(B) ≤ −inf_{B̄} J, which is part (b).

applications.title: Magnetization of an ideal spin-1 paramagnet
applications.inputs: N independent spins σ_i ∈ E = {−1, 0, 1}, each with the uniform law µ = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) at infinite temperature. The magnetization per spin is M_N = N⁻¹ Σ_i σ_i. The target value is m = 8/13.
applications.hypotheses: Sanov's theorem for a finite alphabet gives the large deviation principle of the empirical measure L_N on M₁(E) with the good rate function H(·|µ). The map T(ν) = ν(1) − ν(−1) from M₁(E) to ℝ is linear, hence continuous, and T(L_N) = M_N.

steps.text: The contraction principle gives the large deviation principle of M_N with speed N and the good rate function J(m) = inf{H(ν|µ) : ν(1) − ν(−1) = m}.

For θ ∈ ℝ let Z(θ) = Σ_σ µ(σ) e^(θσ) and ν_θ(σ) = µ(σ) e^(θσ)/Z(θ). For every ν with T(ν) = m, H(ν|µ) = H(ν|ν_θ) + θm − log Z(θ) ≥ θm − log Z(θ), with equality only at ν = ν_θ. So J(m) = θm − log Z(θ) for the θ with T(ν_θ) = m.
The magnetization of ν_θ is T(ν_θ) = 9/13 − 1/13 = 8/13. So J(8/13) = (8/13) log 3 − log(13/9) ≈ 0.3083.

The lower bound for the open interval (8/13 − δ, 8/13 + δ) and the upper bound for the closed interval [8/13 − δ, 8/13 + δ] squeeze N⁻¹ log P(|M_N − 8/13| < δ). Lower semicontinuity of J makes the closed-interval infimum tend to J(8/13) as δ → 0.

applications.conclusion: lim_{δ→0} lim_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log P(|M_N − 8/13| < δ) = −J(8/13) = −((8/13) log 3 − log(13/9)) ≈ −0.3083, where the inner limit is taken as liminf or limsup. The cheapest empirical law with this magnetization is ν = (1/13, 3/13, 9/13).

limitations: Goodness of I is needed. Without it, J need not be lower semicontinuous and the infimum need not be attained.

The principle transfers a large deviation principle only along continuous maps. For maps that are continuous only on approximations, one needs exponentially good approximations or the inverse contraction principle under exponential tightness.

results.name: Bryc's inverse Varadhan lemma
results.statement: Let E be a metric space and let µ_N be probability measures on the Borel sets of E. Assume that (µ_N) is exponentially tight: for every α < ∞ there is a compact set K_α ⊂ E with limsup_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log µ_N(E ∖ K_α) < −α. Assume also that for every bounded continuous f: E → ℝ the limit Λ_f = lim_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log ∫_E e^(Nf) dµ_N exists. Then (µ_N) satisfies the large deviation principle with speed N and the good rate function I(x) = sup{f(x) − Λ_f : f bounded and continuous}. Moreover, Λ_f = sup_{x∈E} (f(x) − I(x)) for every bounded continuous f.
hypotheses: E is a metric space and µ_N are probability measures on its Borel sets.
The sequence (µ_N) is exponentially tight.
For every bounded continuous f: E → ℝ the limit Λ_f = lim N⁻¹ log ∫ e^(Nf) dµ_N exists.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 bounds µ_N of a neighbourhood A_x by e^(Nδ) ∫ e^(N(f_x − f_x(x))) dµ_N with Markov's inequality for an exponential.
Step s5 applies Varadhan's integral lemma to a bounded continuous f, once the large deviation principle with good rate function I is proved.

definitions.name: exponential tightness
definitions.text: For every α < ∞ there is a compact K_α with limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(E ∖ K_α) < −α. All but an exponentially small mass sits on one compact set.

definitions.name: large deviation principle
definitions.text: Probability measures µ_N satisfy the large deviation principle with speed N and rate function I if −inf_{A°} I ≤ liminf N⁻¹ log µ_N(A) ≤ limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(A) ≤ −inf_{Ā} I for every Borel set A.

definitions.name: good rate function
definitions.text: A function I: E → [0, +∞] whose level sets {I ≤ α}, α ≥ 0, are compact.

source.module: Chapter 3 General Theory, Section 3.4 Bryc's Inverse Varadhan Lemma
source.excerpt: (Bryc) Suppose that the sequence (µN)N∈N of probability measures µN ∈ M1(E) over the Polish space is exponentially tight and that the limit in (3.13) exists for all f ∈ Cb(E). Then (µN)N∈N satisfies the LDP on E with rate N and good rate function I(x) = sup_{f∈Cb(E)} {f(x) − Λf} (3.14). Furthermore, Λf = sup_{x∈E} {f(x) − I(x)} (3.15).
source.attribution: © Stefan Adams. Quoted from the author's MA4L3 lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the theorem on a Polish space. The authored statement uses any metric space, because the proof uses only the metric and compactness. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 3.15 on pp. 32-34 for the lower bound and the compact upper bound. It adds the steps that the source leaves to Proposition 3.3 and to Varadhan's lemma: the upper bound for closed sets, the goodness of I, and formula (3.15).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the cited proof of Theorem 3.15, with Proposition 3.3 for closed sets and Theorem 3.10 for formula (3.15). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: the large deviation principle, the goodness of I and the formula for Λ_f.

steps.text: I is a rate function. For bounded continuous f, |N⁻¹ log ∫ e^(Nf) dµ_N| ≤ sup |f|, so Λ_f is a real number. The choice f = 0 gives Λ_0 = 0 and hence I(x) ≥ 0 − Λ_0 = 0. Each map x ↦ f(x) − Λ_f is continuous, and a supremum of continuous functions is lower semicontinuous. So I: E → [0, +∞] is lower semicontinuous.

Lower bound for open sets. Let G be open and x ∈ G with I(x) < ∞. Choose r > 0 with B(x, r) ⊂ G and set φ(y) = max(0, 1 − d(x, y)/r). Then φ is continuous, 0 ≤ φ ≤ 1, φ(x) = 1 and φ = 0 off G. For m ∈ ℕ let f_m = m(φ − 1). It is bounded and continuous, f_m(x) = 0, f_m ≤ 0, and f_m = −m off G. So ∫ e^(Nf_m) dµ_N ≤ e^(−mN) + µ_N(G) ≤ 2 max(e^(−mN), µ_N(G)). Taking N⁻¹ log and the liminf gives Λ_{f_m} ≤ max(−m, liminf N⁻¹ log µ_N(G)). The definition of I gives −Λ_{f_m} = f_m(x) − Λ_{f_m} ≤ I(x). Choose m > I(x). Then −m < −I(x) ≤ Λ_{f_m}, so liminf N⁻¹ log µ_N(G) ≥ −I(x). The supremum over x ∈ G gives the lower bound −inf_G I.

Upper bound for compact sets. Let K be compact and 0 < δ < 1. Set I^δ(x) = min(I(x) − δ, 1/δ). For each x ∈ K the definition of I gives a bounded continuous f_x with f_x(x) − Λ_{f_x} ≥ I^δ(x). The set A_x = {y : f_x(y) > f_x(x) − δ} is an open neighbourhood of x. Since 1{f_x − f_x(x) > −δ} ≤ e^(N(f_x − f_x(x) + δ)), Markov's inequality gives µ_N(A_x) ≤ e^(Nδ − Nf_x(x)) ∫ e^(Nf_x) dµ_N. So limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(A_x) ≤ δ − f_x(x) + Λ_{f_x} ≤ δ − I^δ(x). Finitely many sets A_{x_1}, …, A_{x_k} cover K. Then µ_N(K) ≤ k max_i µ_N(A_{x_i}), and limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(K) ≤ δ − min_i I^δ(x_i) ≤ δ − min(inf_K I − δ, 1/δ). Let δ → 0 to get the bound −inf_K I.

Closed sets and goodness. Let F be closed and let α be a real number with α < inf_F I. Exponential tightness gives K_α. The set F ∩ K_α is compact and I ≥ inf_F I on it, so step s3 gives limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(F ∩ K_α) ≤ −inf_F I < −α. From µ_N(F) ≤ µ_N(F ∩ K_α) + µ_N(E ∖ K_α) and the bound for the larger of the two terms, limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(F) ≤ −α. Letting α increase to inf_F I gives the upper bound for F. For goodness, apply step s2 to the open set E ∖ K_α. It gives −inf_{E∖K_α} I ≤ liminf N⁻¹ log µ_N(E ∖ K_α) < −α, so I > α off K_α. Thus {I ≤ α} is a closed subset of the compact K_α, hence compact. For a Borel set A, the bounds for Ā and A° and monotonicity give the large deviation principle.

Formula for Λ_f. Let f be bounded and continuous. Steps s1 to s4 give the large deviation principle with the good rate function I. Since f is bounded above, it satisfies the tail condition, and Varadhan's integral lemma gives lim N⁻¹ log ∫ e^(Nf) dµ_N = sup_x (f(x) − I(x)). The left side is Λ_f by hypothesis.

applications.title: Low-temperature position of a particle in a potential well
applications.inputs: A particle on E = [0, 1] in the potential V(x) = 4(x − 1/2)². At temperature 1/N its position X_N has the Gibbs law µ_N(dx) = e^(−NV(x)) dx / ∫₀¹ e^(−NV(y)) dy. The question is the exponential rate of P(X_N ≥ 3/4).
applications.hypotheses: E = [0, 1] is a compact metric space, so (µ_N) is exponentially tight with K_α = E for every α. Step a1 computes Λ_f for every continuous f on [0, 1], so the limit hypothesis holds.

steps.text: Laplace method: for continuous g on [0, 1], N⁻¹ log ∫₀¹ e^(Ng) dx → max g. The integral is at most e^(N max g). The set {g > max g − ε} is a nonempty open subset of [0, 1] with some length ℓ_ε > 0, so the integral is at least ℓ_ε e^(N(max g − ε)). Hence Λ_f = max(f − V) − max(−V) = max(f − V) + min V for every f.

Rate function: for every f, f(x) − Λ_f ≤ f(x) − (f(x) − V(x)) − min V = V(x) − min V. The choice f = V gives equality. So Bryc's theorem gives the large deviation principle with I(x) = V(x) − min V = 4(x − 1/2)².
The closed set [3/4, 1] and the set (3/4, 1], which is open in E, have the same infimum of I, namely I(3/4) = 4(3/4 − 1/2)² = 1/4. So lim N⁻¹ log P(X_N ≥ 3/4) = −1/4.
Check formula (3.15) for f(x) = x. The function x − 4(x − 1/2)² has derivative 1 − 8(x − 1/2), which vanishes at x = 5/8. Its maximum is 5/8 − 4(1/8)² = 9/16, which equals both Λ_f and sup(f − I).

applications.conclusion: The position X_N satisfies the large deviation principle with rate function 4(x − 1/2)², and P(X_N ≥ 3/4) = e^(−N/4 + o(N)) as the temperature 1/N tends to 0.

limitations: The theorem needs the limit Λ_f for every bounded continuous f, which is a strong hypothesis. In vector spaces the Gärtner–Ellis theorem uses only linear f, at the price of convexity conditions.
Without exponential tightness the argument gives only the weak large deviation principle, with the upper bound for compact sets.

results.name: Donsker–Varadhan large deviation principle for finite Markov chains
aliases: level-2 large deviations for finite Markov chains
results.statement: Let E be a finite set, let P = (p(x, y)) be an irreducible stochastic matrix on E, and let (Y_k)_{k≥0} be a Markov chain with transition matrix P and Y₀ = σ for a fixed σ ∈ E. Let L_N = N⁻¹ Σ_{k=1}^N δ_{Y_k}, viewed as a vector in ℝ^E. For λ ∈ ℝ^E let P_λ(x, y) = p(x, y) e^(λ_y), and let ρ(P_λ) be its Perron–Frobenius eigenvalue. Then (L_N) satisfies the large deviation principle in ℝ^E with speed N and the convex good rate function I(q) = sup_{λ∈ℝ^E} (⟨λ, q⟩ − log ρ(P_λ)), which does not depend on σ. Moreover, I(q) = +∞ for q outside the simplex M₁(E), and for q ∈ M₁(E), I(q) = sup_{u≫0} Σ_x q_x log(u_x/(uP)_x) = sup_{u≫0} Σ_x q_x log(u_x/(Pu)_x). Here u ≫ 0 means u_x > 0 for every x, (uP)_x = Σ_y u_y p(y, x) and (Pu)_x = Σ_y p(x, y) u_y.
hypotheses: E is a finite set and (Y_k) is a Markov chain on E with transition matrix P, started at a fixed state σ.
The stochastic matrix P is irreducible.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s2, s5 and s6 use the Perron–Frobenius theorem for the irreducible matrices P_λ: a simple eigenvalue ρ(P_λ) > 0 with positive left and right eigenvectors.
Step s3 uses the implicit function theorem at the simple root ρ(P_λ) of det(z − P_λ) to show that λ ↦ ρ(P_λ) is differentiable.
Step s3 applies part (c) of the Gärtner–Ellis theorem to the finite, differentiable limit Λ(λ) = log ρ(P_λ).

definitions.name: irreducible stochastic matrix
definitions.text: A matrix P with nonnegative entries and row sums 1 such that every state can reach every other state through a chain of transitions with positive probability.

definitions.name: Perron–Frobenius eigenvalue
definitions.text: For an irreducible nonnegative matrix B, the eigenvalue ρ(B) > 0 that equals the spectral radius of B. It is simple and has left and right eigenvectors with positive entries.

definitions.name: empirical measure of a chain
definitions.text: L_N = N⁻¹ Σ_{k=1}^N δ_{Y_k}. Its value at x is the fraction of the times 1, …, N that the chain spends at x.

source.excerpt: (LDP for L_N^Y – Sanov's theorem for Markov chains) Under the same assumptions as in Theorem 5.2, the large deviation principle holds for the empirical measures (L_N^Y)N∈N with respect to the Markov chain distribution with rate N and rate function given in (5.9).

source.alignment: The source states Theorem 5.3 with the rate function (5.9) and proves the variational formula with the left action uP in Theorem 5.4. The authored statement collects both, adds the equal form with the right action Pu, which is the classical Donsker–Varadhan form, and notes that the rate does not depend on the initial state. The outline follows the proofs of Theorems 5.1 (e), 5.2, 5.3 and 5.4 on pp. 44-47.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proofs of Theorems 5.1 (e), 5.2, 5.3 and 5.4 in Adams's MA4L3 notes, pp. 44-47. Step s3 takes the differentiability of the Perron–Frobenius eigenvalue from the source, which cites Seneta's book, and the large deviation principle from the Gärtner–Ellis theorem.

steps.text: Exponential moments as matrix powers. For λ ∈ ℝ^E, N⟨λ, L_N⟩ = Σ_{k=1}^N λ_{Y_k}. The Markov property gives E_σ exp(Σ_{k=1}^N λ_{Y_k}) = Σ_{y₁,…,y_N} Π_{k=1}^N p(y_{k−1}, y_k) e^(λ_{y_k}) = Σ_{y∈E} P_λ^N(σ, y), with y₀ = σ. This is the computation in the proof of Theorem 5.2 of the source, with f(y) = (1_x(y))_{x∈E}.

Perron–Frobenius limit (Theorem 5.1 (e) of the source). P_λ has the same zero pattern as P, so it is irreducible. Let θ ≫ 0 be a right eigenvector for ρ(P_λ) and let 1 be the vector of ones. Entrywise, θ/max θ ≤ 1 ≤ θ/min θ, so P_λ^N θ / max θ ≤ P_λ^N 1 ≤ P_λ^N θ / min θ, and P_λ^N θ = ρ(P_λ)^N θ. Hence Λ(λ) = lim N⁻¹ log Σ_y P_λ^N(σ, y) = log ρ(P_λ) for every λ and every σ.

Gärtner–Ellis. The eigenvalue ρ(P_λ) is a simple root of det(z − P_λ), whose coefficients are polynomials in the numbers e^(λ_y). The implicit function theorem then makes λ ↦ ρ(P_λ) differentiable, as the source states with a reference to Seneta. So Λ = log ρ(P_·) is finite and differentiable on all of ℝ^E. With D_Λ = ℝ^E it is essentially smooth and continuous. Part (c) of the Gärtner–Ellis theorem gives the large deviation principle for L_N in ℝ^E with the convex good rate function I = Λ*. The limit Λ does not depend on σ, so neither does I.

The rate is infinite off the simplex. L_N always lies in M₁(E), which is closed in ℝ^E. The lower bound for the open set ℝ^E ∖ M₁(E) gives −inf_{q∉M₁(E)} I(q) ≤ liminf N⁻¹ log 0 = −∞. So I(q) = +∞ for every q ∉ M₁(E).

Lower bound for I (first half of the proof of Theorem 5.4). Let q ∈ M₁(E) and u ≫ 0. Every column of the irreducible P has a positive entry, so (uP)_y > 0. Set λ_x = log(u_x/(uP)_x). Then (uP_λ)_y = (uP)_y e^(λ_y) = u_y, so uP_λ^N = u. Theorem 5.1 (e) with the positive vector u gives log ρ(P_λ) = lim N⁻¹ log Σ_y (uP_λ^N)_y = 0. Hence I(q) ≥ ⟨λ, q⟩ = Σ_x q_x log(u_x/(uP)_x). For the right form set λ_x = log(u_x/(Pu)_x) and D = diag(e^(λ_x)). Then DPu = u, and ρ(DP) = ρ(PD) = ρ(P_λ) because DP = D(PD)D⁻¹. The same argument gives I(q) ≥ Σ_x q_x log(u_x/(Pu)_x).

Upper bound for I (second half of the proof of Theorem 5.4). Fix λ and let u* ≫ 0 be a left Perron eigenvector of P_λ. Then (u*P)_x e^(λ_x) = ρ(P_λ) u*_x, so λ_x = log ρ(P_λ) + log(u*_x/(u*P)_x). For q ∈ M₁(E), Σ_x q_x = 1 gives ⟨λ, q⟩ − log ρ(P_λ) = Σ_x q_x log(u*_x/(u*P)_x), which is at most the supremum over u ≫ 0. The supremum over λ gives equality in the first formula. A right Perron eigenvector v* of DP gives λ_x = log ρ(P_λ) + log(v*_x/(Pv*)_x) and the second formula in the same way.

applications.title: Occupation imbalance of a persistent two-state chain
applications.inputs: A two-state chain on E = {0, 1}, for example a molecule that switches between two conformations, with P = ((2/3, 1/3), (1/3, 2/3)). The stationary law is (1/2, 1/2). The target is the occupation vector q = (2/7, 5/7).
applications.hypotheses: E is finite and all entries of P are positive, so P is irreducible. The initial state does not matter for the rate.

steps.text: Use the right form I(q) = sup_{u≫0} Σ_x q_x log(u_x/(Pu)_x). The functional is unchanged when u is multiplied by a constant, so take u = (1, s) with s > 0. Then (Pu)₀ = (2 + s)/3 and (Pu)₁ = (1 + 2s)/3.

In the variables w = log u the functional is concave, because log (Pu)_x is a log-sum-exp of w. So a critical point is the maximum. The derivative in s vanishes when q₀/(2 + s) = q₁/(s(1 + 2s)), that is, q₀ s(1 + 2s) = q₁(2 + s).
For q = (2/7, 5/7) the value s = 2 solves this equation, because (2/7)·2·5 = (5/7)·4 = 20/7.

For independent fair draws the same imbalance costs H(q | (1/2, 1/2)) = log 2 + (2/7) log(2/7) + (5/7) log(5/7) ≈ 0.0949. The persistent chain makes long runs in one state cheaper, so its rate is about half as large.

applications.conclusion: For the persistent chain, P(L_N is near (2/7, 5/7)) = e^(−N(I + o(1))) with I = (2/7) log(3/4) + (5/7) log(6/5) ≈ 0.0480, about half of the rate 0.0949 for independent draws with the same stationary law.

limitations: The proof uses a finite state space. On general state spaces Donsker and Varadhan proved the principle under strong uniformity conditions, and the lower bound can fail without them.
The rate function I(q) has no closed form in general. The pair empirical measure has an explicit relative entropy rate, and I is its contraction.

results.name: Mogulskii's theorem
aliases: Mogulskii's theorem for sample-path large deviations of random walks
sample path large deviations for random walks
results.statement: Let X_1, X_2, … be independent identically distributed random vectors in ℝ^d, and assume that Λ(λ) = log E e^(⟨λ, X_1⟩) is finite for every λ ∈ ℝ^d. Let Λ*(x) = sup_{λ∈ℝ^d} (⟨λ, x⟩ − Λ(λ)). For N ≥ 1 let Z_N(t) = N⁻¹ Σ_{k=1}^{⌊Nt⌋} X_k for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, and let µ_N be the law of the path Z_N in the space L∞([0, 1]) of bounded functions h: [0, 1] → ℝ^d with the supremum norm ‖h‖ = sup_{t∈[0,1]} |h(t)|. Then (µ_N) satisfies the large deviation principle with speed N and the good rate function I(h) = ∫₀¹ Λ*(ḣ(t)) dt if h is absolutely continuous with h(0) = 0, and I(h) = ∞ otherwise. That is, limsup_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log µ_N(F) ≤ −inf_F I for every closed set F and liminf_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log µ_N(G) ≥ −inf_G I for every open set G of L∞([0, 1]).
hypotheses: X_1, X_2, … are independent identically distributed random vectors in ℝ^d.
The logarithmic moment generating function Λ(λ) = log E e^(⟨λ, X_1⟩) is finite for every λ ∈ ℝ^d.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Markov's inequality for e^(λ|X_1|) to show that the step path and its linear interpolation are exponentially equivalent.
Step s2 applies the Gärtner–Ellis theorem to the independent increments of the path at finitely many times.
Step s2 moves the large deviation principle from the increments to the path values through a continuous linear bijection.
Step s3 uses the Dawson–Gärtner theorem to combine the finite-dimensional principles into one principle in the topology of pointwise convergence.
Step s4 uses Jensen's inequality for the convex function Λ* on each interval of a partition to show I_X ≤ I.
Step s4 uses the Lebesgue differentiation theorem: the averages of the derivative over shrinking grid intervals converge almost everywhere.
Step s4 uses Fatou's lemma for the nonnegative functions Λ*(g^k) to show I_X ≥ I.

definitions.name: Legendre–Fenchel transform
definitions.text: Λ*(x) = sup_λ (⟨λ, x⟩ − Λ(λ)). It is convex, lower semicontinuous and nonnegative, because Λ(0) = 0.

definitions.name: absolutely continuous function
definitions.text: h: [0, 1] → ℝ^d is absolutely continuous if for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that Σ_i |h(t_i) − h(s_i)| < ε for every finite family of disjoint intervals (s_i, t_i) with Σ_i (t_i − s_i) < δ. Then h is differentiable almost everywhere and h(t) = h(0) + ∫₀ᵗ ḣ(s) ds.

definitions.name: exponential equivalence
definitions.text: Two sequences of random elements Y_N and Ỹ_N of a metric space, defined on one probability space, are exponentially equivalent if limsup N⁻¹ log P(d(Y_N, Ỹ_N) > δ) = −∞ for every δ > 0.

definitions.name: exponential tightness
definitions.text: A sequence of laws µ_N is exponentially tight if for every α < ∞ there is a compact set K_α with limsup N⁻¹ log µ_N(K_α^c) < −α.

source.excerpt: (Sample path large deviations for random walks, Mogulskii's theorem) The sequence (µN)N∈N of probability measures µN satisfies in L∞([0, 1]) the LDP with the good rate function I(h) = ∫₀¹ Λ*(ḣ(t)) dt, if h ∈ AC, h(0) = 0, ∞, otherwise
source.attribution: © Stefan Adams. Quoted from the author's MA4L3 lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement collects the setting of Section 7.1: the hypothesis (7.1), the path Z_N in (7.2) and the supremum norm in (7.3), which the source takes over all t ∈ [0, 1]. The source states the theorem with speed N and the rate function (7.4). The outline follows Lemma 7.5, Lemma 7.8, the proof of Theorem 7.6 and the proof of Theorem 7.1 on pp. 58-62. The source calls Theorem 7.6 'Theorem 7.14' in these proofs. The source states Theorem 7.4 for Polish spaces and applies it in L∞([0, 1]), which is not separable. The usual proof of that theorem uses only the metric. The source leaves the case I_X(f) = ∞ for f not absolutely continuous as an exercise, and step s5 gives an argument for it.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow Lemma 7.5, Lemma 7.8, the proof of Theorem 7.6 and the proof of Theorem 7.1 in Adams's MA4L3 notes, pp. 58-62. The source cites without proof Theorem 7.4 (exponentially equivalent sequences have the same large deviation principle), the Dawson–Gärtner theorem and the exponential tightness in Lemma 7.7, which it refers to Dembo and Zeitouni. Step s5 completes a part that the source leaves as an exercise.

steps.text: Lemma 7.5 of the source. Let Z̃_N be the linear interpolation of Z_N, that is, Z̃_N(t) = Z_N(t) + (t − ⌊Nt⌋/N) X_{⌊Nt⌋+1}. Then ‖Z̃_N − Z_N‖ ≤ N⁻¹ max_{k≤N} |X_k|. Because |x| ≤ √d max_i |x_i|, the hypothesis gives E e^(λ|X_1|) < ∞ for every λ > 0. A union bound and the exponential Chebyshev inequality give P(‖Z̃_N − Z_N‖ > δ) ≤ N P(|X_1| > Nδ) ≤ N E e^(λ|X_1|) e^(−λNδ). So limsup N⁻¹ log P(‖Z̃_N − Z_N‖ > δ) ≤ −λδ for every λ, which is −∞. Thus the laws µ̃_N of Z̃_N and µ_N are exponentially equivalent, and by Theorem 7.4 of the source it is sufficient to prove the principle for µ̃_N.

Lemma 7.8 of the source. Fix times 0 = t_0 < t_1 < … < t_k ≤ 1. The increments Y_ℓ = Z_N(t_ℓ) − Z_N(t_{ℓ−1}) are independent, and Y_ℓ is N⁻¹ times a sum of ⌊Nt_ℓ⌋ − ⌊Nt_{ℓ−1}⌋ independent copies of X_1. So N⁻¹ log E exp(N Σ_ℓ ⟨λ_ℓ, Y_ℓ⟩) → Λ_j(λ) = Σ_ℓ (t_ℓ − t_{ℓ−1}) Λ(λ_ℓ), which is finite and differentiable on ℝ^{dk}. The Gärtner–Ellis theorem gives the principle for (Y_1, …, Y_k) with the rate Λ_j*(y) = Σ_ℓ (t_ℓ − t_{ℓ−1}) Λ*(y_ℓ/(t_ℓ − t_{ℓ−1})), because the supremum separates over ℓ. The map from increments to values is a continuous linear bijection, so the contraction principle gives the rate I_j(z) = Σ_ℓ (t_ℓ − t_{ℓ−1}) Λ*((z_ℓ − z_{ℓ−1})/(t_ℓ − t_{ℓ−1})) for (Z_N(t_1), …, Z_N(t_k)), with z_0 = 0. Since |(Z̃_N(t_ℓ) − Z_N(t_ℓ))_ℓ| ≤ √k ‖Z̃_N − Z_N‖, step s1 gives the same principle for the values of Z̃_N.

Projective limit (step 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.6). The finite subsets of (0, 1], ordered by inclusion, index the spaces ℝ^{d|j|} with the coordinate projections between them. The space X of all functions f: [0, 1] → ℝ^d with f(0) = 0, with the topology of pointwise convergence, is their projective limit. The Dawson–Gärtner theorem, which the source cites, gives the principle for µ̃_N in X with the good rate function I_X(f) = sup Σ_{ℓ=1}^k (t_ℓ − t_{ℓ−1}) Λ*((f(t_ℓ) − f(t_{ℓ−1}))/(t_ℓ − t_{ℓ−1})), where the supremum is over all k and all 0 = t_0 < t_1 < … < t_k ≤ 1.

Identification on absolutely continuous paths (step 3 of the source). Let f be absolutely continuous with f(0) = 0 and g = ḟ ∈ L¹. Since f(t_ℓ) − f(t_{ℓ−1}) = ∫ g over [t_{ℓ−1}, t_ℓ], Jensen's inequality for the convex Λ* and the uniform measure on that interval gives (t_ℓ − t_{ℓ−1}) Λ*((f(t_ℓ) − f(t_{ℓ−1}))/(t_ℓ − t_{ℓ−1})) ≤ ∫ Λ*(g) over [t_{ℓ−1}, t_ℓ]. Summing gives I_X(f) ≤ I(f). For the reverse inequality take the partitions with step 1/k. Their sum is ∫₀¹ Λ*(g^k(t)) dt, where g^k(t) is the average of g over the grid interval of length 1/k that contains t. By the Lebesgue differentiation theorem g^k → g almost everywhere. Λ* ≥ 0 and Λ* is lower semicontinuous, so Fatou's lemma gives I_X(f) ≥ liminf_k ∫ Λ*(g^k) ≥ ∫ Λ*(g) = I(f).

Paths that are not absolutely continuous (the exercise in the source). Λ is convex and finite, so it is continuous, and C_M = max_{|λ|=M} Λ(λ) is finite for every M > 0. The choice λ = Mx/|x| gives Λ*(x) ≥ M|x| − C_M. Let f ∈ X with I_X(f) < ∞, and let (s_i, t_i) be disjoint intervals with total length δ. Use a partition that contains all s_i and t_i. All its terms are nonnegative, so M Σ_i |f(t_i) − f(s_i)| − C_M δ ≤ I_X(f). First choose M with I_X(f)/M < ε/2, then δ with C_M δ/M < ε/2. Then Σ_i |f(t_i) − f(s_i)| < ε, so f is absolutely continuous. Hence I_X = I on all of X.

Change of topology (proof of Theorem 7.1 in the source). Each Z̃_N is continuous with Z̃_N(0) = 0, and the domain of I lies in C_0 = {h ∈ C([0, 1]) : h(0) = 0}. By Lemma 3.5 of the source the principle holds in C_0 with the topology of pointwise convergence. Lemma 7.7, whose proof the source refers to Dembo and Zeitouni, states that (µ̃_N) is exponentially tight in C_0 with the supremum norm. That topology is finer, so Proposition 3.9 of the source, which rests on the inverse contraction principle, gives the same principle with the good rate function I in the supremum norm. C_0 is a closed subset of L∞([0, 1]), so Lemma 3.5 again gives the principle in L∞([0, 1]) with I = ∞ outside C_0. Finally step s1 and Theorem 7.4 of the source transfer the principle from µ̃_N to µ_N.

applications.title: A rare excursion of a diffusing tracer
applications.inputs: A tracer particle on a line takes N independent displacements X_k with the standard normal law. Its rescaled position after ⌊Nt⌋ displacements is Z_N(t) = N⁻¹ Σ_{k≤⌊Nt⌋} X_k. The event E_N is that the tracer is at least N/2 to the right after N/4 displacements and back at or left of its start after N displacements, that is, Z_N(1/4) ≥ 1/2 and Z_N(1) ≤ 0.
applications.hypotheses: The displacements are independent and identically distributed in ℝ, and Λ(λ) = log E e^(λX_1) = λ²/2 is finite for every λ. So the theorem applies with d = 1.

steps.text: Here Λ*(x) = sup_λ (λx − λ²/2) = x²/2, attained at λ = x. So I(h) = (1/2) ∫₀¹ ḣ(t)² dt for absolutely continuous h with h(0) = 0, and I(h) = ∞ otherwise.

Evaluation at a fixed time t is continuous for the supremum norm, so F = {h : h(1/4) ≥ 1/2, h(1) ≤ 0} is closed and G = {h : h(1/4) > 1/2, h(1) < 0} is open, with G ⊂ E ⊂ F for the event set E of paths. The theorem bounds N⁻¹ log P(E_N) between −inf_G I and −inf_F I.

Let h(1/4) = u and h(1) = v. Jensen's inequality on [0, 1/4] and on [1/4, 1] gives I(h) ≥ (1/2)(1/4)(4u)² + (1/2)(3/4)((v − u)/(3/4))² = 2u² + (2/3)(u − v)², with equality for the path that is linear on each interval.
On F, u ≥ 1/2 and u − v ≥ 1/2, so I ≥ 2(1/2)² + (2/3)(1/2)² = 1/2 + 1/6 = 2/3. The path with u = 1/2 and v = 0 attains this value.

The minimizing path rises with slope 2 to 1/2 at t = 1/4 and falls with slope −2/3 to 0 at t = 1, because 1/2 − (2/3)(3/4) = 0. The linear paths with u = 1/2 + η and v = −η lie in G and their cost 2u² + (2/3)(u − v)² tends to 2/3 as η → 0, so inf_G I = inf_F I = 2/3.

applications.conclusion: lim_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log P(Z_N(1/4) ≥ 1/2, Z_N(1) ≤ 0) = −2/3. The condition at t = 1/4 alone costs 1/2, and the return to the start adds 1/6. The most probable way for the rare event to occur is the piecewise linear path of step a5.

limitations: The theorem needs a finite moment generating function for all λ. With heavier tails the path can jump, and the rate function and the topology must change.
The theorem gives only the exponential rate. It does not give the prefactor of P(E_N).

results.name: Equivalence of the microcanonical and canonical ensembles
results.statement: For each N let P_N be a probability measure on a measurable space Λ_N, and let h_N: Λ_N → ℝ be a measurable function (the mean energy). Assume that (i) under P_N, h_N satisfies the large deviation principle with speed N and rate function −s, where the microcanonical entropy s: ℝ → [−∞, 0] is upper semicontinuous, and (ii) for every β ∈ ℝ the free energy φ(β) = −lim_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log Z_N(β), with Z_N(β) = ∫ e^(−βN h_N) dP_N, exists and is finite. Let P_{N,β}(dω) = e^(−βN h_N(ω)) P_N(dω)/Z_N(β) be the canonical measures. Then: (a) φ(β) = inf_{u∈ℝ} (βu − s(u)) for every β, so φ is the concave Legendre–Fenchel transform of s. (b) s**(u) = inf_β (βu − φ(β)) is the smallest concave upper semicontinuous function with s** ≥ s, so s = s** if and only if s is concave. (c) Under P_{N,β}, h_N satisfies the large deviation principle with speed N and the good rate function J_β(u) = βu − s(u) − φ(β). (d) J_β(u) = 0 if and only if β ∈ ∂s(u), where ∂s(u) is the set of β with s(v) ≤ s(u) + β(v − u) for all v ∈ ℝ. Hence, if ∂s(u) is empty, in particular if s(u) < s**(u), then u is not an equilibrium mean energy of the canonical ensemble for any β (nonequivalence). If β ∈ ∂s(u) and s(v) < s(u) + β(v − u) for every v ≠ u, then u is the only zero of J_β, and P_{N,β}(|h_N − u| ≥ δ) tends to 0 exponentially fast for every δ > 0 (equivalence).
hypotheses: P_N is a probability measure on Λ_N and h_N: Λ_N → ℝ is measurable for each N.
Under P_N, h_N satisfies the large deviation principle with speed N and rate function −s, where s: ℝ → [−∞, 0] is upper semicontinuous.
For every β ∈ ℝ the limit φ(β) = −lim N⁻¹ log ∫ e^(−βN h_N) dP_N exists and is finite.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 to s3 prove the case F(u) = −βu of Varadhan's integral lemma, restricted to an open or a closed set of energies, with the tail bound from hypothesis (ii).
Step s4 uses the Fenchel–Moreau theorem for −s to identify s** as the smallest concave upper semicontinuous majorant of s.

definitions.name: microcanonical entropy
definitions.text: s(u) = lim_{r→0} lim_{N→∞} N⁻¹ log P_N(h_N ∈ [u − r, u + r]). The large deviation hypothesis (i) is the rigorous form of this definition.

definitions.name: microcanonical ensemble
definitions.text: The law P_N conditioned on h_N ∈ [u − r, u + r], with r → 0. It describes an isolated system at mean energy u.

definitions.name: canonical ensemble
definitions.text: P_{N,β}(dω) = e^(−βN h_N(ω)) P_N(dω)/Z_N(β). It describes a system in contact with a heat bath at inverse temperature β.

definitions.name: supporting line
definitions.text: β ∈ ∂s(u) means that the line v ↦ s(u) + β(v − u) lies above the graph of s and touches it at u. Then s is concave at u. If the line touches the graph only at u, s is strictly concave at u.

source.excerpt: Proposition 4. Assume A1-A2. Then u ∈ Uβ if and only if β ∈ ∂s(u). Proof. We first prove the necessary part of this result. Let u ∈ dom s and assume that β ∈ ∂s(u).

source.alignment: The authored statement collects the thermodynamic level of Section III: the transform (21) in part (a), the concave hull (22) in part (b), Proposition 3 on p. 12 in part (c), and Proposition 4 with the two cases after it in part (d). U_β of the source is the zero set of J_β. Assumption A1 of the source asks for a finite φ everywhere, and A2 is hypothesis (i). The authored statement takes P_N to be a probability measure, which makes s ≤ 0. The source proves Proposition 3 with its Theorem 14, which it cites without proof. Steps s1 and s2 prove the bounds that this needs. The source calls ∂s(u) a subdifferential, and its Appendix A defines strict concavity at u by a supporting line that touches the graph only at u. The macrostate level (Theorem 7 of the source) needs the further assumptions A3 and A4 and is not part of this record.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow Section III of Touchette (2015): the transform (21), the hull (22), Proposition 3 and Proposition 4 with their proofs on pp. 10-13. The source cites its Theorem 14 (large deviations of tilted measures) for Proposition 3. Steps s1 and s2 give that argument for the function −βu in full. The macrostate level of the source is not covered.

steps.text: Lower bound on open sets. Let O be open, u ∈ O with s(u) > −∞, and ε > 0 with (u − ε, u + ε) ⊂ O. On that interval e^(−βN h_N) ≥ e^(−N(βu + |β|ε)). So ∫_{h_N∈O} e^(−βN h_N) dP_N ≥ e^(−N(βu + |β|ε)) P_N(|h_N − u| < ε). The lower bound of hypothesis (i) gives liminf N⁻¹ log P_N(|h_N − u| < ε) ≥ s(u). Let ε → 0 and take the supremum over u: liminf N⁻¹ log ∫_{h_N∈O} e^(−βN h_N) dP_N ≥ sup_O (s(u) − βu).

Upper bound on closed sets. Let C be closed, M > 0 and ε > 0. On {h_N > M}, e^(−βN h_N) ≤ e^(−NM) e^(−(β−1)N h_N), so this part of the integral is at most e^(−NM) Z_N(β − 1), whose exponential rate is −M − φ(β − 1). In the same way {h_N < −M} contributes at most e^(−NM) Z_N(β + 1). Cover [−M, M] by finitely many closed intervals K_i of length at most ε/(1 + |β|). Then βu varies by at most ε on K_i, and the upper bound of (i) for the closed set K_i ∩ C gives the rate sup_{K_i∩C} (s(u) − βu) + ε for the part in K_i ∩ C. The rate of a finite sum is the maximum of the rates. So limsup N⁻¹ log ∫_{h_N∈C} e^(−βN h_N) dP_N ≤ max(sup_C (s(u) − βu) + ε, −M − φ(β − 1), −M − φ(β + 1)). Let M → ∞ and ε → 0.

Part (a). Steps s1 and s2 with O = C = ℝ give lim N⁻¹ log Z_N(β) = sup_u (s(u) − βu). By (ii) this limit is −φ(β), so φ(β) = inf_u (βu − s(u)). As an infimum of affine functions of β, φ is concave. This is the transform (21) of the source.

Part (b). By (a), βu − φ(β) ≥ s(u) for all β and u, so s** ≥ s. Apply the Fenchel–Moreau theorem to f = −s, which is proper because sup s = 0, and has the affine minorant 0. Its conjugate is f*(y) = −φ(−y), and f** = −s**. So −s** is the largest lower semicontinuous convex function below −s. Equivalently, s** is the smallest concave upper semicontinuous function above s. Since s is upper semicontinuous, s = s** exactly when s is concave. If β ∈ ∂s(u), the line v ↦ s(u) + β(v − u) is one such function, so s**(u) ≤ s(u). Hence s(u) < s**(u) forces ∂s(u) = ∅.

Part (c). P_{N,β}(h_N ∈ A) = Z_N(β)⁻¹ ∫_{h_N∈A} e^(−βN h_N) dP_N, and N⁻¹ log Z_N(β) → −φ(β). Steps s1 and s2 give limsup N⁻¹ log P_{N,β}(h_N ∈ C) ≤ sup_C (s(u) − βu) + φ(β) = −inf_C J_β for closed C, and the matching lower bound for open sets. J_β ≥ 0 by (a), and J_β is lower semicontinuous because s is upper semicontinuous. By (a), −s(v) ≥ φ(β′) − β′v for every β′. With β′ = β ∓ 1 this gives J_β(v) ≥ |v| − c, where c = max(φ(β) − φ(β − 1), φ(β) − φ(β + 1)). So the level sets of J_β are closed and bounded, and J_β is a good rate function.

Part (d), which is Proposition 4 of the source. If s(u) = −∞, then J_β(u) = ∞ and ∂s(u) = ∅, because sup s = 0. If s(u) > −∞, then J_β(u) = 0 means βu − s(u) = inf_v (βv − s(v)), that is, s(v) ≤ s(u) + β(v − u) for all v, which is β ∈ ∂s(u). If the inequality is strict for v ≠ u, then J_β(v) > 0 for v ≠ u. Let δ > 0. The closed set {v : |v − u| ≥ δ} meets the compact level sets of J_β, so the infimum a of J_β on it is attained or infinite, and a > 0. Part (c) gives limsup N⁻¹ log P_{N,β}(|h_N − u| ≥ δ) ≤ −a < 0.

applications.title: A paramagnet of two-level atoms
applications.inputs: N independent atoms, each in the ground level (energy 0) or the excited level (energy 1), with the uniform prior P_N on {0, 1}^N. The mean energy h_N is the fraction of excited atoms. The microcanonical mean energy is u = 1/4.
applications.hypotheses: P_N is a probability measure. Under P_N, h_N is the mean of N independent fair Bernoulli variables. Cramér's theorem gives the large deviation principle with s(u) = −u log u − (1 − u) log(1 − u) − log 2 for u ∈ [0, 1] and s(u) = −∞ otherwise. This s is continuous on [0, 1], so it is upper semicontinuous, and s ≤ 0. Also Z_N(β) = ((1 + e^(−β))/2)^N exactly, so φ(β) = log 2 − log(1 + e^(−β)) is finite for every β.

steps.text: On (0, 1), s′(u) = log((1 − u)/u) and s″(u) = −1/(u(1 − u)) < 0. So s is strictly concave on [0, 1], and the tangent at u touches the graph only at u. At u = 1/4 the slope is log 3, because (1 − 1/4)/(1/4) = 3. So ∂s(1/4) = {log 3}.

Part (d) says that β = log 3 is the only inverse temperature whose canonical ensemble has the equilibrium mean energy 1/4. Directly, the canonical probability of the excited level is e^(−β)/(1 + e^(−β)) = (1/3)/(1 + 1/3) = 1/4.

Part (a) at β = log 3: φ(log 3) = log 2 − log(4/3) = log(3/2). The infimum of βu − s(u) is at u = 1/4, where (1/4) log 3 + (1/4) log(1/4) + (3/4) log(3/4) + log 2 = log 3 − log 2 = log(3/2). The two values agree. The partition function per atom is e^(−φ) = (1 + 1/3)/2 = 2/3.

Part (c): J_{log 3}(u) = u log 3 + u log u + (1 − u) log(1 − u) + log(4/3) = u log(4u) + (1 − u) log(4(1 − u)/3). This is the relative entropy of the Bernoulli(u) law with respect to the Bernoulli(1/4) law. At u = 1/2 it is (1/2) log 2 + (1/2) log(2/3) = (1/2) log(4/3) ≈ 0.1438.

applications.conclusion: The microcanonical ensemble at mean energy 1/4 and the canonical ensemble at β = log 3 are equivalent: the entropy is concave, φ and s are Legendre transforms of each other, and the canonical mean energy concentrates at 1/4. For example, the canonical probability that at least half of the atoms are excited decays like e^(−N (1/2) log(4/3)) on the exponential scale.

limitations: Systems with long-range interactions can have a nonconcave entropy. Then energies u with s(u) < s**(u) are not seen in the canonical ensemble at any temperature, and the canonical ensemble has a first-order phase transition in their place.

The record covers the thermodynamic level and the equilibrium energies. Equivalence of equilibrium macrostates and of the measures themselves needs more assumptions, as in Theorems 7, 10 and 12 of the source.

results.name: Jarzynski equality
results.statement: Let S be a finite set, β > 0 and N ≥ 1. Let X = (X_0, …, X_N) be a Markov chain on S with initial law p_0 and transition matrices M_1, …, M_N, where (M_n)_{xy} = P(X_n = x | X_{n−1} = y). Assume that p_0 has positive entries and that each M_n has a stationary distribution p_n (M_n p_n = p_n) with positive entries. This holds, with p_n unique, when M_n is irreducible. For n = 0, …, N let E_n: S → ℝ be an energy function of p_n, that is, p_n(x) = e^(−βE_n(x))/Z_n with Z_n = Σ_{x∈S} e^(−βE_n(x)), and let F_n = −β⁻¹ log Z_n. Let W = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} (E_{n+1}(X_n) − E_n(X_n)) be the work and ΔF = F_N − F_0. Then E[e^(−β(W − ΔF))] = 1. In particular E[W] ≥ ΔF.
hypotheses: S is a finite set, β > 0, and X = (X_0, …, X_N) is a Markov chain on S with transition matrices M_1, …, M_N.
The initial law p_0 has positive entries.
Each M_n has a stationary distribution p_n with positive entries, for example because M_n is irreducible.
E_n is an energy function of p_n: p_n(x) = e^(−βE_n(x))/Z_n for n = 0, …, N.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Perron–Frobenius theorem to show that an irreducible transition matrix has a unique stationary distribution with positive entries.
Step s3 conditions on X_0, …, X_n and uses the tower property to get the one-step recursion for the weighted occupation ρ_n.
Step s6 applies Jensen's inequality to the convex exponential function to derive E[W] ≥ ΔF from the equality.

definitions.name: work
definitions.text: W = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} (E_{n+1}(X_n) − E_n(X_n)): the energy put into the system when the energy function changes from E_n to E_{n+1} while the state X_n stays fixed.

definitions.name: free energy
definitions.text: F_n = −β⁻¹ log Z_n, where Z_n = Σ_x e^(−βE_n(x)) is the partition function of the energy E_n.

definitions.name: stationary distribution
definitions.text: A probability vector p with M p = p, that is, Σ_y (M)_{xy} p(y) = p(x) for every x.

source.citation: Pedro Hack, Sebastian Gottwald, Daniel A. Braun, Jarzyski's equality and Crooks' fluctuation theorem for general Markov chains with application to decision-making systems, arXiv:2202.05576.

source.module: Section 3 Jarzynski's equality for Markov chains
source.excerpt: Theorem 1 (Jarzynski's equality for Markov chains). If X = (Xn)Nn=0 is a Markov chain on a finite state space S whose initial distribution p0 has non-zero entries and whose transition matrices (Mn)Nn=1 are irreducible, then we have, for any family of energies E = (En)Nn=0 of X, ⟨e−β(W(X)−∆F)⟩ = 1, (10) where W = WX,E and ∆F = ∆FX,E.
source.attribution: © Pedro Hack, Sebastian Gottwald, Daniel A. Braun. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source defines the work (4), the energies and the free energies in Section 2.1 on pp. 5-6, with E_0 an energy function of the initial law p_0. The source assumes irreducible transition matrices. The authored statement assumes only a stationary distribution with positive entries for each M_n, which irreducibility gives, because the proof uses nothing more. The source proves the equality with an auxiliary reversed chain on pp. 8-9. The authored proof uses an induction on the weighted occupation E[e^(−βW_n); X_n = x], which rests on the same cancellation. The inequality E[W] ≥ ΔF is (22) on p. 17 of the source. The title of the source prints 'Jarzyski'.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 1 in Hack, Gottwald and Braun (arXiv:2202.05576). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for any finite state space, any β > 0 and any protocol of energies whose Boltzmann laws are stationary for the corresponding transition matrices.

steps.text: Existence of the energies. If M_n is irreducible, it is a nonnegative irreducible matrix with column sums 1, so the all-ones row vector is a positive left eigenvector for the eigenvalue 1. By the Perron–Frobenius theorem the only eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector is the spectral radius, which is therefore 1, and its right eigenvector is positive and unique up to a factor. Normalizing gives the unique stationary distribution p_n, and its entries are positive. For any positive p_n, E_n = −β⁻¹ log p_n is an energy function with Z_n = 1. Any other energy function differs from it by a constant.

Partial work and the base case. Let W_0 = 0 and W_n = Σ_{k=0}^{n−1} (E_{k+1}(X_k) − E_k(X_k)) for 1 ≤ n ≤ N, so W_N = W. W_n is a function of X_0, …, X_{n−1}. Define ρ_n(x) = E[e^(−βW_n) 1{X_n = x}] for x ∈ S. Since S is finite, all these expectations are finite sums. At n = 0, ρ_0(x) = P(X_0 = x) = p_0(x) = e^(−βE_0(x))/Z_0.

One-step recursion. W_{n+1} = W_n + E_{n+1}(X_n) − E_n(X_n) is a function of X_0, …, X_n. By the Markov property, P(X_{n+1} = y | X_0, …, X_n) = (M_{n+1})_{y X_n}. The tower property, conditioning on X_0, …, X_n, gives ρ_{n+1}(y) = E[e^(−βW_n) e^(−β(E_{n+1}(X_n) − E_n(X_n))) (M_{n+1})_{y X_n}] = Σ_{x∈S} ρ_n(x) e^(−β(E_{n+1}(x) − E_n(x))) (M_{n+1})_{yx}.

Induction. Assume ρ_n(x) = e^(−βE_n(x))/Z_0 for all x. Then the factor e^(−βE_n(x)) cancels in step s3, and ρ_{n+1}(y) = Z_0⁻¹ Σ_x e^(−βE_{n+1}(x)) (M_{n+1})_{yx} = (Z_{n+1}/Z_0) Σ_x (M_{n+1})_{yx} p_{n+1}(x). Since p_{n+1} is stationary for M_{n+1}, the last sum is p_{n+1}(y). So ρ_{n+1}(y) = (Z_{n+1}/Z_0) p_{n+1}(y) = e^(−βE_{n+1}(y))/Z_0. By induction from step s2, ρ_n = e^(−βE_n)/Z_0 for every n = 0, …, N.

The equality. Sum ρ_N over S: E[e^(−βW)] = Σ_x ρ_N(x) = Σ_x e^(−βE_N(x))/Z_0 = Z_N/Z_0. Since F_n = −β⁻¹ log Z_n, Z_N/Z_0 = e^(−β(F_N − F_0)) = e^(−βΔF). Multiplying by the constant e^(βΔF) gives E[e^(−β(W − ΔF))] = 1.

The second law. W takes finitely many values, so E[W] is finite. The function t ↦ e^(−βt) is convex, and Jensen's inequality gives e^(−β(E[W] − ΔF)) ≤ E[e^(−β(W − ΔF))] = 1. Since β > 0, taking logarithms gives −β(E[W] − ΔF) ≤ 0, that is, E[W] ≥ ΔF.

applications.title: A two-level atom with a ramped excitation energy
applications.inputs: A two-level atom with states S = {0, 1} at β = 1. The excited level has energy a_n, and the protocol is a_0 = 0, a_1 = log 2, a_2 = log 4, so E_n(0) = 0 and E_n(1) = a_n, with N = 2. The atom starts in equilibrium, p_0 = (1/2, 1/2). Between changes it relaxes partly: M_n = (1/2) I + (1/2) p_n 1ᵀ, where p_n is the Boltzmann law of E_n.
applications.hypotheses: S is finite and β = 1 > 0. p_0 = (1/2, 1/2) has positive entries and is the Boltzmann law of E_0 = 0. Each M_n has positive entries, so it is irreducible, and M_n p_n = (1/2) p_n + (1/2) p_n = p_n, so p_n is its stationary distribution. Here p_1 = (2/3, 1/3) and p_2 = (4/5, 1/5), and E_n is an energy function of p_n.

steps.text: The partition functions are Z_0 = 2, Z_1 = 1 + 1/2 = 3/2 and Z_2 = 1 + 1/4 = 5/4. So the theorem predicts E[e^(−W)] = e^(−ΔF) = Z_2/Z_0 = 5/8.

Each change of the energy raises the excited level by log 2, so W = log 2 · (X_0 + X_1) and e^(−W) = 2^(−(X_0 + X_1)). From M_1 = (1/2) I + (1/2) p_1 1ᵀ, P(X_1 = 1 | X_0 = 0) = (1/2)(1/3) = 1/6 and P(X_1 = 1 | X_0 = 1) = 1/2 + (1/2)(1/3) = 2/3.

The mean work is E[W] = log 2 · (P(X_0 = 1) + P(X_1 = 1)) = log 2 · (1/2 + 5/12) = (11/12) log 2 ≈ 0.635, because P(X_1 = 1) = (1/2)(1/6) + (1/2)(2/3) = 5/12. The free energy change is ΔF = log(8/5) ≈ 0.470, so E[W] ≥ ΔF holds with a dissipated work of about 0.165.

applications.conclusion: For this protocol E[e^(−W)] = 5/8 = e^(−ΔF), although the atom is never in equilibrium with the current energy after the first change. The mean work (11/12) log 2 is larger than ΔF = log(8/5), as the second law requires.

limitations: The equality needs the initial law to be the Boltzmann law of E_0. If the system does not start in equilibrium, it fails in general.
The average of e^(−βW) is dominated by rare trajectories with small work, so estimates of ΔF from few samples can have a large bias.
Crooks' fluctuation theorem gives the full ratio of forward and reverse work distributions under detailed balance, and it implies this equality.

results.name: Lebowitz–Spohn fluctuation symmetry
aliases: Gallavotti–Cohen symmetry for Markov jump processes
fluctuation relation for the action functional of a Markov chain
results.statement: Let (X_t)_{t≥0} be an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain on a finite set S with at least two states and jump rates k(σ, σ′) ≥ 0 for σ ≠ σ′, such that k(σ, σ′) > 0 if and only if k(σ′, σ) > 0. Split the rates as k = Σ_{i=1}^m k^(i), with k^(i)(σ, σ′) ≥ 0 and k^(i)(σ, σ′) > 0 if and only if k^(i)(σ′, σ) > 0, and let a jump from σ to σ′ carry the label i with rate k^(i)(σ, σ′). Let W^(i)(t) be the sum of w^(i)(σ, σ′) = log(k^(i)(σ, σ′)/k^(i)(σ′, σ)) over the jumps σ → σ′ with label i up to time t. For λ ∈ ℝ^m let L_λ be the S × S matrix with off-diagonal entries L_λ(σ, σ′) = Σ_{i: k^(i)(σ,σ′)>0} k^(i)(σ, σ′)^(1−λ_i) k^(i)(σ′, σ)^(λ_i) and diagonal entries −r(σ) = −Σ_{σ′≠σ} k(σ, σ′). Then for every initial law ν and every λ ∈ ℝ^m: (a) the limit e(λ) = −lim_{t→∞} t⁻¹ log E_ν exp(−Σ_i λ_i W^(i)(t)) exists, is finite and does not depend on ν, and −e(λ) is the largest real eigenvalue of L_λ. (b) e(λ_1, …, λ_m) = e(1 − λ_1, …, 1 − λ_m). (c) The Legendre transform I(z) = sup_{λ∈ℝ^m} (e(λ) − ⟨λ, z⟩) satisfies I(−z) = I(z) + Σ_i z_i for every z ∈ ℝ^m. (d) Under P_ν, W(t)/t = (W^(1)(t), …, W^(m)(t))/t satisfies the large deviation principle as t → ∞ with speed t and the good rate function I. For m = 1, W(t) is the Lebowitz–Spohn action functional, and (c) is the Gallavotti–Cohen symmetry of its rate function.
hypotheses: (X_t) is an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain on a finite set S with at least two states.
The jump rates satisfy k(σ, σ′) > 0 if and only if k(σ′, σ) > 0.
The rates split as k = Σ_i k^(i) with k^(i) ≥ 0, and k^(i)(σ, σ′) > 0 if and only if k^(i)(σ′, σ) > 0 for each i.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Dyson formula (the time-ordered expansion of e^(t(A+B)) in powers of B) to identify the path expansion with e^(tL_λ).
Step s1 uses the monotone convergence theorem to sum the nonnegative contributions of the paths with n jumps over all n.
Steps s2 and s4 use the Perron–Frobenius theorem for the irreducible nonnegative matrix L_λ + aI: a simple dominant eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector.
Step s6 uses the implicit function theorem at the simple Perron root to show that e is differentiable in λ.
Step s7 applies the Gärtner–Ellis theorem to W(t)/t, whose scaled cumulant generating function −e(−λ) is finite and differentiable.

definitions.name: action functional
definitions.text: W(t) = Σ over the jumps σ → σ′ up to time t of log(k(σ, σ′)/k(σ′, σ)). It compares the probability of a path with the probability of its time reversal, and in physical models it is the entropy production in units of k_B.

definitions.name: tilted generator
definitions.text: L_λ is the generator L in which each rate k^(i)(σ, σ′) is multiplied by e^(−λ_i w^(i)(σ, σ′)). This gives k^(i)(σ, σ′)^(1−λ_i) k^(i)(σ′, σ)^(λ_i). L_λ is not a Markov generator when λ ≠ 0, because its rows need not sum to 0.

definitions.name: scaled cumulant generating function
definitions.text: Λ(λ) = lim t⁻¹ log E e^(⟨λ, W(t)⟩). Here Λ(λ) = −e(−λ).

source.citation: Alessandra Faggionato, Daniele Di Pietro, Gallavotti–Cohen-type symmetry related to cycle decompositions for Markov chains and biochemical applications, Journal of Statistical Physics 143 (2011) 11–32.

source.module: Section 2 Fluctuation Theorem for sums of Markov generators
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.1. Given a distribution ν on S, for each λ1, . . . , λm ∈ R the limit e(λ1, . . . , λm) := lim_{t→∞} −(1/t) ln Eν[e^{−Σ_{i=1}^m λi W^(i)(t)}] (2.5) exists, is finite and does not depend on ν. Moreover, the following fluctuation relation is valid: e(λ1, . . . , λm) = e(1 − λ1, . . . , 1 − λm). (2.6)

source.alignment: Parts (a) and (b) are Theorem 2.1 of the source, which extends Section 2.3 of Lebowitz and Spohn (J. Stat. Phys. 95, 1999) and gives its own proof in Section 5.1, pp. 17-19. The source states (c) as (2.7) and (d) on p. 6 with references to the theory of large deviations. The authored proof gives both. The source obtains the formula E_ν e^(−⟨λ, W(t)⟩) = (ν, e^(tL_λ) 1) from a differential equation for t ↦ E_σ e^(−⟨λ, W(t)⟩). Step s1 obtains it from the path expansion instead. The limit, the Perron–Frobenius bounds and the transpose identity follow the source.

proof.scope: The full statement for finite state spaces, every splitting of the rates and every initial law.

steps.text: Path expansion. Irreducibility with |S| ≥ 2 gives r(σ) > 0. Started at σ, the chain stays at σ for an exponential time with rate r(σ) and then jumps to σ′ with label i with probability k^(i)(σ, σ′)/r(σ). So the paths with exactly n jumps up to time t, through σ_0 = σ, σ_1, …, σ_n with labels i_1, …, i_n at times s_1 < … < s_n, have the density Π_j [e^(−r(σ_{j−1})(s_j − s_{j−1})) k^(i_j)(σ_{j−1}, σ_j)] · e^(−r(σ_n)(t − s_n)), with s_0 = 0. The weight e^(−λ_i w^(i)(σ, σ′)) turns k^(i)(σ, σ′) into k^(i)(σ, σ′)^(1−λ_i) k^(i)(σ′, σ)^(λ_i), and the sum over labels gives K_λ(σ, σ′), the off-diagonal part of L_λ. With R = diag(r), the n-jump term of E_σ[e^(−⟨λ, W(t)⟩); X_t = σ′] is ∫_{0<s_1<…<s_n<t} (e^(−s_1R) K_λ e^(−(s_2−s_1)R) ⋯ K_λ e^(−(t−s_n)R))(σ, σ′) ds. The number of jumps up to time t is finite almost surely, and all terms are nonnegative. So monotone convergence and the Dyson formula for e^(t(−R + K_λ)) give E_ν e^(−⟨λ, W(t)⟩) = (ν, e^(tL_λ) 1), where 1 is the all-ones vector.

The Perron eigenvector. The off-diagonal entries of L_λ are nonnegative, and L_λ(σ, σ′) > 0 exactly when k(σ, σ′) > 0, by the positivity relations. Take a ≥ max_σ r(σ). Then M = L_λ + aI is a nonnegative matrix, and it is irreducible because the chain is irreducible. By the Perron–Frobenius theorem its spectral radius ρ is an algebraically simple eigenvalue with an eigenvector v whose entries are all positive. Every real eigenvalue μ of M satisfies μ ≤ |μ| ≤ ρ. Put −e(λ) = ρ − a. Then L_λ v = −e(λ) v, and −e(λ) is the largest real eigenvalue of L_λ.

Part (a). e^(tL_λ) = e^(−ta) e^(tM) has nonnegative entries, and e^(tL_λ) v = e^(−te(λ)) v. With v_min = min v and v_max = max v, the vectors satisfy v/v_max ≤ 1 ≤ v/v_min entrywise. So v_max⁻¹ e^(−te(λ)) (ν, v) ≤ (ν, e^(tL_λ) 1) ≤ v_min⁻¹ e^(−te(λ)) (ν, v). Since (ν, v) > 0, taking −t⁻¹ log and t → ∞ gives the limit e(λ) for every initial law ν.

Part (b). For σ ≠ σ′, L_{1−λ}(σ′, σ) = Σ_i k^(i)(σ′, σ)^(λ_i) k^(i)(σ, σ′)^(1−λ_i) = L_λ(σ, σ′), where the sums run over the same labels by the positivity relation for k^(i). The diagonals are both −r. So the transpose of L_{1−λ} is L_λ. A matrix and its transpose have the same eigenvalues, so they have the same largest real eigenvalue, and step s2 gives e(1 − λ) = e(λ).

Part (c). Substitute λ = 1 − µ, where 1 is the vector with all entries 1: I(−z) = sup_λ (e(λ) + ⟨λ, z⟩) = sup_µ (e(1 − µ) + ⟨1 − µ, z⟩) = sup_µ (e(µ) − ⟨µ, z⟩) + Σ_i z_i = I(z) + Σ_i z_i. The middle equality uses part (b). The identity holds in (−∞, ∞].

Differentiability. The entries of L_λ are k^(i)(σ, σ′) e^(λ_i log(k^(i)(σ′, σ)/k^(i)(σ, σ′))), which are smooth in λ, so the characteristic polynomial p(λ, x) = det(xI − L_λ) has smooth coefficients. At λ_0 the root x_0 = −e(λ_0) is simple by step s2, so ∂p/∂x ≠ 0 there, and the implicit function theorem gives a smooth root x(λ) near λ_0. The other eigenvalues of L_{λ_0} have real parts smaller than x_0. Eigenvalues depend continuously on λ, so for λ near λ_0 exactly one eigenvalue lies near x_0, it is real, and it is the largest real eigenvalue. Hence −e(λ) = x(λ) near λ_0, and e is differentiable on ℝ^m.

Part (d). By part (a), Λ(λ) = lim t⁻¹ log E_ν e^(⟨λ, W(t)⟩) = −e(−λ) exists and is finite for every λ, and by step s6 it is differentiable. So Λ is continuous and essentially smooth with domain ℝ^m. The Gärtner–Ellis theorem, whose proof is unchanged when the speed N is replaced by a sequence t_n → ∞, gives along every such sequence the large deviation principle for W(t_n)/t_n with the good rate function Λ*(z) = sup_λ (⟨λ, z⟩ + e(−λ)) = I(z). If a bound failed as t → ∞, it would fail along some sequence t_n → ∞, so the bounds hold as t → ∞.

applications.title: Entropy production of a driven three-state ring
applications.inputs: A molecular motor with three states 0, 1, 2 on a ring. It steps forward σ → σ + 1 (mod 3) with rate 2 and backward σ → σ − 1 with rate 1. Take m = 1. Each forward jump adds w = log 2 to W(t) and each backward jump adds −log 2, so W(t) = (log 2)(N₊(t) − N₋(t)), where N₊ and N₋ count the forward and backward jumps. The test value is z = (7/2) log 2, a net current of 7/2 steps per unit time.
applications.hypotheses: S is finite with three states. All rates are positive, so the chain is irreducible, and each rate has a positive reverse rate. With m = 1 the splitting is k^(1) = k.

steps.text: L_λ has diagonal −3, forward entries 2^(1−λ)·1^λ = 2^(1−λ) and backward entries 1^(1−λ)·2^λ = 2^λ. Its rows have the same sum, so the all-ones vector is a positive eigenvector with eigenvalue 2^(1−λ) + 2^λ − 3. By Perron–Frobenius it is the Perron eigenvalue, so e(λ) = 3 − 2^(1−λ) − 2^λ. The formula is unchanged under λ ↦ 1 − λ, as part (b) states.
At λ = −1 and at its mirror λ = 2: e(−1) = 3 − 4 − 1/2 = −3/2 and e(2) = 3 − 1/2 − 4 = −3/2. The mean of W(t)/t is e′(0) = (log 2)(2 − 1) = log 2, the entropy produced per unit time.

e″(λ) = −(log 2)²(2^(1−λ) + 2^λ) < 0, so e is concave and the supremum in I(z) is at e′(λ) = z, that is, (log 2)(2^(1−λ) − 2^λ) = z. For z = (7/2) log 2 this holds at λ = −1, because 4 − 1/2 = 7/2. So I(z) = e(−1) + z = (7/2) log 2 − 3/2 ≈ 0.926.
For −z the condition holds at λ = 2, because 1/2 − 4 = −7/2. So I(−z) = e(2) + 2z = 7 log 2 − 3/2 ≈ 3.352. Then I(−z) − I(z) = (7/2) log 2 = z, which is part (c) with m = 1.

applications.conclusion: On the exponential scale, P(W(t)/t ≈ −(7/2) log 2) / P(W(t)/t ≈ (7/2) log 2) ≈ e^(−t(I(−z) − I(z))) = 2^(−7t/2). A net backward current of 7/2 steps per unit time is less probable than the same forward current by the factor 2^(−7t/2), and this ratio does not depend on the details of the rate function.

limitations: The theorem needs a finite state space and the positivity relation for each pair of reverse jumps. With an unbounded state space or with unbounded weights, the symmetry can fail for some currents and needs extra conditions.
The symmetry (c) fixes only the odd part of the rate function. The rate function itself depends on the model and is usually known only through the Perron eigenvalue.
