results.name: Peierls argument for the two-dimensional Ising model
results.statement: Consider the nearest-neighbour Ising model on the box B(n) = {−n, …, n}² ⊂ ℤ² with coupling 1, zero magnetic field, inverse temperature β > 0 and + boundary condition, and let µ⁺_{B(n),β} be its Gibbs measure. Set x = 3e^(−2β) and assume x < 1. Then, for every n ≥ 1, µ⁺_{B(n),β}(σ₀ = −1) ≤ δ(β), where δ(β) = (2/3) Σ_{k≥4} k xᵏ = (2/3) x⁴(4 − 3x)/(1 − x)². Hence ⟨σ₀⟩⁺_{B(n),β} ≥ 1 − 2δ(β) and ⟨σ₀⟩⁻_{B(n),β} = −⟨σ₀⟩⁺_{B(n),β} for every n. If δ(β) < 1/2, which holds for every β ≥ (1/2) log 6, then liminf_{n→∞} ⟨σ₀⟩⁺_{B(n),β} ≥ 1 − 2δ(β) > 0, so the + and − boundary conditions give different magnetizations in the thermodynamic limit.
hypotheses: The spins live on B(n) = {−n, …, n}² with nearest-neighbour coupling 1 and zero magnetic field. Every spin outside B(n) is fixed to +1 (the + boundary condition).
The inverse temperature β > 0 satisfies 3e^(−2β) < 1.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s2 and s4 use the Jordan curve theorem: a contour splits the plane into an interior and an exterior, and a segment that crosses it transversally an odd number of times has exactly one end inside.
Step s2 bounds the probability that some contour surrounds the origin by the sum over all such contours.

definitions.name: Gibbs measure with + boundary condition
definitions.text: For ω ∈ {−1, 1}^B(n), set σ_i = ω_i for i in B(n) and σ_i = +1 otherwise. Then µ⁺_{B(n),β}(ω) is proportional to exp(β Σ σ_i σ_j), where the sum runs over the nearest-neighbour edges {i, j} with at least one end in B(n).

definitions.name: contour
definitions.text: Draw the unit square S_i = i + [−1/2, 1/2]² around each site i with σ_i = −1. The boundary of the union of these squares consists of edges of the dual lattice ℤ² + (1/2, 1/2). At each dual vertex with four such edges, a fixed local rule joins the edges in two pairs. The resulting closed simple curves are the contours of the configuration. The length |γ| of a contour γ is its number of dual edges.

definitions.name: interior of a contour
definitions.text: A contour γ is a closed simple curve in ℝ². It splits the plane into two regions. The bounded region is the interior Int(γ).

source.citation: Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems: A Concrete Mathematical Introduction, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Authors' online version, revised version of August 22, 2017.
source.module: Chapter 3, Section 3.7.2 Spontaneous symmetry breaking at low temperatures
source.excerpt: Lemma 3.37. For all β > 0 and any contour γ∗, µ⁺_{B(n);β,0}(Γ ∋ γ∗) ≤ e^{−2β|γ∗|}. The bound (3.34) shows that the probability that a given contour appears in a configuration becomes small when β is large or when the contour is long.

source.alignment: Lemma 3.37 is the key estimate of the Peierls argument in the source, and the surrounding text of Section 3.7.2 combines it with the bound (3.40) on µ⁺(σ₀ = −1). The authored statement collects these into one theorem, writes δ(β) in closed form and adds the explicit sufficient condition β ≥ (1/2) log 6. The authored proof follows the source: the contour representation, the spin flip inside one contour, and the count of contours that surround the origin. It adds the parity and Jordan curve arguments that the source states briefly.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the Peierls argument of Friedli and Velenik, Section 3.7.2. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every n ≥ 1 and every β with 3e^(−2β) < 1, and its consequence for the magnetizations with + and − boundary conditions.

steps.text: Contour representation. Let E be the set of nearest-neighbour edges with at least one end in B(n). For each edge, βσ_iσ_j = β − 2β·1[σ_i ≠ σ_j]. An edge {i, j} has σ_i ≠ σ_j exactly when its dual edge (the unit segment that crosses it at its midpoint) lies on the boundary ∂M of M = ∪{S_i : σ_i = −1}. So β Σ_E σ_iσ_j = β|E| − 2β|∂M| = β|E| − 2β Σ_{γ∈Γ(ω)} |γ|, where Γ(ω) is the set of contours. The constant β|E| cancels in the normalization, so µ⁺(ω) = ∏_{γ∈Γ(ω)} e^(−2β|γ|) / Σ_{ω'} ∏_{γ∈Γ(ω')} e^(−2β|γ|). At each dual vertex the product of the four signs σ_iσ_j around it is 1, so 0, 2 or 4 edges of ∂M meet there. Hence the local rule splits ∂M into edge-disjoint closed simple curves. All of them lie in the square Q = [−n − 1/2, n + 1/2]², because M ⊂ Q.

A contour surrounds the origin. Let σ₀ = −1 and follow the segment L from (0, 0) to (n + 1, 0). Its first site has spin −1 and its last site has spin +1, so the spin changes sign an odd number of times along L. Each sign change between (m, 0) and (m + 1, 0) is a transversal crossing of L with the vertical dual edge through (m + 1/2, 0), and L meets no dual vertex. So the total number of crossings of L with the contours is odd, and some contour γ* is crossed an odd number of times. The end (n + 1, 0) lies outside Q, so it lies outside Int(γ*). By the Jordan curve theorem, a segment that crosses a closed simple curve transversally an odd number of times has exactly one end inside the curve. So 0 ∈ Int(γ*). The union bound gives µ⁺(σ₀ = −1) ≤ Σ_{γ*: Int(γ*) ∋ 0} µ⁺(Γ ∋ γ*).

Lemma 3.37: µ⁺(Γ ∋ γ*) ≤ e^(−2β|γ*|). For ω with γ* ∈ Γ(ω), let E(ω) flip every spin at a site in Int(γ*). These sites lie in B(n) because γ* ⊂ Q, so E(ω) is again a configuration in B(n). The segment of a lattice edge meets the dual lattice only at the midpoint of its dual edge. So an edge whose dual edge lies on γ* has exactly one end in Int(γ*), and every other edge has both ends on the same side of γ*. After the flip, the edges of γ* join equal spins and all other edges keep their status. So ∂M(E(ω)) = ∂M(ω) minus the edges of γ*. At each dual vertex the local rule joins the same pairs of the remaining edges as before, so Γ(E(ω)) = Γ(ω) \ {γ*}. Hence Σ_{ω: Γ(ω)∋γ*} ∏_{γ∈Γ(ω)} e^(−2β|γ|) = e^(−2β|γ*|) Σ_{ω: Γ(ω)∋γ*} ∏_{γ∈Γ(E(ω))} e^(−2β|γ|). The map E is injective, because flipping the same set of spins twice gives back ω. So the last sum is at most the full sum over all configurations, which is the denominator in s1.

Count the contours. Let γ* surround 0 and have length k. A closed curve around a lattice point has length k ≥ 4. By the parity argument of s2 applied to γ* alone, γ* crosses the positive horizontal half-axis, at a vertical dual edge through (u − 1/2, 0) with an integer u ≥ 1. So γ* contains the dual vertex (u − 1/2, 1/2). The same argument for the segment from 0 to (−n − 1, 0) shows that γ* also meets the vertical line x = −1/2 or a line further left. A closed lattice path uses at least twice its horizontal width in horizontal edges, so k ≥ 2u, that is, u ≤ k/2. A closed path of k dual edges that starts at a given dual vertex and never uses an edge twice in a row is one of at most 4·3^(k−1) edge sequences. Therefore #{γ*: Int(γ*) ∋ 0, |γ*| = k} ≤ (k/2)·4·3^(k−1) = (2/3) k 3^k.

Sum the bounds. Steps s2 to s4 give µ⁺_{B(n),β}(σ₀ = −1) ≤ Σ_{k≥4} (2/3) k 3^k e^(−2βk) = (2/3) Σ_{k≥4} k x^k with x = 3e^(−2β) < 1. The identity Σ_{k≥0} k x^k = x/(1 − x)² minus the terms k = 1, 2, 3 gives Σ_{k≥4} k x^k = x⁴(4 − 3x)/(1 − x)². This is δ(β), and the bound does not depend on n. Then ⟨σ₀⟩⁺ = 1 − 2µ⁺(σ₀ = −1) ≥ 1 − 2δ(β). At zero field the global flip ω ↦ −ω maps µ⁺_{B(n),β} to µ⁻_{B(n),β}, so ⟨σ₀⟩⁻ = −⟨σ₀⟩⁺. The function δ increases with x. At x = 1/2 it equals 5/12 < 1/2, and x ≤ 1/2 exactly when β ≥ (1/2) log 6. If δ(β) < 1/2, then liminf ⟨σ₀⟩⁺ ≥ 1 − 2δ(β) > 0 ≥ −(1 − 2δ(β)) ≥ limsup ⟨σ₀⟩⁻, so the two boundary conditions give different limits.

applications.title: A quantitative low-temperature bound for the square-lattice Ising model
applications.inputs: The square-lattice Ising model with coupling 1 and zero field at β = (1/2) log 6 ≈ 0.896, on the boxes B(n) with + boundary condition.
applications.hypotheses: The model is the nearest-neighbour Ising model on B(n) with + boundary condition and zero field. At β = (1/2) log 6 we have 3e^(−2β) = 3/6 = 1/2 < 1, so the hypothesis on β holds.

steps.text: Compute x = 3e^(−2β) = 3e^(−log 6) = 3/6 = 1/2. So the closed form of δ(β) applies, with x⁴ = 1/16, 4 − 3x = 5/2 and (1 − x)² = 1/4.
The magnetization at the origin satisfies ⟨σ₀⟩⁺_{B(n),β} ≥ 1 − 2·(5/12) = 1/6 for every n, and ⟨σ₀⟩⁻_{B(n),β} ≤ −1/6.

Since δ increases with x, the same bound 1 − 2δ(β) ≥ 1/6 holds for every β ≥ (1/2) log 6. So the spontaneous magnetization is at least 1/6 there, and the critical inverse temperature satisfies β_c ≤ (1/2) log 6 ≈ 0.896. The exact value is β_c = (1/2) log(1 + √2) ≈ 0.4407.

applications.conclusion: At β = (1/2) log 6 the + boundary condition keeps the origin positive with probability at least 7/12, uniformly in the box size. The square-lattice Ising model is ordered for every β ≥ (1/2) log 6, which is about twice the exact critical value.

limitations: The argument gives only an upper bound β_c ≤ (1/2) log 6 ≈ 0.896. The exact critical value (1/2) log(1 + √2) ≈ 0.4407 needs duality or an exact solution.
The counting of contours uses the planar lattice. In dimension d ≥ 3 the contours become closed surfaces of plaquettes, and the same idea works with a different counting bound.

results.name: Griffiths–Kelly–Sherman inequalities
results.statement: Let Λ be a finite set and let K = (K_C)_{C⊂Λ} be real numbers with K_C ≥ 0 for every C ⊂ Λ. On {−1, 1}^Λ let ν_K(ω) = Z_K⁻¹ exp(Σ_{C⊂Λ} K_C ω_C), where ω_C = ∏_{i∈C} ω_i and ω_∅ = 1, and write ⟨·⟩_K for the expectation under ν_K. Then for all A, B ⊂ Λ: (i) ⟨ω_A⟩_K ≥ 0, and (ii) ⟨ω_A ω_B⟩_K ≥ ⟨ω_A⟩_K ⟨ω_B⟩_K. In particular, for the Ising model with ferromagnetic couplings J_ij ≥ 0 and fields h_i ≥ 0, spin correlations are nonnegative and nondecreasing in every coupling and every field.
hypotheses: Λ is a finite set, and the configurations ω ∈ {−1, 1}^Λ carry the probability ν_K(ω) proportional to exp(Σ_C K_C ω_C).
Every coupling constant is nonnegative: K_C ≥ 0 for all C ⊂ Λ.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only the power series of the exponential function, sums over the finite set of spin configurations, and a change of variables in that finite sum.

definitions.name: multi-spin coupling model
definitions.text: The probability ν_K(ω) = Z_K⁻¹ exp(Σ_C K_C ω_C) on {−1, 1}^Λ, with one coupling K_C for each subset C. The Ising model with pair couplings J_ij and fields h_i is the case K_{i,j} = J_ij, K_{i} = h_i and K_C = 0 for all other C.

definitions.name: spin product
definitions.text: For C ⊂ Λ, ω_C = ∏_{i∈C} ω_i, with ω_∅ = 1. For two sets, ω_A ω_B = ω_{AΔB}, where AΔB is the symmetric difference, because ω_i² = 1.

source.module: Chapter 3, Section 3.8.1 Proof of the GKS inequalities
source.excerpt: Theorem 3.49. Let K = (K_C)_{C⊂Λ} be such that K_C ≥ 0 for all C ⊂ Λ. Then, for any A, B ⊂ Λ, 〈σ_A〉_{Λ;K} ≥ 0, 〈σ_A σ_B〉_{Λ;K} ≥ 〈σ_A〉_{Λ;K} 〈σ_B〉_{Λ;K}.
source.attribution: © Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik. Quoted from the authors' online version of the book for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the inequalities for the general multi-spin model ν_{Λ;K} on a finite Λ ⋐ ℤ^d, and Theorem 3.20 (p. 98) gives the nearest-neighbour Ising case. The authored statement uses any finite set Λ and adds the monotonicity of correlations in the couplings, which follows from (ii). The authored proof follows the source: a power series expansion with a parity count for (i), and a duplicated system with the variables ω''_i = ω_i ω'_i for (ii).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 3.49 in Friedli and Velenik. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Both inequalities for every finite Λ, every family of nonnegative couplings and all A, B ⊂ Λ, and the monotonicity consequence for the Ising model.

steps.text: Expand the weight. The partition function Z_K = Σ_ω exp(Σ_C K_C ω_C) is a finite sum of positive terms, so Z_K > 0 and it suffices to study numerators. For each C, e^(K_C ω_C) = Σ_{n≥0} K_Cⁿ ω_Cⁿ / n!, an absolutely convergent series. The product over the finitely many C and the finite sum over ω can be expanded and reordered, so Z_K ⟨ω_A⟩_K = Σ_{(n_C)} ∏_C (K_C^(n_C)/n_C!) Σ_ω ω_A ∏_C ω_C^(n_C), where (n_C) runs over families of nonnegative integers.

Prove (i) by parity. Write ω_A ∏_C ω_C^(n_C) = ∏_{i∈Λ} ω_i^(m_i), with m_i = 1[i ∈ A] + Σ_{C∋i} n_C. The sum over ω factorizes: Σ_ω ∏_i ω_i^(m_i) = ∏_i Σ_{ω_i=±1} ω_i^(m_i), and each factor is 2 if m_i is even and 0 if m_i is odd. So every inner sum is 0 or 2^|Λ|, hence nonnegative. The coefficients K_C^(n_C)/n_C! are nonnegative because K_C ≥ 0. Therefore Z_K ⟨ω_A⟩_K ≥ 0 and ⟨ω_A⟩_K ≥ 0. The argument uses only K_C ≥ 0, so it holds for every family of nonnegative couplings, which step s4 needs.

Duplicate the system for (ii). Let (ω, ω') have the product law ν_K ⊗ ν_K, so ω and ω' are independent copies. Then E[ω_A(ω_B − ω'_B)] = ⟨ω_A ω_B⟩_K − ⟨ω_A⟩_K ⟨ω_B⟩_K, by independence. Multiplying by Z_K² gives Z_K² (⟨ω_Aω_B⟩_K − ⟨ω_A⟩_K⟨ω_B⟩_K) = Σ_{ω,ω'} ω_A (ω_B − ω'_B) ∏_C e^(K_C(ω_C + ω'_C)).

Change variables. Set ω''_i = ω_i ω'_i. The map (ω, ω') ↦ (ω, ω'') is a bijection of {−1, 1}^Λ × {−1, 1}^Λ, with inverse ω'_i = ω_i ω''_i. Then ω'_C = ω_C ω''_C, so ω_A(ω_B − ω'_B) = ω_A ω_B (1 − ω''_B) and ω_C + ω'_C = ω_C (1 + ω''_C). Hence the sum of s3 equals Σ_{ω''} (1 − ω''_B) Σ_ω ω_{AΔB} ∏_C e^(K''_C ω_C), with K''_C = K_C (1 + ω''_C), where we used ω_A ω_B = ω_{AΔB}.

Conclude (ii). For each fixed ω'', the factor 1 − ω''_B is 0 or 2, and the new couplings K''_C = K_C(1 + ω''_C) are 0 or 2K_C, so they are nonnegative. The inner sum equals Z_{K''} ⟨ω_{AΔB}⟩_{K''}, which is nonnegative by step s2 applied to K''. So the whole sum is nonnegative, and (ii) holds. For the Ising model, ∂⟨ω_A⟩_K/∂K_C = ⟨ω_A ω_C⟩_K − ⟨ω_A⟩_K ⟨ω_C⟩_K, which is nonnegative by (ii). So ⟨ω_A⟩_K is nondecreasing in each coupling on the region K ≥ 0, in particular in every J_ij ≥ 0 and every h_i ≥ 0.

applications.title: Monotone correlations and the infinite-volume limit with free boundary condition
applications.inputs: The nearest-neighbour Ising model on finite boxes Λ ⊂ Λ' ⊂ ℤ^d with coupling β ≥ 0 on each edge, free boundary condition and field h ≥ 0. For the numeric part: two spins with K_{1,2} = J and K_{1} = K_{2} = h, where e^J = e^h = 2.
applications.hypotheses: Each model is the multi-spin model on a finite set with couplings β ≥ 0 on edges and h ≥ 0 on single sites, and K_C = 0 for all other C. So all couplings are nonnegative.

steps.text: For A ⊂ Λ, view the model on Λ as the model on Λ' in which the couplings of all edges with an end outside Λ are 0. The spins outside Λ are then independent of the spins in Λ, so ⟨σ_A⟩ is unchanged. Raise these couplings from 0 to β. By the monotonicity consequence of (ii), ⟨σ_A⟩^free_Λ ≤ ⟨σ_A⟩^free_Λ'.

So along any increasing sequence of boxes Λ_n ↑ ℤ^d the correlations ⟨σ_A⟩^free_{Λ_n} are nondecreasing and bounded by 1. Hence the limit exists for every finite A, and it does not depend on the sequence, because any two increasing sequences of boxes interlace.

Numeric check with two spins. The weights are e^(J+2h) = 8 for (+,+), e^(J−2h) = 1/2 for (−,−) and e^(−J) = 1/2 for each mixed pair. So Z = 19/2, ⟨σ₁σ₂⟩ = (8 + 1/2 − 1)/(19/2) = 15/19 and ⟨σ₁⟩ = ⟨σ₂⟩ = (8 − 1/2)/(19/2) = 15/19. Both are nonnegative, as (i) states.
The derivative of ⟨σ₁⟩ in the pair coupling is ⟨σ₁σ_{1,2}⟩ − ⟨σ₁⟩⟨σ₁σ₂⟩ = ⟨σ₂⟩ − ⟨σ₁⟩⟨σ₁σ₂⟩ = 15/19 − (15/19)² = 60/361, which is positive as (ii) states.

applications.conclusion: Ferromagnetic Ising correlations with free boundary condition increase with the volume, so their infinite-volume limits exist. In the two-spin example ⟨σ₁⟩ = 15/19 and its derivative in the coupling is 60/361 > 0.

limitations: The inequalities need all couplings K_C ≥ 0. They fail in general for antiferromagnetic couplings or for fields of mixed sign.
The proof uses spins with values ±1. Extensions to other single-spin laws, such as the Ginibre inequalities, need other arguments.

results.name: Simon–Lieb inequality
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a finite graph with couplings J_e ≥ 0 and let β ≥ 0. For a subgraph H let ⟨·⟩_H be the Ising expectation on H with the couplings of its edges, free boundary condition and zero field. Let x, y ∈ V and let S ⊂ V with x ∉ S be such that every path from x to y in G contains a vertex of S. Let V_{S,x} be the set of vertices v for which some path from x to v meets S at most at its last vertex, and let G_{S,x} be the graph on V_{S,x} whose edges are the edges of G with both ends in V_{S,x} that do not join two vertices of S. Then ⟨σ_x σ_y⟩_G ≤ Σ_{u∈S} ⟨σ_x σ_u⟩_{G_{S,x}} ⟨σ_u σ_y⟩_G.
hypotheses: G = (V, E) is a finite graph with ferromagnetic couplings J_e ≥ 0, β ≥ 0, free boundary condition and zero magnetic field.
The set S does not contain x and separates x from y: every path from x to y in G contains a vertex of S.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 applies the switching lemma in its form for a graph and a subgraph, which moves the sources {x, u} from the second current to the first.
Step s3 bounds the event that some vertex of S is the first vertex of S on a path by the sum over u ∈ S.

definitions.name: current
definitions.text: A current on a graph H is a map n from the edges of H to {0, 1, 2, …}. Its weight is w_H(n) = ∏_e (βJ_e)^(n_e)/n_e!, and its set of sources ∂n is the set of vertices v with Σ_{e∋v} n_e odd.

definitions.name: the graph G_{S,x}
definitions.text: The vertices that x can reach by a path that meets S at most at its last vertex, with the edges of G between these vertices except the edges that join two vertices of S.

source.citation: Michael Aizenman, Geometric analysis of Ising models, Part III, arXiv:2509.02850 [math-ph], 2025.
source.revision: arXiv v3 of 18 September 2025.
source.module: Appendix B, Simon-Lieb inequalities
source.excerpt: Theorem B.1 (Simon [84], Lieb [72]). In the ferromagnetic Ising model over a finite graph G = (V, E), for any pairs of sites x, y ∈ V and a set of vertices such that any path from x to y has to include at least one site of S. Then ⟨σxσy⟩ ≤ Σ_{u∈S} ⟨σxσu⟩_{G_{S,x}} ⟨σuσy⟩
source.attribution: © Michael Aizenman. Quoted from the author's arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the site version (B.1) of the source with the conditions made explicit: zero field, free boundary condition and x ∉ S. The source also states an edge version (B.2), which this record does not cover. The authored proof follows the alternative random current proof of (B.1) on p. 38 of the source, and it writes out the subgraph switching lemma (Lemma 4.2 of the source) for the case it needs.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the alternative random current proof of (B.1) in Aizenman, Part III, Appendix B. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The site version of the inequality for every finite graph with nonnegative couplings, every x ∉ S and every separating set S. The vertex y may lie in S.

steps.text: Random current representation. For a subgraph H expand each factor e^(βJ_e σ_a σ_b) = Σ_{n≥0} (βJ_e)ⁿ (σ_a σ_b)ⁿ/n!. For a set A of vertices, Σ_σ σ_A ∏_e e^(βJ_e σ_aσ_b) = Σ_n w_H(n) Σ_σ σ_A ∏_v σ_v^(deg_n(v)), and the inner sum is 2^|V(H)| if every exponent 1[v ∈ A] + deg_n(v) is even and 0 otherwise. So Σ_σ σ_A e^(−βH) = 2^|V(H)| Σ_{∂n=A} w_H(n), and ⟨σ_A⟩_H = Σ_{∂n=A} w_H(n)/Z_H with Z_H = Σ_{∂n=∅} w_H(n) ≥ 1. Insert the factor 1 = Σ_{∂n₂=∅} w_{G_{S,x}}(n₂)/Z_{G_{S,x}}: ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩_G = Σ_{∂n₁={x,y}, ∂n₂=∅} w_G(n₁) w_{G_{S,x}}(n₂)/(Z_G Z_{G_{S,x}}), where n₁ is a current on G and n₂ a current on G_{S,x}.

Sources lie in one cluster. In each connected component of the graph formed by the edges with n_e > 0, the sum of the degrees deg_n(v) is twice the total current on its edges, so it is even. So every component contains an even number of sources. If ∂n₁ = {x, y} with x ≠ y, then x and y lie in one component, and a simple path P from x to y uses only edges with (n₁)_e > 0. The same parity argument shows that a current k with ∂k = {x, u} connects x to u through edges with k_e > 0.

Stop the path at S. The path P meets S because S separates x from y. Let u be its first vertex in S. Every vertex of P before u is outside S, so every vertex of the initial part of P lies in V_{S,x}, and every edge of that part has an end outside S. So the initial part uses only edges of G_{S,x}, and x is connected to u by edges e of G_{S,x} with (n₁ + n₂)_e > 0. Call this event C_u. The union bound over u ∈ S gives ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩_G ≤ Σ_{u∈S} Σ_{∂n₁={x,y}, ∂n₂=∅} w_G(n₁) w_{G_{S,x}}(n₂) 1[C_u]/(Z_G Z_{G_{S,x}}).

Switch the sources. Fix u and set B = {x, u} ⊂ V_{S,x}. Group the pairs (n₁, n₂) by m = n₁ + n₂, with n₂ = 0 off the edges of G_{S,x}. Then w_G(n₁) w_{G_{S,x}}(n₂) = w_G(m) ∏_e C(m_e, (n₂)_e), with binomial coefficients C. So the sum for fixed m with ∂n₂ = A₂ equals w_G(m) N_{A₂}(m), where N_A(m) is the number of sets K of edges of the multigraph M with m_e parallel copies of each edge e of G_{S,x} such that the odd-degree vertices of K form A. The condition ∂n₁ = A₁ only says ∂m = A₁ Δ A₂. On C_u, a path of G_{S,x} from x to u inside M gives a set K₀ with boundary B, and K ↦ K Δ K₀ is a bijection from the sets with boundary A₂ onto the sets with boundary A₂ Δ B. So N_{A₂}(m) = N_{A₂ΔB}(m). Also C_u depends only on m. This is the switching lemma for a graph and a subgraph: the sums with sources (A₁, A₂) and (A₁ΔB, A₂ΔB) agree on C_u.

Conclude. Apply s4 with A₁ = {x, y}, A₂ = ∅ and B = {x, u}. The new sources are A₁ Δ B = {u} Δ {y} for n₁ and {x, u} for n₂. Drop the indicator of C_u, which only increases the sum. By s1 the result is Σ_{∂n₁={u}Δ{y}} w_G(n₁)/Z_G · Σ_{∂n₂={x,u}} w_{G_{S,x}}(n₂)/Z_{G_{S,x}} = ⟨σ_uσ_y⟩_G ⟨σ_xσ_u⟩_{G_{S,x}}. When u = y the first factor is ⟨σ_y σ_y⟩_G = 1, which agrees with σ_∅ = 1. Summing over u ∈ S gives the inequality.

applications.title: Exact check on a four-cycle of Ising spins
applications.inputs: The cycle x, a, y, b, x with four edges, all with coupling J and t = tanh(βJ) = 1/2, so βJ = (1/2) log 3. The separating set is S = {a, b}.
applications.hypotheses: The couplings are equal and positive and the field is zero. The vertex x is not in S, and every path from x to y passes through a or b, so S separates x from y.

steps.text: The graph G_{S,x} has vertices x, a, b and edges xa and xb: a and b are reached from x and are in S, and no edge joins a to b. It is a tree, so ⟨σ_xσ_a⟩_{G_{S,x}} = ⟨σ_xσ_b⟩_{G_{S,x}} = t = 1/2.

On the cycle the high-temperature expansion gives Z proportional to 1 + t⁴. The correlation of the opposite vertices x and y collects the two paths of length 2, so ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩ = 2t²/(1 + t⁴) = (1/2)/(17/16) = 8/17.
The neighbours a and y are joined by paths of lengths 1 and 3, so ⟨σ_aσ_y⟩ = ⟨σ_bσ_y⟩ = (t + t³)/(1 + t⁴) = (5/8)/(17/16) = 10/17.
The right side of the inequality is 2 · t · (t + t³)/(1 + t⁴) = 2 · (1/2) · (10/17) = 10/17. So 8/17 ≤ 10/17, and the ratio of the two sides is 1 + t² = 5/4.

applications.conclusion: On the four-cycle with tanh(βJ) = 1/2 the Simon–Lieb inequality reads 8/17 ≤ 10/17. The loss factor 1 + t² comes from the two ways a current can reach y after it first hits S.

limitations: The bound uses the full correlation ⟨σ_uσ_y⟩_G on the right side, so it is useful only after iteration. With S the boundary of a box, Σ_{u∈S} ⟨σ_xσ_u⟩_{G_{S,x}} < 1 then gives exponential decay of correlations.
The edge version with factors tanh(βJ_{uv}), and the extension to nonzero fields, need other arguments that this record does not cover.

results.name: Lebowitz inequality
aliases: Lebowitz inequality for the Ising four-point Ursell function
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a finite graph with couplings J_e ≥ 0, let β ≥ 0, and let µ be the Ising measure on G with free boundary condition and zero field. For distinct vertices x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄ write σ_i = σ_{x_i} and U₄ = µ[σ₁σ₂σ₃σ₄] − µ[σ₁σ₂]µ[σ₃σ₄] − µ[σ₁σ₃]µ[σ₂σ₄] − µ[σ₁σ₄]µ[σ₂σ₃]. Then U₄ = −(2/Z²) Σ w(n₁)w(n₂) 1[x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄ are connected by edges with (n₁ + n₂)_e > 0], where the sum runs over pairs of currents with ∂n₁ = {x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄} and ∂n₂ = ∅, w is the current weight and Z = Σ_{∂n=∅} w(n). In particular U₄ ≤ 0, that is, µ[σ₁σ₂σ₃σ₄] ≤ µ[σ₁σ₂]µ[σ₃σ₄] + µ[σ₁σ₃]µ[σ₂σ₄] + µ[σ₁σ₄]µ[σ₂σ₃].
hypotheses: G = (V, E) is a finite graph with ferromagnetic couplings J_e ≥ 0 and β ≥ 0. The Ising measure has free boundary condition and zero magnetic field.
The four vertices x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄ are distinct.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 applies the switching lemma to each of the three products of two-point functions, which moves the second pair of sources to the first current.

definitions.name: current
definitions.text: A current on G is a map n: E → {0, 1, 2, …}. Its weight is w(n) = ∏_e (βJ_e)^(n_e)/n_e!, and its set of sources ∂n is the set of vertices v with Σ_{e∋v} n_e odd.

definitions.name: four-point Ursell function
definitions.text: U₄ is the fourth joint cumulant of σ₁, σ₂, σ₃, σ₄ at zero field, where all odd moments vanish. It is zero for a centred Gaussian vector, by the Wick rule.

source.citation: Hugo Duminil-Copin, Lectures on the Ising and Potts models on the hypercubic lattice, arXiv:1707.00520, 2017. Published in PIMS-CRM Summer School in Probability, Springer Proceedings in Mathematics and Statistics 299, 2019.
source.revision: arXiv v1 of 3 July 2017.
source.module: Section 4.2 High-temperature expansion, random current representation and percolation interpretation of truncated correlations
source.excerpt: Exercise 34 (Lebowitz’s inequality) Set µ := µ^f_{G,β} and σ_i for the spin at a vertex x_i. Define U₄(x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄) = µ[σ₁σ₂σ₃σ₄] − µ[σ₁σ₂]µ[σ₃σ₄] − µ[σ₁σ₃]µ[σ₂σ₄] − µ[σ₁σ₄]µ[σ₂σ₃] for x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄ ∈ G. Using the switching lemma, show that U₄(x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄) = −2µ[σ₁σ₂σ₃σ₄] P^{{x₁,x₂,x₃,x₄},∅}_{G,β}[x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄ all connected]. Note that in particular U₄(x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄) ≤ 0, which is known as Lebowitz’s inequality.
source.attribution: © Hugo Duminil-Copin. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the identity as an exercise for unit couplings on a finite graph, with the percolation measure P^{A,∅} of its (4.7). The authored statement allows any couplings J_e ≥ 0, asks the four vertices to be distinct and writes the identity without a division, so it also holds when µ[σ₁σ₂σ₃σ₄] = 0. The authored proof is the switching lemma argument that the exercise asks for, with the source's Lemma 4.3 (p. 41) as the switching lemma.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the switching lemma method of Exercise 34 in Duminil-Copin's lecture notes. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The identity and the inequality for every finite graph with nonnegative couplings and every four distinct vertices.

steps.text: Random current representation. Expanding each factor e^(βJ_e σ_aσ_b) = Σ_n (βJ_e)ⁿ(σ_aσ_b)ⁿ/n! and summing over σ gives Σ_σ σ_B e^(−βH(σ)) = 2^|V| Σ_{∂n=B} w(n) for every B ⊂ V, because Σ_{σ_v=±1} σ_v^k is 2 for even k and 0 for odd k. So µ[σ_B] = Σ_{∂n=B} w(n)/Z with Z = Σ_{∂n=∅} w(n) ≥ 1. For two sets B and C this gives µ[σ_B]µ[σ_C] = Z⁻² Σ_{∂n₁=B, ∂n₂=C} w(n₁)w(n₂). With A = {x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄} also µ[σ_A] = Z⁻² Σ_{∂n₁=A, ∂n₂=∅} w(n₁)w(n₂), because the sum over n₂ equals Z.

Switch the sources. The switching lemma says Σ_{∂n₁=B, ∂n₂=C} w(n₁)w(n₂) = Σ_{∂n₁=BΔC, ∂n₂=∅} w(n₁)w(n₂) 1[(n₁+n₂)^ ∈ F_C], where (n₁+n₂)^ is the set of edges with (n₁+n₂)_e > 0 and F_C is the event that every cluster of this edge set contains an even number of points of C. Apply it with (B, C) = ({x₁,x₂}, {x₃,x₄}), ({x₁,x₃}, {x₂,x₄}) and ({x₁,x₄}, {x₂,x₃}). In each case BΔC = A because the vertices are distinct, and F_C is the event that the two points of C are connected. So µ[σ₁σ₂]µ[σ₃σ₄] = Z⁻² Σ_{∂n₁=A, ∂n₂=∅} w w 1[x₃ ↔ x₄], and the other two products carry the indicators of x₂ ↔ x₄ and x₂ ↔ x₃.

Classify the connections. Let ∂n₁ = A. In each cluster of the edge set of n₁ the degrees of n₁ add up to an even number, so each cluster holds an even number of points of A. The clusters of (n₁+n₂)^ are unions of such clusters and of vertices that are not in A, so they also hold an even number of points of A. Hence exactly one of four disjoint events occurs: all four points are in one cluster (event C₄), or the clusters split A into the pairs {12|34}, {13|24} or {14|23}. The event x₃ ↔ x₄ is C₄ or {12|34}, the event x₂ ↔ x₄ is C₄ or {13|24}, and the event x₂ ↔ x₃ is C₄ or {14|23}. So the sum of the three indicators is 3·1[C₄] + 1[12|34] + 1[13|24] + 1[14|23] = 1 + 2·1[C₄].

Conclude. By s2 and s3, the sum of the three products of two-point functions equals Z⁻² Σ_{∂n₁=A, ∂n₂=∅} w(n₁)w(n₂)(1 + 2·1[C₄]). By s1 the term with 1 is µ[σ_A]. Therefore U₄ = µ[σ_A] − µ[σ_A] − 2Z⁻² Σ_{∂n₁=A, ∂n₂=∅} w(n₁)w(n₂)1[C₄], which is the claimed identity. All weights are nonnegative because J_e ≥ 0 and β ≥ 0, so U₄ ≤ 0. When µ[σ_A] > 0 the identity reads U₄ = −2µ[σ_A]·P[C₄], where P is the probability measure on pairs of currents with weights proportional to w(n₁)w(n₂), ∂n₁ = A and ∂n₂ = ∅.

applications.title: Non-Gaussian four-point function of a ring of four spins
applications.inputs: Four Ising spins on the cycle x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄, x₁ with equal couplings and t = tanh(βJ) = 1/2, so βJ = (1/2) log 3.
applications.hypotheses: The cycle is a finite graph with positive couplings, the field is zero, the boundary condition is free and the four vertices are distinct.

steps.text: The high-temperature expansion gives µ[σ_B] = Σ t^|γ| / (1 + t⁴), where γ runs over edge sets whose odd-degree vertices are B. With t = 1/2 the denominator is 1 + 1/16 = 17/16.

Neighbours are joined by paths of lengths 1 and 3, so µ[σ₁σ₂] = µ[σ₃σ₄] = µ[σ₁σ₄] = µ[σ₂σ₃] = (t + t³)/(1 + t⁴) = 10/17. Opposite vertices are joined by two paths of length 2, so µ[σ₁σ₃] = µ[σ₂σ₄] = 2t²/(1 + t⁴) = 8/17.
The edge sets with all four vertices odd are the two perfect matchings of the cycle, so µ[σ₁σ₂σ₃σ₄] = 2t²/(1 + t⁴) = 8/17.
The identity then gives the connection probability P[C₄] = −U₄/(2µ[σ₁σ₂σ₃σ₄]) = (128/289)/(16/17) = 8/17 for the duplicated currents.

applications.conclusion: For the four-spin ring with tanh(βJ) = 1/2, U₄ = −128/289. The four-point function is strictly below its Gaussian (Wick) value, as the Lebowitz inequality requires, and the duplicated currents connect all four points with probability 8/17.

limitations: The inequality is an upper bound on µ[σ₁σ₂σ₃σ₄] only. The matching lower bound, which gives Gaussian scaling limits in high dimensions, needs the tree diagram bound of Aizenman.
The proof uses zero field. With a nonzero field the odd correlations do not vanish and U₄ has more terms.

results.name: Griffiths–Hurst–Sherman inequality
aliases: Concavity of the Ising magnetization in a positive field
results.statement: Let n ≥ 1, β > 0, let Q be a symmetric n × n matrix with zero diagonal and Q_ij ≥ 0 for all i, j, and let µ ∈ [0, ∞)^n. Let X be a random vector in {−1, 1}^n with P(X = x) = exp((β/2) xᵀQx + µᵀx)/Z_n(β, Q, µ). Then for all indices i, j, k ∈ {1, …, n}, distinct or not, ∂³ log Z_n(β, Q, µ)/∂µ_i ∂µ_j ∂µ_k ≤ 0. This third derivative is the joint cumulant E[X_iX_jX_k] − E[X_i]E[X_jX_k] − E[X_j]E[X_iX_k] − E[X_k]E[X_iX_j] + 2E[X_i]E[X_j]E[X_k]. In particular, for every v ∈ [0, ∞)^n and every i, the map t ↦ E_{µ+tv}[X_i] is concave on [0, ∞).
hypotheses: β > 0 and Q is a symmetric matrix with zero diagonal and nonnegative entries, so the interaction is ferromagnetic.
The external field µ has nonnegative entries.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only the power series of the exponential function, an orthogonal change of variables in a finite sum over spin configurations, and parity counting.

definitions.name: Ising model with field
definitions.text: The law on {−1, 1}^n with probability proportional to exp((β/2) xᵀQx + µᵀx). Here Z_n(β, Q, µ) = Σ_x exp((β/2) xᵀQx + µᵀx) is the partition function, and log Z_n is the cumulant generating function of X in the variable µ.

definitions.name: replicas
definitions.text: Four independent copies X¹, X², X³, X⁴ of X, with the same parameters (β, Q, µ).

source.citation: Nabarun Deb, Rajarshi Mukherjee, Sumit Mukherjee and Ming Yuan, Detecting structured signals in Ising models, arXiv:2012.05784 [math.PR], 2020.
source.revision: arXiv v1 of 10 December 2020.
source.module: Section 4.1 Some Supporting Lemmas
source.excerpt: Lemma 1 (GHS Inequality (Lebowitz, 1974)). Suppose X ∼ P_{β,Q,µ} with β > 0, Q_ij ≥ 0 for all i, j ∈ [n] and µ ∈ (R+)^n. Then for any (i1, i2, i3) ∈ [n]^{⊗3} one has ∂³ log Z_n(β, Q, µ) / ∂µ_{i1} ∂µ_{i2} ∂µ_{i3} ≤ 0.

source.alignment: The source defines the model in its (1) on p. 1, with Q symmetric with zero diagonal, states the lemma with a citation of J. L. Lebowitz, GHS and other inequalities, Comm. Math. Phys. 35 (1974) 87-92, and gives no proof (Section 4.6 says that the proofs of Lemmas 1-4 follow from the cited references). The authored proof is the four-replica rotation argument that is usually credited to that paper, but it was not compared with Lebowitz's text. The record quotes only the first sentence of the lemma and adds the concavity of the magnetization, which follows directly.

proof.scope: The inequality for every finite ferromagnetic Ising model with nonnegative field and all index triples, and the concavity of each magnetization along nonnegative field directions.

steps.text: Replicas. Since log Z_n is the cumulant generating function of X in µ, its third derivative u = ∂³ log Z_n/∂µ_i∂µ_j∂µ_k is the joint cumulant in the statement. Let X¹, X², X³, X⁴ be independent copies of X. Expanding the product into eight terms and using independence gives u = E[(X¹_i − X²_i)(X¹_j − X³_j)(X¹_k − X⁴_k)]. Hence Z_n⁴ u = Σ (x¹_i − x²_i)(x¹_j − x³_j)(x¹_k − x⁴_k) exp(Σ_ℓ ((β/2) x^ℓᵀQx^ℓ + µᵀx^ℓ)), where the sum runs over x¹, x², x³, x⁴ ∈ {−1, 1}^n.

Rotation. At each site m put a_m = (x¹_m + x²_m + x³_m + x⁴_m)/2, b_m = (x¹_m + x²_m − x³_m − x⁴_m)/2, c_m = (x¹_m − x²_m + x³_m − x⁴_m)/2 and d_m = (x¹_m − x²_m − x³_m + x⁴_m)/2. This is an orthogonal linear map of R⁴, so Σ_ℓ x^ℓ_m x^ℓ_p = a_ma_p + b_mb_p + c_mc_p + d_md_p, and Σ_ℓ x^ℓ_m = 2a_m. Also x¹ − x² = c + d, x¹ − x³ = b + d and x¹ − x⁴ = b + c. So the summand is (c_i + d_i)(b_j + d_j)(b_k + c_k) exp(Σ_{m,p} (β/2)Q_mp(a_ma_p + b_mb_p + c_mc_p + d_md_p) + Σ_m 2µ_m a_m).

One site. The 16 values of (x¹, x², x³, x⁴) give 8 points where one of a, b, c, d is ±2 and the other three are 0 (all four spins equal, or exactly two equal to −1), and 8 points with an odd number of −1. A direct check of (−1, 1, 1, 1) and its permutations and their negatives shows that the last 8 points go injectively, hence bijectively, onto the set of v ∈ {−1, 1}⁴ with v₁v₂v₃v₄ = −1. For exponents (p, q, r, s) let S = Σ a^p b^q c^r d^s over the 16 points. The first 8 points give a term that is ≥ 0, and nonzero only if all exponents are even. The last 8 give (1/2)Σ_{v∈{−1,1}⁴} (1 − v₁v₂v₃v₄) v₁^p v₂^q v₃^r v₄^s = 8·1[all even] − 8·1[all odd]. So S > 0 if p, q, r, s are all even, S = −8 if they are all odd, and S = 0 if their parities differ.

Expand and count parities. Because βQ_mp/2 ≥ 0 and µ_m ≥ 0, the exponential is a convergent power series in the a, b, c, d variables with nonnegative coefficients. Multiply out the prefactor into eight monomials and sum over the spins term by term, which is allowed because the spin sum is finite. Each resulting monomial ∏_m a_m^{p_m} b_m^{q_m} c_m^{r_m} d_m^{s_m} sums to ∏_m S(p_m, q_m, r_m, s_m) by s3. The exponential part has even total degree in the b variables, because each factor b_mb_p adds 2 to it, and the same holds for c and d. A nonzero product needs equal parities at each site, so Σ_m q_m ≡ Σ_m r_m ≡ Σ_m s_m (mod 2). The prefactor monomials c_ib_jb_k, c_ib_jc_k, c_id_jc_k, d_ib_jb_k, d_id_jb_k and d_id_jc_k add total degrees in (b, c, d) of mixed parity, so they give 0. The two others, c_id_jb_k and d_ib_jc_k, make Σ_m q_m odd. At a contributing site q_m is odd exactly when all four exponents are odd, so the number of all-odd sites is odd and the product is ≤ 0. Hence Z_n⁴ u ≤ 0.

Concavity. For v ∈ [0, ∞)^n the field µ + tv stays in [0, ∞)^n for t ≥ 0. The second derivative of t ↦ E_{µ+tv}[X_i] is Σ_{j,k} v_jv_k ∂³ log Z_n/∂µ_i∂µ_j∂µ_k at µ + tv. Each term is ≤ 0 by s4, so the map is concave.

applications.title: Concave magnetization of two coupled spins
applications.inputs: Two spins with β = 1 and Q₁₂ = Q₂₁ = log 2, so that (β/2)xᵀQx = J x₁x₂ with J = log 2 and e^{2J} = 4, and the uniform field µ = (h, h) with e^{2h} = 1, 2 and 4, that is h = 0, (1/2) log 2 and log 2.
applications.hypotheses: The coupling is nonnegative and the fields are nonnegative, so the theorem applies with v = (1, 1).

steps.text: With u = e^{2h} the magnetization is m(h) = E[X₁] = e^{2J}(u² − 1)/(e^{2J}(u² + 1) + 2u). With e^{2J} = 4 this gives m = 0 at u = 1 and m = 12/24 = 1/2 at u = 2.
At u = 4 the magnetization is 4·15/(4·17 + 8), which equals 15/19.
The three fields are equally spaced, so concavity requires m at the middle field to be at least the mean of the outer values. The gap 2·(1/2) − (0 + 15/19) is positive.

applications.conclusion: The magnetization of the two-spin model grows from 0 to 1/2 to 15/19 over equal steps of the field, so the second step adds less than the first, as the GHS inequality requires.

limitations: The inequality needs the field to be nonnegative. For fields of mixed signs the third cumulant can be positive.
The proof is specific to spins with values ±1 and to pair interactions. Extensions to other single-spin laws, such as the Ellis–Monroe–Newman class, need separate arguments.

results.name: Onsager's formula for the free energy of the two-dimensional Ising model
aliases: Onsager solution of the two-dimensional Ising model
results.statement: Consider the nearest-neighbour Ising model on Z² with unit coupling and zero field, and let Z_{n,β} = Σ_σ exp(β Σ_{x∼y} σ_xσ_y) be its partition function on the n × n torus Z²/nZ². For every β > 0 the free energy per site ψ(β) = lim_{n→∞} n^(−2) log Z_{n,β} exists and equals ψ(β) = log 2 + (1/(8π²)) ∫_0^{2π} ∫_0^{2π} log[cosh²(2β) − sinh(2β)(cos θ₁ + cos θ₂)] dθ₁ dθ₂. In terms of x = tanh β, the high-temperature part satisfies lim_{n→∞} n^(−2) log Z(G_nn, x) = (1/(8π²)) ∫∫ log[(1 + x²)² − 2x(1 − x²)(cos θ₁ + cos θ₂)] dθ₁ dθ₂, where Z(G_nn, x) is the sum of x^|γ| over even subgraphs γ of the torus.
hypotheses: The lattice is Z² with nearest-neighbour coupling 1 and zero magnetic field, with periodic boundary condition on the n × n torus.
The inverse temperature satisfies β > 0, so x = tanh β lies in (0, 1).

prerequisites.reason: Step s5 uses the dominated (bounded) convergence theorem, as the source does, to pass from Riemann sums of the logarithm of the Kac–Ward symbol to its integral.

definitions.name: even subgraph
definitions.text: A set γ of edges such that every vertex meets an even number of edges of γ. The high-temperature expansion is Z(G, x) = Σ_γ x^|γ| over even subgraphs.

definitions.name: Kac–Ward determinant
definitions.text: P^{z,w}(G, x) = det(I − T^{z,w}), where T is indexed by oriented edges, T_{e,e′} = ϕ(e) e^{iα(e,e′)/2} x_e when e′ continues e without backtracking, α(e, e′) is the turning angle and ϕ(e) is z or w to the power of the crossings of e with two fixed cycles of the torus.

source.citation: David Cimasoni and Hugo Duminil-Copin, The critical temperature for the Ising model on planar doubly periodic graphs, arXiv:1209.0951 [math-ph], 2012.
source.revision: arXiv v1 of 5 September 2012.
source.module: Section 4 The critical temperature
source.excerpt: Lemma 4.3. For any x ∈ (0,1)^{E(G)}, log Z_x = (1/(2(2πi)²)) ∫_{T²} log P^{z,w}(G, x) dz/z dw/w. Proof. The proof is inspired by the proof of [22, Theorem 3.5]. First note that P^{z,w}(G, x) > 0 for any (z, w) ≠ (1, 1) by Lemma 4.2 …
source.attribution: © David Cimasoni and Hugo Duminil-Copin. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source proves Lemma 4.3 for every planar non-degenerate doubly periodic weighted graph, with log Z_x the free energy per fundamental domain of the high-temperature expansion, (6) on p. 13. The authored statement is the special case of the square lattice with unit couplings (Example 1 of the source), written as Onsager's formula, which Friedli and Velenik state without proof as (3.14) on p. 93 of their book. The Kac–Ward symbol of the one-vertex torus and the change to hyperbolic functions are computed for this record and checked numerically. The outline follows the source's proof of Lemma 4.3 on pp. 13-14.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Lemma 4.3 in Cimasoni and Duminil-Copin, The critical temperature for the Ising model on planar doubly periodic graphs, Section 4, pp. 13-14, specialized to the square lattice. Steps s3 and s4 take Lemma 4.1, Proposition 2.1 and Theorem 2.2 from the source. Steps s2 and s6 are explicit computations for the square lattice.

steps.text: High-temperature expansion. By the identity exp(βσ_uσ_v) = cosh β (1 + tanh β σ_uσ_v), (1) of the source, the torus G_nn = Z²/nZ² with n² vertices and 2n² edges gives Z_{n,β} = (cosh β)^(2n²) 2^(n²) Z(G_nn, x) with x = tanh β. Hence ψ(β) = log 2 + 2 log cosh β + log Z_x, where log Z_x = lim_{n→∞} n^(−2) log Z(G_nn, x) is the free energy per fundamental domain of (6) in the source, once this limit is shown to exist.

The Kac–Ward symbol. The fundamental domain G = G_11 has one vertex and two loop edges (Example 1 of the source). Its four oriented edges point east, north, west and south, with ϕ = z, w, 1/z and 1/w, and the turning angles are 0 and ±π/2. Expanding the 4 × 4 determinant of Definition 1 gives P^{z,w}(G, x) = (1 + x²)² − x(1 − x²)(z + 1/z + w + 1/w). On the unit torus z = e^{iθ}, w = e^{iφ} this is (1 + x²)² − 2x(1 − x²)(cos θ + cos φ) ≥ (1 + x²)² − 4x(1 − x²) = (x² + 2x − 1)² ≥ 0. Since 2x(1 − x²) > 0, the inequality is strict off (z, w) = (1, 1), which is Lemma 4.2 of the source in this case. Near (1, 1), 1 − cos θ ≥ 2θ²/π², so log P is integrable on the torus.

Factorization over the torus. Lemma 4.1 of the source states that P^{z,w}(G_nm, x) = ∏_{u^n = z} ∏_{v^m = w} P^{u,v}(G, x), because translation invariance makes the Kac–Ward matrix of G_nm block diagonal in a discrete Fourier basis. So for (ε, η) ∈ {(−1, −1), (−1, 1), (1, −1)}, n^(−2) log P^{ε,η}(G_nn, x) = n^(−2) Σ_{z^n = ε} Σ_{w^n = η} log P^{z,w}(G, x). None of these grids contains (1, 1), so every term is finite by s2.

Sandwich for the partition function. Proposition 2.1 of the source writes P^{±1,±1}(G_nn, x) as squares (Z₀₀ ± Z₁₀ ± Z₀₁ ± Z₁₁)², where Z_α ≥ 0 sums x^|γ| over even subgraphs in homology class α. Theorem 2.2 of the source gives Z(G_nn, x) = (1/2)(−P^{1,1}(G_nn, x)^{1/2} + P^{1,−1}(G_nn, x)^{1/2} + P^{−1,1}(G_nn, x)^{1/2} + P^{−1,−1}(G_nn, x)^{1/2}). The source deduces P^{−1,1}(G_nn, x) ≤ Z(G_nn, x)² ≤ (9/4) max{P^{−1,−1}(G_nn, x), P^{−1,1}(G_nn, x), P^{1,−1}(G_nn, x)}.

Passage to the limit. The sums in s3 are Riemann sums of log P^{e^{iθ},e^{iφ}}(G, x) on shifted grids of mesh 2π/n. For x ≠ √2 − 1 the integrand is continuous and positive on the whole torus, so they converge to (1/(4π²)) ∫∫ log P dθ dφ. At x = √2 − 1 the source uses the bound log P = O(log(|z − 1| + |w − 1|)) and the bounded convergence theorem. All three sums have the same limit, so s4 gives 2 log Z_x = (1/(4π²)) ∫∫ log P dθ dφ, and the limit defining log Z_x exists. With dz/z = i dθ and dw/w = i dφ this is Lemma 4.3 of the source.

Onsager's form. With x = tanh β, 1 + x² = cosh(2β)/cosh²β and 2x(1 − x²) = sinh(2β)/cosh⁴β. So P = [cosh²(2β) − sinh(2β)(cos θ + cos φ)]/cosh⁴β, and (1/(8π²)) ∫∫ log P dθ dφ equals (1/(8π²)) ∫∫ log[cosh²(2β) − sinh(2β)(cos θ + cos φ)] dθ dφ − 2 log cosh β. Adding log 2 + 2 log cosh β from s1 gives ψ(β) = log 2 + (1/(8π²)) ∫∫ log[cosh²(2β) − sinh(2β)(cos θ₁ + cos θ₂)] dθ₁ dθ₂.

applications.title: The singularity of the square-lattice free energy
applications.inputs: The square-lattice Ising model with unit coupling, at e^(2β) = 3 and at the β with sinh(2β) = 1.
applications.hypotheses: Both values of β are positive and the model is the nearest-neighbour Ising model on Z² with zero field, so the formula applies.

steps.text: Put s = sinh(2β). Since cosh²(2β) = 1 + s², the integrand is 1 + s² − s(cos θ₁ + cos θ₂) ≥ 1 + s² − 2s = (s − 1)², with equality only at θ₁ = θ₂ = 0.
For e^(2β) = 3, s = (3 − 1/3)/2 = 4/3, and the minimum of the integrand is (4/3 − 1)² = 1/9 > 0. So the integrand stays away from 0, and ψ is analytic near this β.
For sinh(2β) = 1 the minimum is 1 + 1 − 2 = 0 at the origin of the torus, so the logarithm in the integrand is singular there.
Hence the only β > 0 where the integrand vanishes is the one with sinh(2β) = 1, that is β = (1/2) log(1 + √2). This is the critical inverse temperature of the square-lattice Ising model.

applications.conclusion: Onsager's formula is a smooth parameter integral except at sinh(2β) = 1, where its integrand vanishes at one point. This locates the phase transition of the square-lattice Ising model at βc = (1/2) log(1 + √2).

limitations: The formula is for zero magnetic field. No closed form is known for the free energy of the two-dimensional Ising model in a nonzero field.
The outline relies on the Kac–Ward results of the source (Proposition 2.1, Theorem 2.2 and Lemma 4.1) and does not reprove them.

results.name: Yang's formula for the spontaneous magnetization of the two-dimensional Ising model
results.statement: Consider the Ising model on Z² with horizontal coupling J₁ > 0, vertical coupling J₂ > 0 and zero field at inverse temperature β > 0, and put k = (sinh(2βJ₁) sinh(2βJ₂))^(−1). Let m*(β) = µ⁺_β[σ₀] be the spontaneous magnetization, that is, the magnetization of the infinite-volume plus state, which equals the limit as h ↓ 0 of the magnetization density in the field h. If k < 1, then m*(β) = (1 − k²)^(1/8). In the isotropic case J₁ = J₂ = 1 this reads m*(β) = (1 − sinh(2β)^(−4))^(1/8) for every β > βc = (1/2) log(1 + √2).
hypotheses: The model is the nearest-neighbour Ising model on Z² with couplings J₁, J₂ > 0 and zero magnetic field.
The temperature is below the critical temperature, k = (sinh(2βJ₁) sinh(2βJ₂))^(−1) < 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses the Szegő strong limit theorem, in its form for smooth nonvanishing complex symbols with zero winding, to compute the limit of the Toeplitz determinants.

definitions.name: Toeplitz determinant
definitions.text: For a function ϕ on the unit circle with Fourier coefficients ϕ_k = (1/2π)∫ e^(−ikθ) ϕ(e^(iθ)) dθ, D_n(ϕ) = det(ϕ_{j−l})_{j,l=0}^{n−1}.

definitions.name: Onsager symbol
definitions.text: ϕ_ons(e^(iθ)) = [(1 − γ₁e^(iθ))(1 − γ₂e^(−iθ)) / ((1 − γ₁e^(−iθ))(1 − γ₂e^(iθ)))]^(1/2), with γ₁ = z₁z₂*, γ₂ = z₂*/z₁, z₁ = tanh(βJ₁), z₂ = tanh(βJ₂) and z₂* = (1 − z₂)/(1 + z₂).

source.citation: Percy Deift, Alexander Its and Igor Krasovsky, Toeplitz matrices and Toeplitz determinants under the impetus of the Ising model. Some history and some recent results, arXiv:1207.4990 [math.FA], 2012.
source.revision: arXiv v3 of 1 December 2012.
source.module: Section 4 Back to Ising
source.excerpt: Remark 4.1. Let E_Λ(σ) denote the interaction energy in a rectangular box Λ of size M × N as in (10) above, … What Yang proved in [Yan1] was that, for T < Tc, M_Y ≡ … = (1 − k_ons²)^(1/8) = M₀ ≡ lim_{n→∞} ⟨σ_{1,1}σ_{1,n}⟩^(1/2).
source.attribution: © Percy Deift, Alexander Its and Igor Krasovsky. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source is a survey. Remark 4.1 states Yang's 1952 result with k_ons from (19), and (93) on p. 24 states that the physical spontaneous magnetization equals (1 − k_ons²)^(1/8) for T < Tc, with references to Lebowitz–Martin-Löf and Benettin–Gallavotti–Jona-Lasinio–Stella. The authored statement writes this in terms of β, J₁, J₂ and the plus state. The outline follows the Toeplitz route of Montroll, Potts and Ward as described on pp. 24-25 of the source, not Yang's original computation.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the derivation of Montroll, Potts and Ward as presented in Deift, Its and Krasovsky, Section 4, pp. 24-25, with Szegő's theorem from Section 3 (Theorem 3 and (85)). Step s1 takes the Toeplitz formula (94) from the source, step s3 takes the strong Szegő limit for complex symbols (85), and step s5 takes the identification (93) of the source.

steps.text: Row correlation as a Toeplitz determinant. Formula (94) of the source, due to Potts and Ward and to Montroll, Potts and Ward, states that the infinite-volume correlation along a row is ⟨σ_{1,1}σ_{1,1+n}⟩ = D_n(ϕ_ons), the n × n Toeplitz determinant of the Onsager symbol (25)-(26). The source defines M₀ = lim_{n→∞} ⟨σ_{1,1}σ_{1,n}⟩^(1/2) in (91), see also (20). So it suffices to compute lim D_n(ϕ_ons).

No winding below Tc. By (27), 0 < γ₁ < 1, and by (30), γ₂ < 1 exactly when k < 1. So for k < 1 the four factors 1 − γ₁e^(±iθ) and 1 − γ₂e^(±iθ) do not vanish on the unit circle and have zero winding, and log ϕ_ons = (1/2)[log(1 − γ₁e^(iθ)) + log(1 − γ₂e^(−iθ)) − log(1 − γ₁e^(−iθ)) − log(1 − γ₂e^(iθ))] is smooth. Expanding log(1 − u) = −Σ_{ℓ≥1} u^ℓ/ℓ gives (log ϕ_ons)_ℓ = −(γ₁^ℓ − γ₂^ℓ)/(2ℓ) and (log ϕ_ons)_{−ℓ} = (γ₁^ℓ − γ₂^ℓ)/(2ℓ) for ℓ ≥ 1, and (log ϕ_ons)₀ = 0, which are (95)-(96) of the source.

Strong Szegő limit. Szegő's strong limit theorem (Theorem 3 of the source) in the form (85) for smooth nonvanishing complex symbols with zero winding, proved by G. Baxter and by Kac's method, gives lim D_n(ϕ)/e^(n(log ϕ)₀) = exp(Σ_{ℓ≥1} ℓ (log ϕ)_ℓ (log ϕ)_{−ℓ}). By s2 the exponent is −Σ_{ℓ≥1} (γ₁^ℓ − γ₂^ℓ)²/(4ℓ) = (1/4)[log(1 − γ₁²) + log(1 − γ₂²) − 2 log(1 − γ₁γ₂)]. Hence lim_{n→∞} ⟨σ_{1,1}σ_{1,1+n}⟩ = [(1 − γ₁²)(1 − γ₂²)/(1 − γ₁γ₂)²]^(1/4).

Elementary algebra. With z₁ = tanh(βJ₁), z₂* = (1 − z₂)/(1 + z₂) = e^(−2βJ₂), γ₁ = z₁z₂* and γ₂ = z₂*/z₁, the source states that elementary algebra using (26) turns this limit into (19). Indeed (1 − γ₁²)(1 − γ₂²)/(1 − γ₁γ₂)² = 1 − k², with k = (sinh(2βJ₁) sinh(2βJ₂))^(−1). This identity was checked numerically for 1000 random couplings and temperatures with k < 1. So M₀ = (1 − k²)^(1/8).

Identification with the plus state. The source defines the physical magnetization M_phys in (92) as lim_{h↓0} lim_{|Λ|→∞} of the magnetization density in the field h, and (93) of the source, citing Lebowitz–Martin-Löf and Benettin–Gallavotti–Jona-Lasinio–Stella, states M_phys = M_Y = M₀ = (1 − k²)^(1/8) for T < Tc. By Theorem 3.34 and (3.9) of Friedli and Velenik, the limit as h ↓ 0 of the magnetization density is the right derivative of the pressure at h = 0, which is µ⁺_β[σ₀] = m*(β). Hence m*(β) = (1 − k²)^(1/8). For J₁ = J₂ = 1, k = sinh(2β)^(−2), and k < 1 exactly when sinh(2β) > 1, that is β > (1/2) log(1 + √2).

applications.title: Spontaneous magnetization of the square-lattice magnet below Tc
applications.inputs: The isotropic square-lattice Ising ferromagnet (J₁ = J₂ = 1) at e^(2β) = 3, where sinh(2β) = 4/3, and at sinh(2β) = 2.
applications.hypotheses: Both temperatures have sinh(2β) > 1, so k = sinh(2β)^(−2) < 1 and the formula applies.

steps.text: Hence m*(β) = (175/256)^(1/8), about 0.954. At this temperature 95 percent of the full order remains.

Near βc, write sinh(2β) = 1 + ε. Then 1 − (1 + ε)^(−4) = 4ε + O(ε²), and ε is proportional to β − βc, so m*(β) behaves like a constant times (β − βc)^(1/8). This is the critical exponent 1/8 of the two-dimensional Ising model.

applications.conclusion: The square-lattice magnet keeps about 95 percent of its full magnetization at e^(2β) = 3 and about 99 percent at sinh(2β) = 2. Near the critical point the magnetization vanishes like (β − βc)^(1/8).

limitations: The formula is for temperatures below Tc. At and above Tc the spontaneous magnetization is zero, which needs separate arguments.
The outline relies on the Toeplitz formula (94) and on the identification (93), which the source cites from the literature and does not prove.

aliases: Critical point of the square-lattice Ising model
Beffara–Duminil-Copin theorem for the critical point of the Potts model
results.statement: Consider the nearest-neighbour Ising model on Z² with Hamiltonian H(σ) = −Σ_{x∼y} σ_xσ_y at inverse temperature β ≥ 0. Let µ⁺_{Λn,β} be its measure on the box Λn = {−n, …, n}² with plus boundary condition, let m*(β) = lim_{n→∞} µ⁺_{Λn,β}[σ₀] be the spontaneous magnetization and let βc = inf{β > 0 : m*(β) > 0}. Then βc = (1/2) log(1 + √2), equivalently sinh(2βc) = 1. So m*(β) = 0 for β < βc and m*(β) > 0 for β > βc. More generally, the random-cluster model on Z² with cluster weight q ≥ 1 has critical parameter pc(q) = √q/(1 + √q), and the q-state Potts model on Z² (q ≥ 2 an integer) has βc(q) = ((q − 1)/q) log(1 + √q).
hypotheses: The lattice is Z² with nearest-neighbour edges, which is planar and isomorphic to its dual lattice.
The interaction is ferromagnetic with unit coupling, H(σ) = −Σ_{x∼y} σ_xσ_y, and the magnetization is taken with plus boundary condition.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Edwards–Sokal coupling, in its version with monochromatic boundary condition, to write the magnetization as a connection probability of the random-cluster model.
Step s2 uses Euler's formula for planar graphs to identify the law of the dual configuration in the duality relation.

definitions.name: random-cluster model
definitions.text: On a finite graph, the law φ_{G,p,q}(ω) ∝ p^{o(ω)}(1 − p)^{c(ω)} q^{k(ω)} on edge configurations ω, where o and c count open and closed edges and k counts clusters. The superscripts 1 and 0 denote wired and free boundary conditions, and φ¹_{p,q}, φ⁰_{p,q} are the infinite-volume limits on Z².

definitions.name: self-dual point
definitions.text: The value p_sd(q) = √q/(1 + √q), which is the unique p with p = p*, where pp*/((1 − p)(1 − p*)) = q.

source.citation: Hugo Duminil-Copin, Lectures on the Ising and Potts models on the hypercubic lattice, arXiv:1707.00520, 2017. Published in PIMS-CRM Summer School in Probability, Springer Proceedings in Mathematics and Statistics 299, 2019.

source.module: Section 2.4 Computation of the critical point for random-cluster models on Z2
source.excerpt: Corollary 2.16 (Beffara, DC [12]) The critical inverse-temperature of the Potts model on Z² satisfies βc(q) := ((q−1)/q) log(1 + √q).
source.attribution: © Hugo Duminil-Copin. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.

source.alignment: The source states the corollary for the q-state Potts model, whose case q = 2 is the Ising model with H = −Σ σ_xσ_y, after Theorem 2.15 (pc = √q/(1 + √q) for q ≥ 1). The proof of Theorem 2.15 is on pp. 35-36, where it is headed 'Proof of Theorem 2.16', and the corollary follows from it by (1.11) on p. 13. The authored statement writes the case q = 2 in Ising notation and keeps the general forms. The outline follows that proof and the coupling of Section 1.2.2.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 2.15 and Corollary 2.16 in Duminil-Copin, Lectures on the Ising and Potts models on the hypercubic lattice, Section 2.4, pp. 35-36, with the coupling of Section 1.2.2. Step s4 takes the exponential decay below pc from Theorem 2.12 of the source (Duminil-Copin, Raoufi and Tassion), and step s5 takes ergodicity, uniqueness of the infinite cluster and Theorem 1.12 from Section 1.3 of the source.

steps.text: Coupling. With p = 1 − e^(−2β), which is (1.4) of the source for q = 2, Proposition 1.3 and Corollary 1.4 of the source give µ⁺_{Λn,β}[σ₀] = φ¹_{Λn,p,2}[0 ↔ ∂Λn], and Corollary 1.9 gives m*(β) = φ¹_{p,2}[0 ↔ ∞]. This connection probability is nondecreasing in p, and p is increasing in β. So (1.11) of the source gives βc = −(1/2) log(1 − pc(2)), where pc(q) = inf{p : φ¹_{p,q}[0 ↔ ∞] > 0}. It remains to prove pc(q) = p_sd(q) = √q/(1 + √q). Then βc = (1/2) log(1 + √2), because 1 − p_sd(2) = 1/(1 + √2).

Duality. Proposition 2.17 of the source states that for a finite planar graph G with planar boundary condition ξ, if ω has law φ^ξ_{G,p,q}, then the dual configuration ω*, with ω*_{e*} = 1 − ω_e, has law φ^{ξ*}_{G*,p*,q}, where pp*/((1 − p)(1 − p*)) = q. The proof uses Euler's formula in the form k(ω) = k((ω*)¹) + o(ω*) − |V|, which turns the weight (p/(1 − p))^{o(ω)} q^{k(ω)} into a constant times (p*/(1 − p*))^{o(ω*)} q^{k((ω*)¹)}. The fixed point p = p* is p_sd = √q/(1 + √q). Letting G grow to Z², the dual of φ¹_{p,q} is φ⁰_{p*,q}.

Crossings at the self-dual point. Let Hn be the event that the rectangle of size (n + 1) × n is crossed horizontally by open edges. If Hn fails, the dual configuration crosses the rotated dual rectangle vertically, and this event is Hn rotated by 90 degrees. With s2 at p = p_sd this gives φ¹_{p_sd,q}[Hn] + φ⁰_{p_sd,q}[Hn] = 1 for q ≥ 1. Hn is increasing and φ¹ dominates φ⁰, so φ¹_{p_sd,q}[Hn] ≥ 1/2 ≥ φ⁰_{p_sd,q}[Hn], which is (2.16) of the source.

Upper bound pc ≤ p_sd. A horizontal crossing of the rectangle starts at one of n + 1 vertices on its left side and reaches distance n from it. By translation invariance and the union bound, φ¹_{p_sd,q}[Hn] ≥ 1/2 gives φ¹_{p_sd,q}[0 ↔ ∂Λn] ≥ 1/(2(n + 1)), so the connection probability does not decay exponentially. Theorem 2.12 of the source (Duminil-Copin, Raoufi and Tassion) proves that for every p < pc there is c_p > 0 with φ¹_{Λn,p,q}[0 ↔ ∂Λn] ≤ exp(−c_p n). Since φ¹_{p,q}[0 ↔ ∂Λn] ≤ φ¹_{Λn,p,q}[0 ↔ ∂Λn], p_sd < pc is impossible, so pc ≤ p_sd.

Lower bound p_sd ≤ pc. If φ⁰_{p,q}[0 ↔ ∞] > 0, then φ⁰_{p,q}[Hn] → 1. The source proves this as for Bernoulli percolation (Proposition 2.1), with ergodicity (Lemma 1.11), almost sure uniqueness of the infinite cluster (Theorem 1.10) and the FKG inequality. Since φ⁰_{p_sd,q}[Hn] ≤ 1/2 by s3, φ⁰_{p_sd,q}[0 ↔ ∞] = 0. For p < p_sd, Theorem 1.12 of the source (φ¹_{p′,q} = φ⁰_{p′,q} except for countably many p′) gives p′ ∈ (p, p_sd) with φ¹_{p,q} ≤ φ¹_{p′,q} = φ⁰_{p′,q} ≤ φ⁰_{p_sd,q} in the stochastic order. So φ¹_{p,q}[0 ↔ ∞] = 0, every p < p_sd is at most pc, and p_sd ≤ pc.

Conclusion. By s4 and s5, pc(q) = √q/(1 + √q) for every q ≥ 1. For an integer q ≥ 2, (1.11) of the source gives βc(q) = −((q − 1)/q) log(1 − pc(q)) = ((q − 1)/q) log(1 + √q). For q = 2 this is βc = (1/2) log(1 + √2), and e^(2βc) = 1 + √2 gives sinh(2βc) = ((1 + √2) − (√2 − 1))/2 = 1. Monotonicity of m* from s1 gives m*(β) = 0 for β < βc and m*(β) > 0 for β > βc.

applications.title: Ordered and disordered phases of the square-lattice Ising magnet
applications.inputs: The square-lattice Ising ferromagnet with unit coupling at the two inverse temperatures with e^(2β) = 2 and e^(2β) = 3, so β = (1/2) log 2 and β = (1/2) log 3.
applications.hypotheses: The lattice is Z² with nearest-neighbour ferromagnetic coupling 1, and the magnetization is taken with plus boundary condition, so the theorem applies.

steps.text: By the theorem, the phase is ordered exactly when sinh(2β) > 1 and disordered when sinh(2β) < 1. In physical units the critical temperature is k_B Tc/J = 2/log(1 + √2), about 2.269.

In the random-cluster language p = 1 − e^(−2β) gives p/(1 − p) = e^(2β) − 1, and p < p_sd(2) exactly when (p/(1 − p))² < 2. For e^(2β) = 2 and 3 the squares are 1 < 2 and 4 > 2, which agrees with a2 and a3.

applications.conclusion: At e^(2β) = 2 the square-lattice Ising magnet has no spontaneous magnetization, while at e^(2β) = 3 it has a positive one. The transition lies at e^(2βc) = 1 + √2.

limitations: The theorem locates βc but does not say whether m*(βc) is zero. For the Ising model, Yang's formula gives m*(β) = (1 − sinh(2β)^(−4))^(1/8) for β > βc, so the transition is continuous.
The proof uses the self-duality of Z². It does not give the critical point of the Ising model in dimension 3 or more, where no closed form is known.

results.name: Kasteleyn–Temperley–Fisher formula for domino tilings
aliases: Kasteleyn's formula for the number of domino tilings of a rectangle
results.statement: Let R be a region of the plane that is a union of unit lattice squares and is bounded by a simple closed lattice polygon. Let G be its dual graph, with one vertex for each square and an edge between squares that share a side. Let K be the matrix indexed by the vertices of G with K_uv = 1 if u and v are horizontal neighbours, K_uv = i = √−1 if they are vertical neighbours, and K_uv = 0 otherwise. Then the number of domino tilings of R is √|det K|. For the m × n rectangle (m, n ≥ 1) this gives T(m, n) = ∏_{j=1}^{m} ∏_{k=1}^{n} (4cos²(πj/(m+1)) + 4cos²(πk/(n+1)))^{1/4}, and for m and n both even T(m, n) = ∏_{j=1}^{m/2} ∏_{k=1}^{n/2} (4cos²(πj/(m+1)) + 4cos²(πk/(n+1))).
hypotheses: R is a union of unit lattice squares bounded by a simple closed lattice polygon, so R is simply connected.
For the product formula, R is the m × n rectangle with m, n ≥ 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 uses the Jordan curve theorem to show that the vertices strictly inside an alternating cycle are matched among themselves.

definitions.name: domino tiling
definitions.text: A covering of R by 1 × 2 and 2 × 1 rectangles (dominoes) with disjoint interiors, each made of two lattice squares of R.

definitions.name: Kasteleyn matrix
definitions.text: The weighted adjacency matrix K of the statement, with weight 1 on horizontal edges and weight i on vertical edges of the dual graph.

source.citation: Richard Kenyon, An introduction to the dimer model, lecture notes, arXiv:math/0310326 [math.CO], 2003.
source.revision: arXiv v1 of 20 October 2003.
source.module: Section 2 The number of domino tilings of a chessboard, Sections 2.1 Combinatorics and 2.2 Rectangles
source.excerpt: Theorem 1 [Kasteleyn, 1961] The number of domino tilings of R is √|det K|, where K is the weighted adjacency matrix of the graph G, with horizontal edges weighted 1 and vertical edges weighted i = √−1.
source.attribution: © Richard Kenyon. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Theorem 1 of the source is the general counting theorem for a region R bounded by a simple closed polygonal curve, with its proof on pp. 1-2. The product formula for rectangles is derived without a label in Section 2.2 on p. 3, which gives the eigenvalues and det K. The authored statement combines both and adds the explicit fourth-root and even-side forms. The outline follows Kenyon's proof and his computation for rectangles.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow Kenyon's proof of Theorem 1 in Section 2.1 (pp. 1-2) and his rectangle computation in Section 2.2 (p. 3) of An introduction to the dimer model. Step s3 takes the sign rule for a cycle from Lemma 1 of the source, which the source states with the remark that it follows by induction.

steps.text: Matchings and the bipartite block form. A domino covers exactly two squares that share a side, so domino tilings of R correspond bijectively to perfect matchings of G. Colour the squares as a chessboard. Then G is bipartite, and with the white vertices first K = [[0, A], [Aᵗ, 0]], where A_wb = 1 or i for horizontal or vertical neighbours w, b. If the two colour classes have different sizes, there is no perfect matching, and det K = 0 because rank K = 2 rank A is less than the size of K. Otherwise A is square and |det K| = |det A|².

Terms of the determinant. det A = Σ_σ sgn(σ) ∏_w A_{w,σ(w)}, where σ runs over bijections from white to black vertices. A term is nonzero exactly when every w is adjacent to σ(w), that is, when the edges {w, σ(w)} form a perfect matching. So the nonzero terms correspond to the tilings, and each has modulus 1 because all weights are 1 or i. Hence |det A| equals the number of tilings if and only if all nonzero terms have the same complex phase.

Comparison along one cycle. The union of two perfect matchings M₁ and M₂ is a set of doubled edges and disjoint even cycles, and M₁ becomes M₂ by exchanging the edges along each cycle in turn. So it suffices to compare matchings that differ along one simple cycle C of length 2k. Their permutations differ by a k-cycle, which gives the factor (−1)^(k−1). Lemma 1 of the source states that the weight products m₁ and m₂ of the two alternating edge sets of C satisfy m₁ = (−1)^(n+k+1) m₂, where n is the number of lattice points strictly inside C. So the ratio of the two terms is (−1)^(k−1)(−1)^(n+k+1) = (−1)^n.

The number of enclosed vertices is even. Because R is bounded by a simple closed curve, every lattice point strictly inside C is a vertex of G. By the Jordan curve theorem, a lattice edge from a point strictly inside C to a point strictly outside C would meet C. This is impossible, because two lattice edges meet only at lattice points and neither end lies on C. The vertices on C are matched along C. So M₁ matches the n interior vertices among themselves, and n is even. By s3 all nonzero terms of det A have the same phase, and by s1 and s2 the number of tilings is |det A| = √|det K|.

Eigenvectors for the rectangle. For the m × n grid, (Kf)(x, y) = f(x − 1, y) + f(x + 1, y) + i f(x, y − 1) + i f(x, y + 1), with f = 0 outside the grid. Section 2.2 of the source states that f_jk(x, y) = sin(πjx/(m+1)) sin(πky/(n+1)) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ_jk = 2cos(πj/(m+1)) + 2i cos(πk/(n+1)). This follows from sin(θ(x − 1)) + sin(θ(x + 1)) = 2cos θ sin(θx) and from sin(0) = sin(πj) = 0, which match the zero values outside the grid. For 1 ≤ j ≤ m and 1 ≤ k ≤ n the f_jk are orthogonal, so they form a basis and det K = ∏_{j,k} λ_jk.

Product formula. Since |λ_jk|² = 4cos²(πj/(m+1)) + 4cos²(πk/(n+1)), s4 and s5 give T(m, n) = √|det K| = ∏_{j,k} (4cos²(πj/(m+1)) + 4cos²(πk/(n+1)))^{1/4}. If m and n are even, j ↦ m + 1 − j changes the sign of cos(πj/(m+1)) and has no fixed point, and the same holds for k. So each factor with j ≤ m/2 and k ≤ n/2 occurs exactly four times, and T(m, n) = ∏_{j=1}^{m/2} ∏_{k=1}^{n/2} (4cos²(πj/(m+1)) + 4cos²(πk/(n+1))). For m = n = 8 the source evaluates this as 12988816.

applications.title: Dimer configurations of small square boards
applications.inputs: The 4 × 4 square and the 2 × 4 rectangle, seen as dimer models with all dimer weights equal to 1.
applications.hypotheses: Both regions are rectangles bounded by simple closed lattice polygons, and both have even sides, so the even-side product formula applies.

steps.text: With m = n = 4 the angles are π/5 and 2π/5. Put A = 4cos²(π/5) = (3 + √5)/2 and B = 4cos²(2π/5) = (3 − √5)/2, so A + B = 3 and AB = (9 − 5)/4 = 1.
The four factors are 2A, A + B, A + B and 2B, so T(4, 4) = 4AB(A + B)² = 4 · 1 · 9 = 36.
With m = 2 the only angle in the first factor is π/3 and 4cos²(π/3) = 1. So T(2, 4) = (1 + A)(1 + B) = 1 + (A + B) + AB = 5, which is the Fibonacci number for a strip of width 2.

applications.conclusion: The formula gives 36 dimer coverings of the 4 × 4 board and 5 of the 2 × 4 board, which agree with direct counts. The same formula gives 12988816 for the 8 × 8 chessboard.

limitations: The proof uses a simply connected region. On a torus or a region with holes, one determinant is not enough, and Kasteleyn uses a combination of four determinants.
The asymptotic growth exp(Gmn/π + O(m + n)), with G the Catalan constant, needs a further Riemann-sum argument that this record does not prove.

results.name: Heilmann–Lieb theorem on the zeros of the monomer-dimer partition function
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph with n vertices and let each edge e have a weight w_e > 0 (w ≡ 1 gives the unweighted case). For k ≥ 0 let m_k be the sum over all matchings M with k edges of the products ∏_{e∈M} w_e, so m_0 = 1. Then the matching polynomial µ_G(x) = Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k m_k x^{n−2k} has only real roots. Equivalently, every zero of the monomer-dimer partition function Z_G(λ) = Σ_{k≥0} m_k λ^k is a negative real number.
hypotheses: G is a finite simple graph.
Every edge weight w_e is strictly positive.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof is a direct induction on the number of vertices that uses only the vertex recurrence of the matching polynomial and arithmetic of complex numbers.

definitions.name: matching
definitions.text: A set of edges of G no two of which share a vertex. The empty set is a matching with 0 edges.

definitions.name: monomer-dimer partition function
definitions.text: Z_G(λ) = Σ_k m_k λ^k, where λ is the activity of a dimer (a matched edge) and every unmatched vertex is a monomer. It satisfies µ_G(x) = x^n Z_G(−1/x²) for x ≠ 0.

source.citation: Adam W. Marcus, Daniel A. Spielman and Nikhil Srivastava, Interlacing families I: Bipartite Ramanujan graphs of all degrees, Annals of Mathematics 182 (2015) 307-325, arXiv:1304.4132 [math.CO].
source.revision: arXiv v2 of 3 March 2014.
source.module: Section 3 2-Lifts and The Matching Polynomial
source.excerpt: Theorem 3.1 (Theorem 4.2 in [22]). For every graph G, µG (x) has only real roots.
source.attribution: © the authors. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source defines µ_G(x) = Σ_i x^{n−2i}(−1)^i m_i for an unweighted graph just before the theorem, attributes Theorem 3.1 to Theorem 4.2 of O. J. Heilmann and E. H. Lieb, Theory of monomer-dimer systems, Comm. Math. Phys. 25 (1972), and remarks that the proof is elementary and uses only recurrence formulas, but gives no proof. The authored statement allows positive edge weights, which Heilmann and Lieb also treat, and adds the equivalent form for Z_G. The authored proof is the standard induction with the vertex recurrence. It was not compared with the text of Heilmann and Lieb.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the recurrence method that Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava name for their Theorem 3.1. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Real-rootedness of µ_G and negativity of the zeros of Z_G for every finite simple graph with positive edge weights.

steps.text: Vertex recurrence. Put µ = 1 for the graph with no vertices. For a vertex u of G, split the matchings by the edge at u. Matchings that do not cover u are the matchings of G − u, with the same sign and weight and one extra factor x. Matchings that contain the edge uv are {uv} ∪ M′ with M′ a matching of G − u − v, with one more edge, so an extra factor −w_uv. Hence µ_G(x) = x µ_{G−u}(x) − Σ_{v∼u} w_uv µ_{G−u−v}(x).

Induction claim. For every graph H with at least one vertex, every vertex u of H and every z with Im z > 0: µ_H(z) ≠ 0, µ_{H−u}(z) ≠ 0 and Im(µ_H(z)/µ_{H−u}(z)) ≥ Im z. For one vertex, µ_H(z) = z and µ_{H−u} = 1, so the claim holds. Assume it for all graphs with fewer than n vertices and let H have n ≥ 2 vertices. Then µ_{H−u}(z) ≠ 0 by the induction hypothesis applied to H − u, which has n − 1 ≥ 1 vertices.

Induction step. By s1, f = µ_H(z)/µ_{H−u}(z) = z − Σ_{v∼u} w_uv/g_v with g_v = µ_{H−u}(z)/µ_{H−u−v}(z). For each neighbour v, the induction hypothesis for the graph H − u at its vertex v gives µ_{H−u−v}(z) ≠ 0 and Im g_v ≥ Im z > 0. Then Im(1/g_v) = −Im g_v/|g_v|² < 0, and since w_uv > 0 each term −w_uv/g_v has positive imaginary part. So Im f ≥ Im z > 0, f ≠ 0 and µ_H(z) = f µ_{H−u}(z) ≠ 0. This proves the claim for H.

Real roots. By s2 and s3, µ_G has no zero in the upper half-plane. Its coefficients are real, so µ_G(z̄) is the complex conjugate of µ_G(z), and µ_G has no zero in the lower half-plane either. Hence all roots of µ_G are real.

Monomer-dimer form. For x ≠ 0, x^n Z_G(−1/x²) = Σ_k (−1)^k m_k x^{n−2k} = µ_G(x). Suppose Z_G(λ₀) = 0. Then λ₀ ≠ 0 because Z_G(0) = 1. If λ₀ were not a negative real number, then −1/λ₀ would not be a positive real number, so a square root x₀ of −1/λ₀ would not be real. But µ_G(x₀) = x₀^n Z_G(λ₀) = 0 would contradict s4. So every zero of Z_G is a negative real number.

applications.title: Monomer-dimer zeros of the six-cycle
applications.inputs: The cycle C₆ (the carbon ring of benzene) with unit edge weights.
applications.hypotheses: C₆ is a finite simple graph and all weights equal 1 > 0.

steps.text: C₆ has 6 edges, 9 pairs of disjoint edges (15 pairs minus 6 adjacent pairs) and 2 perfect matchings. So Z(λ) = 1 + 6λ + 9λ² + 2λ³ = (1 + 2λ)(1 + 4λ + λ²).
The linear factor vanishes at λ = −1/2, which is negative.
The quadratic factor λ² + 4λ + 1 has discriminant 12 > 0, so its roots −2 ± √3 are real, and they are negative because their sum is −4 and their product is 1.
At unit activity the mean number of dimers is Z′(1)/Z(1) = (6 + 18 + 6)/18.

applications.conclusion: All three zeros −1/2 and −2 ± √3 of the monomer-dimer partition function of C₆ are negative reals, as the theorem states. So µ(x) = x⁶ − 6x⁴ + 9x² − 2 has the six real roots ±√2 and ±√(2 ± √3).

limitations: The theorem locates the zeros for each finite graph. The absence of a phase transition in the monomer-dimer model at positive activity needs a further limit argument, which this record does not prove.
The bound 2√(d − 1) on the roots for maximum degree d (Theorem 4.3 of Heilmann and Lieb) is a separate result.

results.name: Edwards–Sokal coupling
aliases: Edwards–Sokal coupling of the Potts and random-cluster models
random-cluster representation of the Potts model
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a finite graph, let q ≥ 2 be an integer, let p ∈ (0, 1) and let J = −ln(1 − p). On {1, …, q}^V × {0, 1}^E define the probability measure P(σ, ω) = Z⁻¹ ∏_{xy∈E} [(1 − p) 1{ω_xy = 0} + p 1{ω_xy = 1} 1{σ_x = σ_y}], with Z the normalizing constant. Then: (a) the law of σ is the q-state Potts measure μ(σ) ∝ exp(J ∑_{xy∈E} 1{σ_x = σ_y}). (b) The law of ω is the random-cluster measure φ(ω) ∝ p^{o(ω)} (1 − p)^{c(ω)} q^{k(ω)}, where o(ω) and c(ω) count open and closed edges and k(ω) counts the clusters of (V, open edges), isolated vertices included. (c) Given ω, σ is constant on each cluster, and the values on distinct clusters are independent and uniform on {1, …, q}. (d) Given σ, the edges are independent, an edge xy with σ_x ≠ σ_y is closed, and an edge with σ_x = σ_y is open with probability p. (e) For all x, y ∈ V, μ(σ_x = σ_y) = 1/q + (1 − 1/q) φ(x ↔ y).
hypotheses: The graph G = (V, E) is finite.
The number of spin values q ≥ 2 is an integer, and p ∈ (0, 1) is related to the coupling constant by J = −ln(1 − p).

prerequisites.reason: Step s5 averages the conditional probability of {σ_x = σ_y} given ω over the law of ω.

definitions.name: Potts measure
definitions.text: The probability measure on {1, …, q}^V proportional to exp(J ∑_{xy∈E} 1{σ_x = σ_y}). For q = 2 and spins ±1 it is the Ising measure at inverse temperature J/2.

definitions.name: random-cluster measure
definitions.text: The probability measure on {0, 1}^E proportional to p^{o(ω)} (1 − p)^{c(ω)} q^{k(ω)}, with free boundary conditions. For q = 1 it is Bernoulli bond percolation.

definitions.name: compatible pair
definitions.text: A spin configuration σ and an edge configuration ω are compatible if σ_x = σ_y for every open edge xy. The measure P gives positive mass exactly to compatible pairs.
